review_text:

There's nothing gripping here, no groove to settle in.....it often seems like a re-telling of the earlier book, including a premeditated car crash into innocent people. review_title: Obsessive behaviour makes for compelling reading.
review_text:
The sequel to Mr Mercedes takes place in post Bush-recession America, in the very town where the Mercedes killer had committed his atrocity four years previously.

It's an intriguing tale of robbery, obsession, murder, and a battle of wits between a teenage lad and a senior citizen parolee.

Hodges and his quirky crew come into the story fairly late on, almost as a distraction. I was fascinated by the behaviour of the teenager who desires to do the best for his family whilst simultaneously forming an invisible tie between himself and antagonist Morris by succumbing to the same obsession.

As with all enjoyable books it's a little sad to get to the end, but there's a third Bill Hodges book to come in the near future.

title: Fifty Shades Of Grey: Book One of the Fifty Shades Trilogy (Fifty Shades of Grey Series, 1)

author: E. L. James
review_text:
I got suckered into reading this book after it being highly recommended by my hairstylist. I had avoided this book clearly because of the hype, so saying I had high expectations for this book is an understatement. After the first 3 chapters, I knew I was in trouble. E.L. James really needs to rethink her choice of profession, because her writing is so atrocious I was screaming at Ana through the whole book. Let's start with a synopsis of the main characters shall we:

We have Anastasia Steele, or Ana as she prefers to be called. Ana is shy, reserved, virginal, and scared of life. Ana has the misfortune of having to interview Christian Gray. Mr. Gray is incredibly hot, with intense Grey eyes and very "controlled". Get used to the word control, in all it's contexts because that is a word that is strewn about this book like dirty clothes on the floor. Ana, while interviewing Mr. Grey, thinks to herself what a control freak he is, and he wholeheartedly agrees with her. Mr. Gray is smitten with young, shy, weak as a doormat and scared of life Ana. He stalks her, has her phone tracked, and after a friend drunkenly tries to kiss her, he comes to her rescue. At this point Ana has seen the contracts and the NDA (what kind of freak is this guy) and is still *gasp* (another word you need to get used to) into Mr. Gray. He finds out that while he suspects she's inexperienced, she is a virgin to boot. So, he deflowers Ana and here proceeds to the most boring and unrealistic sex scenes I've ever read. Seriously, who writes this stuff. Ana has the uncanny ability to orgasm at not only the command from Mr. Gray to "come for me", but at any word from him. I've heard of responsive women, but even this is a stretch. Once she's no longer a virgin, she comes off as having some serious hang-ups about sex. She likes it, but is somehow concerned that she is not enough for our domineering and controlling Mr. Gray. She is so weak and pathetic I want to slap her silly.

We have Christian Gray, who after being exposed to the BDSM lifestyle by Mrs. Lincoln (Mrs. Robinson as Ana calls her), is a complete and total control freak. Anyone who gets themselves involved with him soon discovers this. Christian refers to himself as a Dom, but we see this with a rarity. He wants Ana to be his sub, but we discover that she can't hang with that, so he takes the "vanilla" sex. Speaking of the sex, this is nothing near erotica. This is about as erotic as the Penthouse Forums. Anyway, Christian wants complete and total control of Ana. He wants to know her every move, tell her when she can and cannot leave, where she can and cannot go. When Ana tries to set him straight, he gets angry with her. His anger ranges from mad to furious and is often scary to watch. He does not get how Mrs. Lincoln is a molester, and much to Ana's horror, maintains a friendship with her. While he gets jealous if she hangs out with her friend Jose', she is not allowed to have the same courtesy with wanting Christian to stay away from her. He is abusive, and Ana walks on eggshells with him so as not to make him really angry. This is hard to do because she never knows what is going to set him off. Personally, I loathed this character so much that I wanted to stomp on his nuts on more than one occasion.

Ana finally gets smart and leaves him when he beats her with a belt. She realizes that he enjoyed hurting her, and that was to much for her. However, she will go back to him in the next book.

Again, seriously, who writes this drivel? I cannot fathom how anyone would find this book to be a love story. This is more a story about abuse and how much a person can handle.

title: Fifty Shades Of Grey: Book One of the Fifty Shades Trilogy (Fifty Shades of Grey Series, 1)
subtitle: Paperback – April 3, 2012
author: E. L. James
review_title: Looking for something romantic, erotic and intriguing?
review_text:
Unfortunately, this book succeeds only partially as any of these things. How about formulaic, clumsy and predictable? There are moments in the story that suggest that in the hands of a decent writer and better editor, this could have been a great book or at least a fun book. But this is sloppy, juvenile writing that spoils a lot.

Passages show the writer's ignorance on many themes. (And am I the only one who winced when I read Ana's decription of Jose's American Hispanic toothy grin? Wow.) This reads like a draft for a filmed mini-series (and then this happened, and then he did this...)This book is only for the curious who want somewhat titillating escapism or for a young audience even though, confusingly, this book cannot possibly be intended for a teenaged audience.

First, the odd choice of telling this story in the first person. This might work if the lead character, Ana, actually took us on her sexual journey with any authenticity. Instead, we are subjected to a "cute", dim witted and certainly not erotic inner voice of an adolescent who refers to her (cheesy and trite) inner goddess metaphorically dancing, waving pom poms, gesturing disapproval, etc., or to her subconscious. The writer really needs to look up the word "subconscious" and its grammatical forms. If one hears their subconscious on a conscious level, then it isn't their subconscious.

Secondly, I know by page 10 how "hot" and seductive Christian Grey is because Ana says this over and over again with each turn of the page. Though restraint shows up in the story, it desperately needed to show up in the writing. Ana gapes, blushes, swoons and bites her lip at the beauty of Christian Grey and all of his material possessions. This is recycled through many scenes. Other than the oft mentioned wealth and beauty of Christian and Ana's bewilderingly immediate physical response, I will have to take Ana's word that Christian is the most amazing man ever.

There is no build up to anything, no resistance, no intrigue--in fact, it seems that Ana is so immediately smitten that there really is no edge in the story, no conflict. There are a few obligatory lines of Ana feeling shocked and uncertain about their "arrangement", but none of the events show any actual resistance to anything. I'm told she's shocked, but it seems coy and insincere. The sex comes easily and as often as the smirks and the hitched breathing, without any build up or increasing tension. While BDSM elements enter into the picture, the elements are graphic but not really shocking, if anyone is worried (or hopeful). It all reads like wish-fulfillment. Over and over, I am told that these two characters are helplessly drawn to each other, but the author doesn't draw me to them. I didn't feel that I was taken through any of the fears or excitement of Ana's sexual introduction, I just had Ana's word for it. I don't need to have it spelled out for me what someone thinks after every email, every glance, every touch. Christian is the hottest man ever, I get it.

Personality-free Ana, who has never had sex, has never masturbated (???), never had too much to drink, has never eaten an oyster for that matter (and she lives in Washington near the coast?) nor noticed any man ever seems a likely foil for a dominating man looking for a blank canvas of a woman to groom--or one as hung up as himself. With the exception of Christian, Ana is oddly dismissive of the other men who pay attention to her in the story, despite the fact that they are also very attractive, moderately successful people. I guess only a billionaire could win the heart of a hardware store clerk.

Yet the author brushes for one mere moment against the possibility that Ana may have some of her own quirks which makes her a set up for a man like Christian. This is totally fumbled and we are expected to buy the implausible notion that ordinary Ana is only going along out of love. Of course, it's probably just a pathetic effort to make Ana seem hesitant and resistant though she never, ever is.

It takes some skill for a writer to cross sexually darker lines in a way that is still sexy. The writer is not up to that, as demonstrated by the bizarre juxtaposition of a damaged, abused character who says he likes to cause pain with a fluffy, female character who, I think, is written to be Bridget Jones-style funny. It is obvious that by the end of the book this story is working toward some revelation about Christian--not Ana. Ana is just a cipher. I understand that the other books throw in distracting plot diversions and evil characters, but those have to be red-herrings for the real story--will Ana and Christian be able to have a genuine relationship on more conventional terms? In other words, this is a run-of-the mill romance with a little drama, a little humor and some kink thrown into it--a botched mix, to say the least.

The dramatic conclusion ends on a rather abrupt, serious note. Is this because the author has decided to write a more thought provoking story or simply a convenient device to set up a cliff-hanger? Either way, it's effective and so is the incredibly good marketing of this book. Incompetent writing looks like high brow erotica and much money is being made off of this--though the ensuing discussions and hype are probably more interesting than the book itself. And I know that the argument is being made that this started out as fanfiction, but it's being sold as a book. I'm not going to cut it any slack- it needs to be held to the same standards as other printed books. This is not the best book of its type, but it certainly is the best presented to the mainstream consumer.

review_text:
Recipe for bestseller:
Step 1: Take a current bestseller
Step 2: Edit out the vampire line. The main male character must be compensated for the lack of magical skills, for example, by making him "stunningly handsome" and "rich beyond imagination". Any other cool skills could be added to the taste, with salt and pepper.
Step 3: Use "Edit/Replace" function as much as possible (for example: replace "gaze" by "peek", "stutter" by "mutter"). Hint: don't forget to change the names of the characters (for example, replace "Bella" with "Ana"); there is no need to update the main characteristics.
Step 4: to ensure the book popularity, make the language as simple as possible. Don't use long complicated words. For the best results, limit the vocabulary to grade 6 reading level and repeat the words a sufficient number of times. Suggestions: "Smirk", "Grin", "roll the eyes". (Hint: to compensate for this drawback, make the heroine to major in English, so she would be able to recite the poetry in between erotic scenes).
Step 5: Close your eyes and remember your teenage erotic dreams . Write it down - anytime you don't know what else to put on the page. Repeat until you feel a little nauseous.
Step 6: Call your publisher. Ask NOT to edit the book, to keep it fresh and original.

Serve to the public.

P.S. At least, this book made me laugh. Hence one star.

title: Fifty Shades Of Grey: Book One of the Fifty Shades Trilogy (Fifty Shades of Grey Series, 1)
subtitle: Paperback – April 3, 2012
author: E. L. James
review_text:
I'm not sure why so many intelligent people recommended this book. I will begin by saying that the only intelligent thing that the "heroine" did is her last action of the novel. Sadly, I see that she reverses that heroic action in the following novels. As a former victim of a controlling and abusive boyfriend, I found the "romantic" relationship between the main character and her stalker/control freak/abuse victim of a boyfriend anything but sexy and romantic. I feel that if a reader finds this book "hot" and sexy, then they clearly (and thankfully) have never been controlled or abused by someone they love. This is not the kind of Heroine I want my daughter to look up to. We should be encouraging young women to walk away from controlling and emotionally abusive men like Christian, not glorifying and romanticizing them. This man meets all the qualifications of an abusive partner. He controls her emotionally, physically, financially, and sexually. He attempts to alienate her from her friends and family. He stalks her when she does try to get some space, tells her when and what to eat, how to exercise, how to dress, and how to behave. It is irresponsible to romanticize an abusive relationship like this. Trust me, being controlled and abused is SCARY, terrifying, and NOT SEXY. You feel alienated, scared, sad, and many times you blame yourself. Ana feels all these things in the novel. I have no issues with the BDSM lifestyle--if that is one's cup of tea (bag out), that is fine. However, I believe that when one enters into a consentual BDSM relationship, they know what they are getting into and enjoy that lifestyle. Our main character states clearly several times that she does NOT enjoy it and afterward is emotionally devastated. She reacts like a victim of domestic abuse and doesn't tell anyone what is happening, makes excuses for her abuser, blames herself, and goes back to him when he is apologetic. It is HARD to leave an abuser--that is why so many victims suffer in silence. It is sad that respected people and media are promoting this kind of trash. This novel is making a physically and emotionally abusive man seem like Prince Charming. I have friends who wish their husbands or boyfriends were like this creep. Sadly, they don't know what they are wishing for.
In addition to being irresponsibly written, it is also TERRIBLY written. Clearly the author possesses a workbook of SAT vocabulary words, but unfortunately she doesn't know how to use them. Her phrasing is out of date. I haven't heard anyone say they paid peanuts for something since I was a small child. She clearly has no concept that Portland, Oregon is not in Washington state. She also must not know how technologically savvy young people are these days, let alone how sexually savvy they are. Her main character has two little people ( the subconscious and inner goddess) who live in her head AND have their own furniture! I suppose they have a house in there too. STUPID! I feel as though I got dumber as I read this book (double crap!). The vocabulary is asinine, the inner dialogue not worthy of a college grad, and the story line a push/pull, back and forth struggle with tons of holes in the plot and meaningless characters with no follow through. I am sorry I wasted $10 to make this EL James person wealthier and her novel more popular.

review_text:
Pros: Easy to read, if a bit boring at times. I can see how this would be construed as mommy porn because the sexual scenes are pervasive but not incredibly explicit. Good cliffhanger at the end, and although I didn't care for the book, I wanted to read the next one to see what would happen between Christian and Ana.

**Spoiler alert** I think there is a lot of potential in this had the author had more time/experience/good editors. The whole idea of a damaged dom teaching an inexperienced sub while both of them had vanilla feelings for each other could be a great basis for a novel, unfortunately I didn't feel that this was exploited enough in the actual book. **end spoiler**

Cons: It's fan-fiction. I can see glimpses of the Twilight character outlines (dominant male, submissive female, beauty, power, etc.), and I actually think that takes away from the storyline because this was written for adults. Teens handle flat characters fairly easily, but I expect something more.I'd have loved to learn more about "the scene" . . . I felt that kind of background was lacking.

Summary: Quick, erotic read that you can breeze through in a weekend. Don't expect too much - it's just a fan-fiction romance novel - and that's the entire plot. As someone who has read the Twilight books, the comparison between the two lies only in the archetypes of the characters and the basic plot of mutual fascination between the main characters.

title: Fifty Shades Of Grey: Book One of the Fifty Shades Trilogy (Fifty Shades of Grey Series, 1)
subtitle: Paperback – April 3, 2012
author: E. L. James
review_text:
From the get-go Christian Grey is willing to go wherever Anastasia Steele is and do whatever she wants. He's determined to own her in any and every way possible.

Equally early on, Anastasia Steele is uncomfortable with her feelings for Christian Grey, scandalized by the kind of sex life he wants them to have, and irritated by the extent to which he wants to control her life.

If he weren't an extraordinary specimen of manhood with charm and money to boot this story wouldn't have taken place, because Anastasia Steele would have been as indifferent to him as she is to every other male in her life that has wanted to be more than friends.

The author does speak about the chemistry Anastasia has with Christian from the moment they meet and that it reveals itself as a current of electricity running through her when they touch for the first time. Anastasia herself speaks of the feelings and sensations Christian awakens in her that nobody before him has, but her constant mention of his beauty makes the reader feel that his looks are the first and foremost thing on her mind when she's around him.

The fact that both behave as petulant children masquerading as consenting adults does make them a match made in heaven, though.

He's willing to drop everything for her, constantly tells her how enthralled he is by her, is enthusiastically trying to prevent her from ever being able to comfortably sit again, and she's not sure what he feels for her (?!?!).

She, on the other hand, is convinced his dominant-submissive lifestyle as well as other emotional quirks are a result of all sorts of hidden trauma and abuse; in other words twisted and cruel, and yet she's willing to give it a try. Why? Because she doesn't want to lose him she tells herself and the reader, but the sequence of events in the novel say otherwise. They indicate that she's insecure beyond measure and that the thought of being entitled to such a gorgeous man has her going down whatever path is necessary.

Throughout the odd actions they take to establish their relationship, these two talk and write to death. Their so called feelings are dissected to an unhealthy extent; they stop adding anything new almost from the beginning and are just re-hashing the same argument over and over. Their relationship is going nowhere except where their fancy-of-the-day takes them but they think all their nonsensical babble is actually moving them beyond constant sex.

Since "Fifty Shades of Grey" is the first book in a trilogy, I guess Christian and Anastasia's relationship is going somewhere. How interested I am in reading through more 1-word sentences, in enduring more endless descriptions of Christian Grey's beauty, or in pitying/mocking Anastasia's "inner goddess", to find out where indeed it's going, is another matter.

Alas, my curiosity being what it is and not being immune to an intensely passionate and beautiful man expressing his love, I read the first chapter of the next 2 books in the trilogy to get a feel of what could be in store and if I would be intrigued enough to read them.

Sorry to say that those first chapters were more of the same: Christian is drop-dead-gorgeous, Anastasia is constantly insecure. He wants to own her; she doesn't know anything except he's the most handsome man she's ever known.

I think if the author had focused on more "showing" than "telling" this novel could have been an exhilarating ride. Anastasia would have had to be a more perceptive woman for that, though. She would have had to be better equipped for describing those very famous "shades of grey". That would have made her more interesting and it would have made Christian Grey simply irresistible.

At one point she's like, "What do you see in me?" and he's like, "You're interesting when you blush." Dangit, that was kind of a big plot point in Twilight.

title: Fifty Shades Of Grey: Book One of the Fifty Shades Trilogy (Fifty Shades of Grey Series, 1)
subtitle: Paperback – April 3, 2012
author: E. L. James
review_text:
I heard about this series from a radio personality. She raved about it. I like the romance genre so I thought I'd give it a try. I read the reviews here on amazon and it seems to split mostly down the middle where the reader either loved it or hated it. I figured it would be a bit cheesy like Twilight but basically a good, easy read. I found myself hating the book in the second chapter. I decided to push on and finish it since I paid ten dollars for it.

A few reasons why I hate it:

1) Christian, the love interest, is creepy. I need to love the hero to like the book, but he is so weird I have a hard time getting past it. The author tries to make up for his weirdness through money, looks, and unbelievable talents. It doesn't work.

2) I am not a feminist but spanking a woman as punishment pisses me off. I feel like the author sets women back a couple hundred years by making Anastasia get off on it even though she is humiliated by it. I can wrap my head around S&M spanking for pleasure but this was very one sided pleasure. It was hard to not just feel angry after reading it.

3) I also have a hard time getting past the fact that Anastasia is basically a British woman in American skin. I feel like the author should write what she knows. Just base the stupid book in England if she wants the main character to reflect her native country. She uses British slang, loves classic British literature, drinks hot tea in place of coffee, and desperately wants to visit England. I don't know anyone like this in Texas.

4) Too much sex. I found myself getting bored with all the sex and I really just wanted the author to get on with the plot. Every two pages they are going at it like rabbits.

5)I don't want to have to use a dictionary to read a romance/erotica novel. Most of the book is poorly written and edited and then out of the blue the author interjects a word I have never even heard of.Really!? Why is that necessary?

Now I will shamefully admit that I actually purchased the second book. The author piqued my interest in the last few chapters. She abruptly ends with a cliff hanger. I wrestled with myself over whether or not to purchase the next book and decided that I would. Looks like I will end up reading the trilogy to find out what happens to the characters. The main character is interesting and realistic enough for me to care about the plot so on I read. The "speed bumps"(when I put the book down) seem to happen at the numerous sex scenes.

In conclusion, I seem to lean mostly to the hate side but, there is something about it that I don't understand that has me reading on. If you don't like the occasional trashy romance novel, don't read this book. I would only recommend this book if you can read it for free. Borrow it from a library or a friend but don't waste money on it.

So, if repetition annoys you, you probably should just let the hub-bub die down and forget it (or get it from your library, but you have been warned). The writing is repetitive.

*SPOILER ALERT*
**SPOILER ALERT**
***SPOILER ALERT***

Just in case anyone missed it, there may be spoilers ahead.

The story is also circular, which is frustrating and just another way of being repetitive. Ana is constantly worried about certain sexual acts, yet she keeps on drifting through what passes for a relationship in this novel. I really don't know how many times Ana thinks it, but "it always comes back to this" is featured quite a few times. It made me roll my eyes so many times because before getting halfway through the book, you know it's an issue, she knows it's an issue, Grey knows it's an issue, and yet they dance around it constantly.

The characters keep talking about how smart Ana is, but really she's an idiot by what we're shown. Or at the very least uncomfortably naive. Uncomfortable because if she's old enough and mature enough to have sex, she should be old/mature enough to discuss things or be able to call her vagina something other than "down there." Seriously. It gets really grating.

And yet, I read it to the end and wanted to know what happened. I'm not sure yet if it was because I cared about the characters or it was more of a morbid fascination. Regardless, I read the trilogy.

title: Fifty Shades Of Grey: Book One of the Fifty Shades Trilogy (Fifty Shades of Grey Series, 1)
subtitle: Paperback – April 3, 2012
author: E. L. James
review_text:
Warning this review comes with a lot of passion and gushing so if you hate the book, this is probably not the review for you. ;)
Any who, I loved this story and simply ate it up in a few days. The book is filled with a roller coaster of a romance that I truly loved watching it progress. I've heard a lot people complain that the writing is not good. Is it like Edgar Allen Poe's brilliant literary style? (Who I Love), No. However, the writing is not nearly as bad as people have stated. My only issue with it was it was kind of repetitive but other than that I thought it was natural and frankly brutally honest. I think we reviewers get caught up in the mechanics of writing a little too much sometimes, shouldn't books be about wonderful storytelling? I give this book and A+ for story telling.

Yes, I fell head over heals in love with Mr. Grey. I loved constantly guessing about what his mood was going to be or how he was going to handle a situation. He is a very complex character and definitely 50 shades of complexity.....and lusciousness. He is a character you want to dream about but not sure if you should... you can't help yourself though.

I liked Ana overall, some of her actions were annoying but as a whole, I liked her. I found a lot of her story easy to relate to personally ( so not expounding on that lol). The inner goddess thoughts were so good, I think a lot of women have this going on in their head, they just don't want to admit. ;) Their email exchanges were fun to read to and kept me glued to the pages.

The ending left my craving more. I had to think long & hard before writing this review because as many have said before me it simply leaves you speechless. I mean sure there is a lot of sex (I mean a lot) but all the scenes make sense and I personally never got tired of it (did I just say that out loud)?

I would recommend this to Adults only who either like the erotica genre or like me was experimenting it. It is a fine representation that I cant stop talking about. If your on my twitter or facebook you know I simply can't stop gushing.

I never read a series all the way through ( for fear I'll get bored with it) and to keep up with reviews I always read a book I want to read followed by a book I have to review. After I read my review book, bring on book #2!

title: Fifty Shades Of Grey: Book One of the Fifty Shades Trilogy (Fifty Shades of Grey Series, 1)
subtitle: Paperback – April 3, 2012
author: E. L. James
review_title: Get your inner goddess doing cartwheels
review_text:
I approached this book with trepidation. I'm really not keen on books that are surrounded by hype, where they seemingly appear from nowhere and EVERYONE is reading, as I ultimately end up disappointed. (I notoriously hated the first Harry Potter book, but I'm glad I continued reading them now.) So after reading a couple of reviews, and getting a couple of people telling me "You HAVE to read it", I bought a copy.

Do you remember in school when people used to pass around certain books (ahem Jackie Collins!) for the certain passages those contained? Those were nothing compared to this book. Those were tame, innocent, timid compared to this book.

I can genuinely say I was sucked straight into this book. Wow. Definitely my favourite read of 2012 so far. I loved the characters, and the mysteriousness of Christian's character. He actually strongly reminded me of guys I've known (apart from the whole BDSM bit obviously) and I could see a lot of myself in Anastasia's character. Which is probably a major reason why I loved this book.

Yes there are issues with the writing and editing. It could have been cut down a little. But I have to be one of the few people who actually liked Ana's subconscious and inner goddess. I definitely need to give my inner goddess a good kick up of the backside. Mine certainly doesn't do cartwheels and sexy dances. The subconscious I felt was very well paired up against her inner goddess. All she needed to do was give them names!

I loved the chemistry between Ana and Christian. Wow. Each word he spoke (wrote?) was literally dripping with innuendo. This is a really good couple with a really good story just springing from this page.

If you haven't got an open mind, and are the slightest bit intimidated by the thought of spanking, then this isn't the book for you. Put it down, and go back to something more tame, like Catherine Cookson. This is the kind of book that will make you blush when reading on the bus (tube, whatever), partly because of the content, but also because you know everyone's looking at you, KNOWING what you're reading. You will come off the bus fanning yourself with the book. This book tells you every single detail you could possibly want to know about certain sexual acts and then some!

I ended up finishing this book on the bus, and I was almost crying, the ending was so amazing. I had to go and buy the next two straight away, and started on Fifty Shades Darker immediately while having something to eat.

Each to their own, this book is a bit of a hit and miss. You're either going to love it or you hate it. I really did expect myself to end up on the hating side of things, but I'm really impressed that I liked it so much. Yes, the book is not going to win any awards, but I think this is going to be a little guilty pleasure of mine, and definitely will be re-read. Every girl needs a little bit of Christian Grey in their lives.

subtitle: Paperback – April 3, 2012
author: E. L. James
review_text: My hats off to Ms. James-she has an incredibly vivid imagination, but if the manuscript for "50 Shades of Grey" ever saw an editor's desk, they should be fired! I almost wanted to get out my blue editing pencil from college journalism classes and go to it. The writing is horrendous, the characters are cliches, and the plotline is beyond far-fetched. But let's face it- "50 Shades" is not meant to be a "literary classic," but it is becoming a cultural icon. If you can get past the writing, and are looking for "escapist romantic fiction," this is a book for you. At its heart, "50 Shades of Grey" is a love story-it reminded me of both "An Officer and a Gentleman," and "Pretty Woman"-because both of these movies featured a tormented, but "longing to be loved" protagonist, much like Christian Grey. I think the allure of Christian lies in the fact that he is flawed, and because his character takes along time to develop-you know there is more to him than kinky sex pervert-the reader can make Christian into whatever you imagine him to be. It is the mystery surrounding what drives Christian to behave as he does that kept me reading. I think "50 Shades" is a book that readers will feel passionate about-both literally and figuratively-and there is no "black and white" here-but many more shades of grey than the naked eye can see.

title: Fifty Shades Of Grey: Book One of the Fifty Shades Trilogy (Fifty Shades of Grey Series, 1)
subtitle: Paperback – April 3, 2012
author: E. L. James
review_title: Hyped fan favorite still offers something new to BDSM romance
review_text:
Courtesy of Happy Endings Reviews

Fifty Shades of Grey, pop culture phenomenon and hot topic book of the year, exploded on the scene early in 2012 after a fanatic online following turned into a cultural obsession. With a set-up eerily similar to its paranormal inspiration Twilight, Fifty Shades opens with college student Anastasia Steele, a fairly plain heroine whose inner voices, not-so-ingeniously named "inner goddess" and "subconscious," become almost schizophrenic by book's end, meeting billionaire entrepreneur and god Christian Grey. An initial pull between the two quickly develops into strategic meetings as a fascinated Christian pursues an equally mesmerized Anastasia. But when worldly Grey unveils his secret BDSM lifestyle to virginal Ana, complete with confidentiality agreements, contracts, and a "Red Room of Pain," she wonders what she's entered into and questions if they can really make a relationship work.

Much like Twilight, it's a mystery exactly why this book became the widespread hit the way it did. Like Twilight, it's not the most exciting or creative plot. It's really not a novel concept, despite what a large population of the American public seems to think - erotic romance novels with a BDSM theme have existed long before Fifty Shades, and many are better written too. And certainly, certainly it's not the simple, silly writing that has made it stand out. The only conclusion is that James manages to spin that elusive magic that every romance author hopes for - pure chemistry between the lead couple. Christian and Ana's evolving, shifting relationship is the best thing about the book, and James was wise to center page after page with scenes between just the two of them.

There's something to appreciate here for even the highest brow romance reader: Ana's vicarious innocence and Christian's overwhelming, all-consuming passion and intensity; sex scenes that were surprisingly emotional and delicious; and deeper than it may appear on first glance, that universal joy of watching two people with very different backgrounds and personalities navigate their way through that beautiful, raw process of falling in love. My favorite part of the book, the point where I knew it had worth, was the moment when Christian learns Ana is a virgin. The hardened man who swore he doesn't make love, who vows to keep emotional and even physical distance from his submissives, takes her hand and leads her to his own bedroom, where he tenderly loves her and stays with her all night. In a genre where there are simply countless "first times," this one stands on its own as something really special and provides a real connection between the hero and heroine.

That's not to say Fifty Shades can't claim its many, many faults. Ana is naïve, making her, at times, annoying. I could forgive her lack of strength as a character because this is journey that we take through her, a coming-of-age story of sorts, but more than that, she isn't fleshed out as well as her counterpoint. Christian Grey is one of those truly fascinating characters, a woman's fantasy and a psychologist's dream, and he tends to overshadow any other character in the vicinity, which isn't necessarily bad in literature, but is sorely noticeable in romance.

The BDSM is stilted, with pages of contract and then an endless merry-go-round of discussion about what they want and what they need. And maybe it's not a very realistic representation of a BDSM relationship, maybe there's not enough incorporation of Dominant/submissive behavior, not enough play. But to an extent, that's the point: the central conflict is, can Christian and Ana forge their own rules, their own definition of a relationship with some amount of BDSM? It's an intriguing study of human behavior, and I enjoyed seeing a woman who isn't sure if she is at heart a submissive, who actually asks herself if, as much as she loves him, can she give him what he needs in this way?

As much as you fall in love with Christian Grey, I couldn't help the nagging feeling that I would feel uncomfortable with him as Ana often does. He is very closed off and doesn't give answers even as he demands them from her. He too has a journey, and this is the crux of it, but I could sympathize with Ana's confusion. The concessions he does make, like quickly doing away with his rule of not staying the night with a woman, melt your heart. But he snaps and punishes and throws off mixed signals as much as he smiles and softens, and it's jarring. His punishments can be brutal, and I felt in this book that Ana gives more than Christian does. That is my issue with the power exchange here: I wasn't sure that Ana as the submissive really did hold all the power.

However, Fifty Shades of Grey is a love story that got to me in that way that we always hope for, and I'm glad I'm not too cynical a romance reader that I can't still be influenced by the crowd.

author: E. L. James
review_text:
Lots of people are complaining about how graphic this book is. And how it is all about BDSM and bondage, etc. It has a lot of sex, yes. But very little bondage/BDSM. Perhaps to the "vanilla" reader, it might be packed full, but in reality, it really has very little in it.

The story line is excellent. I love the author, she makes you feel everything that you are reading. I only wish there were more books in this series. Through the trilogy, I have laughed, cried, and have even been stunned at times. I edit stories, and have found nothing whatsoever to complain about. The spelling is good, punctuation is great, and I love how the author brings in larger vocabulary all the way throughout.

I am a very picky reader, and have not been able to put these books down. I do hope Ms. James writes more in the near future!

review_title: Not much besides a place to put your tiny fingers
review_text:

The pages have holes punched in the food items that the caterpillar has eaten. He would regularly return to this book but lose interest once we got past the holes. Ezra Jack Keats would be a better choice for collage art. Try "The Snowy Day" or "Peter's Chair" to get started. You could easily abridge one of those books as you read aloud and then read the whole thing when your kids are older.

-Mae Hodges

The book is well-written, but it's sick and disgusting. Will not buy or read another book from this author, even though the writing itself is quite skilled.

I got about a third of the way through it, abandoned it, and returned it to Amazon for offensive content (I've never done that before, and was surprised to learn you can do that with Kindle books). I'm not a Holocaust denier--I know all I need to know about the Holocaust. I don't need to wallow in violence-porn.

Tempted to put my Kindle through the washing machine...

review_text:
I read a lot and I have read almost all of Jodi Picoult books, and I always look forward to a new one being released. I have never done a book review on amazon, but I really thought I should about this book. I did finish it, however I started to just put it down. Maybe a stronger stomach is needed to be able to read the chapters that took place in the camps. I must have a weak stomach because they made me feel ill. I dont feel that the graphic descriptions added one single thing. I feel there should be a warning somewhere in the description of this book about the graphic details. Everybody is different, and some just can't take it!! I can understand some of the descriptions, but this was TOO much, in my opinion.
I will look forward to another book by Jodi, but I will do more research before purchasing next time. I have read so many wonderful books by her, but I do regret this purchase.

author: Jodi Picoult
review_title: Terribly written: Flat, slow and nothing new
review_text: I looked forward to reading this book as I have read many books surrounding the Jewish Holocaust (due to my family’s history) and there are so many well-written books on this topic.  This book is probably the worst I have read in this genre. I wish I had not wasted my money (another benefit if I had gone to the library and checked the book out instead). First: The main character (Sage - which is ironic and would have been amusing had this book been a comedy) isn’t even likable. Her “woe is me” attitude is unbelievable given the context this book deals with the Holocaust. Second: The book is slow. Third: The friendship between Sage and Joseff doesn’t feel natural, nor believable due to the lack of substance.  Fourth: The vision of Jesus in the bread loaf? Really,  that was just plain silly. Lastly, the only good part of the book is Minka’s story and there is nothing new or fresh. It’s not written with feeling in my opinion. The book is just flat. This is the 2nd book of Picoult's that I've tried to read and I guess it boils down to the fact that I don't like her writing style so it’s time to move on. I seriously don't know how this book got so many 5-star ratings.

review_title: Good writing but too many disappointments, question marks and loose ends.
review_text: This was well-written enough, but an utter slog to get through (I found myself speed-reading through Minka's italicized story within the story, within the story; it was too disjointly rendered). Mainly, I waited patiently to "get" Sage, including what was behind the facial scar issue -- all of her hiding. But I couldn't; she never came alive for me. [Mild spoiler alert coming up....] And then the surprise ending, the unilateral decision she made behind Leo's back, had me disliking her immensely. I get the symbolism of her action, but it wasn't necessary; the entire story itself made the "we're all capable of good and evil" point just fine. So, what did such a disappointing ending leave the readers with? The assumption that she went on to live out a grand lie for the rest of her life -- with Leo, particularly in light of what he does for a living? Minka's Holocaust story was most compelling; otherwise, just ... no, including all the loose ends. This was the first of this author's books I've read. Not sure I'll read another.

review_text:
I am getting tired of reading, and finding myself continually loving, Jodi Picoult and so always read her with a little bit of a jaundiced eye. Her last couple weren't my favorite, of hers. She has become predictable in her unpredictability and that gets a little old, however once again she drew me in and as much as I did not want to, I loved her book. Many people have written about the horrors of the holocaust but she did it from a bit of a different angle. The book pulls 4 stories, each which can stand alone, into one well woven story. You have a modern day fragile woman, a Polish Jew who is a victim of the holocaust, surprisingly a view from a Nazi soldiers side, and a fairy story. It was excellent.

I have read this book twice. Not impressed the second time around. I was very disappointed in this book because it felt like a bit of a cheat. As if Picoult took the most tender and horrific remembrances written by historians and survivors like Ellie Weisel and cherry picked the most atrocious ones to push onto 2 people and squeeze into one book to shock the senses.
A terrible period in time. It deserved more respect from the author.

review_text: I have always been drawn to the horrible atrocities of the holocaust, but seldom does a novel come along that brings to life new, unexplored human condition aspects and touching as well as controversial feelings like this novel has. Were all soldiers, police, every Nazi in World War II inherently evil? They did horrible atrocious crimes for which there is not a hot enough hell to stone for. But did they all start off this way and end this way? What is sin without forgiveness? This novel touches so many raw and unmentionable emotions that it makes it difficult to put into words. However, one thing becomes clear to hate all those who committed the crimes and to harbor the inability to forgive will only hurt the soul that cannot forgive, and the hate will only perpetuate hate one cannot cancel out the other. The Jews have shown us this with their grace, poise and eternal justice in the face of many a millennia of persecution. This same grace, poise and forgiveness is brought to light in one of Jodi Picoult's best most heart wrenching novels to date. She never fails to touch your heart, stir your anger and surprise you in the end!

review_text: im giving it 2 stars because i was interested enough to finish it, but like others i also skipped pages. the writer has no subtlety or sense of restraint. this is the second book ive read by her and the other one suffered from similar problems. she shows her hand too early in the books and then tries to muddy up the plot and ends up with preposterous climaxes (small spoiler alert, but i knew instantly when i read she was pregnant that she'd go into labor during the climax of the book, just lots of non surprising "twists"). i wanted to like both books because they started out with interesting premises, but both times the main character was unlikable (as were most of the side characters) and she threw so many curve balls that it just ended up being a mess. i wanted to like emma, but she made so many awful decisions and didnt even seem to have a firm identity. at some points it got so absurd that it felt like a bad horror movie where the main character does everything to make the situation worse. amazing how many villains abound in one small town of 400 people. too bad, a better writer could've made this story good.

review_text: This book drove me crazy. I am not sure what was more important to the author – writing a thriller mystery or having a constant internal emotional dialogue about the pain and trauma of losing a child – yes, it is painful – and trying to live with the emotions only to have them opened again.  All types of information is swirling around the main character – and yes, it is often hard to see the forest for the trees – but I knew who the perpetrator was less than a fourth of the way into the story.  I really did not connect to the main character and was more interested in the silent child who stays silent until the very end. So, it was rather anti-climactic. I only kept reading because I try not read the last chapter of a book just to confirm my conclusion in the hopes there might be another twist.

author: Sarah A. Denzil
review_title: Began With Promise, Then Went and Ruined It
review_text: Spoiler Alert. This wasn't the worst book I've ever read, but it certainly cannot be called "Good". It begins with promise, but quickly devolves into a trite, implausible, and irritating story that makes me never willing to trust the author enough to read anything else by her. I knew who the kidnapper was (and person holding the child) very quickly...too quickly to not want to hurry to the ending. Unfortunately, the author spends way too much time telling us how damaged both the mother and son are. The mother's actions don't make any sense (they go to opposite ends of the pole, from action to action), nor does the therapist's. The police in the story don't do any of the things any decent police would do to investigate. And the uncovering of the kidnapper goes from finding his lair to him telling Emma (the mother) all about himself and how and why he's done it in just a few pages. Not only is it not believable, it's totally amateurish. I didn't give it one star, arguing that it began with promise and the premise was good. The author simply didn't have the talent to pull it off.

review_text: I was excited to read a book so well rated and reviewed.  I was looking for takeaways to be used inspirationally or for reflection.  I had to be careful with this book as I 'read' it via audible while driving.  The reality is you could replace Michelle's name with Jane Doe and the luster behind the foundation of this book cracks.  I found myself asking why I am continuing to read this?  It is about as dynamic as overhearing two people discuss their weekend activities in a coffee shop.  It is well written from a structure standpoint but content is so dull and un-relational that I was asking myself if I wanted to continue to the next chapter or invest the time in something else entertaining or informative.  This puppy is boring.  That is not a demeaning critique.  It is just reality.  I wouldn't force someone to read my biography either.  My successes and failures might be interesting on a surface layer but who cares?  Her first album, neighborhood, kiss, and progress might be interesting to some.  Inspirational; how?  Interesting; in what way? Revealing; who cares?  I got a refund and put it into Marcel Proust.  Michelle may be more successful in life than Proust but as an author, Proust, and a reader, muối, the material provides something to reflect on.  This book is not bad but rather irrelevant to the reader.  I will say this.  So many reviews are calling this inspirational for women.  Ladies, if you want to be strong, stop calling yourself strong.  if you need to state your strength, power, equableness, and relevance then the foresaid is questionable. Stop saying you are strong but rather be strong in position and character. You already are.  Congratulations to Michelle for her accomplishments.  Reading about them is causing my car to veer off the road as my forehead touches the wheel.

review_text: This book is brilliantly written. I have recently read three books - James Comey's "Higher Loyalty" (unreliable narrator), "Fear" by Woodward (too scary), and this one. Of those three books this one is by far the best and the best written. It is probably the most brilliant book written by a First Lady. It's really about growing up black and female in the United States and not about politics at all. Or it might be all about politics. In some ways Michelle reminds me of Katniss Everdeen in the "Hunger Games" books, in that she just keeps on becoming a big political deal even though she really is just interested in marrying the right guy. The book has three parts which I think are called "Becoming Me", "Becoming Us" and "Becoming More". They tell 3 different stories. The first story is the one of her growing up. I was instantly annoyed that she started a book on "Becoming" with her first memory when she was 4. It seemed like a book about becoming should start in the womb, or about her parents. But it is about her first memory. She talks a lot about growing up black in the South Side of Chicago, and it is a very good story, sometimes reminding me of Harper Lee's Go Tell a Mockingbird. The second part "Becoming Us" is the love story between her and Obama and their unconventional marriage, and the way she copes with that (it turns out his idea of marriage is to married to his philosophical ambitions and not coming home for dinner). The third part, which is the best part, is about her raising her 2 pre-teen/teenage daughters in the White House. It was finally the third part that made me like her a lot. It is a book about what it is like to be a black female teenager in the United States in the 21rst century, something as a white male I only know about this by my friendships with them. I believe this book is very honest. At the end, she says she will never run for president. If you like this type of book - it is a must read.

review_title: A story of constant evolution and growth
review_text:
"For me, becoming isn't about arriving somewhere or achieving a certain aim. I see it instead as a forward motion, a means of evolving, a way to reach continuously toward a better self. The journey doesn't end."

Whenever a new president is elected, it is inevitable that the people vacating the White House eventually publish a memoir. I've read Bill Clinton's My Life, George W. Bush's Decision Points, and will no doubt read whatever book Barack Obama eventually publishes. While Hillary Clinton is the only First Lady whose writings I've read, Michelle Obama's book was one of last year's must-reads. I never got around to reading it during 2018, so it was a natural choice to start off my reading in the new year.

Even if she never became First Lady, Michelle Obama's life story would be remarkable. Her family rented out the upper level of a home in the south side of Chicago, laying the foundation for her future and her appreciation of the privilege she would earn later in life. Her parents never had the money to lavish their kids with gifts or vacations, but they did make a marked effort to invest in their children's education. Obama defied the disadvantages of her gender, race, and class to earn a law degree from an Ivy League university and carved out the future that her parents always dreamed she could achieve.

Naturally, a large portion of the book focuses on the Obama family's time in the public eye. Michelle writes about the oft-repeated story of her not wanting her husband to run for office. As he prepared to step into the political limelight, Barack was already stretched thin between his duties as community organizer, author, college professor, father, and husband. Obama writes of the effects of her husband's political and professional obligations in a way that any working wife and mother are sure to relate to.

What struck me most about the aptly titled Becoming, was the ways in which Michelle Obama's story of finding herself and constantly evolving align with the aspirations of the country that her husband was elected to lead. Her trajectory in life was achieved through hard work, humility, and seeking to always learn and grow. At a time when our country is more divided than ever, I think it is vital that we look to stories like Michelle's to find our common humanity. At the end of the day, we are all still 'becoming', and the only certain thing is that each day will offer something new to love, challenge, and hopefully learn from.

title: The Shoemaker's Wife: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Adriana Trigiani
review_title: Nice words don't make a nice book
review_text:
I love early 20th century stories. It’s a time when mysteries still abound. The world holds such promise. The bustling city, the war, the pursuit of the American dream, are all promising ideas. This book, about a love that just can’t pull itself together, had promise.

The author, clearly, did her research before writing this book; and she put every tidbit of research into the novel. It was very descriptive, even when a description was not necessary. There were so many wasted words. There were ideas, and characters, and actions that did not move the story forward or enrich the act of reading in any way. I felt that, had the author trimmed the fat, the story may have been tolerable. Tolerable, not good.

“Tolerable” because, frankly speaking, this is a poorly written book. I tried to find a way to excuse the writing. “Maybe this is her first novel,” I told myself. I could definitely excuse a little bad writing if it was her first novel. Nope. It’s her 10th. She should know better.

Aside from the unnecessary descriptive language, Trigiani is bold enough to break Cardinal Writing Rule # 1: Show don’t tell. Now, I’m all about rebels and rule breakers, but it didn’t work in this case. Written in the 3rd person omniscient (is that ever a good idea?), Trigiani tells the reader what the characters are thinking and feeling. The dialogue is often used as an “info dump”, and the characters never show their emotions through their actions. The result: two-dimensional characters buried under a mountain of useless words. I was so unconvinced of the connection between the two lead characters, Enza and Ciro, that it was terribly anti-climactic when they finally decided to give their relationship a chance.

The bottom line is, there is so much wrong with this book at its core, that I could end up writing a five page review. However, I will attempt to end on a positive note, as always.

A teacher once told me that some stories are better realized as novels, while others make better scripts or plays. Perhaps, Adriana Trigiani should have written this as a script. I could visualize the story playing out as a Hallmark mini-series, and I probably would watch it. If you enjoy the immigrant experience, and long-winded passages, you might just like this book. I felt so bad about having to write such a negative review (but, hey, I’ve got to be honest) that I was tempted to read something else written by the author in an effort to vindicate her. Sadly, I just couldn’t stand the idea of putting myself through that. The fact that this is her 10th book, clearly, indicates that there are some loyal readers out there.

title: The Shoemaker's Wife: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Adriana Trigiani
review_text:
I give up.
After reading this most unsatisfying book, I realize I can never again trust “5” star reviews.
How is it possible this most disappointing book received glowing recommendations and more importantly, why are readers willing to settle for so little in the books they choose to read?
I cannot ever remember reading a book, nearly 500 pages long, whose characters remained one-dimensional and undeveloped, with choppy, infrequent dialogue and scant character interaction.
I soon realized the story and characters were secondary to the author’s seemingly endless descriptions and details of locations, food and fabric.
These unimportant, overly-descriptive passages added nothing to the development of the story or it’s characters.
What it did add was pages, possibly making this book twice as long as it needed to be, which convinced me the author was being paid by the word.
I will donate this book, will never read another Adriana Trigiani book and will forever be suspicious of “5” star reviews.

subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Adriana Trigiani
review_title: What in all that's holy do people like about this book?
review_text:
I would say that the people who gave this book 5 stars must like romance novels. That's why they like it and I don't. I'm not a fan of the genre. Except, I've read the odd "bodice ripper" and I've enjoyed them. No, the problem isn’t the genre. What I can't abide is poor, flat, bloodless writing and this book has that in spades.

I want to give specific examples of this writing. Here's a line from early in the book when the boys’ mother leaves them at the convent and the townspeople are waking up and moving around the streets. "The presence of the others helped Eduardo gain control of his emotions." That's as gripping as a sign post reading "Your tax dollars at work."

How about this one from later in the book when the now teenage boy, Ciro (Ed's brother) finds out the truth about the pretty Concetta. "Ciro held his head in his hands. The pangs of unrequited love stung his heart for the first time. There was nothing worse than never having the opportunity to express true romantic feeling to the person who inspired them." Oh I can think of many things far worse than that.

Here's another: "A father mourns, but a mother, whose child is born of her body, remembers the soft kisses that become the act of two loving bodies joined together in sweet privacy, which begets the first flutter of joyous pregnancy, to the soft, slippery kicks as the baby grows in her belly, to the moment when her body opens up to bring a new life to the world, and yields to a despair that will never leave her." Oh please. Shoot me. Shoot me now.

This is the work of a lazy writer. She doesn’t trust the characters’ actions to speak louder than words, show rather than tell. It’s either that or she wrote it while watching a soap opera.

The descriptions of the characters lives, as others have noted, are teeth-clenchingly sugared-coated details of idealized peasants. You've read this stuff before when you were 12 and curled up with the book "Heidi". In that book it went something like this: The warm sun bathed her face as she listened to the soft silvery bells of the goats high in the mountains grazing on the sweet spring grass. She opened her eyes to see Peter smiling, holding out a wooden bowl he'd carved from the native trees that dotted the landscape, filled with the fresh milk that had strengthened him and helped make him the young healthy man that he was today.

Pass the bucket!

Again, I want to think that people who like this book can look beyond the nauseating narrative and enjoy the thin plot of romance denied, found, denied, found, denied.... But I can't. I can't stand it when a writer thinks I'm so befuddled that I have to be told what a nod means. I get it! She agrees!!! I cannot bear the tone-deaf dialog of a 10-year old telling her mother that the family can't bear one more child, that 6 is enough. I know the young girl is called "wise" beyond her years. I'm thinking maybe wiseass. And I laughed out loud when the mother, just before she says goodbye to her boys, tells them to listen "to the most important thing" I'll ever tell you. And then launches into a detailed instructional about how to build, light and maintain a fire in the fireplace. Oddly, another character remembers his father giving him advice, not a simple "Do unto others" easy to remember nugget but a long laundry list of how to run a business. Is she serious writing this, are we supposed to be touched at these moments by the emotional tension?

This is irresponsible writing. And the people who are drooling over it and giving this such high praise ought to sit quietly in a corner and rethink their lives.

review_text:
The Italian Alps, New York, the Metropolitan Opera, the great Caruso--this author had a lot of enticing ingredients to whip up a masterpiece of Italian immigrants coming to the United States in the early part of the twentieth century. But instead of a delicious dish, she throws her ingredients against the wall to see what sticks (anyone for spaghetti?)

The story rambles, jumps from unrelated paragraph to unrelated paragraph, serves up predictable plot points--all in a pedantic style that lacks artistry and nuance. An example of lack of writing talent (and the lack of a good editor) is three consecutive paragraphs all beginning with the same three words (Enza and Laura). This doesn't pass muster with discerning readers who are looking for more than a romance novel/chic lit.

I felt like I was watching a bad Lifetime movie. Every cheesy device (no Parmesan, just plain old cheddar) was thrown into this story, including the heroine stumbling into her lost love on her wedding day to another man. Of course, she left her groom at the altar, at which point I finally gave up. I'm pretty sure the author will end the saga by tying all the threads of her story up into a nice big bow. After all, the heroine is a seamstress.

review_text:
2.5 stars. It took awhile for me to get into this book because of its excessive descriptiveness. I'm not a fan of overly long books, and feel that 100 pages could have been cut without any impact to the story. I kept putting this book down for another one that was better at holding my attention.

However, once Ciro goes to America--and Enza follows soon after (at about the 25% mark, for Kindle readers)--the story picked up for me. They both live in NYC and do occasionally see each other, but their meetings are brief and somewhat casual. They basically live their lives separately for a majority of the book.

Ciro and Enza are connected in a way that's hard to immediately understand. The characters are also somewhat flat. I certainly didn't feel much affection coming from either of them when they first kissed, but that formed the basis for their long-surviving love for each other.

Ciro is quite a ladies' man for the time period in which the story is written. While his casualness around women somewhat disappointed me, he is still an admirable character, working hard in his apprenticeship and signing up for the Army to gain US citizenship.

Enza works harder than anyone, initially in indentured servitude with the family who agreed to take her in, then later in her employment with the theater and with her husband later in life. She finds a friend and steadfast companion in Laura, and they are good to each other, never competing for employment and always supporting each other's successes.

When Enza and Ciro do finally get together, I found it to be quite an abrupt decision/transition. But I was also thinking, well it took you long enough!

Then things moved very quickly throughout their lives, with years passing by in a matter of pages. The pacing was certainly all over the place from the beginning of the book in comparison to the end. And the events were not all happy, either.

While many other reviewers loved this book, I didn't wholly connect with the characters or story. Issues with descriptiveness, pacing, and character development were too glaring for me to be able to fully enjoy the story.

title: The Shoemaker's Wife: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Adriana Trigiani
review_text:
The Shoemaker’s Wife by Adriano Trigiani
The sights and sounds of the eastern Italian Alps are still in my mind. They are so beautifully and lovingly described I was not surprised to discover that the author, Adriana Trigiani, finds her ancestry there. In fact, the novel is a fictionalized story of Ms. Trigiani’s grandparents’ great and true love story. Some will probably find that there is too much emphasis given to setting details.

The pace of the novel is sweet and gentle, there is nothing that will startle or scare you, but the story is compelling and the pages just fly by. We begin our immigration story in a small village in the Alps above Bergamo, nestled in the foot of the famous mountain, Pizzo Camino. Poverty is bracing the country and many men have left Italy for America seeking work building the infrastructure of America while sending life-saving money home. It is in this situation that we find our protagonists, Ciro and Vincenza, called Enza. This two have had their youth upended by poverty and misfortune. Sacrificing for the needs of your family is the theme of the book and it is born out of the hardship of the era and deep family commitment.

The novel sweeps us out of the Alps and into New York where we are treated to a sample of what life was like in the early 20th century. Ciro is in New York apprenticed to a shoemaker and Enza is a seamstress in in Hoboken, New Jersey. Through a series of admittedly hard-to-believe coincidences the two friends meet on a few occasions. Ciro eventually dramatically whisks Enza away from her dear friend and the beautiful life she has found working at the Metropolitan Opera House with none other than The Great Caruso. It seems true love has been fully realized and bests all else.

From here we are whisked up to the iron-ore mines of Minnesota, the exact place where Ciro’s father lost his life in the infamous Hibbing mine disaster of 1904. Here Ciro develops a thriving business serving the miners’ need for work boots. Their family grows and Enza is also able to develop her talents for business and sewing. The life of this international immigrant community comes alive with Ms. Tragiani’s detailed descriptions. It is a happy and fulfilling time. Enza is able to send her Italian family enough money to build an ample house with land enough for a productive garden and a small business to support them. Her goal in coming to America was reached and this gives her great peace of mind.
Prepare to drop a tear or two as the story proceeds. The conclusion will leave you with a desire for a continuum.

Regarding the title, I will add that this is a reason for dropping a star. In the title Enza, the wife, is placed in a subordinate position to her husband. In fact, she is a strong protagonist. The title might better have been the Seamstress and the Shoemaker.

Missing 1/3 of the information in a book causes it to be unreadable. Judging from the sample(was not missing any pages) i would have enjoyed reading this novel and do wish i still had the option on my kindle... too bad.
After amazon care center contacted me i downloaded this book again which became readable. It is an entertaining novel and i look forward to reading the 2nd book. Although the story takes its time evolving, the first 2/3 of the information creates an abstract main character surrounded by great supporting characters as well as more than one antagonists that bring the last of the portion hurtling into chaos, despair, and pain, all which is wrapped by LOVE and PASSION from Mercy(the main character suitably named). review_text:
I can see I'm out of step with the other reviewers, but I had to force myself to finish this book. And I only succeeded by skimming lots of the last third of it.

A number of reviewers have commented that the majority of the book was slow. It seemed to me that the author wrote a bunch of short stories about the same character and then plopped them side by side to make up the first third of the book. Take the first chapter for instance. It has nothing to do with the story and doesn't do anything to illuminate Mercy's character.

The main story points were easy to figure out. I just kept reading through the filler and waiting for the events to happen.

There's not any suspense when you know that magic is going to intervene to smooth over any problems faced by Mercy.

review_title: Simply awful -  a bad joke on the paying reader
review_text:
This is possibly the worst kindle book I have bought!
I read the sample chapters and bought the book on the strength of these - but once past the sample it was downhill from there. The writing is about the standard of a high school homework essay - and not a very good one at that!
Its like the Author once read the jacket cover of an Anne Rice novel [[ASIN:B00F1W0DEU The Mayfair Witches Series 3-Book Bundle: Witching Hour, Lasher, Taltos (Lives of Mayfair Witches)]] or saw an episode or two of American Horror Story [[ASIN:B005SZADQS Pilot [HD]]] and decide to fudge it from there - unfortunately not very well at all.....I think the Author must have been laughing out loud as they dreamed up the improbable plot twists to get the main character in/out of trouble - it really is a joke on the paying reader. The plot moves along like a very bad dream - you know the kind where things happen completely randomly and without really hanging together.

OK, so the plot's not a winner and the writing style is a bad joke...what about the characterisation...?
The main character of the book is constantly being betrayed by her close family - all the characters are so impossibly one-dimensional and unlikeable that the feel of the novel just comes across as very immature. I cannot recommend this novel at all.

The semi-predictable plot twists lent enough steam to keep the story flowing and the reader engaged. The witchcraft served as a quiet undercurrent, dished up in small doses, leaving the reader searching for more. Throughout the book, it felt as though the author was providing only the infrastructure of what could potentially evolve into a solid series. Shallow narratives beg for expansion for the reader to become truly immersed in the lives of Savannah's Taylor witches. Questionable editing made for frustrating navigation through some sections, almost as though entire pages eluded the editing process. It will be interesting to see how the author weaves the next installment of Witching Savannah.

review_text:
Please keep in mind I am not providing spoilers, so this review will be deliberately vague.

I immediately found myself insulted by the author providing some of the characters with stereotypical speech and action. As well as the way he chose to make intelligent people start speaking the same way. The author tried in so many ways to make this story work by switching up the most evil character, but this grew irritating.

I read the first 10 chapters and could not get into this book. I finally gave up and walked away for several hours. I, however, decided I needed to find out why this book was so highly recommended. I was also curious to know why it was compared to the All Souls Trilogy.

I tried picking up where I left off, but found I was bored again. So I flipped ahead a few chapters and found that I still couldn't get into it. So I decided to skim as I headed to the ending, where things finally picked up and got better. At first, I thought oh this is going to have a predictable ending. Then I thought, ok so not predictable. In the end, it was predictable.

This slight twist and turn is why I am providing a 2 star rating instead of a 1 star.

title: The Line (Witching Savannah Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: J.D. Horn
review_title: Starts off great...doesn't continue that way
review_text:
I don't even know what the hell happened here. My foundation is shaken. I'm left perpetually baffled. I just don't understand how a book can start off somewhere and then end in another place that's so completely left field that you can't actually see that damn field anymore. It's not even left field. It's freaking off center. What has The Line done to me?

Here's the thing: The Line starts off pretty damn great. And then it tapers off a bit. And then it gets great again. I was slightly disillusioned with its inconsistency (what with the ups and downs and all arounds), but overall, I decided it was a pretty okay read, especially since I felt that people who wanted me to stop reading this book would have to pry my Kindle out of my cold, dead hands. Needless to say, The Line was straddling the line (no lame pun intended) between a 3 and a 4 star read. And then, a twist happened. Seeing as how, a lot of the time I'm up for a twist I was like "Oooh, twist!" And then another twist happened. And then another. And then another. And then another, etc. So, not only did I get literary whiplash, I've come to the conclusion that people should remain at least 50 feet away from Mercy (our heroine) because that chick has the worst luck in the entire world and you'll probably be six feet under if you're anywhere near her.

I liked Mercy at the beginning. She was witty, kind of sarcastic, the black sheep in the family, so I identified with her. However, I was starting to dislike her a bit when I found out she had fuzzy feelings for her sister's boyfriend. And then all of this bad stuff started to happen to her. I get it, we need angst. But after a while (or numerous life-threatening, murderous escapades that all happened between paragraphs of each other), enough was enough. Mercy wasn't a Mary Sue, but she was a perpetual damsel in distress. Sure, sometimes she saved herself, but still...Once you're in THAT many situations, I'm going to start calling you just a tad bit gullible. Also, The Line started to give me horrid One Tree Hill flashbacks where a chick does something crappy with a guy and once we dislike that her, we find out that her friend did something equally crappy with another guy, so therefore that should negate all the bad feelings we have towards our heroine and make us go "awww, poor bbby!" But it doesn't. Not if you're me.

Not all of The Line was bad. Again, it was an extreme page turner and once you get over Mercy and her penchant to attract trouble of all kinds, in every conceivable way possible, you have a really interesting storyline. I love witches. They are always fascinating. In JD Horn's world, they're even more so. Plus, it has an awesome supporting character in Jilo. In fact, the only reason I'm planning on picking up the next installment of this series is because I'm interested in seeing how that relationship plays out...only that relationship. Well, I'm also interested to know more about Maisie and Mercy, but mostly it's Jilo keeping me coming back for more. Mercy and her inner teenage angst doesn't interest me at all. Neither does her development.

So overall, I found The Line to be just meh. I will check out the second installment of this series if its free, and I'll hope that it's better than this one...And that it has slightly more less twists.

title: The Day the Crayons Quit
subtitle: Hardcover – Picture Book, June 27, 2013
author: Oliver Jeffers
review_title: I don't think it's "fair" that I bought this book...
review_text:
The only positives: The art work is fun. The naked crayon was humorous. The first half of green crayon's letter was almost happy.

The negatives:
If you're looking for a book where all of the characters are complaining and *itching about life not being fair, then this is the perfect book for you and your children. If you'd like to reinforce phrases like "it's not fair" and "I'm tired of that" with your children then by all means purchase this book. Page after page, you read letters of complaining crayons...what parent want to sit down and read this with their toddler?!

This book will help your kids learn that by throwing a tantrum and refusing to participate in normal, everyday tasks they can get what they want. After all, the little boy gave into the crayons demands.

The end also lacked any sort of real resolution...we jump from all these nasty letters back to two pages of the little boy coloring. And very little text is used on these pages to help complete the story or address his thought process. I've got kids to take care of, so I'm not going to spend another ounce of energy on this piece of *rap book.

BTW...if I'd done my research I'd have realized what i was getting, so the "it's not fair in the subject" is supposed to be a little ironic. I made my own bed and am stuck with this until garage sale season. Don't make the same mistake.

review_text: My 5-year old son received this book and its sequel as a gift. I think this aggrieved tone is meant to appeal to adults, not children, because the only thing my son really loves about this book and its sequel are the "off-color" (no pun intended) bits such as the naked crayon, the pooping bear (from the sequel), a crayon stuck in a pair of underpants, etc. He also guffaws at the use of some language (i.e., "hate", "stupid") that we typically try to discourage. I also hate reading this book because the crayon scrawls are a little difficult to discern in his dimmer bedroom lighting. I think as soon as he loses interest in reading these books EVERY. SINGLE.
