title: The Day the Crayons Quit
subtitle: Hardcover – Picture Book, June 27, 2013
author: Oliver Jeffers
review_text: This story looked cute enough, but as a mom, I pretty much disliked it.  The premise is adorable: the crayons go on strike list their grudges and there's a happy ending.  The pictures are pretty cute too and the artwork was well done and matched the text well.  I had two big problems with it.  The first is that the book just isn't really for kids.  It's the kind of book that adults think is funny and will enjoy reading, but I don't think really appeals to kids.  I was laughing, but my kids were both like, enough whiny crayons already, where's the story?  So if you put it in the same category with Go the $%^ to Sleep, it's a winner.  My kids 4.5 and 2.5 were just kind of bored.  My big problem though is with the tongue-in-cheek page about pink being a "girl's color."  I know, the book was trying to point out how silly and limiting that is.  Bravo to the book for trying to change the minds of kids who think that.  The thing is, my kids don't really think that yet.  Maybe someday, they will, but I'd like for them to feel as though they have the whole rainbow to explore unencumbered for as long as possible.  It's like books refuting the existence of Santa, or teaching about monsters under the bed.  Fine, yes, someday they will pick that up at school and we'll deal with it then, but I'd rather not be the one to introduce the concept.  We may love this book in a few years when my kids get the joke, and my daughter is languishing in a pink abyss, but by then I suspect they'll have outgrown picture books.

title: The Day the Crayons Quit
subtitle: Hardcover – Picture Book, June 27, 2013
author: Oliver Jeffers
review_text:
While I like the creativity and format of this book, I have removed it from our at home "library" and we no longer read it.

The book tells a story of a box of crayons who write letters to their "boy," telling him what they like or do not like to be used to color (ie - Red Crayon says "I even have to work on holidays!"). I like the general idea, but the constant complaining from each color turned me off. I have two little kids (2 and 3), and they mimic and use phrases and attitudes from any books that we read. Instead of picking up positive comments from Green Crayon, they started copying the complaining from Orange and Yellow Crayon (and Red and Blue and White, etc).

Again, cute in the idea but not a fit for us. Were my kids a bit older I might have kept it as an example for how to express yourself appropriately (and inappropriately), but since most of those nuances go over their heads at this point, this book is going away.

review_title: This book colors out a rating of... 4 White Cats in the Snow!!
review_text:
The Day the Crayons Quit comes from the Crayons point of view. Each Crayon crayols out a personal note they leave for Duncan expressing either their satisfaction or dissatisfaction with the lot they have in life.

Each page is filled with life like looking notes and crayon drawing's featuring the Color writing the note. Some Crayons get used to much, some not enough. Some don't like being used for drawing huge pictures of elephants, and some don't like being solely used for princess gowns. It's like a community in labor bargaining negotiations and your lucky kid reading gets to be the Mayor!

Learning the back story of each Crayon could provide a parent and child the opportunity to discuss ways that the Crayons different complaints could be resolved. Not only will this book spark the imagination, but it could be the basis for some critical thinking... Problem solving on a kid level.

The Day the Crayons Quit is written by Drew Daywalt and has pictures from Oliver Jeffers.

This book colors out a rating of... 4 White Cats in the Snow!!

author: Oliver Jeffers
review_title: Some people need to learn to think outside the box.
review_text:
I was skeptical about reading this book with my 5 1/2 year old tonight after reading through some of the weird reviews. As someone who regularly works with children and has a masters degree in a psych field, I found no issues with this book!

1.) This book is about thinking outside the box, considering others' feelings and opinions, and having empathy.

2.) The book shows unintended consequences that can go on without us realizing we may be impacting others in a potentially hurtful way.

3.) My 5 year old found the "naked" peach crayon in the crayon box absolutely hilarious. "Crayons don't need underwear!" He says. He has more of a sense of humor than some of y'all lol.

4.) Pink was actually considered a masculine color not too long ago in modern history (look it up). Don't overthink the pink crayon page.

5.) I LIKE that the purple and pink crayons address coloring in the lines...because guess what? In Kindergarten now it is a rigid expectation! The book isn't being harsh with it...and no one says kids have to do it all the time...but understanding it is going to be a useful skill to work on by school-age/a fine motor skill goal is important too. Positive labeled praise for coloring in the lines is given by the pink crayon in reference to the litle sister as well.

Don't read into the book so much. I did not find it to be politically leaning one way or the other. We had a lot of fun reading it and using different voices. The way the main character tries to solve the problem in a way that attempts to make everyone happy is overly simplistic...but it's a book for littles! It also brings the message home about things not needing to be so rigid/strict. I am glad I ordered the book despite goofy reviews by people who clearly missed the point.

title: Secret Garden: An Inky Treasure Hunt and Coloring Book for Adults
subtitle: Paperback – Coloring Book, March 26, 2013
author: Johanna Basford
review_title: Overrated and not that great compare to other coloring books out there
review_text:
I purchased this book a year ago after hearing all the hype about it and I must say it did not live up to my expectations. The paper is not pure white it is an ivory color. The designs are nice but they are way too intricate and most of them are repetitive. To be honest, my eyes hurt just looking at them because they're so intricate and detailed it's difficult to focus on the focal points in the majority of the designs. Another thing that bothers me about this book is not all of the pages are completely illustrated. From an artist point of view, I understand that the illustrator wants you to be as creative and create your own designs in the book but it's a coloring book it should not require you to do more work other than coloring especially for people who can't draw and just simply want to color. So far I've experimented Prismacolor premier colored pencils and Faber Castell polychromos in it and I must prefer the polychromos over the Prismacolor premier for this book although I think water based markers would be the best media to use for this particular book. I started coloring in this book and so far I've only completed 2 designs. There's not a lot about this coloring book that's "wow" me.

I would only recommend this coloring book for people that are more experienced in adult coloring. For people who just started out or are new to the adult coloring world but want that similar feel to this book, I really recommend you try Joyous Blooms to Color by Eleri Fowler - trust me you will love it! Over all, I think this book is way overrated and there are many better adult coloring books out there that have that similar feel and spark more interests than this one.

I was quite disappointed when I got the book and found that so very many pages had "instructions" on them. The preview pictures and even the colored pages that reviewers have uploaded really avoid those pages so you don't get to find out the truth until you open the book. Over 1/4 of the total coloring pages in the book (22 of 84) have extra instructions written on them, telling you to do things such as fill flower pots or draw more butterflies, etc. Many of these are on pictures that are over two facing pages, so this affects about 1/3 of the total coloring pages in the book. This may not be important to many people, but it is quite unappealing to me. I suspect it is not very appealing to others as well considering that almost none of the uploaded pages of color have any of these instructions on them.

Overall I like the artwork but I know I will avoid the pages with instructions. I wouldn't mind filling in the blank spaces on my own with my own doodling and coloring, but I really don't like the idea of having the instructions scrawled across the page around my drawing. All of the instructions are integrated into the drawings so they aren't even anything you can crop out. I don't think this necessarily "ruins" the book, but for my preferences, it does ruin the pages in question. Considering that I thought I was getting a lot more coloring pages, I really am disappointed. Of the 96 pages listed, 12 of them are introductory pages, instructions, and answers to the hidden mystery objects. The other 22+ that are undesirable because of their instructions, plus perhaps another half dozen that are joint pages with some of those instruction pages, means that less than 60% of the listed pages are pure coloring pages. That's not what I thought I was paying for, and I just thought others might want to make sure they know exactly what they are getting.

Finally, all of the pages are double sided, leaving none for you to easily choose to use markers with. I have only used colored pencils because it is obvious that bleed will ruin half of this book otherwise. The drawings look like they would be truly vibrant with markers but I don't want to lose even more pages with so many already of questionable use. The drawings also stretch all the way into the binding, requiring you to bend the spine just to be able to almost fully color many of them. If this bothers you, that leaves several more pages of questionable usefulness.

I got this because the reviews were amazing and I really loved the few pages I had gotten a preview of. Unfortunately it seems that I'd already seen all of the best of the best, and in a book with 96 pages, that left me feeling quite let down.

title: Secret Garden: An Inky Treasure Hunt and Coloring Book for Adults
subtitle: Paperback – Coloring Book, March 26, 2013
author: Johanna Basford
review_text:
There can be little doubt that the illustrations in this book are simply magnificent. They are as artful as they are complex, and the time it takes to colour them is certainly restorative and calming. What a pity the book itself is so cheaply put together.

The pages bleed if you use felt tip pens. Even if you take the time to track down a set of the Staedtler Fineliners Johanna Basford herself recommends on her blog; a post I might add that is dedicated solely to Staedtler products. Perhaps I am the fool for failing to recognise such blatant product placement or sponsorship.

Furthermore, far from the crisp white images you see in most photos of this books contents, the pages are decidedly yellowed. I would accept this if the pages were made from recycled paper, but this is not stated anywhere that I can find. At any rate, the thing is labelled as being printed in China, and it feels as cheap and nasty as a stereotypical Chinese product.

I simply could not recommend this product, unless you are willing to pull the book apart, scan the images, and print them on better quality paper yourself; something I may find myself doing to have a useable product.

I LOVE this book. I'm having so much fun with it. I was a little hesitant after reading some of the other reviews that mentioned poor quality paper with bleed-throughs from markers, but I really don't know what they're talking about. title: The Cuckoo's Calling (Cormoran Strike Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Robert Galbraith
review_text:
If you are a scholarly bibliophile, you’ll love the Latin quotes that precede each section of JK Rowling’s first detective novel, as well as the literary allusion in the title. If you are a detective novel junkie with a special love for the private eye subgenre, you’ll likely appreciate the extraordinary level of detail that characterizes The Cuckoo’s Calling. Detail, in fact, that seems to be both Rowling’s greatest strength and also greatest weakness. In the Harry Potter books, Rowling was creating a world of wonder and imagination, like our own, but Other, and lit with a magical luminescence. Details were essential to this world, in all sorts of things from Quiddich to Bogles, because these things do not exist in our Muggle dimension. The heart of Rowling’s consummate storytelling is the details, in fact: it’s the zip of a Golden Snitch, the droopy elastic arms rendered boneless by a spell, and the nicked and filthy cover of the Half-Blood Prince’s potions book. These are the tiny particulars that make fiction real, which by definition it is not. For fantasy, these minutiae are essential, because fantastical stories are generally set in entire worlds that do not even exist. But for detective fiction, the situation is altered. Many readers who consume mystery novels are looking for a complex and interesting plot and some level of suspense that plays out through a relatively fast-paced story. Some readers, admittedly, are only looking to have some fun, some are looking for quirky and humorous characters, and still others are looking to overcome their deep-seated feelings of frustration with the overwhelming tides of injustice washing through their lives. (At least in detective novels, if not in real life, the bad guy is always punished and the murderer is always caught. Or at least 99% of the time, anyway. No true detective fiction is likely to be very successful unless this predictable but essential element is present. Ok, now we’re on a Freudian tangent.) But too many details tend to kill a mystery novel, because too much external description destroys internal suspense.

To a point, Rowling’s novel is extremely believable due to its level of detail: halfway through, the reader has unconsciously memorized the brand of beer the detective drinks, knows how to remove a prosthetic leg, and can tell you how to sneak a shower at a university even if you aren’t a student there. These particulars do an outstanding job of bringing the character to life, which is a rare and beautiful sight in a detective novel since that genre usually focusses on plot and pacing at the expense of character. The problem here is that any possibility of suspense, the foundation of the genre, is drowned in the sea of details. Halfway through you begin to wonder why in blazes you’re continuing to read, since the book so far appears merely to be an incredibly detailed account of the research of a private sleuth who is getting nowhere. Meaning no disrespect, Rowling should fire her editor. I mean, c’mon—100 pages of Harry and his friends wandering in the woods literally doing nothing in The Deathly Hallows? Two hundred some pages of detective Cormoran Strike using the restroom, getting drunk, surfing Google, and pining for his vindictive girlfriend? Really? Rowling’s writing is extremely high-quality, but her penchant for describing everything, especially places and scenes in which nothing happens for hundreds of pages, needs the assistance of a better editor.

The two other serious flaws that The Cuckoo’s Calling displays as part of the detective genre are first, that Rowling never drops any clues about the murderer’s motive, so that comes as an implausible surprise at the very end, and second, as a result, the entire climax is wildly improbable. Not only does the murderer have no compelling motive, but also he/she has an ironclad alibi until the very crux of the climax, which is replaced at that point by the most truly ludicrous actions of any fictional murderer that I’ve ever encountered. Put simply, Rowling commits the cardinal sin of poor mystery writers: she cheats. It’s considered extremely bad form for a detective novelist to never drop a single hint to her readers of the murderer’s true motives or true actions on the day of the murder, and Rowling does neither, so it is impossible for her audience to solve the crime along with the detective. The audience is simply provided with useless non-information from all of the suspects for the entire first 3/4 of the novel, so the reader can literally skip the entire first 75% of the book and not have missed anything at all except for character and place description. Not character development, mind you—merely description. There isn’t even a second murder until 75% of the way through the novel.

Despite the fact that Rowling’s detail-oriented style does not, at least so far, lend itself particularly well to the urban detective novel, one significant strength integral to The Cuckoo’s Calling in addition to quality style is the astonishing variety of voice in the work. Rowling’s greatest gift, it would seem, lies in that field which is often such a disaster for so many lesser writers, myself included: Rowling possesses an extraordinary capacity to create diverse voices for her characters. No two sound alike in this novel, a feat that isn’t nearly as prolific in the Harry Potter novels. In The Cuckoo’s Calling, each character talks in a unique, believable dialogue that leaves the reader marveling how on earth Rowling could capture the personality of so many different people so effectively through their spoken words. The main character of the detective himself, as well as to a limited extent his assistant and ex-fiancée, are developed more through narrative than dialogue, but all the other characters are illuminated through that most golden of fiction-writing maxims: show, don’t tell. And Rowling shows, through the dialogue of her characters, that she is an absolute master of character voice, and on a wider scale characterization in general. She’s one of the best voice writers I’ve ever seen, in fact, possibly even the best, because unlike Harper Lee or Lemony Snickett who write novels in one nuanced and extraordinary voice, Rowling seems capable of writing as anyone, in nearly any kind of voice, and does just that throughout the course of the book. If you’re a student of voice and character, do yourself a favor and pick up this modern Dickensian detective novel. If your primary love is fast-paced suspense/mystery novels, don’t go anywhere near this book, unless you want to read yourself to sleep.

title: The Cuckoo's Calling (Cormoran Strike Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Robert Galbraith
review_text:
Let's get the issue of Rowling out of the way before I get into the actual book review. First of which is to say that I'm not going to discuss Rowling beyond saying that the fact that she doesn't know when to shut her mouth shows that having lots of money can affect the way that anyone views themselves and the world. She's at that stage where she believes that she, because she is who she is, is right and doesn't need to listen to other people, so she has continued to dig her hole bigger and bigger rather than just shutting up and keeping her opinions to herself. That she didn't shut up shows an amount of entitlement which is disappointing.

The other thing I want to say is that I started reading this book... well, so long ago that I don't remember when it was. I picked it up during some free promotion thing just to check it out and have been reading it in bits and pieces ever since. It's on my Kindle, and I don't really read from my Kindle all that often. I don't carry it places with me like I do physical books, so I lag a lot with books on there unless they are really engrossing. Which tells you that this book was not. Seriously, I've been working on it for over a year, maybe closer to two.

What this book has taught me is that I need to read some Agatha Christie, something I've been meaning to do for a long time and have never gotten around to. Maybe I don't like detective novels? I don't know. I like Butcher's Dresden books, but they're hardly detective novels after the first few. Beyond those, I can't recall any mystery novels I've ever really liked, including this one.

Which is not to say that I didn't like it, I just didn't much care for it. Rowling doesn't make it possible for the reader to really solve the mystery as they're reading, which seems to me to be the point of detective novels, because she doesn't reveal crucial information until the actual reveal at the end of the novel, and the reveal was one of the most contrived things I've ever read. And this is an ABSOLUTE SPOILER, so turn away now if you don't want to know who the killer is...

I'm waiting...

Still waiting, because I'm absolutely serious that I'm going to spoil the ending of this book. And let me just toss out there that I never spoil a book that I think you ought to read. If I spoil it, it's because I don't think it's really worth your trouble.

Having said that, the book itself was just fine. By that, I mean it's readable. Mostly engaging, though not engaging enough to prompt me to read it more quickly. It's... typical. Down on his luck private eye getting a high paying, juicy case which might just get him out of debt. Your basic story about an underachiever finally getting a break and getting to show the world who he really is. Honestly, after Harry Potter, I expected something less... cliché.

So the book goes along with our detective -- the son of a famous rock star, seriously? -- gathering up evidence about a case that is several months cold. And closed. But he's hired by the brother of the murdered woman because the brother believes it was a murder though the police ruled it a suicide. And this is the hitch and what I'm sure Rowling thought would make it a clever story: the brother is the murderer. So Strike is hired by the murderer to discover who the murderer is. The motivation for this is never explained adequately since the murderer had already gotten away with the crime.

What the novel mostly does, as most mystery shows do (I don't know about mystery novels, as I said, but I have watched a lot of detective shows) is to show that everyone had a motive for killing the victim. Rowling walks us through the suspects over and over again almost always strengthening the case for why each person might have wanted Lulu dead. In fact, the only person not shown to have a motive, not until the very end of the book, basically not until just before the reveal, is the actual murderer. Of course, the motive is money, but we don't get to find out the murderer's money issues until Strike is sitting alone in a room with the murderer revealing all the things the murderer already knows.

The reveal was clumsy and contrived. The fact that Bristow (the murderer) sits through Strike's walkthrough of the entire crime is, frankly, unbelievable. The fact that Bristow then attacks Strike is even more unbelievable considering that Strike is a bear of a man and ex-boxer while Bristow is your very stereotypical account type, even though he's a lawyer, not an account, a "gag" that is run into the ground over the course of the book.

I want to say that Rowling's strength as a writer is her characters but, as I'm thinking of this now, she has no real strength in that, either. Her character's tend toward the stereotype, including pretty much all of the characters in Harry Potter. In Harry Potter, we're able to overlook that, though, because the world is so new and interesting, but this world, the world of C. B. Strike, is not new or interesting so the fact that all of the characters are two dimensional really stands out. The most real character in the book is Strike's temporary secretary, Robin, and she's really just a pale reflection of Hermione Granger.

Also, the title of this book is stupid. It's just tossed in somewhere over the halfway mark of the book that "Cuckoo" is a nickname of the murdered woman that only one character in the book ever called her. It's a throwaway excuse to have "Cuckoo" in the title. Without that very vague reason, the title of the book is meaningless.

So, yeah, I suppose I am actually disappointed with this book and don't really understand all the praise for it. Again, maybe I just don't really like detective novels; I don't know. This book doesn't inspire me to try more, though.

review_title: Cormoran and Robin, a great new series by RA aka JKR
review_text: Too rarely do I begin a book and know within a few minutes that I am in for a very enjoyable read.  Such is the case with "The Cuckoo's Calling" by Robert Galbraith (J K Rowling).  This is the first in a series, the author having announced that book #2 is recently finished and will likely be published sometime in 2014.  Cormoran Strike, the protagonist, is quite a character - offspring of an androgynous rocker and a deceased addict and groupie,  injured Afghan war vet, and barely surviving PI.  He no longer shares the bed of his ex girlfriend, a wealthy glamour girl who wants him back, or does she?  Things are so tough for Strike that he sleeps on a foldup bed in his office and showers at the ULU, whatever that is, perhaps a London University.  But things begin to look up early on when in the span of a few hours he gets a client he was praying for and a lovely temp that he didn't want.  The case involves the supposed suicide of a well known model, victim of a jump from her expensive apartment virtually to the feet of a horde of papparazzi (paps).  Soon, a dozen or so friends, half relatives, hangers on etc are introduced and questioned at lenth by Cormoran, sometimes with the assistance of Robin.  At the end there is a lengthy dialog between Cormoran and killer where everything is explained, everything.  Too often, these long and detailed revelations bore me but not this one, just one more indication of how well written the story is.  I particularly liked all the characters, even the many obnoxious ones, and I liked the getting-to-know-you between Cormoran and the engaging (and engaged) Robin.  Looking forward very much to #2.  By the way, Rowling in real life, has some very interesting neighbors in her little community near Edinburgh and it is not surprising that she has finally tried on crime fiction.

review_text:
I know! Oh boy there are a lot of readers who will COMPLETELY disagree with this rating. Many of my friends loved this book. Let's begin with what I liked about this novel - the main character's connection to nature and the scientific facts presented throughout the story.

Now for the novel's downfalls...

SPOILER ALERT!

This story is just too improbable. From Kya raising herself beginning at a very young age, to EVERYONE leaving her, to her killing someone it was all too much for me. Kya never got sick or badly injured, needed a doctor, dentist? This strong character goes to school for one day and is bullied away? She had a wonderful relationship with her brother Jody, who then leaves her and never contacts her again for years. He left her to live in a dilapidated shack ,with an abusive, irresponsible, neglectful father. That is not something this character would have done. Next, Tate befriends her and presumably loves her. He knows everyone has left her and he does also. How could you do that to someone you love? Neither character has a reasonable excuse for not contacting her in any way for years.

Overall, the author used too much drama to develop the character she was trying to create. Owens needs to show that she believes in the intelligence of her readers and not author-splain constantly. Yikes! I did not like this one.

title: Where the Crawdads Sing
subtitle: Hardcover – August 14, 2018
author: Delia Owens
review_text:
Last time I checked 24,157 people had written reviews of Where the Crawdads Sing, and 87% of them gave it 5 stars. Can all those people be wrong? That would be crazy, right? So let's not use the word 'wrong.'
But really, I am completely baffled.
In the beginning I was engaged and thought the writing was lovely. And then as the pages wore on it seemed the author became more interested in finding new ways to describe things than in telling the story, and so it went on and on with pages of tedious description, quotes from nature books, poetry, etc.
I am a writer. I'm not well-known, I don't have a NY Times best seller, but I am published. I write and read and study writing continuously. So whenever I read there's a little critique going on in my head. When something annoys me or pulls me out of the story I highlight it so I know not to do that in my own work.
Here are things I highlighted in this book (they became more frequent as I continued on and by the end I was skipping large passages):
1. The book is written in the point of view of Kya but every once in a while it switches POV, out of the blue, to explain something.
2. Then, about 1/4 of the way in there is even an omniscient narrator (another POV) who tells the story of Kya's parents. Annoying.
3. Another POV switch to explain why Tate never came back. Again, jarring, pulling me out of the story. It could be explained later when he returns.
4. Then, it all of a sudden changes to present tense, when all along (and through the rest of the book) it is past tense.

WHERE IS HER EDITOR, FOR GOD'S SAKE?

5. There are long passages from the nature articles Kya pours over, because even though she did not learn to read until she was a teenager, she suddenly is reading scientific materials. I am not interested in those passages, and they don't move the story along.
6. She goes to the library to request those scientific books (let me just say her sudden knowledge is a huge credibility stretch) and the librarian offers to get them for her. How do you get a library card if you live in a marsh and have no i.d. and no address?
7. Then, guess what? She writes a nature book and gets it published. Talk about a suspension of disbelief. And then at some point she gets a check for $5000 from her publisher. She could not receive a check from a publisher without having a completed W9 which would require a social security number. She continues to get substantial checks, so let's just say that COULD happen - how would she cash them? She has no bank account.
8. When she fixes up her shack (which she's lived in her whole life - since age SIX, all alone - without toilet facilities or heat or running water or a place to plug in her blow-dryer) and puts in running water and electricity, did she get permits? Does her contractor just come in and jury-rig all the utilities?
9. She orders stuff from the Sears catalog. With what?
I could go on...
The last 1/4 of the book is tedious and repetitive with much unnecessary description. And then I kept thinking I'd reached the end and I'd be so relieved, and then I'd turn the page and it would just continue on.
The trial scene, in particular, could be cut entirely. There's nothing new or revelatory there. It's predictable and mind-numbing.
Ok, I'm done.
Books are subjective, we all know that. But I can't believe 21,016 people could be so wrong.

title: Where the Crawdads Sing
subtitle: Hardcover – August 14, 2018
author: Delia Owens
review_title: This is most definitely NOT the North Carolina Carolina I know
review_text:
Is there anyone out there who disliked "Where the Crawdad Sings" as much as I? I'm so confused. This book has received reverential treatment, including a piece on the author on CBS Sunday Morning that talked about this book like it was the next To Kill a Mockingbird. I can't believe the author ever set foot in North Carolina! I am from New Bern near where this story supposedly takes place. I went to college in Greenville. There are many coastal dialects,
all beautiful in their own way. None of them sound remotely like the dialogue used with any of these characters. This dialect is more akin to Snuffy Smith in the comics. There is no way that a gentleman farmer from the mountains, of landed means, as the "pa" is described, would say things like,
"Ah reckin we can git us some rest'rant vittles." And she had people driving clear across the great state of North Carolina to get supplies in Asheville! During the 50s, 60s and 70s, it would take an entire day to travel from the coast to the mountains. Most people would do it in two days. NO ONE would drive from the coast to Asheville to buy neckties. Or a bicycle.
ALSO, and this really drove me crazy, no one ate cheese grits. Especially for supper. We ate grits, lots of grits. Often with country ham. For breakfast. That is an invention of Quaker Oats, probably in the late 70s. Cheese grits are not the iconic southern food they are depicted to be in this book. Cheese biscuits, yes. Cheese grits, no.
Finally, this story is just ENTIRELY unbelievable. Nothing about it rings true. Hearing this author compared to Barbara Kingsolver and Harper Lee is just crazy.

title: Where the Crawdads Sing
subtitle: Hardcover – August 14, 2018
author: Delia Owens
review_title: The crawdads don’t want any part of this idiocy
review_text:
This is one of the worst books I have ever had the misfortune of reading. The only upside is that it was a library, so only time, not money, was lost. The characters are either wooden, one dimensional, gross stereotypes, unbelievable, or, in many cases, all of the above. The “mystery” (flash forwards and flashbacks to reveal the mystery throughout the book) is so stupid it hurts. Man falls and dies in the woods. What, no footprints in the SWAMP? By cracky , it must be a murder! The plot of the book is a preposterous bore. I only read to the end because a friend told me there was a great “twist” (spoiler alert: unless you are catatonic- which, come to think of it, you might be by the end of the book- you know exactly what is going to happen. The author does add in a few more unbelievable bits (swamp girl is a brilliant scientist, author, watercolorist, AND a remarkable poet! Despite being abandoned in the swamp at age 6. Oh, and she is gorgeous, too. And supporting herself, since childhood, by digging mussels every day. ) Swamp girl is also a magician: later in the story, after having her best-selling book published, she is able to make all sorts of modern additions to a dilapidated shack in the swamp. Abracadabra!

SPOILER: the end. The end! It reads like a children’s story that no one wants to read. Swamp girl and lab boy live happily ever after in in the modernized shack. Swamp girl is recognized for her brilliance as a naturalist, awarded honorary doctorates, and then... just dies in a boat. Really. She and lab boy are out in the boat and next thing you know, she’s dead. It is so dumb, and poorly written, you want to throw the book in the nearest swamp (until you remember it is a library book; screaming into a pillow will have to suffice ). Oh, and then we are told that swamp girl is eventually forgotten about in the small town, to the point where some wonder if she was just a “legend “ (wha-huh???!!! Umm, the trial? All of her best-selling books? Her recognition as a brilliant naturalist? It makes no sense, at all).

So, we find out that swamp girl did indeed do it, creating two costumes (!!!) to wear on the bus, luring fancy boy to the swamp in the middle of the night , and pushing him to his death (reason never explained— years later still feeling scorned? ) Oh, and returning by bus in order to come back again, hours later, by bus.

title: Where the Crawdads Sing

author: Delia Owens
review_title: Turn off your brain to enjoy this one.
review_text: All my family and friends recommended this book, so I got it for a summer read. I started it and almost immediately had to suspend any attempt at believing the story of a 6 year old who could wear the same overalls for over four years and never grow out of them. She lived in the swamps barefoot for over a decade. Her only injury is a massive puncture wound through her foot, from which she recovers on her own - at seven! She never goes to school, but picks up reading so quickly she becomes a researcher and writer. She makes money selling her books and becomes famous. She knows the Latin roots of words in her twenties with no formal education! This might be great for a beach read, but I just couldn’t suspend all reason enough to appreciate it.

author: Delia Owens
review_text:
Another book I read because of Taylor Swift. Only this time, Blondie let me down. I was underwhelmed… Maybe WHERE THE CRAWDADS SING has just been too overhyped at this point? I hate using that phrase, but I expected more. I honestly think at this point I’ve read better historical fiction. I can see why in 2018, it might have been fantastic - and have Reese pick it - but now, I’m meh about it. It makes me sad as a Swiftie that so many people will pick this book up when there are many better books without plot holes and stereotypes. The only positives I liked were Deliah Owens’ prose and the poetic - albeit questionable - ending.

Let’s do a double negative compliment sandwich since I was not too fond of this one…

+ Owens prose is lovely, especially if you are fond of nature descriptions. You’ll feel like you’re in the marsh.

- Plot-holes. I don’t give spoilers, but I was frustrated reading this because things didn’t add up even when I suspended belief as a reader.

- Stereotypes. An author can write a book about an era and its people respectfully or as stereotypes. Owens did the latter with Jumpin’ and Mabel, and it felt uncomfortable to read about these characters.

+/- The end. It did give me a whoa moment. But at the same time, we go back to plot-holes because really?! 🤔🤐

I hope the movie will affect my negative criticisms and fix the flaws because I liked this book’s overall idea. I also did like Kya being a strong, independent,$ wild woman. I plan on seeing the movie when it’s available to stream on something I already pay for. 🤣

Many people love this book - Reese Witherspoon, Taylor Swift, and my best friend are included in that group. It wasn’t for me. I wish I loved it being a Swiftie, but I wouldn’t be me if I weren’t honestly reviewing it. Maybe I’ll like the movie! 🙂🙃

Content Warnings: domestic abuse, child abuse, abandonment, alcoholism, sexual assault, racism, bullying, familial death, grief, classism

title: Where the Crawdads Sing
subtitle: Hardcover – August 14, 2018
author: Delia Owens
review_text:
I love good books and had high hopes for this one -- especially after reading all of the wonderful reviews. The premise of an isolated, almost feral young woman being accused of murder sounded enticing so I settled in for a good winter's read that turned into an incredulous chuckle. Yes, fiction does require a willing suspension of disbelief, but this tale requires a constant state of said suspension. The underlying premise of abandonment is faulty from the get-go: No loving mother leaves a young child to deal with her abusive father; No loving brother abandons a six year old to the same fate; No caring society turns its back on a six-year-old living alone in a dangerous environment. But if for some reason you manage to get past the incredulous premise, the characterization of the two young men involved in Kya's life seals the deal. We're expected to accept that Chase, the young man who never forced himself on Kya for years, suddenly tries to violently rape her. Yes, his flaws are made clear from the beginning, but he cultivates his relationship with Kay slowly and carefully; he isn't a raging animal bent on having her for himself until it becomes convenient for the plot. Similarly her relationship with Tate is questionable. Like everyone else in Kya's life, he abandons her until his return is convenient for the plot. Tate's big discovery at the end of the novel is a convenience as well. It's supposed to tie all the loose ends together, but it leaves many questions unanswered -- and that's because there aren't any logical answers to those questions.

Long story short, if you enjoy immersions in implausibility, then read this book. But if you like your fiction to hold some semblance of truth, walk away.

title: Where the Crawdads Sing
subtitle: Hardcover – August 14, 2018
author: Delia Owens
review_title: Intriguing story with beautiful descriptive passages
review_text:
I enjoyed this book immensely, particularly the beautifully written descriptive passages about the marsh. It was easy to visualize the places and wildlife described by Delia Owens but I found many of the characters to be cariacatures. There is the ‘Nice Man’, Tate and the ‘Bad Man’, Chase among others.
Some of the plot points did not ring true for me. It seemed unlikely that such a young girl abandoned to live alone in a marsh would escape the Truancy Lady so completely and that authorities would never be able to find her and place her in care. The people who came to care about her, Tate, Jumpin’ and Mabel would surely have done more to look after her instead of leaving her alone for such large stretches of time.
I would like to think that Jodi and her other siblings would have written to her or found a way to come and visit and check on her rather than simply abandoning her.
I also felt that her mother would have written many times and probably Kya would have been able to intercept at least one of the letters. Although she herself couldn’t read, they would surely have assumed, as Jodi did, that she had gone to school and could have asked someone to read their letters to her.
Kya’s education was entirely gained from reading books left for her by Tate and yet she becomes extraordinarily smart and insightful. I’m not sure this is possible without more human interaction and study of subjects other than those open to her.
In addition to these plot holes, the policemen seemed to have no evidence that Chase’s death was a murder and very little evidence to suggest Kya had been Involved. That whole chunk of the story did not ring true for me. The murder of Chase Andrews was an intriguing story arc, but did not seem to mesh well with this story of a girl abandoned by her family and living alone in the marsh. Perhaps it would have worked better as two separate books.
Having said all of this I did thoroughly enjoy the book and its final reveal, and felt haunted by the loneliness and sadness of Kya’s story. I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys scenic descriptions with an added love story entwined within a murder mystery.

title: A Gentleman in Moscow: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Amor Towles
review_text:
We read this book for our December library book club selection. I'm the only one out of fifteen that didn't like it. There were all sorts of sighing over the writing--wonderful similes and metaphors--and love and admiration for the Count. The general opinion was that it was a tremendous picture of a man who acted well and gracefully under pressure.

Towles gets a star for writing a novel, and another star for some interesting language use. But for me the setting was unreal, and the plotting slow, somewhat cliched, and too long.

SPOILERS

I simply cannot buy that a 21st century writer would know how a Russian count would react when caught in a world-shattering event such as the Bolshevik/Communist revolutions. Oh, wait, the count DIDN'T face any any of the REAL consequences of being hated royalty during the horrific overthrow of the Russian aristocracy. There is very, very little of the reality of the Bolshevik revolution in this book. Towles has his character confined to a 4-star hotel, where he forms friendships with the staff, gets three meals a day, is not running or in hiding for his life, and finally gets the better of the communist manager, and escapes. Oh, and the count also raises a little girl who is dropped off by her mother, who is running from the Russian authorities.

As for grace under pressure, it's not hard to retain one's courtliness when you're not fighting for food or a shower or looking for a safe place to hide--and, oh yeah, there's that little matter of the hollow chair leg that you can remove and pull out a couple of pieces of gold whenever you need them.

Perhaps I read it at the wrong time: I had just finished "Looking Like the Enemy," a memoir of the Japanese internment camps. Now THERE were people who really lost everything, and they didn't get sent to four star hotels.

Truthfully, the plot of the story-beginning to ending-could have been written in 75 pages or less.  Way too much filler, and just boring, but I kept on reading-took me way to long-just to see how Mr Towles was going to end it, which, by the way, was certainly not unexpected, and, sorry, just added to the complete boredom. Maybe Mr Towles is just too intellectual for me, but I doubt it!  A very boring man he must be for people like me, but others must be impressed.

Amor Towles it seems never fails to disappoint. A Gentleman in Moscow is even more beautifully written than The Rules of Civility. Towles is so adept at capturing the historical period of Moscow that the reader cannot fail but to feel a time traveler.
A book is best defined, however, by its character development and this book does not disappoint. Count Rostov's character is so beautiful that I was immediately in love. The Count and all the other wonderful members of this lovely Hotel Metropov which in itself is a character are such a loving family. I learned many lessons of "civility" and character and love yet again.
If you are looking for a fast paced book this book is not for you but if you are looking to slow down and enjoy a well written book about history, love and friendship across all ages, classes and political beliefs, then read a Gentleman in Moscow.

review_title: Good Bones, Was Not Fleshed Out
review_text:
A fresh-out-of-the-box lawyer takes the only job he can find, one with a rather sleazy law firm, and his second case is for capital murder. And because the murder was done in front of witnesses, it is pretty hard to refute or defend.

Despite some implausibility issues, this very short book has the bones of a good story. Unfortunately, that is all there is – bones of a story. The characters are not fleshed out much, there are potential storylines that are not explored, especially the mentions of the Russian mafia, and the story is a bit too predictable.

There was a horrible description of child torture which I found hard to read. As so much of the story was glossed over, I do wish this part had been, as well.

While this book does have potential, it just didn't live up to that potential.

I read this e-book through my Kindle Unlimited membership.

title: The Burning Room (A Harry Bosch Novel Book 17)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Michael Connelly
review_text:
I always look forward to a new book by Michael Connelly, whether it’s Harry Bosch or Mickey Haller. Connelly’s latest, The Burning Room, is good but not great. I just thought that this novel was missing something, although I still enjoyed this Harry Bosch novel.

LAPD Detective Harry Bosch is still working on open and unsolved cases. He has a new partner, the young Lucia “Lucky Lucy” Soto. Soto was moved to detective after being the hero of a shootout. The plan is that Bosch will mentor her in his last year with the department. They pull a case that is 21 years old. A Mariachi musician, Orlando Merced, was shot and ended up paralyzed. When he dies years later of sepsis related to this shooting, the case is now ruled a homicide. The original investigators thought Merced was the victim of a random, gang-related shooting. But Bosch and Soto find new evidence that shows otherwise. Soto also takes an interest in a second old, unsolved case—an arson in an apartment building where 9 people died, many of them children. Soto was one of the few children who survived in the basement day care center. The two detectives go back and forth between both cases while receiving lots of pressure from the top as the Merced case has political implications.

I always enjoy Michael Connelly because not only is he a talented writer, but you get a real sense that he knows all aspects of the LAPD—procedures, politics, the press, etc. For instance, police work has changed over the course of Bosch’s career. The LAPD was “becoming a deskbound institution. Keyboards and cell phones were the main tools of the modern investigator. Detectives sat in twelve-hundred-dollar chairs and wore sleek designer shoes with tassels.” As for working a case, “Bosch also liked returning to a crime scene. He called it listening to the scene. There were nuances and small details that could be picked up even years after the crime. Plus there was a sense of ghosts, some sort of presence of those who had been murdered.” As a former police-beat reporter for the Los Angeles Times, Connelly certainly knows about newspapers: “Now the paper [Los Angeles Times] looked like somebody who had been through chemo—thin, unsteady, and knowing the inevitable could only be held off for so long.”
Although there was much to like about The Burning Room, it was lacking something that I can’t quite put my finger on—maybe passion or suspense. But despite this, Connelly is a fine writer and even when he’s not quite on top of his game, his novels are still much better than those of many other authors.

Now that Bosch is nearing retirement, I wonder what will happen to this series. Will Connelly move to build a new series around Lucia Soto? Bosch’s 12th-grade daughter, Maddie, wants to become a cop. Maybe the focus will pass to her. I guess we’ll just have to wait and see.

author: Michael Connelly
review_title: Superb Cold Case Drama with Harry Bosch
review_text:
All of Connelly's novels are good. This one is particularly good.

Working with a new young female partner Harry pursues two unrelated cold cases. The first is that of a musician paralyzed in an apparent drive-by approximately ten years earlier When he dies from complications caused by the bullet that had been lodged in his spine, the case is resurrected as a murder.

The second is a 1992 robbery/murder that had become a legend in L.A. police history.

Both cases are worked simultaneously as Harry mentors his new partner. Both have the usual complement of twists and turns which Connelly develops in his unique way. The books is tightly written with never a dull moment. To say much more could be a spoiler.

If you like the Harry Bosch series, you will love this. Recommend highly.

title: 10-Day Green Smoothie Cleanse
subtitle: Paperback – July 15, 2014
author: J.J. Smith
review_title: WAY too much fruit and not enough protein.....
review_text:
This may work for some people, but not for me. I normally eat a low carb diet of proteins, vegetables, nuts, seeds, with very limited dairy and 2 fruits a day. I usually have a protein smoothie with added greens for breakfast. Getting adequate protein insures that I don't get too hungry and keeps my blood sugar stable.

I was surprised when I saw just how much fruit is in these daily smoothies. Lots of high sugar bananas, grapes, and mangos which I knew I would have to sub out for something else. So, with trepidation I started the program two days ago. It didn't go well. I was STARVING all the time, even adding a scoop of protein powder to the smoothie, eating an egg for a snack and a handful of walnuts. Not only is there just not enough protein to keep you full, but all the fructose in the fruit raised my blood sugar more than normal. I managed to get through two days, but felt like I was gobbling snacks way too much, and desperately craving protein. And by bedtime, I couldn't think about anything but food. Today, after two days of this nonsense, I had GAINED two pounds.

So, if you're young and have no blood sugar issues, then this might work for you. Obviously lots of people have done well on it. For people with blood sugar issues though, too much fruit, especially blended up so it goes straight into your bloodstream, is almost as bad as eating sugar. Combine that with not enough protein and good fat, and you get what I got; extreme hunger and weight gain. I'd like to send the book back, but I dog-eared lots of pages. :( The title is pretty misleading. It should be called 10-Day Fruit-To-Cover-Up-the-Taste-of-Greens.Starvation Smoothie Cleanse.

I had heard nothing but positive things about this product when I was searching customer reviews for people's opinions and experiences. I am sure that this cleanse would have worked if I did not suffer from hypoglycemia, but unfortunately I do. I knew that the cleanse would cause certain side affects such as stomach cramps, irritability, fatigue, and even nausea (I got this info straight from the book). Because I have this deficiency, I was not getting enough sugar. This caused the normal symptoms to escalate exponentially. I was unable to function. The most serious symptom was exhaustion-close to fainting.

The reason I wrote this review was not to criticize or complain about the cleanse, but to inform potential customers of my experience so that others may not have to struggle in the same way.

Pluses: The book is easy to read, well organized, very handy when needing to go back to the grocery list, the recipe, or tips. So far the 1st 5 days recipes don't taste too bad for someone who is already used to drinking healthy smoothies.

Minuses: The recipes should have the calorie count and other important nutrition facts like the sugar content. I find most of the recipes to be very high in sugar. Also, without the calorie count, some people (example: male who requires more calories) would find the recipes not enough to get them through the day without getting very hungry. The book claims that the cleanse will also help you get a good sleep (as most cleanse do) but I had the opposite effect, my mind was just awake most of the night. My hubby had headaches, but this could be also attributed to him not drinking the required amount of water.

Me & my husband did not finish the cleanse, we only did it for 5 days as I was worried about the high sugar. I will probably try doing the cleanse again using this book once I completed the nutritional facts on each recipes and do more research about this type of cleanse.

I do believe in the healing properties of green smoothie. Since doing smoothies, we are less likely to get sick and my hair grows fast!

title: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, Parts 1 & 2, Special Rehearsal Edition Script
subtitle: Hardcover – July 31, 2016
author: J.K. Rowling
review_title: I wanted to like it. I really really did
review_text:
I want to start this by saying that I am a huge Harry Potter fan. I grew up with Harry, I went to midnight premiers of the books and movies. I was so excited for this play. I wanted to like it. I really really did. If you are a fan I would say read it and form your own opinion. Here is what I thought:

- Where was George?
- Where was Teddy? Because he was in the station in th epilogue.
- Where was Hugo? You know the other child Ron and Hermione have.
- Lily and James Potter… MIA for most of the play. Like James? Was he even in it?
- Why was Ron running the joke shop? He is an Auror. WHAT HAPPENED TO GEORGE? WHY WASN’T HE RUNNING THE SHOP?!
- Let’s talk about Ron. Why was he so non-Ron like? His character, all jokes no supporting and listening to Harry and Hermione. Also he is hardly in the play.
- Harry’s relationship with Albus. Everything about this is upsetting.
o In the last book when they are dropping off the children at the Hogwarts express, the kids are genuinely confused as to why everyone is looking at them and Ron makes a joke saying “I’m famous”. It is deduced that the kids do not know the extent of everything their parents went through to save the world. Yet Albus feel the weight of his dad’s legacy. Huh.
o Then we have Harry SEPARATING Albus and Scorpious. Let’s go back to that epilogue where they all see Draco with his family and a joke gets made about not playing with his son. Which then Hermione corrects and Ron says to beat him on test but not to get too cozy and marry him. Again, making it seem that everything in the past is in the past. Then there is Harry’s history of friends at Hogwarts. He knows. He would not separate his son from his ONLY friend.
- Albus choosing Slytherin for a friend? Awesome.
- The rumors of Voldemort having a child and that not being stopped by the ministry? Stupid. The ministry would have stopped panic about an heir being possible. Also Voldemort was conceived without love. He never cared about having an heir because he wanted to be in power. An heir would have been competition for him.
- More on that point. Bellatrix pregnant. She would have loved to mother the Dark Lords child; there would have been no greater honor. But. This does not work with the original time line. Bella is never pregnant, she fights at the battle. And then the gang goes to Malfoy manor there is no baby in sight. And if. IF. Voldemort would have wanted an heir; wouldn’t he have made it a horcrux and offered it more protection?
- Sexual tension between Scorpious and Albus. Yet Albus has a crush on Delphi and Scorpious on Lily. I feel as though either they should have been opened about their romantic feels towards each other or this should have not been included.
- The flashbacks/dreams Harry has. When Dudley is mentioned (yay!) and you find out petunia is dead. I know she was horrible but I do think Harry would have deep feelings about his mother’s sister passing. I liked the blanket part.
- Bellatrix husband somehow got out of Azkaban and raised Delphi. How did he escape Azkaban? Because there is no way he got pardoned. So how did he escape? And after escaping how was there no alarm over him escaping. Sirius Black escapes and the freaking muggle minister is alerted! Then there is a massive breakout and it is all over the daily prophet. But hey, this guy who tortured the Longbottoms into insanity he escapes and it’s cool. Yeah, sounds legit.
- The new prophecy. First of all: how did it happen with no one knowing about it except Delphi. Who made it? It’s sounding more and more as if this witch convinced herself that she is the heir of the dark lord.
- Cedric. Cedric a character who was noble and good and died oh so tragically. This character who was loyal and kind and helped Harry turns DARK SIDE?!?! BECAUSE HE LOSES THE CUP. WHAT?!?! CEDRIC A DEAD EATER HAHAHAHA NOPE NOT FUNNY. Thank you for turning a good character and completely changing him for the worse. Thank goodness you did not include Sirius Black in your play.
- On that same characters changing note. The trolley lady…. Hm. I will just leave it at that.
- Polyjuice potion. That s*** takes a month to make. I read the chamber of secrets. Many times. It takes an effing month. And you need a piece of the person you are changing into. But wait not, here I got some polyjuice potion here in my back pocket and I just happen to carry my dad and his best friends hairs at all times. So let’s change into them and break into the ministry.
- Btw that potion is not necessary because you can transfigure a HUMAN. Seven books and that never came out. Must be very dark magic.
- On the dark magic note. Harry duels Delphi (a eighteen year old) and she is stronger? Um. Do we not recall Harry being a teenager and he beat Voldemort. His wand is the s***. So yeah how does this even make sense?
- The no sugar diet. WHAT. Sounds like something movie Ginny would do, not book Ginny.

author: J.K. Rowling
review_title: Killing the goose that lays the golden eggs: Not true Potterverse and NOT AT ALL true JKR writing
review_text:
Reads badly like a story in a monthly magazine written for subscribers. I feel they disrespected the Potter fans worldwide and am returning this book pronto.
Found glaring plotholes(IMO) and like another reviewer said, the characters do not stay true to their own values from the original series.
Really bad fanfic! Not at all worth the hype and the fact that there is a "Definitive script" also being released later at some point shows that the publishers and whoever else is making even a single penny off this book have published it for the money.
Should not say this is the "Eighth story, 19 years later" and tarnish the memories and expectations of the readers. Especially when JKR keeps blowing her trumpet saying that her Potter writing is done fully and finally, but still keeps churning content regularly!
Personally, I would like to say to JKR that she should have waited to publish this work and ironed out all the discrepancies and issues first instead of what seems to be a very rushed and improperly vetted publication.
Not even worth 10$ and they are selling it for 18$ on Amazon to make that fast buck before everyone catches onto the absolute rubbish that this book is.
I don't mind it being a play OR a script but even as either it seems terrible with magical beings making muggle references in dialogue amongst other terrible nuisances this book creates.
JKR, it's OK to not put out more HP stuff, we can live with what's already out there but please don't ruin it for everyone by giving your blessing to such ditchwater writing. Sorry John Tiffany and Jack Throne, maybe your own creative characters would have had more justice done than for you both to have used the names of the favourites of millions worldwide and disappointing them such.

author: J.K. Rowling
review_title: Tremendous disappointment,  None of the characters are recognizable.
review_text: There are multiple problems with this work, including an improbable, convoluted plot.  But the worst parts of this script are the utterly unrecognizable characters.  This is absolutely unforgiveable and leaves me baffled.  Who are these people?  How did this get so screwed up?  Since when is Draco Malfoy a source of wisdom and advice to Harry Potter?  Why change Snape into a weird buddy-buddy defender instead of the delghtfully unpleasant character who is heroic despite himself? Yes, Scorpius is genuinely attractive as a person, and that is fine.  But does any of this REALLY feel like the orignal series?  Or honestly, isn't this like Imposter Harry Potter - and a transparent fail?  My advice is, skip this.  Don't pay a dime for this.  Borrow it from the library if you must, but please do not spend your hard-earned money.  This book is a tremendous disappointment.

subtitle: Hardcover – July 31, 2016
author: J.K. Rowling
review_title: Like bad fan fiction - so disappointed
review_text: I am a huge fan of the Harry Potter series and was so excited for the Cursed Child to arrive.  Having just finished it, I'm extremely disappointed.  I knew it was written as a play, so it's not the format that's the problem - it's the story.  It reads like bad fan fiction -  all the magic of the original series is gone.  Harry, Ron, Hermione and many of the original characters appear, but are sad, flat versions of themselves.  Albus Potter, as the protagonist, is completely unsympathetic and his motives, which drive the plot, never seem justified.  The storyline is not compelling, just depressing.  And there are serious flaws in the plot which render it all ridiculous....SPOILER ALERT: Bellatrix Lestrange secretly gives birth to Voldemort's child just before the Battle of Hogwarts?!? For that to be true, she would have been obviously pregnant in several scenes in Book 7.  How would no one have noticed that?!?!?  Also, Polyjuice potion cannot be brewed in a day. And how, if the Potters' house is protected by the Fidelius charm, did they find the Potters and steal the blanket???  Perhaps with the spectacle of a theater production, this story might be more engaging on stage, but in my view, the Cursed Child is an unnecessary and unworthy addition to the Harry Potter canon.

Another nice example of how it is important to stop and leave at a right moment. Unfortunately this story brings almost nothing to the HP Universe. At the same time it alters the magical laws and provides even more questions than we had before. And the characters are not saving the situation this time. If you still remember them from the books then I would advise you to forget them. Almost all of them are out of character. If you are hoping to find good dialogs here, I guess, you would probably be disappointed as well. Most of them are pointless, some of them are full of pathos. Well, there are some nice jokes and lines. But they are lost in the whole mess.
In conclusion, this play looks like a very bad fanfiction. I personally would never consider it as the 8 HP story.

review_text:
Hi, yes, if you love Harry Potter and wish to keep the same image of it in your head, do not read this. My world has been tainted by the knowledge of this complete and utter fan fiction filth. Now that I know the things I know I can no longer look at certain characters the same way ever again.
My world was shattered. I'm not kidding. I was so happy to buy this and read it, but I literally threw it across the room when I was done.
My heart was broken because the books were my Hogwarts and Hogwarts was BURNT TO THE GROUND. MY HOGWARTS IS GONE. ITS FOREVER TAINTED AND HARRY IS NEVER GOING TO BE THE SAME FOR ME AGAIN.
I've tried pretending. I told myself "it's not real, I doubt this is cannon...." but it's cannon. Everything that happens in this book is cannon and goes along with the original books.
So, don't buy it. Stay naive. Save your Hogwarts, keep the HARRY Potter in your mind the way it was meant to be.

Don't waste your money.

title: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, Parts 1 & 2, Special Rehearsal Edition Script
subtitle: Hardcover – July 31, 2016
author: J.K. Rowling
review_text:
What this reads like to me is a rough outline of what should have been a whole new series of Harry Potter novels - which Mrs. Rowling couldn't be bothered to actually write, so she handed the draft off to a couple of theater guys, who crammed 4 or 5 books into 1 and called it a 'play'.
The tensions between Harry and his son alone would have made an excellent novel 8 in the series, before we even get back to Hogwarts.
Things like character development, layering of plot lines and the building of interest are lost arts in literature (and even more so in movies and TV !), but Mrs. Rowling is quite capable, her other books are proof of that.
Not sure why she took the VERY easy way out on this one.
Many of the characters are basically caricatures of their original selves, the plot has more holes than thinly sliced Swiss cheese, the whole thing's kind of a mess.
It's ok if you look at it as a potential theater production, which has to be shortshort by necessity - can't keep the audience in the theater for 3 weeks - but it should come with a neon pink warning label : THIS IS FAN FICTION, NOT J.K. ROWLING !

It reads like fan fiction written by a teenager. We've waited 9 years for another HP story. I'm happy for any chance to get back into that world. But this could have been done so much better. It's kind of like really wanting chocolate cake for your birthday, and getting vanilla instead. It's better than nothing. You'd try to be happy. Yet you'd be thinking "really? That's the best you can do? I wanted something better."

title: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, Parts 1 & 2, Special Rehearsal Edition Script

author: J.K. Rowling
review_text:
If you're on here, debating whether or not to buy the book, and using reviews to help you STOP NOW.

First, let's be clear: this is a script, not a book. I've read play scripts before so I wasn't too worried about the format, but for some reason this seemed pretty jumpy.

I think a lot of my issues come with the writing. I felt the characters that we potter-heads knew and loved were somehow changed into characters we'd never met before. I realize that this story focuses less on our beloved characters and more on their offspring. Unfortunately, even these new characters seemed one dimensional and undeveloped.

The plot was... Meh, somewhat predictable.

Overall I was just disappointed. If anything, this makes me want to re-read the actual series again.

title: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, Parts 1 & 2, Special Rehearsal Edition Script
subtitle: Hardcover – July 31, 2016
author: J.K. Rowling
review_text: Disappointed. Story focuses on the characters' flaws, not strengths. (In the other books, the characters are real and flawed, yes, but their strengths are the focus, making us love them so much as they overcome their problems.) I didn't think I'd mind the script format, but it's super sparse with very little to guide you. Found it hard to picture the setting or hear the character's tone of voice. Part of the pleasure in reading are the way words come together to paint a picture, and this lacks that completely. Just step-by-step dialogue. But mostly, I was disappointed in the story itself, which spends a lot of time showing the characters' flaws and not enough time making us love them. Even the old characters I already know and love so much came across as surprisingly unlikable.

title: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, Parts 1 & 2, Special Rehearsal Edition Script
subtitle: Hardcover – July 31, 2016
author: J.K. Rowling
review_text:
If the books of Harry Potter are the ocean, deep with meaning and story, etc. this playwright, is like jet skiing, just skimming the surface (such is the form by it's very nature). Second, as stated on the cover "based on an original new story by J.K Rowling," the play is actually by Jack Thorne, and you can tell, **especially** after Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them came out. The magic in her work is just not there in "The Cursed Child." When reading this, I really got a taste of fan service; dynamics... characters... scenes... so much of the story felt just so hackneyed. On the other hand, other scenes and major characters seemed to behave in non-canonical ways, which is just disappointing.

I will say, this probably was still cute on stage. Cheesy, but probably far more entertaining than reading. So, perhaps I'm judging too harshly on reading a text that was meant to be performed and not read.

If you're debating on whether or not you should buy this book, I'll pose the question to you that I did to my mother when she asked if she ought to read it: Do you want this book for this collection, to further prove you are a Harry Potter nerd, like myself? Will you feel the story isn't complete unless you pick it up? If yes, you probably have it already, or will buy it regardless of what reviews say.
On the other hand, if quality is a standard of yours, and you don't want your final impression of the Harry Potter saga to be on a sour, or at the very least flat, note. You might want to pass. Best of luck! ~Mischief Managed.

title: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, Parts 1 & 2, Special Rehearsal Edition Script
subtitle: Hardcover – July 31, 2016
author: J.K. Rowling
review_text:
There's a stage direction where Ron is doing a magic trick that I think accurately sums up this play:

"His hand is empty. It's a lame trick. Everyone enjoys its lameness."

In the same way Trump just isn't presidential, "Harry Potter and the Cursed Child" just isn't Harry Potter. I wish JK Rowling had written this instead of Jack Thorne. Maybe Jack Thorne is a genius of a playwright, but he does not treat the wizarding world like a serious play-world. The dialogue lacks wit, the plot lacks coherence, and the characters lack complexity. Also, the magic. It's gone. All the little moments where we fell in love with this world.

I wish so badly Rowling had written this (or another prequel) in a novel form. JK Rowling is a visual mastermind: she tells stories with the cinematic flare and caricature of Dickens--creating scenes that are seeable, but also profoundly true to human behavior. She builds mysterious plots and empathetic communities in our minds so that "Harry Potter & the Deathly Hallows" felt more like a movie in my mind than a binding of pages. It felt real, and here for me. I miss reading her.

Honestly, I am way more excited about the script of "Fantastical Beasts and Where to Find Them" that will be released in November. Possibly even more than the film. Not because it's another Harry Potter addition, but because it'll be written BY JK ROWLING.

I love Harry Potter. But what I love even more is JK Rowling's way of writing Harry Potter. Her way of making reading such a rich & immersive activity. November, hurry up!

author: J.K. Rowling
review_title: this felt like I was revisiting a badly written version of earlier ...
review_text: I am a big fan of all of HP novels and have been reading the books since I was 11 years old. Unfortunately, this felt like I was revisiting a badly written version of earlier books. I was expecting a play that gave me more of an insight on Harry's life, his work at the Ministry, his new role as a husband and father, other magical worlds, etc. The first thing that annoyed me in the scene descriptions was the phrase "this is magic. this is chaos", which seemed like a condescending gesture toward the reader and which in hindsight actually seem to excuse the unimaginative plot.The time-turner is grossly overused and seems like a cheap plot device. I might have as well watched Back to the Future again . The simultaneous use of two time-turners was even more ludicrous. (So on one time turner they had only 5 minutes to change the past and on another they had more minutes--wouldn't this have had some kind of effect?---otherwise why point out the difference between time-turners... It really seemed like the characters spent hours awkwardly waiting for Voldemort at Godrick's Hollow) The story lacked verisimilitude. Many characters (Rose, Delphi, Ron, Hermione), were left undeveloped. Delphi's intervention at the end seemed forced. She did not play that much of a leading role at the beginning when they were trying to bring Cedric back then she suddenly appears at the end, only after receiving an Owl from Albus. If she really was planning to bring back Voldemort she would have intervened earlier. Finally, the idea that Voldemort and Bella had sex in some room of Malfoy's Manor was laughable and implausible, given Rowling's characterization of Voldemort.

title: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, Parts 1 & 2, Special Rehearsal Edition Script
subtitle: Hardcover – July 31, 2016
author: J.K. Rowling
review_text:
I bought this book locally on sale. If I could have, I'd have given it a 2½ because I'm swinging between it being just bare okay and being disappointed in it. Harry seems like a different character than in the original series. Actually, all of them are significantly changed to the point that they are hard to recognize ( just dropped the rating back to 2). I can't see Harry relating to his son the way he does in this play. Voldemort has a daughter? Come on. Overall it feels like a not quite as bad Highlander II movie that was so far removed from the first movie that it was a whole other story. The beginning is so choppy it reminds me of Ralph Bakshi's attempt toe retell the entire 3 volumes of LOTR in a single 133 minute animated film. I would hate to be the director who had to make sense of the sudden and chaotic shifts between scenes of the early first act without a narrator announcing them so that the audience could follow what each was. The plot line borrows heavily from other stories like Back to the Future, the main character(s) go back in time and mess things up, then have to go back again to straighten things out, etc. It is disappointing.
Addendum: I confess that I wrote the above after reading only Parts 1-3 and I was debating whether to finish reading the book/play. I did finish. It did not change my opinion. I agree with those who object to the alterations of the characters and plot of the original books, especially the alteration of Ron. He was not the jokester in the novels, that was Fred and George, nor did he come off as someone who would be so drunk at his wedding that he wouldn't remember it. Ron was a sober character in the novels, quite the opposite of the way he is portrayed in this play. I feel that the characters of Harry and Hermione have been diminished badly also. Upon reading part 4, I was particularly struck by Harry telling Albus that because he didn't have a father as an example, he didn't know how to be a father. I was in that same boat with my children and I can say with certainty that any man as brave and loyal as Harry was portrayed in the novels and as sensitive would never tell his child "I wish you weren't my child". Growing up without a father present makes one acutely aware of the need to be a good parent even if one fumbles with how to do that and saying something that hurtful to a child would not happen.
Finally, I turn to the flaws of logic (yes, I know it is a magical world). Harry's scar hurt because it connected him to Voldemort via the piece of Voldemort that was in him making him the last Horcrux. When Harry died and returned he no longer was connected in that way to Voldemort. That is why he was able to kill Voldemort. As long as that was in him, Voldemort could not die. But there was nothing about the scar that connected Harry to Voldemort's daughter and Voldemort was dead, thus no reason for the scar to hurt. Lastly, it was impossible for Albus to bring Voldemort back in the way described, i.e. by causing Cedric Diggory to turn to a Death Eater, followed by Voldemort's victory and the death of Harry so that Albus was never born. If Albus wasn't born he could not have gone back in time to interfere in the Tri-Wizard Tournament. Without that interference, the outcome of the Tournament would not have been changed nor would all that this story alleges followed. It is an impossible chain of events. The person causing the change is not born, therefore it can't happen.
A story about a child born to the famous Harry Potter being troubled by living in the shadow of his father is ripe with possibilities but this tale does not live up to those possibilities IMO.

title: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, Parts 1 & 2, Special Rehearsal Edition Script
subtitle: Hardcover – July 31, 2016
author: J.K. Rowling
review_title: Don't Make This Your First Impression of Harry Potter!
review_text:
I have a few things I really didn't like about this script and I will try not to spoil anything for those who have not yet read it.

My biggest negative after reading this as a Harry Potter fan was that the dialogue of the returning Harry Potter characters (Harry, Hermoine, Ron, etc.) felt very unnatural to the characters from the original series. I understand that Harry is now in his late 30s, early 40s in this play but there were times when I was reading his lines, and other returning characters' lines, where it just felt like that isn't something that character would say. There was also some dialogue that was really "cheesy" and felt like the writer was trying to force a laugh which made the line seem unnatural.

It is also missing the descriptive quality that made the original series so good, I understand it's a play and that quality would be lacking a bit but it was almost entirely absent in the scene descriptions.

The story line was pretty predictable (even the "twist" at the end was predictable) and was used much more effectively in other movies that had used it before.

I hope this review helps and I didn't spoil anything. I think any Harry Potter fan will check this out regardless of the reviews, as I did. But, if you're new to the Harry Potter series please read the original series and don't make this your first impression of Harry Potter.
