title: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, Parts 1 & 2, Special Rehearsal Edition Script
subtitle: Hardcover – July 31, 2016
author: J.K. Rowling
review_title: A Nostalgic trip back to Hogwarts
review_text:
The 8th installment in the Potterverse – “Harry Potter and the Cursed Child” joins the Hogwarts alumni nineteen years after the close of “Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows” and is truly a nostalgic romp through the previous seven books. Revisiting familiar places, people and events the Cursed Child is a nice catching up with old friend and also some perceived enemies. Harry, now grown with three kids of his own sends his second son Albus off to Hogwarts. Who he meets there, the friends he makes and the things he gets up to well… you’ll have to read the book if you want to know because I will not give away anything here.

Written as an Official Script book for the play, this definitely reads slightly differently than the previous installments. After taking a few pages/scenes to familiarize myself with the formatting I think I actually preferred this format for the purpose of this story, it worked very nicely. The scenes are sketched in basic format and it is left to the reader to fill in the blanks… as grand or minimal as you like. Clocking in an a little over 300 pages, I’m fairly certain that if this were a traditional novel we would have been looking at closer to 500 pages.

After reading “Cursed Child”, I find myself nostalgic for the Wizarding World and would love to see more installments of the grown up Hogwarts alum and the new generation of wizards. As far as if that will become a reality, I guess only Professor Treylawney knows for sure; but I would definitely be game for seeing the stage production if it ever makes it stateside.

subtitle: Hardcover – July 31, 2016
author: J.K. Rowling
review_title: as a huge theatre geek I actually quite liked the script format
review_text:
I'm giving this script four stars. I will be honest, I didn't want to set my expectations too high (despite waiting in line and attending a pre-lease party to grab the hardcover at midnight), so I did not reread the series this summer as I normally do, as readers should understand although Rowling is given some credit I give most credit to the other two, especially due to the format and style.

POSSIBLE SPOILERS, READ AT OWN RISK
Pros:
1. Personally, as a huge theatre geek I actually quite liked the script format, adding to why I rated this so high. Yes, I miss J.K. Rowling's writing and would prefer her for Harry rather than this, but I got used to the format. People must understand THIS WAS WRITTEN AS A PLAY and not a book, and that the printing of this just gave opportunity to muggles, witches, and wizards alike who don't have the chance to apparate, use floo powder, or fly (on brooms and planes alike) to see the show in London. Unfortunately, I do admit that because of the script format, it is also difficult to really immerse the reader into the setting.
2. IT'S FREAKING HARRY POTTER. It was nice to see the old crew again. This book/script gave me the chance to fully be apart of and understand what it is like to wait in line, be part of crazy big crowds donned in costumes, and quickly read as soon as released. Plus, another story is another chance to read, well, another story based on a world so many have come to love.
3. Hermione as Minister for Magic. Yessss. Seeing her as a mean teacher was interesting too. Oh, and Ginny rocked as the voice of reason.
4. Scorpius! Love him. Also liked Draco and relationship with his son, and both their relationships with Astoria.
5. I liked how every little small thing the boys changed in time impacted the present.
6. Alternate worlds were interesting.
7. Giving props to old characters, little details that nodded to the series.
8. Harry and Albus, not so much their characters or shouting that they wish they didn't have each other as a father/son, but some of the raw relationship, such as being honest that the reason they don't understand one another isn't just because Albus is put into Slytherin.
Cons:
1. This story seemed more like fanfic.
2. The children besides Albus and Scorpius are introduced and then forgotten (besides Rose being savage). And I reallyyyy wished that there would be a main child/character who was in Ravenclaw or Hufflepuff, not just Gryffindor (Surprise! All kids except Albus from the main three are Gryffindor. No hate, I love all you guys, just babbling my opinions; it makes sense because of her their parents, but doesn't hurt to wonder).
3. Cedric becoming a deatheater because of his humiliation? Two best friends wanting to save him despite thinking about the consequences of messing with time? Oh boy.
4. What happened to our beloved characters? And the new ones? I understand that the format limits the description, but the dialogue sometimes... Ron as a comedic relief seemed to provide nothing to the story, make his character a bit corny, and his want of public affection with Hermione (not to mention Albus kissing his aunt because of this)? I don't know. Additionally, Albus seemed like a "poor-me" kid, Delphi seemed forced, etc ... Maybe it is just me ¯\_(ツ)_/¯
5. The whole freakout with Harry: "I'm going to protect myself even if it means taking his only happiness, his friend Scorpius, because there is a black cloud over him. Also I am now threatening my previous professor-now-headmaster into watching his every move because she can't be busy with anything else." I know it was a different world, and it was interesting; Harry doing anything for his son is believable, but I just couldn't settle on thinking Harry would go so far as to be so manipulative and threatening to his friends in a selfish (even though it was for his son) way.
6. Harry acting as/transfiguring into Voldemort. I don't think this was necessarily bad, I just don't know how to feel about it. I don't know how I feel about warrior Hermione or the fact that kids were able to get the time-turner from her office either (come on Hermione, you're smarter than that).
7. I feel there was this opportunity to show how the wizard world has changed since when the trio were students, and it wasn't used.

Okay, this is getting too long... phew. Thank you for reading, I hope my review didn't seem too whiny or dramatic! Overall, I think it is worth a read. I'll just leave it with this quote:
ROSE: The rumor is that [Scorpius] is Voldemort’s son, Albus.
It’s probably rubbish. I mean… look, you’ve got a nose.
– Act One, Scene Three

title: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, Parts 1 & 2, Special Rehearsal Edition Script
subtitle: Hardcover – July 31, 2016
author: J.K. Rowling
review_text:
Expectations are dangerous things, and realize this is a play, not a full blown book. It's also a play of a series that's been done and finished for many years now, movies and everything, even if the world itself hasn't quite died with Rowlings great charity books and new Magical Beasts movies.

Still, this story is good. It fits Harry Potter, and is fun to read. There's just under 300 pages of actual story and because it's written as a play there's little to know description for any of the characters or settings as you're expected to know what they look like already, and the read is extremely fast. There's enough twists and turns to make this a great page turner and I'm happy to add it as the 8th story to my Harry Potter shelf.

If I had any complaints, it's that the story definitely feels written by a guy who doesn't really know the world or characters well enough and whose name I'll never see anywhere but on this book. A lot of the story uses repeated events to get itself going rather than inventing anything new, and sticks with replaying events already written by the master JK Rowling. As a result it is a rehashing story, but it's done well enough that I'll excuse most of it to call it a great play-book. The ending is also completely tied in an extremely tight package that one would expect from any "they lived happily ever after" story, rather than the world-changing events that happened at the end of the 7th book. While this isn't a problem for fantasy tales, I still feel it would have been better had something meaningful been added at the end instead of the two heroes looking out over the sunset. Then again, it isn't my story, and my expectations are always going to be greater than what's delivered.

title: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, Parts 1 & 2, Special Rehearsal Edition Script
subtitle: Hardcover – July 31, 2016
author: J.K. Rowling
review_title: Not the Novels, but Still Fun for HP Fans
review_text:
4/4.5 stars.

I had very mixed feelings about how to review this. I'm a huge HP fan, and so reading this was of course super-exciting for me, and I did really enjoy it. At the same time, it was clear to me that reading a play script is not the same as reading one of the novels. I've heard great things about the play and by reading the script it sounded amazing; however, the script in and of itself, while interesting, was a less fabulous experience than reading the books.

Of particular interest to me as a writer was the fact that the script, by leaving out (as scripts do) all the "slow" stuff that fills up novels, was a less rewarding reading experience. Scripts by their nature can't have any internal monologue or reflection: everything has to be said out loud, or portrayed by the actors' physical movements on stage/screen. Scripts also have very minimal descriptions of settings and background, and the action is by necessity compressed. The result is something very spare--I finished the entire thing in a couple of hours--that is more like a sketch than a book. It's a book in which the author has taken the common command these days to "tighten up your writing" and "cut filler" to its maximum possible expression, and the result is something that is not really a book. All the empty space on the page between is just...empty space on the page, lacking the depth that the novelistic form provides. Which is not to say that this is bad, per se, it just highlighted for me the unique benefits of the novel, which allows for a depth and introspection that other forms do not.

All that being said, Harry Potter fans like me are probably going to enjoy this. Aside from the genre differences, reading it was more like a cruise through a greatest hits album with the occasional original track thrown in than a fully-fledged new book, but a lot of the old magic is still there.

title: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, Parts 1 & 2, Special Rehearsal Edition Script
subtitle: Hardcover – July 31, 2016
author: J.K. Rowling
review_title: A fun read for Harry Potter lovers
review_text:
I had heard a lot of mixed reviews about this book and quite a few spoilers that planted my feet firmly on the "I'm never going to read that book" side of things. Someone even told me that the Weasley's were the villains in this book! For all those reading this review and have heard the same thing, let me put your mind at ease. That's absolutely not true. But that's all I'm going to say as far as plot and whatnot go because I don't want to give any spoilers. I'm not going to be one of those people.

I will say that, because this is written as a play, it takes a quick minute to get the hang of how to read it. It was slow going at first because I kept skipping over the name of the person who is saying the line and then thoroughly confusing myself. Tip #1: read the name of the person who is saying the line. It's important. Eventually you get a handle on it and then it's like reading any other book.

Well, except that pretty much all the descriptions are missing from this book. Because it is a play, you don't get a lot of details about the setting or what people look like or what they are thinking, which I really missed. But I ended up really enjoying the book! Despite the spoilers, I finished the book more pleased than I was expecting to be. But, I mean, my expectations were really low so take that as you will.

It's a quick read, it's a fun read, especially for any fellow Potterheads. It's worth the afternoon, if nothing but to revisit some of the magic of Hogwarts and the Wizarding World that we've been missing.

review_title: No excuse for this level of writing and editing
review_text: I'd been introduced to Michael Connelly's Bosch novels a few months ago with one of the first books, and I was so impressed  to find a detective story that was also truly well written, page after page showing craft and care in the construction of each sentence and paragraph. Soon after I decided to read The Wrong Side of Goodbye ahead of the planned Bosch sequel tv series, and was astounded at the difference. This book reads like a badly edited early draft. Really Page One newbie writing moves--this isnot a direct quotation, but along the lines of, "She raised her eyebrows in a sarcastic gesture that he knew from way back meant she didn't believe him." And this kind of thing happens over and over, almost as if Connelly has taken, "Tell, Don't Show" as his motto--but to my mind, he settled on a too-early draft that could have this kind of thing cleaned up in no time. The plot deficiencies won't harm the new series, I don't think, but no writer who was ever worth his salt should be satisfied getting away with this kind of sloppiness.

review_text:
I cannot recommend this book. I am a loyal fan of Mr Connelly, and have read all his books. I cannot believe he published this.
The book drags on for 250 pages of torturously detailed, boring descriptions of - nothing - following Harry Bosch around, describing every minute of his pedantic search for an old man's heir.
No crimes. No action.

When something does happen, it is covered superficially and dispensed with quickly, returning us back to the original boring plot. Connelly brings Mickey Haller into the story, a character from other Connelly books (The Lincoln Lawyer is one of my favorites), and reduces him to a two dimensional paper cut-out version of a wonderfully complex and interesting character.

I feel we fans have been ripped off. We will buy anything Connelly writes, and he took advantage of that with this pot-boiler.

title: The Wrong Side of Goodbye (A Harry Bosch Novel Book 19)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Michael Connelly
review_text:
I like Michael Connelly. But I don't like LA. And as a rule, I don't much like LA cops. But it's not that simple. In both cases, it's more of a love/hate relationship, with the hate portion edging out the love part. Somehow, Connelly manages to infuse his stories with this mix of emotions. My suspicion is that he doesn't do this by design. It's just part of who he is.

There's that. And then there's the fact that taken as a whole Connelly's novels are much better than if they are considered one at a time. He's never written a really great novel, but his body of work verges on greatness--a rarity among authors.

So usually I am inclined to cut him a lot more slack, than I am willing to grant with this novel.

In The Wrong Side of Goodby almost all the background that concerns the US Marine Corps in Vietnam, and most especially helicopter and Force Recon operations, is simply wrong.

I don't want to belabor this fact because: 1. This is not a book about Marines in Vietnam. And 2. Almost no one knows enough about the Vietnam War to worry about getting the facts correct. In fact, there are so few people with my level of knowledge about that war that, statistically, I don't even exist.

Still . . . It rankles. If I can't trust what he says about Marines and Navy Corpsmen, then how can I trust anything else that he says? Simple answer: once again, when it comes to Connelly, it's not that simple. In this novel, I trust him less than I don't trust him. But I still trust him.

I was a Marine helicopter gunner and crew chief in Vietnam. The better part of two tours. We didn't fly "slicks." Slicks were Hueys with only a crew chief and gunner. The Army had slicks. When I was there, the only Hueys that the Marine Corps had were "guns." They had mini-guns and rocket pods. Their primary function was to shoot people and things, not to transport people and things. To transport troops we had UH-34, UH-46, and CH-53 helicopters. The 34s were Korean War vintage, and had a bulbous front nose that housed a reciprocating engine. The 46 was a tandem-rotor helicopter that was much more powerful, and could thus carry a lot more a lot faster than the 34. The 53 came along toward the end of the War. It is a very large, very powerful helicopter that, in Laos, could carry more than 35 Hmong troopers. Versions of it are still flown by the USMC today.

(An aside: El Toro Marine Corps Air Station was fixed wing. Santa Ana--the old, giant dirigible hangars--was helicopters.)

All of these helicopters were crewed by a pilot and a copilot, a gunner and a crew chief. Basically, the plane belonged to the crew chief. When it was on the ground, he had control. He was responsible to maintain it. The gunner was there to help kick cargo, to shoot from the other side of the aircraft, and in general to do whatever the crew chief told him to do. An added benefit of the gunner was that he was usually not a mechanic. He was trained in a maintenance field other than mechanical--avionics, electrical, hydraulics, etc. This meant that if the plane developed any problems, his knowledge could easily be the difference between getting it back in the air or putting it down somewhere and waiting for a technician to be flown in to repair it. The gunner probably flew missions no more than one or two months total in a 13-month tour. Which was plenty of time to see a lot of action, and to acquire a raft of air medals.

Force Recon insertions and extractions were nearly always exciting, even if no gunfire was involved. Extractions often involved some of the most dangerous missions of the War. This was because Recon had a habit of calling for an extraction only as a last resort. A hot LZ was a given. The last plane out was often overloaded to a dangerous degree--but since it was the last plane out, and anyone left behind was not going to survive . . . Well, you get the idea.

I cannot recall a Navy Corpsman being with a recon team. Maybe later in the war. All the combat corpsmen I knew were with large units, mostly grunt units. We had a single corpsman for our entire squadron. There were only so many to go around. The attrition rate was right up there with radiomen and 2nd Lieutenants. To this day, if I have a chance, and if he will let me, I will not allow a former combat corpsman to buy a drink, a meal, or even gas for his car or truck.

None of that comes through in Connelly's treatment of a character who was a Navy combat corpsman.

To put it in writing terms: the Navy corpsman should have stolen every scene he was in, and even a few in which he was only talked about. He didn't. He couldn't. Connelly didn't know him well enough.

It would have been a much harder novel to write, but if the author had gotten that character right, it could easily have been the difference between a mediocre novel and a good novel--maybe even a great novel. As a Navy combat corpsman, the character should have reverberated through the entire novel.

Semper Fi does not apply to only Marines and Navy combat corpsmen, Mr. Connelly. It also applies to authors.

title: The Wrong Side of Goodbye (A Harry Bosch Novel Book 19)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Michael Connelly
review_title: Back with Bosch in The Wrong Side Of Goodbye: A Bosch Novel by Michael Connelly
review_text:
While he has spent most of the last year suing the LAPD over his forced retirement, these days Harry Bosch is a private detective when he isn’t working as a reserve officer for the San Fernando PD. Bosch works for free as the small department does not have the funds to pay him. For Bosch it is a chance to wear the badge and work any of the city’s many unsolved cases. One of the cases Bosch is working on is the serial rapist case as the “Screen Cutter.” That case is the prominent secondary storyline of The Wrong Side Of Goodbye.

Bosch got the job at SFPD because of his old LAPD contacts. He gets his private detective jobs by way of referrals. Sometimes those referrals happen by the way of his former colleagues. While he might be an enemy of some in LAPD who are angry over the lawsuit there are plenty of others folks very aware that nobody is a better detective then Bosch on a case.

That ability and those contacts lead him to a meeting with the 85-year-old reclusive billionaire Whitney Vance. Creator and owner of Advance Engineering, Whitney Vance expanded the family legacy considerably from a modest start dating back during the California gold rush. Whitney also believes he may have expanded the family legacy another way-- by fathering a child.

While in film school at USC in 1949, he met someone. Hispanic and underage, she was not somebody that the family would appreciate. They had a brief relationship and she became pregnant. After Whitney told his father, who was convinced that the young woman was looking to become a married citizen, certain people talked to her about not having the child. She then vanished and Whitney has no idea what happened to her or the baby.

Whitney’s independence was now over as his father had leverage on him to make him conform. She was under age so there was that potential legal issue as well as the family embarrassment if the story cane out and was public. He did as he was told and left film school and transferred to Cal Tech. Eventually graduating and further expanding the family legacy.

All these years later, he can tell Bosch little at this point other than her name, Vibiana Duarte, and that she used to work at the student cafeteria known as “Everybody’s Kitchen.” Those facts and a couple of others give Bosch enough to go on. That hunt for the heir becomes the prominent storyline of The Wrong Side Of Goodbye.

This latest book in the Bosch series is far more straightforward than earlier books in the series. Bosch divides his time between both cases, with occasional side excursions to see or call his daughter, as the pages fly by. There is zero character development for anyone in the novel as Bosch and his family were fleshed out long ago. Even characters new to readers are barely more than cardboard cutouts and interchangeable as spare parts. Instead, it is about the hunt for a rapist and the heir.

It wouldn’t be a Bosch novel without a bit of workplace friction. That function is served here by having Bosch work in the San Fernando PD under a boss that has a bit of a bureaucratic bent. It isn’t surprising that Bosch flaunts a rule that he sees as petty only to have it become an issue for another character. The reader that pays attention to detail will see the setup for this coming a mile away.

Overall, the latest Bosch novel is a good one. Though it lacks the complexity of some of the earlier novels and a couple of the twists are a bit obvious, The Wrong Side Of Goodbye is a good read. The only real problem is that this read is nowhere near the high bar this author consistently set for most of this very entertaining series. Good on its own, The Wrong Side Of Goodbye, does not come close to the books earlier in the series.

Material supplied by the good folks of the Plano Public Library System.

Kevin R. Tipple ©2017

review_text: Trying to read these in order and so far, I'm impressed with the plot within plot style - not so convoluted that you lose the thread - just right.  Good characters. title: Laugh-Out-Loud Jokes for Kids
subtitle: Paperback – August 1, 2010
author: Rob Elliott
review_title: Too few rimshots for most readers to find the "humor," but it might some use.
review_text:
This book, like many similar "joke" books, takes the position that a play on words is funny. The reverse may be true - something funny may also be a play on words, but correlation is not causation here or anywhere else. A play on words is not automatically funny. Often it's just annoying. So this awkward collection may remind you of certain sitcoms that supplant their writing with heavy applications of the laugh track, lacking anything so rare these days as true wit. Yes, even a stopped clock is right twice a day, and this collection may hit a good one now and then, but this joke book is seriously flawed.

I will grant the parents and grandparents one thing - if it gets a poor reader to read, even at the risk of damaging his appreciation for true humor, maybe it's still worthwhile. You need the attention span of a flea to read a joke, and a flea's intelligence to understand these, so maybe it will draw kids into reading as a stepping stone toward better, hopefully much better, stuff.

author: Gill Paul
review_text:
One and half stars. This book is not what the blurb made me believe it was. I wouldn't call this historical fiction because there isn't really any true history in it. There are facts that are true here and there but that's about it. I believe for a book to be considered historical fiction it has to have a strong historical background running through it based on true historical facts. You should be able to learn from it. This book teaches nothing about Russian history.

I found it a really difficult read. I couldn't find much to like about any of the characters. That's a sad statement when you consider the fate of the Romanov family. I couldn't like Kitty either because she has no backbone and seemed to blame others for her situation and lack of knowledge of her ancestors. I know everything possible about my ancestors because I ASKED QUESTIONS. Doesn't most everyone?

The story seemed clunky, there was too much angst with little effort to change situations, boat loads of self pity and stories of love based on nothing real. I'm sorry but love at first sight is a fallacy found only in romance books. I could find nothing that would cause a deep, abiding, life long love between Tatianna and Malama. Friendship maybe, love no.

One and a half stars for editing. Even though this is a publishing house book there were still editing errors so I can't even give that a full two stars. Even words are misused.

I rarely leave a horrible review but felt this book so overrated I had to.

author: Gill Paul
review_text:
A Real Brain Teaser
This novel is a real brain teaser, in that it requires your complete attention. It is not a light read. There are two concurrent stories running side by side that are three generations apart. One takes place in Russia during the beginning years of World War I, and through the Bolshevik revolution; the other takes place at Lake Akanabee, New York State, USA., year 2016.
It’s a very compelling tale, but as I said, one must keep close attention, to keep track of all the characters. Some have more than on identity, and it becomes a bit confusing at times. There is also a bit of gore in the description of the Romanov family execution. But even though there is fiction involved, there is also a good bit of Russian history, also. It’s a fascinating read, well worth the time.

title: The Secret Wife: A captivating story of romance, passion and mystery: Love. Guilt. Heartbreak.
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Gill Paul
review_title: this book examines the notion of what life might have looked like if Tatiana
review_text: This is an interesting look at one of the major mysteries of the 20th century the killing of the Romanov family.  While I believe it's been more recently settled that both the parents and all the children were killed, this book examines the notion of what life might have looked like if Tatiana, the youngest child had escaped death.  The story is well written, well researched and certainly contains all the elements of suspense.  It looks at the life of one soldier hopelessly in love and takes us on a journey that includes an amazing story of love lost, love found and the time tremendous cost of that found love.  The book was not at all what I thought and it is told through the eyes of a great-granddaughter who finds herself lost and faced with the decision of how to deal with an unfaithful husband. It's a very good read.

title: The Shack: Where Tragedy Confronts Eternity
subtitle: Paperback – July 1, 2007
author: William P. Young
review_title: The Problem of Evil Seen as "No Problemo"
review_text:
Dear Reader -- You will find many reviews that point out the many discrepancies between "The Shack" and the Bible. And like me, you will agree with some, disagree with others, and fail to comprehend still others.

My beef with "The Shack" is that it tries to tell us that when the main character's little girl is abducted and being tortured and murdered, she really did not suffer, because she was in the presence of Jesus. That she was in the presence of Jesus after she died, I do not dispute, but to make her murder less than horrible to the end is foolish poppycock.

Are we to believe, by extension, that when hundreds of thousands of innocent people die in a tsunami, they are in the presence of Jesus as the wave sweeps over them? That when children lie crushed and screaming in a collapsed school building, they are in the presence of Jesus? That when a bombed soldier observes his life blood soaking into the roadside sand, he is in the presence of Jesus?

My belief is that there is no rational explanation for the contradiction between evil (especially impersonal evil) and belief in a loving God. Much as it may irk the modern "scientific" mind to not be able to solve this problem, it remains amystery.

title: The Shack: Where Tragedy Confronts Eternity
subtitle: Paperback – July 1, 2007
author: William P. Young
review_text: I won't repeat the many points made in warnings of this book. Many people who defend this book seem to be "hiding" behind the idea that is fiction so it is okay to read. The problem with this thinking is twofold. One, despite it being fiction, people are reading this book and applying it to their Faith and what they know and believe about God. This book is clearly taking you down the wrong path and Satan is most likely having a huge chuckle over this. He is afterall, the father of lies...and what a great lie this book provides. How deeply troubling that non-believers and those early in their Christian walk come across this highly praised book and fall prey to the lies and misguidance. Second, whether something is fictional or not, we are to guard our hearts. Reading this will certainly affect us even slightly. We are always affected by what we read or watch-despite it's fictional status.  The worst thing about this book that I have found is the author saying, "Jesus is the best way"-WRONG! Jesus is the ONLY way. Shame on every Christian for reading, praising and sharing this book. If you want a deeper understanding of God's love for us, the trinity and how to walk your Christian life faithfully, then submerge yourself in the source-HIS word!  If you don't understand the Bible, pray for God to bring you understanding-as only He can-and go to church and to bible studies.  Guard your heart and thoughts and stay away from reading garbage like this.  Max Lucado does an EXCELLENT job in helping gain an understanding of God's word in a light, easy to read, enjoyable and often funny way.  Read him before reading this!

title: The Shack: Where Tragedy Confronts Eternity
subtitle: Paperback – July 1, 2007
author: William P. Young
review_text:
I am really saddened by how so many people think this is a Christian book. The Trinity in this book is not at all the God of the Bible. Much of what is taught in the book is false. It teaches the exact opposite of what the Bible says in many cases. It does not matter that this book is fiction, because so many people read it and come away saying things like, "This book has completely changed my views about God! I feel so much closer to him now." That is because the God as described in this book is only something that people made up to suit themselves, and will not bring you closer to Christ. You can't trust your heart on this. Instead, trust God's Word to tell us about God. (Jeremiah 17:9 "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?")

You may think I'm negative for saying these things. I'm not trying to be. I'm just trying to stand up for the truth of Christ and His Word.

There are already some thorough reviews about the serious problems with this book, so I will not add any more. If you want to read a time-tested best-selling book to learn more about God and to be faithful to Christ, I recommend "Knowing God" by J.I. Packer. It's not nearly as easy a read as "The Shack," but at least it is faithful to the true identity of the Trinity.

title: The Shack: Where Tragedy Confronts Eternity
subtitle: Paperback – July 1, 2007
author: William P. Young
review_text:
As an atheist/agnostic type, I read this book at the insistence of a Christian friend in turn for her reading an atheist book of my choosing.

It is absurd how many people think this book might actually report a true story, including my Christian friend. The story is all fiction, admitted by the author, even the main character of Mack was made up. I don't understand how individuals can ever believe a epic dream where the person flies, swirls in color and is serenaded by forest animals. Furthermore, after being emotionally distraught over his loss and experiencing massive head trauma, he supposedly remembers intricate details of his encounter with God totaling 150 pages and containing numerous long theological discussions.

There are plenty of flaws in the books presentation and content, but one stands out as most humorous. God appears to Mack as a big black woman in order to not reinforce a stereotype of God as a bearded middle aged white man. From a visual perspective this explanation make sense. However, when majority of the shack encounter involves this big black woman doing and saying the most stereotypically black things, this character choice becomes terribly ironic.

title: The Shack: Where Tragedy Confronts Eternity

review_text: I believe the reason so many gave positive reviews, is that so many do not possess real wisdom or discernment.  It takes the power of the Holy Spirit to reveal truth and deception to us.  Many fall for numerous things that appear to be good. God tells us to accept Him, which is the better, but most want to accept the good they think comes from man. In fact, one sign of the end times will be that what is called evil will be called good, and good, evil.  This may not fall into the category of evil, but deception is within its pages. When a whole book is written from the standpoint of the pain man must endure, never focusing on what Christ endured for man, to free him forever from that pain, than it's focus is self-centered. Humanism is all about self-centered man. This is what originated the fall of man in the first place.  Pride always takes us to our own perceived self-importance.  People who continually speak about themselves and their personal painful past, and not about the overwhelming goodness of God, have taken the enemy's bait.  Just listen to people... do they continually speak about the difference and hope Christ made in their life.  And do they tell you how their life of pain was turned around and was eventually blessed and used by God in a mighty way. What is the focus.  This reads as if an overly emotional, melancholy woman wrote it. Once we become a Christian, our focus needs to turn to the One who changed our focus.  This is what gives others reason to hope!

title: The Shack: Where Tragedy Confronts Eternity
subtitle: Paperback – July 1, 2007
author: William P. Young
review_title: The Shambles: A Very Poor Attempt at Conveying the Christian Message
review_text:
Before and after an incredible encounter with God, main character "Mack" remains a fellow, we are told, who is not particularly "religious." While some truths may be expressed in this book, author Wm. Paul Young appears to have great fun, having his version of God also express some offbeat ideas. He seems to enjoy taking swipes at "hierarchy," "institutions," and "ritual," while quietly promoting a type of [[ASIN:0879736690 syncretism]]. Rather than try to create God in "Willie's" image, Wm. Paul Young would be well served by a review of classic apologetics, such as is found in the [[ASIN:0830817743 Handbook of Christian Apologetics]].

In the second chapter, we are told that Mack likes to share a tale with his kids about a princess, in which "After praying and giving herself to the Great Spirit, she fulfilled the prophecy by jumping without hesitation to her death on the rocks below." Romanticizing suicide to kids is akin to child abuse. Tragically, Mack (& Wm. Paul Young?) view this suicide as akin to Christ's acceptance of death on the cross!

In the fourth chapter, we are reminded that "Something in the hearts of most human beings simply cannot abide pain inflicted on the innocent, especially children....Even in such a world of relative morality [i.e., prison], causing harm to a child is still considered absolutely wrong. Period!" Amen!!! Unfortunately, the book does not stop there....

Near universal condemnation of harming a child points to the existence of moral absolutes and the "natural law." While our ability to distinguish right from wrong has often grown weak through lack of exercise (among other factors), J. Budziszewski says that moral truth is [[ASIN:1890626546 What We Can't Not Know]](Though we sure do our darndest to run from it & to deny it.). The existence of the conscience for knowing moral truth is a classic argument for the existence of God.

We can know truth! I would love the opportunity to meet Wm. Paul Young and urge him to review the [[ASIN:1574557203 Compendium of the Catechism of the Catholic Church]].

review_text:
Meh... this book is dangerous.

A novel? Yes. Well written? Not so much. Fiction? Most definitely! Scriptural? No, not in the least. This book is a New Age take on Christianity.

The author portrays a Godhead that eschews hierarchical structure and a Holy Spirit who is flighty and embraces chaos and randomness. Our (true) God is a God of order not chaos. God created hierarchy as a framework for authority which is what the power of the Kingdom of God is driven by. We combat satanic attacks using the authority of Jesus' name. Apostolic churches are founded based on submission to God's authority, Without hierarchy there can be no authority, and without authority God's power is impotent on earth. The Bible clearly teaches that there is a hierarchical structure within the heavenly (and satanic) hosts. The story of Jesus and the Centurion lays out the importance of structure and authority. There are many, many other examples in the Bible that pretty much nullify this author's misguided perceptions of God.

This fallacious reasoning is all the more dangerous in that this appears to a be a somewhat popular book that holds itself out to be Christian writing with study guides and whatnot. I wound up throwing this book away. My recommendation to anyone who views this book as anything other than pure fiction with no scriptural foundation should skip it. There are other Christian novels out there that are good writing AND still maintain fidelity to basic scriptural truths.

subtitle: Paperback – July 1, 2007
author: William P. Young
review_title: "Did I hear God call me an idiot?"
review_text: I have learned to be leery when a book is gifted to me with a broad beaming smile and the coo, "This book changed my life - and I want you to read it."  I handle it delicately - knowing it is likely to blow up in my face.  A few such books have had amazing impacts ["Life of Pi" for example].  However, too often (SHACK being one of them), the book is derivative and deliberate in its efforts.  SHACK sets off in this manner.  The narrator/author demures that he will be a silent witness - but steers the narrative constantly to cinematic details that the main character is not observing ["Unnoticed by Mack, the room lightened..."]  Willie is an overbearing Uncle Remus.  The revelation of God as a sassy trio of women smacks of "Steel Magnolias".  That's right, honey.  The unfolding of book's messages and ultimate miracles and the teasing out of the books "secrets" which really are pretty basic and very obvious and were mostly anticipated and decoded by page 25 just compounds the books issues.  Re-editing and a better comprehension of base concepts [how do you get Pandora's Box wrong?] - a severe reduction of overwrought similes/metaphors ["a significant lump had already formed, emerging like a humpbacked whale breaching the wild waves of his thinning hair." - Egads!].  Back to the cinematic drivel: there's even a page of "push" at the rear of the book to send the numbers in publication high enough to get a film producer to pick this one up for production.  Well, who saw that one coming?  So - our Mack is right when warning the reader that the story "wasn't primarily written for you."  The message that might easily be overlooked: a pearl is both a layered gem and lacquered excrement.

title: The Shack: Where Tragedy Confronts Eternity
subtitle: Paperback – July 1, 2007
author: William P. Young
review_text:
This part one from a series of blog posts on The Shack found here:[...]

Recently a friend from work lent me her copy of the Shack. I have read the reviews, am aware of the controversial nature of the book, and know that my perceptions of this read are going to be colored by the aforementioned. Even so, and even if the wave of controversy surrounding The Shack has long since crested, I will now put down other titles I am reading, focus on the Shack, and render my thoughts on the book as I read my way through it.

First, I know that The Shack was dearly loved by many. It's lengthy stay on the New York Times best-seller list attests to that fact. I think it brought a since of solace to many and made God seem warmly imminent, perhaps for the first time in their lives. I think many people have their own "Shack" somewhere in their history, and I know I do. We all, to some degree, struggle with the very real and very theological problem of persistent evil in the world, and The Shack is one such story, perhaps a theodicy of sorts.

Next, I am aware of the theological controversy surrounding this book. The reformed tribe, among others, found egregious error, even heresy, in much the theological assertions in the shack. Others pontificated that this is not a theological textbook, but a mere novel. "Lighten up, man!' However, I say any theological talk, be it in a novel or a systematic theology, especially when it is warmly received my much of the American evangelical community, is worthy of critique, and what follows is mine.

The First Five Chapters:

From the first page, I find Young's writing, quite honestly, a bit cloying, as if written by an earnest fourteen year old school-girl with a modest amount of talent with the written word. Second, I hate overt emotional manipulation. Before going further, let me state that I am a bit of a romantic, at times. At the end of the movie, The Gladiator, my eyes were a bit moist. I found the framing device of Saving Private Ryan a bit sentimental, but, again, my eyes were moist when Tom Hank's character dies at the end of the film. I have to admit, too, that as a father, Young's writing made me feel Mack's pain. I did get a bit misty.

However, is it possible to construct a more cynically and emotionally manipulative framing device than the one presented by The Shack?

First, we find Mack and Missy having just had a discourse on the nature of grace and sacrifice in Mack's recounting of the story of the Multnomah princess, supposedly an analog of the Gospel, though I think a profoundly weak one. In that story, the princess voluntarily sacrifices her life by jumping off a cliff to her death, something apparently required by an Indian prophesy to save the men of the tribe who were all dying from some illness. As an omen, perhaps, young Missy later asks Mack if God would ever ask her to jump of a cliff? Mack says no.

Soon after, we find Josh and Kate, two of Mack's five children, involved in a canoeing mishap wherein Mack, his instincts as a life-guard in his younger days rising up at this moment of crisis, dives into the water and saves his son Josh from drowning. Upon returning to shore, crisis over - at least that one - everyone safe and sound, Mack finds his youngest daughter, ten years old, if memory serves, ominously missing. The stage for The Great Sadness is set.

As the story unfolds, Missy's body is never found, but the dress, now blood-stained, worn when she was abducted by her killer is located. It is found in a shack in the woods.

I am at the point now where Mack has received an invitation from a character called Papa, in the form of an unstamped letter in the mail, to visit him at the shack, a proposal of which Mack is understandably quite dubious, though intrigued.

Again, is it possible for a Young to construct a more emotionally manipulative framing device, the abduction and murder of his ten year old daughter by a serial killer who preys on young girls for a narrative than the one found in The Shack? He has constructed a literary device of great manipulative and visceral power seeming designed so as to emotionally deconstruct any critical thought.

I will end this initial installment with a quote, found below, starting at the end of page 65 of the soft-cover edition. My next post, when time allows and sooner rather than later I hope, will be to deconstruct this wretched, sophomoric, post-modern intellectual detritus that passes for profundity and then perhaps examine the next few chapters....if I can muster up the where-with-all to stay the course...

...the thought of God passing notes did not fit well with his theological training. In seminary he had been taught that God had completely stopped any overt communication with moderns, preferring to have them only listen to and follow sacred Scripture, properly interpreted, of course. God's voice had been reduced to paper, and even that paper had to be moderated and deciphered by the proper authorities and intellects. It seemed that direct communication with God was something exclusively for the ancients and uncivilized, while educated Westerners' access to God was mediated and controlled by the intelligentsia. Nobody wanted God in a box, just in a book. Especially an expensive one bound in leather with gilt edges, or was that guilt edges?

title: The Shack: Where Tragedy Confronts Eternity

author: William P. Young
review_text: I will leave the theology discussions to other posts, and will just write about how horribly written this book is. It is as sappy and sophomoric as an after-school TV special.  I rolled my eyes so many times I thought they would get stuck. After a weak but not completely uninteresting start, it becomes an endless, lame fantasy that tries to make what are likely concepts that we can't completely comprehend into pat, perky platitudes. But I have to say what really irritates me is how the foreward and afterward state that this is a work of non-fiction, that this really happened to the author's friend Mack. I guess I have become accustomed to thinking that the foreward and afterward are parts of the book where the author breaks away from the content of the book itself and writes from outside of the "fourth wall" again. However, in fact, there is no Mack, no daughter, no murder, no serial killer:  this is completely a work of fiction -- just view the author's web site to read about it.  I find this to be deceptive and disrespectful of the reader, not to mention how it thus positions itself to be the "true" representation of what the universe's higher power is -- negating any different, non-complying beliefs, unless you happen to find out the truth.

If you want to understand and know the true nature and character of God then read the Bible with a broken and repentant heart and ask the Holy Spirit to reveal God the Father to you in the Name of God the Son through the power of God the Holy Spirit..The Shack is one man's opinion of God and does not even come close to the true revealed nature of God revealed in the scriptures...Be like Paul in Phillipians 3:10 and pray that I may know him and the power of his resurrection and the fellowship of his sufferings...It's sad when people go to novels for their theology.Whatever happened to reading the Bible,studying the Bible, meditating on the Bible? Man's opinion outside the scriptures always ends up being politically correct and watered down...It bothers me that hundred of comments like the shack changed my life and I've been a Christian for 10-20 years and now only after reading the shack do I understand that God loves me...In Colossians Paul states that the gospel has the power to change your life. Also in Colossians Paul states that the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily in Jesus and that the secret of the ages is Christ in you the hope of glory.It's a sad commentary when "Christians" go to the local Christian book store and look to the latest Christian celebrity author to get their theology...I have written a couple of Christian fiction novels that are not allegory..The first is The Palace Theatre..[[ASIN:1424129990 The Palace Theatre]....]The second is Changing Seasons..[[ASIN:1413700845 Changing Seasons]]..Would encourage comments...especially constructive critism...

Added later...I haven't read anything in these posts about the book of Job.Job goes through a lot more "great sadness" than Mack ever thought about and God didn't appear to him to cook him meals, "splain" things to him or hold his hand. God had some tough questions and didn't tell Job any reasons behind the suffering. When God was done interogating Job he said to God in Job 42:5-6,"I have only heard about you before,but now that I have seen you with my own eyes I take back everything I said,and sit in dust and ashes to show my repentance."

The Shack creates a wordview where everyone is forgiven without the need for repentance mentioned.I know God.God knows me. I love God. God loves me.I have a personal realtionshiop with Him. He is a God of love,mercy, forgiveness faithfullness,holiness judgement,wrath,righteousness. author: William P. Young
review_text: Just one line in the book put me right off. On p.96, Papa says (s)he never left Jesus on the cross. I for one do not believe Jesus was deluded when he called out, very loudly, "My God, My God, why have you forsaken me?" He was forsaken so that we would not be forsaken. He was wounded for our transgressions, pierced for our iniquities, and had the iniquities of us all laid on him, (Isaiah 53). I tried to read this book with an open mind, remembering that it is a work of fiction and not the Bible, but when I read what Papa said I was horrified, it was just too much. Certainly the Father suffered as well as the Son, something we might tend to forget, and the author brings that out on p.95-96, but for me at least, to say or imply that Jesus was not really forsaken is an extremely serious error and should never be taught, whether in a work of fiction or non fiction.

review_text: While I welcomed the attempt to expand our view of God which is presented in The Shack, I found the theology to fall short.  As a Catholic, I was especially alarmed at the individualistic tone of the entire book.  There is no concept of the Kingdom of God or the beatitudes.  It is as if the message and purpose of Jesus doesn't matter as long as one has a personal relationship with Jesus.  The value of community, sacraments and ritual are ridiculed in the theology that is put forth.  I also found the emphasis to be quite anthropocentric at times at the expense of the rest of creation.  While this book may serve as a comfort to evangelical Christians, I find it to be disturbing and not consistent with Scripture and Tradition.

It's true in the sense that it's only parables relating to his life and how he rose from the depths of despair. Had I known it was not true, I probably would have got bored with it.  Once I found out, I was kind of angry I was "taken" yet it's  not the author's fault people think that way. Clearly the book on the outside cover says it's FICTION! title: The Shack: Where Tragedy Confronts Eternity
subtitle: Paperback – July 1, 2007
author: William P. Young
review_title: You're not supposed to think about it
review_text:
(big spoilers herein)

In this story, a man gets past the grief he feels after a tremendous tragedy by spending a few days with a physical personification of God. Neat!

As of this writing, some bad things are happening to me. I understand I'm supposed to believe that in spite of this, God loves me as much as He loves the dude in this story. But the dude in the story only gets over his trouble once God meets up with him in the most literal, physical way possible, and directly speaks with him and hugs him and counsels him. Well, maybe God has met with me and I didn't notice it etc. But He definitely hasn't met with me in the most literal, physical way possible--so I guess it makes sense for me to go on not caring about Him, right? I don't think that's really the Christian view, though, and I doubt that William P. Young wants me to use this book as a justification to go through the rest of my life being disinterested in God. So... WHY should I have faith in God, when my weekend with Him is, by all appearances, not on the calendar? Well you're not supposed to think about that I guess. Not in Young's view, anyway.

Through a lot of the early part of this story, I perceived a build-up toward an important communication between God and the protagonist: The guy's daughter was probably tortured to death for no apparent reason, and the guy had suffered over this himself for a long time, and he needed to find out why God would let that happen, or make it happen. I was a little bit excited, even, to learn what answer would be given to this important question! As the story progressed, the dad got to see his daughter being happy in the afterlife, and even to feel her contentment with the state of things. He got to argue his piece with various incarnations of the ostensible Almighty, and he eventually even got to find and bury her previously hidden body. These events weren't really God's answer to the question, but they made up most of God's response to it, and that seemed to be good enough for the distraught dad. It seemed to me that maybe Young wouldn't even try to give an answer--how tricky of him! But in a few little bits that didn't receive much emphasis, his answer did come through: Evil exists because there's some cosmic balance that prevents good from existing alone. And even God cannot get around this balance. Sooo God isn't all-powerful. Well, what are the limits of God's power, then? If God has limits, is there something greater than God? What kind of a person gets a chance to ask God herself (OR HIMSELF DON'T FREAK OUT) this question, and then doesn't? Somebody who accepts that you're not supposed to think about it, that's who! But... if he truly accepts that faith is superior to reason, then why, at the start of the story, was he having so much trouble believing God had a higher purpose in letting his daughter die? I don't think you're supposed to think about that either. :(

Young says right in the foreword to The Shack (in the voice of the protagonist) that if you don't like this book, then it wasn't written for you. In this way he suggests that criticism itself doesn't matter, if it's made by people who think about things. You're not supposed to think, and people who like to think, well... does God love them too? Presumably He does, at least to the extent that He exists and behaves as the Christians say He does. Is that healthy, for people to be pushed away from an account of how God's love can heal a wounded person, just because they're smart and they think about things? Maybe it is, maybe it isn't. But you're not supposed to think about that.

If you think you're supposed to think about all these things, and you still somehow like this book, then I think you're missing the book's point! Good thing I don't have a God to sic on you. You might want to send yours after me, though. But good luck with that--for all you know, I just might be the Keeper of the Cosmic Balance. For all you know, I have the power to get rid of your god! It's not like you've thoroughly thought the matter through. Better be nice to me! And to yourself and everyone else, while you're at it. :)

author: William P. Young
review_title: Let's make up our own religion
review_text: First, the good part--this book will cause people to revisit their views of God.  The big downside--a subtle message that we people can do no wrong in God's eyes and that He, make that she, is fine with almost any behavior of ours.  Although some of the explanations the various "characters" who are posing as God give to the main character are close to Christian teaching, they are still off the mark. This book tries so hard to make God a non-threatening chum that it strips God of His qualities of majesty, justice, and truth. It is a thinly disguised attempt to rail against mainstream, organized religion and it leaves the reader with the message that anyone can make up their own version of religion as long as it makes you feel warm and fuzzy inside.

review_text: I read the book first and then the reviews on here. Yes, it's a simple read and probably with more grammatical and English writing errors than sand on a beach. Is the plot/main story impossible? Probably. God as a black woman? Who says that he/she isn't? What mattered to me and what I tried putting into perspective while reading the book was the philosophy behind all of the imperfections. Even if you don't believe it actually happened, there's some good advice here about living in today, releasing control over things you don't have control over and trusting in the relationships you have with your loved ones and the ability to forgive those who has committed the most vile of crimes. What's wrong with that wisdom? In the end, it's the message you take from the book, not how the author phrased his metaphor.

review_title: makes you think about yourself, and God...
review_text:
The Shack is a rather unique book - and has become quite a phenomenon. Near the top of the best seller charts for several months now, I somehow avoided hearing much about it until my brother mentioned it in a phone call. Strangely enough, a couple hours later a friend gave it to me.

It starts off a little uneven, but you quickly get a sense of the characters and their emotions. It isn't spoiling anything to say there is good reason for Mack to have "The Great Sadness" as it is put, and there is certainly a horrific ordeal at the center of that, but the details are thankfully not elaborated on.

Mack's return to the shack is when the magic begins. What happens there, and how it unfolds, is compelling reading. I do not have the theologian background to argue for or against specifics within those events; I can only relate how the book made me feel and think while reading it. And as to that, it made me want to examine my own life and actions, my own relationship with God and with the people around me. For that alone, the book is worth reading.

I had a couple things figured out as the book neared the end, but there were still a couple surprises for me and that made the ending that much more satisfying. All in all, an enjoyable read that can make a difference in your life if you let it.

title: The Shack: Where Tragedy Confronts Eternity

author: William P. Young
review_text:
I love that this book addresses many of the questions that we ask ourselves day to day. I hate that it uses the pain of a family to answer said questions. We've all been in a predicament where we ask ourselves, "What if I had only did...? What if I hadn't done...?" These are questions that Mack wrestles with after the abduction of his daughter, Missy. He places blame on himself (and God) for the terrible circumstances surrounding her disappearance. In midst of tragedy, He finds himself asking, as I am sure you can relate, "Where is God in my pain?" After reading a book that addresses many of these concerns, I didn't feel so alone. I feel God truly does understand that "when all you see is your pain, perhaps that is when you lose sight" of God (page 98).

I also loved how this book encompassed what God expects of us regarding forgiveness. Mac has a really troubling situation in which he must forgive someone who hurt him dearly. He struggles with how to forgive and justifies his hatred of the individual until God intervenes and shows him the freeing power of forgiveness.

A final important topic which this book alludes to is the human ability to be judge and jury of our brother/sisters. I felt complete conviction during the chapter in which Mac was to the judge at the risk of saving only one of his children and forsaking the other. Wow! Completely powerful!

If you haven't picked up this book to read, you should!

author: William P. Young
review_text:
For me "The Shack" was an excellent book because it did an excellent job of helping me to understand with a fresh perspective the nature of God's love for me and the kind of relationship He wants to have with me too. I don't know about you but I am constantly fighting my old paradigms about a judgmental, vengeful, legalistic, religious oriented God even though I know intellectually that is not really His nature. "The Shack" gave me a much needed fresh, healthy reminder of the kind of love our God has for His children, which is so far beyond our human ways of perceiving and quantifying love. We all need some help with this one. Seeing love and relationship from God's perspective is very hard, if not impossible, for most humans. This book has done the best job so far in helping me to comprehend.

As a disclaimer, I would like to state that there are some theological shortfalls and errors in "The Shack" in my opinion, however, my theological understanding is strong enough to see through those shortfalls and allow me to benefit from the larger and deeper non-religious message. If you are a new believer in Christ then you may want to consider waiting to read this book until your own theological understanding is deeply rooted in the truth of the New Testament Word of God. With that understanding as a back drop you will be in a much better position to read "The Shack" and receive the badly needed macro message of the book without getting mislead or distracted with theological detail and debate.

Truthfully, the non-religious disarming perspective and tone is part of the books charm, as well as necessary perhaps in order to effectively get the full and pure message of the book across to the reader. This is especially true of readers like me who easily and frequently find themselves caught up in legalism and thus sometimes get distracted from the simple message of God's love. Again, what is compelling to me about this book is that it sidesteps religious theology in order to powerfully reconnect me to that over arching truth: God wants to be in a relationship with me.

We as humans so frequently view, experience and quantify love and relationships from our flawed human perspective and on our selfish terms. "The Shack" does an excellent job juxtaposing our human view of love and relationship with the far superior perspective God has and wishes for us to experience with Him/Her.

title: The Shack: Where Tragedy Confronts Eternity

author: William P. Young
review_title: Even if You Don't Consider Yourself Religious, There's Much to Gain From Reading this Book
review_text:
I read this book primarily because it was chosen by my book club, not because I had a great desire to read it. However, I'm glad that I read it. Since there are many reviews that discuss and debate the value of the book for its Christian messages, I won't comment on its value as a tool to bring people closer to God. Instead, I will discuss what I thought about it aside from that.

I couldn't read the first half of the book fast enough. The first 100 pages told the story about what led to Mack's daughter, Missy, being murdered. (I'm not giving away anything here--you get this from reading the back cover.)

However, my reading pace slowed a bit when I arrived midway through the book, at the part which introduces Mack's life-changing weekend at "the shack." What kept me reading was the author's creativity and the quality of the writing, which I thought was excellent. The book challenges our stereotypes of God and makes some significant points which transcend religion and offer applicability to life in our society and make you stop and really think.

A few such examples include:

"Being always transcends appearance-that which only seems to be. Once you being to know the being behind the very pretty or very ugly face, as determined by your bias, the surface appearances fade away until they simply no longer matter."

"Authority, as you think of it, is merely the excuse the strong use to make others conform to what they want."

"...the value of the individual is constantly weighed against the survival of the system, whether political, economic, social or religious -- any system actually. First one person, and then a few, and finally even many are easily sacrificed for the good and ongoing existence of that system. In one form another this lies behind every struggle for power, every prejudice, every war, and every abuse of relationship."

While I think the author does an outstanding job of challenging our stereotypes of God, my strongest criticism of the book is that I think he sometimes reinforces unhelpful gender stereotypes.

Overall, I think The Shack was very well written, creative, and intelligent. Was it life changing for me? No. Was it enjoyable and did it challenge me to think at a different level? Absolutely!

review_text:
For every person who has struggled with seeing God, as a loving God, this book is worth reading. Many of the things that are brought out in this book will challenge you. I myself personally do not usually like to read fictional books, but this book had so much life in it. It is not the bible and does not promote itself to be gospel truth. That's why it's called fiction. But it will open your eyes to see a God who loves you and desires more than anything to have a relationship with you and everyone else in this world. It brings picture images to your mind that will help you to understand God's love as well.

I read this book out loud to my husband and he and I fell in love with it. We not only desire a closer relationship with God but also we desire to have a closer relationship with each other, our 6 children, and those around us. We desire to love as God loves us. People say that this book is Heresy, and yet from someone who has tried to walk softly with God my whole life, I find this book to reveal God closer to His nature than many other books. I find myself feeling closer to Him, not further from me. I feel more loved by God, not less.

I think that it's funny that some are so against a book that isn't word for word scripture but watch tv shows and movies that leaves you feeling afraid of tomorrow and the things that could come.

I believe this book opens a door that many of us see as closed. It opens a door to having a relationship with God as a friend, father, and God. I treasure my relationship with Him and pray that all will experience it as well.
God bless all of you and enjoy reading!

review_text:
I have read some of the reviews and feel that people have taken something that could be inspirational and condemned it. The bottom line is that if you are looking for a book to save people, in a Christian way, that's what the Bible is. This book takes a deep despair and transforms it into compass with God as due north.

The strongest lesson put forth by the book, to me, was that no matter what you call "it", "God" is love, and your notions of what he/she is make little difference to the truth of God. The "truth" of God isn't dependent on what people think. We have been flawed from the fall of Adam and Eve, and God understands that. Free will is fact, but God using the outcomes of that free will--good or bad--is part of God's glory and insight.

I feel that this book is a wonderful read. My family truly enjoyed it. I cried and felt uplifted. I plan on reading it again.

review_text:
I loved this book! It really gets to the heart of God and His passionate pursuit of us. It cuts through dry religion and leaves you longing for a relationship with a living PERSON-Christ Himself.

Although I don't agree with every theological nuance of the book, I was swept away by the truth and reality of the love within the Godhead-and how that love extends to us and draws us in. The book does an incredible job communicating the inexhaustible grace of our God, and His behind-the-scenes work in our lives, to weave EVERYTHING into a beautiful expression of His love and glory.

I found that the book "fleshed out" much of what I've been reading in another book-"From Eternity to Here", by Frank Viola. This book gives a biblical and theological explanation for the concepts in the book. It explores the amazing eternal purpose of our God-the purpose that satisfies HIS longings (and ours in the process). I found my heart beating rapidly at times, stirred by the relentless passion of my Lord for His Church. I think you'll find yourself in awe of the hidden treasure he unearths. Viola is a gifted storyteller-much of the book reads like a novel-but it's so much more than that. You can pick up a copy here or at Parable Books, where it's on 33% discount for the rest of March: [...] .

review_text:
The BEST work of Fiction I have read in Years. UNEQUIVOCALLY THE Best Fiction Book of 2007.

I am changed. I pray indelibly. My oh my!

Donald Miller, Jim Palmer, Jim Henderson, Jeff Jacobson --- now William P. Young --- refreshing, timely, powerful new voices, gifted story tellers God has raised up to speak to those who need to hear His voice, feel His love, comprehend God's presence today in their lives. This book pierced dimensions of my soul in ways that defy explanation through the written word --- it's just that powerful.

I must tell you I almost delayed reading this book (it was sent to me for review). I just wasn't in the mood for reading something that had a subtitle of "Where Tragedy Confronts Eternity." Don't make the mistake I almost made: You must not delay in reading this book. In fact, get 4 copies and give them to folks.

This story is a unique blessing, supernaturally infectious, and intended to distribute its blessing well beyond the initial reader who comes into contact with its contents. Whatever you're reading, drop it and get this book.

I promised I wouldn't share the story line. I'm going to keep that promise. This book was terribly special to me as I had spent several days last April with my boys smack dab in the midst of the geographic area (the Wallowa) where the story line takes place. Buy this book now. See the website at [...].

I will read this book once a year for the rest of my days. My prayer is that this is the first of many books to come from William P. Young. If no more books are ever written by Mr. Young, I will remain forever grateful for this one.

"Living unloved is like clipping a bird's wings and removing its ability to fly." P. 97. This book renewed the strength in my wings and deepened my appreciation for my ability to soar.

Prepare for lift-off! Soar with The Shack. Mr. Young, I am especially fond of you. Read the book - You will come to understand what I mean.

Bill Dahl
Author, Creator, Editor

author: Dr. Seuss
review_text:
This is fun and inspirational for all ages. I should read this more often to uplift my spirits when I am having a rough time; I know a lot of adults that could use it. I remember the Valedictorian of my graduating high school class read this for his speech and I thought it was perfect. It gives anybody encouragement no matter where they are in life. I like how it gives you hope that you can be the best YOU but there will also be ups and downs along the way that can be overcome. I read it to my kids and they liked different parts of the story. My young daughter liked the spooky bit, my middle son liked the silly games “there is fun to be done” (which suits his personality), and my oldest son liked the page where everyone was waiting for something (which he understands more at his age).

It teaches personal accountability for your choices and living up to your potential. “You have brains in your head. You have feet in your shoes. You can steer yourself any direction you choose. You’re on your own. And you know what you know. And YOU are the guy who’ll decide where to go.”

title: Killing Floor (Jack Reacher, Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Lee Child
review_text:
So I normally don't read thrillers, right. I took about a week to research various authors and decided to buy Lee Child's first Jack Reacher book, right. After I started reading it, I realized something was bothering me, right. How about because every person in the book ends their sentences with the word "right". At first, I thought Child was trying to use it as a southern Georgia type of accent, but no matter who was in the book, they said it. The professor in NY, the FBI guy, Jack himself, right. Granted, the book is dated, but I could have lived with that. The story was decent and did something with counterfeiting I never heard off. Pretty good. But the use of the word "right" was so overwhelmingly annoying, I couldn't take it. Also, the in depth description of certain things, like how Child described ever turn on every street that someone took...I turned left here, then right here, then drove 2.35 miles, then made another left. I think he was just trying to show how detailed Reacher's mind was, but it also got annoying.
The only more annoying thing than this book is the fact that Tom Cruise was just caste to play Reacher in an upcoming movie. Reacher is about 6'4", blond military type. Cruise is 5'6", dark hair, and although he can pull off a kick butt movie, he just isn't Reacher. Get the guy who plays Eric Northman from True Blood. He is exactly who I pictured.

review_text: This book includes over 500 pages of short, abrupt non-sentences (more than half are just fragments) with no sentence variety, no character development or growth, no editing for unnecessary repetition, and an over-the-top fantasy that might appeal, at best, to the reluctant adolescent male reader. Plus it's incredibly boring. Mr. Child needs a good fiction writing course.

title: Killing Floor (Jack Reacher, Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Lee Child
review_text:
I was not impressed with this book. I can't believe the rave reviews the Jack Reacher series is getting. I had just completed Vinnce Flynn's, Mitch Rapp series and was looking for another great hero to follow. Through tons of research, I was led to Lee Child's "Jack Reacher" collection. I was extremely disappointed in the very first chapter. The story read like a bad low budget movie. The sentences were very short and choppy. Example: I looked at her. She looked back at me. We stood there looking at each other. She never spoke. I never spoke. We both turned and walked away.. These were not actual lines from the book but merely a close representation of Child's writing style. Because of the reviews I had read, I drugged on hoping it would get better but it never did. I completed the book but felt like I wasted my entire time. I even skipped forward several books in the Reacher series to see if they got any better. Nope, they all read the same.
Based on that, I will not be reading any more of Child's books. If you want to read an awesome series, check out Vince Flynn's collection of Mitch Rapp books.

review_text:
I've never read a book so poorly researched. There's artistic privilege and then there's vandalism.

If you're looking for something to read during your lobotomy, this is the rag for you. If you're looking for something to engage with, you need to look a little further.

review_text: I wanted to sample one of Child's Reacher books and chose this title because it is the first book in the series. There is not much to like or admire about the Reacher character in this story.  Ostensibly he is one of the good guys but several of his actions reveal him to be as morally bankrupt as the criminals he is pursuing. title: Killing Floor (Jack Reacher, Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Lee Child
review_text: I was quite frankly surprised at just how bad this book was given the author's popularity.  The plot becomes implausible very early in the book and its main characters act in ways that are unrealistic.  A coincidence that occurs before the middle of the book pushed me over the edge.  At page 200, I came back to read the one star reviews on this site noting that many reviewers were turned off by the very same implausibilities.  The story line had potential if you could get past the amateurish writing.  If I read "he just shrugged" one more time, I knew I would fling the book.  I can only presume that this writer's later efforts are substantially better given his popularity, but I do not plan to read more of his work.

title: Killing Floor (Jack Reacher, Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Lee Child
review_title: I really wanted to give it more stars
review_text:
Jack Reacher should be an incredibly deep character, but instead, in this book, he's a victim of luck, apparently.

It seems rather weak that some guy with a deep past decides to randomly tour the East coast, but he does, and *immediately* stumbles upon some incredible conspiracy. If there was even ONE iota of suggestion that that was the reason he landed there, this book would have immediately been worth four stars. But the connection is weak.

Nope, this dude accidentally landed in a conspiracy -- and COINCIDENTALLY involves his long-lost brother -- and the rest of the book is basically about Jack being in the right place at the right time. And it's just lucky that Jack has the skills to solve the problem. And that he's met the right people at the right time. And that things happen randomly the way they do. And...

No, this book should be rewritten, because it's a great idea, but very poorly executed.

title: Killing Floor (Jack Reacher, Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Lee Child
review_text:
I almost always finish any book I start, no matter how bad it turns out to be. So you understand when I say this is the worst book that I ever finished: there have been worse, but not many.

The protagonist is made of cardboard in every respect. He can disable or kill any number of antagonists without ever suffering a scratch. The story is implausible if not completely absurd. Worst of all: the mean length for each sentence is about 4.5 words. It reads like a cheap 1950s movie script.

I'm done with this series after reading just the first entry.
