title: Killing Floor (Jack Reacher, Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Lee Child
review_title: Really Wanted to Like This Book, But...
review_text:
I don't think I've ever written a bad review of a book even if I didn't like it, but I have to make an exception here. This is honestly the worst book I've ever read. It was painful to read and I hope the other Jack Reacher novels are better than this, but I won't be reading them.

The plot and sequence of events are so absurd that they are insulting. It's almost like it was made up as it went along. I found myself saying, "Oh, for God's sake!" at the impossible and implausible things that happen in this book. As I read I couldn't help but see Puddy from Seinfeld as Jack Reacher, Lee Child's franchise character. It was that comically bad. In a 536-page book that is arguably 250 pages too long, when you use the word "shrugged" 123 times, there's a serious problem. Fiction is fiction, but the characters are unbelievable in unbelievable situations. There were pages that repeated almost exactly what was written the page before which only doubled the agony.

I really wanted to like this book and find a new Michael Connelly or James Lee Burke, but I was never more glad to finish a book.

The author obviously did no research and just made stuff up as he went along. Maybe it'll end up being awesome, but I don't think so.

Update: This is basically unreadable. I put it down after the main character pocketed an item taken from a victim's car, and a 20 year detective from Boston, who is standing right there, doesn't even notice. This is only one of many stupid plot points. Sheesh, what a waste of ten bucks! If only there was a way to give it negative stars...

Reacher's logic for making some of his kills in the way he did flew in the face of reason, and his weapons of choice were also a bit odd. I put this down to an inexperienced author who has no prior knowledge in this area. I also question whether anyone in the book, good or bad, would have been as blood-thirty in real life as the author portrayed them.

All in all, The Killing Floor was very good an well worth reading.

title: The Storied Life of A. J. Fikry: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Gabrielle Zevin
review_text:
I don't like to give negative reviews because I'm not a writer, so I've never faced the challenge of a blank page. And because what one person enjoys, may not be another's cup of tea. However, I am completely unable to fathom the enthusiasm generated by independent booksellers for this book. I was lucky and got it from the library; if my favorite indie bookseller had recommended this to me, I'd be appalled: the book is just not good. It is amateurish and mawkish: people die off to further the plot line. The booksellers first wife has died some years ago so he's free to fall in love; the mother of Maya conveniently kills herself, but not before leaving her child in the bookstore with a note to the owner asking him or her to raise her baby cause booksellers are naturally compassionate people. The social worker (who doesn't die) manages to circumvent an entire state's bureaucracy so the bookseller can keep the baby without any hassle (would be nice if real-world adoptions were so easy!). Voilà, do you see a family in the making?

I picked up this book because it was hyped in the indie press. I don't understand why it was lauded so; is it simply because it takes up the cause of bookstores? Why would a bookstore manager or owner who values his customers hype such mediocrity?

subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Gabrielle Zevin
review_text:
I was attracted to this book by its name, "The Storied Life of A. J. Fikry". It immediately put me in mind of books like The Unlikely Pilgrimage of Henry Fry" and "Major Pettigrew's Last Stand" and others that I put in the genre of "Gentle Reads". What I loved about the book was it's author, Gabrielle Zevin, and by association, her main character, A. J. Fikry's absolute love of all things BOOK! The story is about books, bookstores, who we are when we read books and who we are not, change and ultimately love.

I think I wanted more from the book, maybe more depth in the characters and I thought it ended too soon. But it was filled with thoughts and ideas worthy of highlighting, such as: "it is better to be alone than to be with someone who doesn't share your sensibilities and interests. (It is, right?)" and "What If there is only an equal ratio of happiness to unhappiness in the world at any given time?" One of my favorite aspects of the book was the references throughout to literature. What bothered me is that the author mixed in made up books with actual ones. I found that confusing and almost unfair. After all if the mentioned book sounded worthy, I'd immediately take a quick break and put it on my Wishlist, as I did when I first referenced The Storied Life of A. J. Fikry. Between
3 1/2 and 4 stars.

title: The Storied Life of A. J. Fikry: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Gabrielle Zevin
review_text:
I love books about books. I can’t help it, I just do. We meet A.J. Fikry when he’s in a place of despair. His book store is failing, his wife is dead, his best friend is a womanizing drunk. A.J is a grump. He’s a book snob. He reminded me of my husband (a former book seller)-who I love dearly-but he is also a book snob (and maybe a grump).

“Everyone thinks they have good taste, but most people do not have good taste. In fact, I’d argue that most people have terrible taste. When left to their own devices– literally their own devices– they read crap and they don’t know the difference.”

How can you not love A.J. Fikry? We learn what A.J. expects from his books:

“If a gun appears in act one, that gun had better go off by act three.”

YES! I loved that each chapter began with a book review by A.J. I loved how we learned what books he chose for Island Books changed as he changed himself. This was a book about books; more importantly it was a book about life, about how we make family and about love. I think this is one that it is best to read without knowing too many details, so I’ll stop here. This book made me laugh and made me tear up. What a life A.J. Fikry had.

One more quote, because as I know I had this experience and I want to know who else did too:

…”I always wanted to try the Turkish Delight in Narnia. When I read The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe as a boy, I used to think that Turkish Delight must be incredibly delicious if it made Edmund betray his family, A.J. says. I guess I must have told my wife this, because one year Nic gets a box for me for the holidays. And it turned out to be this powdery, gummy candy. I don’t think I’ve ever been so disappointed in my whole life.”

RIGHT? That stuff is so gross! Such a let down.

Read it and tell if you loved this too! Also-survey please on Turkish Delight. My husband has never tried it and I’m appalled. I feel like this disappointment is a milestone in life.

5 stars!!

All quotes were taken from an uncorrected galley proof subject to change in the final edition

Thank you NetGalley and Algonquin Books for this advanced read copy in exchange for an honest review!

review_text:
First I want to say I really really wanted to like this book. After watching the movie I was blown away. Being a video gamer and seeing this virtual reality world with so many references and action packed fun I had to check out the book. Because books are so much better than the movie right?
That’s when I decided to go to my local bookstore and purchase a hardcover copy. I took it home and wasn’t 10 pages in till the main character compares God to the Easter bunny and calls him Bulls***. Man what a low blow to readers. I found this comment extremely distasteful and just.... well unnecessary. With as much arguments going on in the world today and politics,me and most every reader wants to escape that and jump into a story.
Shame that the author had to subliminally place his own personal views into the book. I tried to read past it and forget it was there but the comment just got under my skin. It’d been nice if the author didint discriminate against religion. I’ll be getting rid of this book soon. Shame though.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_text: Oh my, where do I begin? As a gamer myself READY PLAYER ONE should have been a slam dunk. Sadly, however, it’s a resounding rebound. For me at least, it was on a downward trajectory from page one, when I realised that it was one of those stories where the outcome is obvious right from the start. There really could be no other resolution, and once this becomes clear all the mystery and tension that the story may otherwise have had vaporises instantly. Then begins the endless cultural references. The 80s was a formative decade for me and I have many fond memories of the era. And although I’m not averse to some well-used references the tedious info-dumps that  persist throughout RPO left me cold. There are also a number of technical issues relating to VR technology as described in the book, mostly concerning, but not limited to, the movement of a player through the environment (luckily for you I won’t bore you with those). And there is at least one occasion where the obvious solution is for Parzival to simply to quit the game, but he does not do so (later in the book the author adds a note as to why this is not possible, but his explanation does not apply to the incident I have in mind). There are no investible or credible characters (how on earth could anyone so young memorise verbatim so many movie scripts, song lyrics, and become master of so many video games?), and the hero of our story is often callous and annoying. As for the story; well to be honest I found it dull and lifeless, as is Cline’s prose. Most of the plot seems to have been reverse-engineered in order to accommodate the rather simplistic, 80s-related clues and the lacklustre quests required to find the keys. There’s even a whiff of deus ex machina thrown in at the start of the final act (where was the god when people were dying?). The most interesting aspect of the story is the concept of a dysfunctional USA where many people live in precarious trailer towers. There is the nub of a good idea here but it’s not developed at all. I wish I could be more positive but I really can’t, and I suspect that many readers have allowed the warm fuzziness of nostalgia to override their critical faculties when assessing the merits of this book. Very disappointing.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_text:
One: A Novel (Paperback)
This book starts with a great premise (post apocalyptic future where real life and an online video game have merged to form parallel realities), but is finished by the terrible writing, uninspired plot line and vapid character development.

I'll try not to spoil the plot, but here are some examples of just how bad this book is:
1. When two Japanese characters are first introduced to the story (as online Samurais no less) their only dialogue is commenting on how dishonorable (x) is. Really? Cliche much?
2. The author dedicates at least several pages to dialogue in which the characters call each other offensive names (edit: Amazon actually nixed my original review that contained the offensive names used by the author). You know, to really drive home the point that the characters are just regular dudes.
3. I would say more than 40% of the book is just the main character rehashing things he remembers from the 80s. The author/editor should have cut at least half of that out.
4. The bad guy in the story is a super evil corporation that will stop at nothing to get what it wants. Gasp!

The list can go on, but hopefully you get the point. The saddest part of this book is that the author actually thanks his editor for all of her hard work. This could mean one of two things. His editor mailed it in on this one, or the original drafts were so bad that this was the best thing they could put out. How this book has so many 5 star reviews is beyond me.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_title: Nothing more than a name-dropping, info-dump 80s reference book
review_text:
As a preface to this review, I was born in the early '80s and grew up with a deep-rooted love and nostalgia for the decade. I have fond memories of watching The Breakfast Club, Lady Hawk, Willow, Goonies, and other iconic '80s movies with my brother. These movies colored my childhood and earliest memories. In fact, I remember believing that I would marry Michael J. Fox and be swept away in The DeLorean. I cut my gaming teeth on my grandfather's Commodore 64 and learned the fine art of platforming with the original Mario Bros. My parents raised us to love Star Trek, be avid readers, and embrace the things that others thought weird. To be blunt, I am a geek.

After listening my husband's roommate praise Ready Player One, I was excited to delve into its uncharted depths. Sadly, it broke my heart.

Where do I even start with this book? It is nothing more than one big cluster-flip of trivia and "Ooo, look at me, I'm the most epic geek of all time because I know so much stuff!" Before I even address how Ernest Cline tried to single-handedly ruin my childhood, I will put on my English teacher/editor hat.

Let me begin with the story. Aside from movies like Tron, The Matrix, Gamer, etc., this book has a very interesting premise. Using '80s trivia and geeky-awesomeness as the vehicle for the plot made me geekgasm. It is also interesting to note that this book seemingly gave rise to Lit. RPG as an actual genre. Honestly, some amazing books have come out of it. Unfortunately, that is where it ends . . . This book lacks originality at its core and borders on plagiarizing myriad '80s movies. While it can be argued that there are no more original stories, Cline takes that to another level by hijacking everyone else's ideas, bastardizing them, and dumbing them down to spoon feed them to the masses. This is evident in his characters. Cline has never met a stock character that he didn't like. Not only are his characters extremely one-dimensional and severely underdeveloped, Wade is no more than a badly written copy of Luke Skywalker. As well as being an orphan raised by his aunt, he was the only one who could go against IOI (*couch* the Empire *cough*) to save the OASIS. And, let me not forget, Wade—like Ernest himself—is the G.O.A.T. (Greatest Of All Time).

At no point can he fail. Even if he does not have the skills or necessary knowledge, Wade always has to succeed.

In addition to the stock characters, the whole story of Halliday and Morrow was a two-bit copy of the formation of modern day computers. In fact, Halliday and Morrow mirror Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak. It was easy to figure out how the relationship would play out if you watched Pirates of Silicon Valley or know anything about that dynamic.

Moving on, Ernest either needs to invest in a good editor or fire the one he has. The glaring inconsistencies in this book were outrageous. For example, on page 161, Wade approaches the replica of Halliday's childhood home and notes, "Two late-'70s Ford sedans were parked in the driveway, one of them up on cider blocks." However, as Wade makes his great escape from the house after cleared the first gate, he grabs "The keys to the Halliday family car were on the pegboard next to the refrigerator. I grabbed them and rushed outside. The car (the one that wasn't up on the blocks) was a 1982 Ford Thunderbird." (p. 178). Um, a 1982 Ford Thunderbird is a not a late-'70s sedan. To add insult to injury, the continual run-on sentences, fragments, and incorrect grammatical structure for a list series nearly made my eyes cross. I am almost too terrified to ask what the original, unedited manuscript looked like.

Ready Player One is chock-full of frivolous details. If the book was distilled down to the story, it would probably cap out around 100-200 pages. Instead, Cline spends the majority of the book inundating the audience with pointless movie references, incorrect geeky trivia, and pages of detailed explanations of why Wade is the G.O.A.T. Cline relies too heavily on several bad plot devices such as the dreaded deus ex machina, hidden knowledge, and the Mary Sue. All of these elements are characteristics of immature writers. Unfortunately, these elements work together to create a book that is nothing more than a name-dropping info dump and testament to Cline's belief in his own "geek prowess".

The lengths to which Cline goes to incorporate all geekdom from the past several decades is laughable. In his attempt to show his godlike knowledge of all things geeky, Cline—surprisingly—got many things wrong. First of all, a Bag of Holding is a pocket dimension that is larger on the inside than the outside. It does not get heavier as you put more objects into it. Therefore, I am unsure why Wade could no longer fill the bag with gold or loot as he worked through the dungeon. Second, he cannot study the map of the dungeon to know where every single monster is located. In many of those old D&D books, wandering monsters were common and could not be predicted. Aside from the bosses and larger battles, it was a roll of the dice and up to the DM to decide what players would encounter. I don't even want to address what he did to the DeLorean or the Serenity . . . It made me weep and my husband homicidal. (Ernest Cline, if you are reading this, you do not deserve to have your picture taken in front of the DeLorean nor do you deserve to be lauded at ComicCon. Can the shit, you're not a geek or a nerd!)

Cline's desire to create the magnum opus of geekdom did nothing more than alienate true geeks and nerds by bastardizing what they love the most.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_text:
If you didn't live through the 1980s, this book's nostalgia appeal will be lost to you. If you actually paid attention to living through the 1980s, the sheer volume of factual inaccuracies and misrepresentation of the bygone pop culture this book pretends to celebrate will infuriate you.

Within the first chapter, the book claims that the 1985 version of Oingo Boingo's song Dead Man's Party opens with horns before vocals and that the Atari game Adventure contained the first video game Easter Egg. Neither is true, and that Klein couldn't be bothered to run web searches on the very sort of minutiae that he expects his characters to be obsessed with. This lack of accuracy, fact checking, and editorial competence permeates the book, with at least as many errors cropping up in each subsequent chapter.

Instead the author expects that his typical reader will have lived through the 1980s, but forgotten both the details and how to check them. As a former 1980s nerd, this is downright offensive, and I cannot believe that this book became the commercial success it is.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_title: Save yourself the time and find something better.
review_text:
Do you like being in a conversation where the other person only speaks in references and then sporadically reminds you of where those references came from so that you can both acknowledge that you consumed the same media before moving on? Would you like to read something where the author's idea of humor is making yet another reference that's barely connected to anything going on in the "story"? Do you want an extremely simple book that never challenges you or the main character with big words, meaningful conversations, or an actual challenge? If yes, fine, read this book from the library if you can.

As someone who plays video games and loves other nerdy media, I'm still not going to recommend this and I definitely don't think you should pay for it. It's obvious that Cline enjoys checking off lists of things he thinks are great to compare and gloat over other people with shorter lists. And now he's writing books to do it. This story has so many plot holes, one dimensional characters, and references that aren't needed that it hurts to call it a story. The main character is a NiceGuy that has somehow memorized thousands of hours of movies and tv shows, hundreds of books, hundreds of video game solutions, who knows how many "classic" albums, and is so amazing at all of the challenges that the amount of time he describes stalking (and he calls it stalking and tells her that he's stalking her) the main female character is longer than the time it takes for him to overcome any of the "obstacles" he faces.

Seriously, skip this book.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_title: I as a reader amleft wondering "How did this get published, given how many IP rights they must have bought?
review_text:
I'm about to say (LOTS OF SPOILERS) nothing good about a work of fiction that an author has worked on (WITH LOTS OF SPOILERS), and furthermore, which has proved popular with a lot more people than just me (WHO APPARENTLY ENJOY LOTS OF SPOILERS). I'm about to violate the golden rule; if you have nothing nice to say, say nothing. I'm also about to violate the silver rule, which is don't give away (LOTS OF SPOILERS)

Ready Player One is about some random teen whose parents are so negligent, his mom decides to name him similarly to a comic book character because his absentee father liked comic books.

The story basically follows a Mary-Sue from the moment they're offered a prize to the moment they win the prize, and they never do anything wrong unless it's already been established as a part of their backstory *why* they might do it wrong, but the story never goes so far as to address why or how they might go about learning, growing, or doing it right the second time around. The main character jumps off the backs of nameless, worthless, single-dimensioned characters in order to reach new heights, which was great in 1986 but does not make for compelling literary fiction.

And what's worse, the author knows that he has a one dimensional story. Again, there is no character growth, there isn't even a sense of tension, as one of the main character's Mary-Sue talents is to hide *within the ranks of the enemy that is seeking to kill him.* The author decides to cover up this (the absolute failing of the novel- a lack of a growth or tension narrative) by drowning both the character and the novel itself in pulp culture references that appeal to the demographic this author is targeting. Firefly, Gauntlet, Dungeons and Dragons, and about forty more other specific pieces of intellectual property appear in this novel, and I...

I as a reader am left wondering "How did this awful piece of literature make a profit, given how many IP rights they must have bought just to get it approved for publishing?"

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_text:
Disappointing, it reads like a Reddit forum when it comes to the dialogue between characters right at the start and it is dripping in "Remember the 80's?" nostalgia. Which, quite frankly, is boring. For the story to be set so far in the future, yet everyone is obsessed with the past, it is very much making fun of the current 25-30 year olds living in the real world.

Wade lives in his Virtual Reality (VR) headset and admits to being a fat kid, who's VR avatar is the opposite of what he looks like. Great kid, you're not special a lot of people do that. But he walks around thinking he's superior to everyone else since he knows every obscure bit of science fiction which he intentionally alienates himself from the rest of the VR community because he thinks he's that special. Which, if you have ever played an MMO, you know that Wade is an utter moron. He sits moping about, unable to leave the school planet because he doesn't have enough money to transport off, doesn't have a high enough level to fight anything for XP, yet claims he can't ask for help because it would be rude and he wants to do everything himself. He claims every player starts off on a spawn planet and then later moves on, but he couldn't. Which makes no sense because he's been living in the VR world for 5 years at this point and has only made it to level 3? I don't think so. Wade is a lame hero

The reason for my title of the review was I initially thought this book looked good and interesting. However, after flipping through the pages it suddenly dawned on my that Ernst Cline basically ripped off the plot to Sword Art Online (SAO), and barely changed the details. With those unfamiliar, SAO is a VR world were players get to be knights and fight in medieval settings such as WoW, Skyrim, Dragon Age, etc. However, on the day of the launch, 10 thousand people are trapped inside the headset because if they take it off the headset will short circuit and fry their brains. If they die in the game, the same result. So the players are forced to complete 100 levels of the Tower to clear the game and save everyone, after two years and rough 400-500 people dead, a lot of people have given up getting out and are living normal lives. Turns out the creator of the game is living in the game with everyone and the main character kills him and the game is over.

In Ernest Cline's version, the creator of the game died and now everyone is trying to find hidden clues to unlock gates so they can be the owner to the copyright of the VR company. So people live inside the headsets basically and live normal lives as the real world sucks. Everyone ends up living in a dudebro's arcade fever dream of the 80s, which perhaps is a far worse fate.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel

review_text:
I want to support writers and rarely return books. But this disappointed me from chapter one. I thought this would be so interesting. Loved the 80’s references. But this is fiction, and heavy-handed diatribes, eg hating on religion, inserted as internal thought with little attempt to even hide them in the plot don’t belong in story.
It’s funny that he can go from having Wade long for the kind of family in the sitcom “Family Ties” to knocking everything about the society that built that kind of security and stability. That TV show at least showed characters who had differing attitudes, conservative and liberal, deep and shallow.
The author goes on to blast God and organized religion at least three times in chapter one. When he does present a religious character, I thought, “Good. He is going to give a different viewpoint from the author’s own bias.” Instead, he presents her devotion as eascapism equivalent to his video game hunt. Why would this kind of bias be slammed for racism but accepted here? Sorry, but this book is just not for me.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_title: Totally disappointed after reading all the hype
review_text:
I wanted to love this book, but ended up not even really liking it. I give it two stars only because it has a good-heart and some fun ideas, especially with regards to technology and classic 80's pop culture (such as how Zork and Joust are used in the book).

The cons however are numerous:

The prose is truly terrible. I felt like a well-written eighth-grader wrote this, including prose style, character development, and plotting.

Too much exposition. Too many descriptions of things in the 80's that I already knew, or didn't care about if I didn't. A quick mention is fine. We have google, you know.

Predictable. What's to say? I bet you can guess how it ends 5 minutes into it.

The "bad-guys" are typically flat. The main character is okay; likable, but boring. The love interest is fine, but not terribly deep as far as female leads go either.

Not many plot twists. The one there was, was also predictable.

Also it's hard to tell who this is written for: nostalgic 40-somethings looking back on the 80's, or adolescents ? Either one I would think would be disappointed, and yet the other reviews here make it clear it's probably succeeding well with both groups. For me it was a big disaster. I'm in the nostalgic 40-somethings camp. I liked parts of it, but overall I enjoyed just watching WarGames over more than actually trudging through this mess.

review_text:
As much as I enjoyed Gödel, Escher, Bach, I have only so much appetite for the self-referential. Here we have a piece of fiction about a fictional world obsessed with nostalgia (another piece of fiction). The icing on the cake is that Spielberg is going to make a movie (another fantasy world) to cap this exercise. The pretext for the action (the hunt for the fortune) is hardly sufficient to make me spend the time with this.
The second star is given in gratitude for not having to read it, or see the flick.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_text:
Way too many cringe-worthy moments throughout the book for me. There's a reviewer quote printed on the book that states "...The grown-up's Harry Potter" Um, no. Harry Potter (even as a kids series) is honestly 100x more intelligent, interesting, and well-written. If this book is supposed to be for adults, it completely misses the mark. I also have to mention the fact that apparently in the future there are no females, because somehow half the world's population is not shown to exist in this story's world. The only capable female character is basically a manic pixie dream girl who the main character has a crush on. That's it! It's a total boy's club from start to finish.

Also I just have to say this, the line "My God, it's full of stars" was NOT from Kubrick's 2001: Space Odyssey adaptation like Cline said it was. The line is a classic from Arthur C. Clarke's novel, which Kubrick chose not to include. Inconsistencies like this make me think Ernest Cline is a complete faux nerd, who instead of actually being genuinely passionate or interested in the 70's/80's, just googled a bunch of stuff and attempted to throw in as many references as he could cram in. I'm truly surprised how many people seem to like this book. I gave it two stars for the concept, which I think could have been great in another writer's hands.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_title: "Holy Grail of Pop Culture"? Let's be serious.
review_text:
The "Holy Grail of pop culture"? Come on, now. It should be titled "That's Familiar! References to Things That You've Heard Of."

Man is this a bad book. Firstly, there is no tension, whatsoever, because in order to succeed in it, one must merely have an encyclopedic knowledge of books/movies/TV shows/video games/comic books from the 80s. Not just a passing knowledge of or familiarity with, but a note-for-note, word-for-word, action-for-action rote recitation ability to recreate any random bit of 80s(ish) pop culture that gets thrown at you. Which is convenient because Wade Watts (who is clearly a thinly veiled attempt at Cline making himself the hero of his own story) has memorized every possible bit of late 70s, 80s and early 90s pop culture trivia (as well as some random references from the 50s and silent movie eras, for some reason), and any other thing a person in his 40s in 2018 might remember from his childhood. Oh hey, Ernest Cline is a person in his 40s in 2018, isn't he? Weird.

Not only are the references so frequent and repetitive that they are oppressive, they are, for the most part, entirely pointless to the story. The majority of these references are cheap throwaway gags. The sheer volume of material Wade is supposed to have read, seen, or played, and memorized by the age of 18 (or whatever he is) demonstrates a total lack of grasp on the author's part of how time works. Every single book by Stephen King. Every episode of Family Ties (multiple times). Every movie by John Wu or John Hughes. Every obscure Japanese Anime show or book. He's played Pac Man so much a perfect game is no challenge whatsoever. Same for Joust. He's seen War Games something like 130 times, and knows it even better than he does The Breakfast Club and... some other "classic 80s" movie I can't recall off the top of my head. Which he has also seen, presumably, more than a hundred times. He's also seen Monty Python and the Holy Grail tens of dozens of times, and has every bit of dialog, every scene, every gesture memorized. But still managed to find the time to play every other game from the 80s, see every other movie from the 80s, watch every TV show from the 80s, read every comic book, sci-fi, and fantasy novel from the 80s... And yes, he knows every one of them by heart. As it is convenient to the story. But totally absurd to life in general. Even for a bookish nerd who says things like "going outside is highly overrated." Literally nothing seems so obscure or so unlikely for a person to enjoy in 2040-whatever that he hasn't completely immersed himself in its world enough that he knows it almost precisely as well as every other thing he has completely immersed himself in. Yet he still has time to hang out in chat rooms to argue the finer points of Star Wars with other nerds. To the glee of everyone watching, I might add. Because people enjoying watching nerds argue is timeless.

Some of this would be forgivable if it weren't just plain badly written. If Cline had an editor, this book would be half as long as it is. It is repetitive, it is overly descriptive of silly minutiae, except for the times when something merely serves as a platform to make a throwaway reference to a "classic" movie/book/TV show/video game ("classic" apparently meaning "something from the 80s you've heard of). Also its fawning treatment of all things 80s is over the top. I lived in the 80s, not everything was that great. (Zork? Really? They spend time in a virtual reality in which literally anything is possible, and they use it to play text-based adventure games from 1977?) It's also pretty gross in its descriptions of sex, masturbation, and general human relationships. Speaking of which, not a single character, not even the narrator, is a fully fleshed out, let alone remotely believable human being that you should possibly care about. All of this is ignoring the dozen or so uses of deus ex machina. Which get to the point of being so predictable, it is impossible to imagine any scenario that Wade Watts isn't going to just realize his way out of with his pitch-perfect knowledge of a "classic 80s" movie/TV show/video game/comic book/, or conveniently have already purchased the thing he needed to get out of it all along, he just failed to mention it before then. Man did I hate this book.

Now, some would probably be quick to suggest that I am not the target audience. But I am a 43 year old white male, who grew up in the 80s, consumed loads of 80s pop culture, and remember much of it rather fondly. I even recall the Christmas I got my Atari 2600 and Boba Fett with Slave One as being probably the best one of my entire childhood, except maybe the one when I got my Nintendo Entertainment System. So it's hard to know, if I am not the target audience for this book, who might be. People who don't care if a book is compelling or well written, as long as it's referential, I guess.

Anyway, I'm adding an extra star for no other reason than grading on the curve. This is not the worst book I have ever read. Not by a long shot. But it is definitely much, much less than what it has been made out to be. This is a bad book, and that needs to be said. And I'm guessing his next one, the plot of which sounds awfully familiar to The Last Starfighter, will also be pretty terrible. But good for him, I guess, for finding a way to monetize cheap nostalgia. I'd suggest he should invest his money well. This is not built to last.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_text:
After reading some initial reviews, I had high hopes for the novel. I was pretty disappointed.

First, the good news: The novel moves along like very well. It would be a good book to pick up at the airport newsstand if you want to forget you are flying from San Antonio to Milwaukee. It would also not be worth the effort to carry it off the plane when you finished.

But as chipper as the protagonist tries to be about his universe, it is an incredibly dismal, derivative and ultimately tawdry place. Imagine a world where the highest ideals of mankind are expressed in 80's video game culture. The dialog is about as deep as Pacman and Mario.

It feels like a cheesy script for a B-list summer blockbuster.

The cover blurb compares it to the Matrix. Ir reads like a cheap rip-off of The Hunger Games. HINT: Instead of reading a book that praises William Gibson and Neal Stephenson, READ William Gibson and Neal Stephenson. Or if dystopia is your thing, might I suggest Margaret Atwood?

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_text:
Reading this was physically painful but I kept on trucking until the very end. Overall I would describe this as a nostalgia fueled autistic fan-fiction crammed with illogical political posturing and pontification.

Pros:
Parts of the book, particularly the bits that revolved around the actual, advertised plot, were quite good. There were times where I legitimately enjoyed reading this book.

Cons:
Extreme progessivist slant, to the point where Cline's world-building suffered immensely. Within the first 25 pages I almost put it down, never to read it again. However, being that I am supposed to read this as part of a book club, I had to soldier on. No real explanation for these holes in the world, I guess Cline was expecting his target audience (virtue signalling gamur gurls and nu-males) to just accept it. Many parts of the novel were cringe-inducing, autistic and awkward, especially the entire romance sub-plot. I think the very worst part of the novel in this regard was the surprise character reveal near the end. When Cline indicated it was going to happen, I paused for a second to concoct the worst progressive, Tumblr, racist, trash fan-fiction reveal I could think of in my head and continued to read. As it so happens I was nearly spot on, getting only one thing wrong (The character was not in a wheelchair). Too predictable, too much pandering.

I rate this book 3/10, would not read again, nor would I recommend it.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_title: SPOILERS: Ironically, the main characters and the quest were one dimensional...
review_text:
As a child of the 80's, I really wanted to like this book. Unfortunately, I don't think it's well written. You have to give the author some credit on the imaginative aspects of the book. His ideas about how an VR world would work and appear are interesting. I also enjoyed his descriptions of the real world (which were few because most of the time was spent in VR...hence the moral of the story). That's about where my enjoyment ended.

I read that most people did not enjoy the first half of the book and I didn't find that to be true myself...I had a hard time getting though the end. Every chapter was another nauseating repeat of the previous chapters 80's references and copy/paste of the previous "challenge" with some details changed. Spoiler: The last gate that you are anxiously awaiting the entire novel, which you believe must be much more difficult than the previous two...is..wait for it..the exact same as the first one, with a different theme. The main character jokes about how easy it is. Which is really my biggest critique..why does he constantly talk about how easy everything is? There is no tension and when there's a problem, the solution is that the characters magically figure it out. Light bulb! It takes away from the reader engaging and trying to figure it out too. Unless you are the type that would know obscure references to a fictional characters childhood manifesto (which is not shared with the reader).

I also felt that there were forced topics, just thrown in for shock value: religion bashing (I thought his slew of angry anti-God quotes at the beginning would lead to something at the end, they didn't), the race, gender and sexuality of a character at the end(her male avatar was IRL a female, black, homosexual - this was *shocking* to the main character and again did not drive the plot forward, answer any questions or was shocking at all to the readers)and the big corporations are horrible was so forced, I think it would've been better played with more subtlety and less complete villains.

Also, one last thing: anyone else have a hard time with the main character's love interest? I felt nothing between them except an undying love from him and a complete hatred from her. Then at the end, you're just supposed to believe that all of her mean comments, selfishness and negativity go away and she was really in love with him too? I just didn't buy it.

I really enjoyed the descriptions of Wade's real world, how the OASIS worked, and the details about Halliday. Ironically, the main characters and the quest were unbelievable and one dimensional. Taking a cue from the Hunger Games-- the world and your characters are more important than the actual game. The upcoming movie could be good if they make the characters more relatable and flesh out the "game" more. I think seeing it on screen will be more entertaining than the "telling" that was done in the book.

review_text:
I am obviously in the minority here, but I didn't care for this book.

Cline has a clear, direct writing style. that's good, particularly in this age age when many best-sellers are almost incoherent due to pretentious prose.

I grew up in the 1980s. I enjoyed 1980s TV, music, movies, video games and other pop culture. but smashing every possible 80s item together in virtual reality doesn't necessarily make for a good story to me.

after the scene where the protagonist plays the arcade game Joust against a reanimated wizard called a Lich ... I just couldn't take the story seriously. it was too silly, and shattered my suspension of disbelief.

the Spielberg film will probably be a smash hit. perhaps I'll enjoy the movie more than the book.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_title: Looking for a way to turn your brain off? Weed and video games not cutting it anymore? Try this!
review_text:
This is honestly a pretty terrible book. If I wanted something as mind-numbing as this, I would watch a Twitch FPS stream or do countless other mindless activities. Typically, when I pick up a book, it's not to turn my brain off, it's to gain stimulation.

I feel like the majority of words in this book serve not to develop characters or plot but as an excuse for the author to regurgitate pop culture references and play out fantasies through his insufferable teenaged protagonist.

The final straw that motivated me to waste more time on this book, writing this review, came after I started counting Ernest Cline's use of the words "perfect" and "perfectly." He seems to think that it's the "perfect" adjective for all situations. It's not. It's just a lazy, cop-out way of inserting a description without actually developing an image or atmosphere.

"But the book is written from the perspective of a teenager, it's meant to sound juvenile," you might say. No. Maybe that excuses the weak vocabulary and egocentric main character, but that's not the limit of the poor writing in this book. By highschool, one should know that a story told from the first-person perspective should not simply state what one did.

A fake excerpt from the book: "I walked into the house, then I saw the bad guy, then I shot him in the perfect spot that I knew would kill him. My gun made a sound that perfectly immitated the Star Wars saber sound effect because I hacked it to do that. It was a perfect replica of a Star Trek phaser except with a Ghost Busters logo on it, the old 80's classic that I had watched literally millions of times in my 17 years of sentience."

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_title: Welp, reads like an amateur novel, that's for sure.
review_text:
I don't get it.

I am usually very open to books, but this reads like an English high school project. It's full of one-dimensional characters whose sole purpose was to prop up the protagonist. Exposition after exposition made the whole book feel like a pilot episode of a television show that wasn't all that great to begin with. I appreciated all of the throwbacks to the things I especially loved about my own childhood, but maaaan, after a certain point my eyes just rolled out of my head and onto the floor as I turned into a skeleton and died.

The whole setup for the plot feels like a fever dream to me. It feels like a weak episode of Black Mirror with a premise that you've seen countless times before. It reads like someone got inspired to write a novel after a weekend binge on video games and manga. And that feeling never leaves. There is this weird disconnect throughout the whole novel that keeps reminding you, the reader, that this is indeed a book, and it was written by an author, and the whole thing is just one big joke.

I dunno, maybe I'm being a bit harsh, but I just found this whole book completely predictable and honestly, kind of a snoozefest.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_text: This book was obviously written by a man, and it’s painful. The description and dialogue of Art3mis is ‘manic pixie dream girl’ in overdrive. Halliday is hardly Willy Wonka charming, but I guess what tech giant is? Wade gives me little to root for besides the fact that he’s poor. And he’s kinda transphobic for someone who claims he doesn’t care what someone looks like. The 80s references are abscure enough to really only be fun if you were literally a nerd who actually lived in the 80s. Not sure why the phrases “noob” and “posers” had to show up. 40 years into the future and we’re still calling opponents gay online? And if you are thinking about buying this book because you enjoyed the movie, don’t. But the final straw was that despite this ‘shove it in your face’, pop culture confetti, I MADE AN OBSCURE REFERNCE IM SMART attitude, you managed to misspell Tatooine. Un. Forgive. Able.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_title: Cline's vindicating his nerdy past with weak writing.
review_text:
I was told to read this by many people who have always given me great reviews. For a road trip I decided to download this book and listen through Audible. This is the first time in a long time where I gave up on a book. The premise of the book sounded great, I grew up in the 90s and love video games and sci-fi stories and could almost be the second target audience for this book. Sadly I could not believe how lazy and weak the actual writing was. Multiple times the writer would create a set up for "Chekhov's Gun" (literary device) with out any delivery. If an object or ability or topic is reference early in the book, it should become relevant during the story. The best example I could think of is after Wade finds the Copper key. Wade tells the reader " the key cannot be traded or stored and if the player holding is killed while holding the key, they will drop the key and it will disappear from their inventory as I would later find out". I might have the quote wrong but I finished 3/4s of the book until I finally gave up because of the use "I would later find out." There was never any pay off.

The Oasis is an interesting playground for Cline where he could make anything happen. Unfortunately he relies on the readers understanding of 80s pop culture to fill in his inability to create an impressive world. Cline does not describe what an object looks like, instead he more-or-less is asking the reader "Did you watch Knight Rider, Back To The Future, and Ghostbusters? Great, that's this vehicle" or "The ship was an exact replica of The Bebop from Cowboy Bebop". If these objects are not going to be important to the story, why even describe them with a nerdy nod? That is how fan-fiction is not a great book.

Wade Watts, our guide and hero, is one of the most unbelievable characters I have seen in fiction. He is a 17-18 year old in high school when the book begins who we are told is an expert on the 80s due to The Hunt. The Hunt begins when Wade is a child and dedicates his life through self profession that he has perfect memorized of every sitcom, drama, commercial, movie, and pop culture books of the 80s. About 3/4th through the book Wade has to play a guitar and admits "he has never held an actual guitar but can shred on a virtual one easily." Assuming he is 7 when The Hunt begins, we as the reader are to assume that in 10 years a child has actually become an expert on topics that are over 60 years old when the story begins while performing in school, and has great proficiency at playing a musical instrument. Sorry Cline, this is isn't realistic and killed my interest in not just your story but you as an author.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_title: Reads like the lovechild of Stephanie Meyer and Dan Brown. Run. Now.
review_text:
There's maybe a handful of scenes in the entire thing. It's just the writer telling the reader things. The characters never feel like they're in any real trouble, and the most interesting parts of the world are glossed over in a whirlwind of nostalgic lip service which grows tedious. The author also employs cheap tactics like having the narrator hide information from the reader despite the narrator having the information. Continually, the author sandwiches things into parenthesis because he didn't edit or fully develop and earlier part of the story.

Honestly, the setting is powerful and amazing. That save this from being one star. However, the writer bungles the telling of the story unfolding against that setting.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_title: "Fortunately, I had prepared for this in advance." THE END
review_text:
Look: I literally played Zork on a Commodore 64, as a teenager in the 80s. I pumped quarters into Joust. I watched WarGames a million times. I should have fallen in love with this book. Unfortunately, it's UTTERLY BORING. It was given to me four months ago, and I still haven't quite finished it -- and I usually finish a novel of this length in two days! Instead, I have found excuses to read other books. I have read books I've read before. This never happens! I've still got a bookmark at the 7/8ths mark of Ready Player One, and if I'm still bored, THAT far into the novel, it's an extremely bad sign.

There is no suspense whatsoever. Even if you forget that the protagonist tells us, right up front, that he has won, and the actual story is one long flashback, you will be frequently reminded, by the way no threat or problem lasts long, or seems possibly unbeatable. Wade can't fail, and doesn't even come close to it. You know up front he wins, and the rest of the story is a long, boring description of his countless and immediate victories.

Every threat or problem the protagonist faces is immediately solved, because the protagonist is ridiculously clever, and already has the solution, because he's prepared for everything. Even when he's imprisoned as an indentured servant, for all of eight days -- which should be a horrible experience that makes us worry for him -- it was his plan to be imprisoned, he's there under a false identity, and within those eight days, he effortlessly fools his captors, and escapes with the vital data he needs to continue winning.

That's about where I've left off. When I have time to kill -- waiting for a doctor's appointment, etc. -- I'll continue reading, from one clever and immediate victory after another, knowing our hero wins the game and gets the girl. I will not be changed or moved in any way. Aside from showing off the author's 80s-geek cred (which is both unrealistic and cringeworthy), this book seems to have no point at all.

I liked the setup, but once it really got into the story, I knew it was going to be bad.  I should have stuck with my gut and quit.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_text:
I got this after seeing the movie and hearing from a few friends about how different the book is. My two main points after reading this book in 3 days:

1. Love the 80's pop culture references integrated into the story. No book I've ever read has ever gone this deep into 80's game, movie, TV, music references. The writer is obviously a true 80's fanatic and geek. No doubt about that, this guy has lived it and did his homework.

2. The main character is completely unlikable. He never arcs or changes, even at the end (finding 'love' is not a character change). Honestly, I've never read a book where the main character is just a complete and utter unlikeable character even to the end. You never really want this jerk to succeed. His inner workings and thoughts are as just about as bad as the main villain.

Conclusion-
Steven Spielberg did a brilliant job taking the meat of this story and actually making the primarily character LIKEABLE because the writer was just down right horrible at it. If the filmmakers had followed the book, no doubt it wouldn't have been successful. I did enjoy the 80's references, but too bad the main character was unlikable.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_title: an epic journey for a niche audience
review_text:
pooled ink Reviews:
2.5 Stars

This book is truly an ode to the origins and spirit of classic videogames. The plot bleeds gaming geekdom and was like stepping into an 80s game quest itself. It was a blend of the relatable and creative but also of the cliché. If you have a love for classic gaming algorithms brought into a high-tech dystopian age then you’ll probably really like this.

I, however, had expected it to be more of a fast-paced action plot with gaming elements but the emphasis on gaming was intense. Rather than a race against time that gets dirty for the prize of a lifetime set within a dystopian world that escapes within virtual reality, this was…this was largely an info guide for all computer systems, gaming systems, and video games from the 1980s packed in with other 80s trivia.

Overall this book was a struggle for me to get through, not because it wasn’t cool or interesting but just because the plot struggled to move forwards constantly hindered by the lengthy explanations and info dumps that in the grand scheme of things really weren’t necessary. It was like watching a cult classic movie only to have your friend constantly press ‘Pause’ just to vomit up a bunch of movie trivia that you really don’t care about nor need to know to understand or enjoy the movie.

I think if you’re a true fan of 80s gaming then you really might enjoy this book. I bet the boys from Stranger Things would love this book. So if that’s you then huzzah! And if not then maybe wait a few months and check out the movie instead.

**Read the full review on Wordpress: Pooled Ink

title: Ready Player One: A Novel

author: Ernest Cline
review_title: I had heard about this book earlier this year from ...
review_text:
I had heard about this book earlier this year from one of my students, but it didn't sound THAT intriguing to me, so I put it on the back burner of my "to read" list. In early January I was scrolling through a Buzzfeed article about books that were going to be turned into movies in 2018. Ready Player One was on that list, and then a few weeks ago I found it on the shelf at Half Price Books. I knew I just had to pick it up.
Once I started reading this book, I just couldn't stop! The story is so interesting and I was dying to know who would find the Easter Egg in "The Oasis" first. While science fiction/dystopian may not be the most original genre, this story is truly one of a kind.
The pop-culture references also make this a book that can span many generations, I understood many of the references, but I know my parents would have found them even more entertaining. That is one pitfall of this novel though, I think it runs the risk of becoming dated very quickly.
However, I think the basic premise is extremely interesting and I am excited to see how they adapt it to the screen!

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_title: A well-created blend of fun and important messages
review_text:
Ready Player One technically has a very specific ideal target audience -- aficionados of 80s culture who are fans of video games and dystopian-sci-fi lit. Being born in the late 1980s, I didn't quite fall into the ideal audience. However, I am a fan of video games, dystopian/sci-fi, and clever books. Thus, I found Ready Player One to be an enjoyable joyride. In Cline's futuristic world, video games and social media and escapism have collided to bring the world the "OASIS." The OASIS is everything: a game, the internet, social networking, school, the world's biggest public library containing just about every piece of writing, music, or video, there for the taking. It is also an escape, a world that isn't crumbling while the real world outside falls to pieces. It is being threatened by the IOI, a corporate entity that wants to take the virtual utopia and monetize it so only the rich can afford to utilize it.

I found the dichotomies present in Ready Player One to be quite interesting. While it is clear that Cline set out to make a dystopia where people would rather spend their time in a perfect, fake world than fix their real one, I found certain elements of the story quite optimistic. For instance, that users with no money, like the protagonist, could access every book ever written, every song ever listened to, and every video ever watched. In our day and age of extremists against freedom of information, of Big Hollywood pushing laws like SOPA and CISPA ever closer to passing, of pundits who act like online piracy will be the downfall of civilization as we know it... Well that right there would very nearly make me willing to live in Cline's world, because I think we are headed in the complete opposite direction of such free culture. In the same vein, I have a hard time believing that file-sharing programs will be around, like the Guntorrent Wade mentions.

Getting off the soapbox on that controversial point, I bring up another thing I doubt our culture will have sense enough to hold onto: privacy. I feel it is overtly optimistic to the point of absurdism to believe that in 32 years, there will ever be such a degree of privacy where the company running the OASIS wouldn't even be able to look up an avatar's true identity. Again, we're headed in the opposite direction. We don't even have this degree of freedom right now, and I doubt the Supreme Court is going to change for the better in the future.

However, it is clear that the society Cline has created is deeply flawed. Little to no human interaction occurs in this world. Humanity spends all of its collective free time in the OASIS. Society has shifted to cater to this -- ways to allow people to never have the leave their rooms; new systems to make the OASIS seem more real than reality ("The real world looked washed-out and blurry by comparison.") Elections in the OASIS come to matter more than the government's. The economy is now based on a credits system that the OASIS uses. Instead of living in the real world and taking a break in the OASIS, people live in the OASIS and feel that any breaks to reality are forced and undesired. Such a society cannot continue on as such indefinitely.

Overall, I greatly enjoyed Ready Player One. The writing was entertaining, humorous, and poignant in all the right places. Cline's voice speaks not only to those who are fans of the 80s culture the hunt revolves around, but to current internet users, video game players, and people who are concerned about the way our society is headed. The events in the OASIS are action-packed, but Cline doesn't let the events in the real-world fall flat, either. The world he has built, both the real and virtual sides, is immensely interesting. The characters are also quirky and well-developed, adding much to the story. If anything about the premise of Ready Player One appeals to you, I'd encourage you to pick it up. It's a fun novel, with messages that speak to you long after you've put it down.

title: Ready Player One: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – June 5, 2012
author: Ernest Cline
review_text:
In the not-too-distant future it turns out Al Gore et al. were right - we've burned through most of our fossil fuels, triggered severe global climate change, and life is miserable for the average person. Much of humanity copes by spending a large part of their lives in the virtual world of the OASIS (basically a virtual reality MMORPG that has become the primary means of interfacing with the internet). When the eccentric multi-billionaire creator of OASIS dies his will leaves all of his assets to whoever can find an "Easter egg" he hid in the OASIS. The main clue is hundreds of pages of a rambling journal centered around his obsession with 1980's pop culture (especially of the nerdier variety). The book is the first person account of the "gunter" (egg hunter) who made the first major breakthrough in finding the Egg.

This whole thing is an excuse to revel in 80's geekiness. However, it has enough edge-of-your-seat treasure hunt kind of tension that even someone who isn't an uber-geek should still be able to enjoy it. Stylistically speaking, this isn't a masterpiece of writing/plotting. There were parts I found annoying like occasional preachy/ranty bits, quite a few "colorful metaphors," and plot points that were just a little too convenient and/or predictable. Despite all that, my nerdy born-in-1980 side really enjoyed it, and I wouldn't be surprised if it makes my top-5 fiction reads of the year list in December.

review_text:
Awesome book for anyone who was a teen in the 80s. I totally got most of the culture references and knew several super nerds who had a terrifyingly deep knowledge of (pick one), RUSH (songs, liner notes, band bios, etc), video games, movies, Japanese cartoons, 80s sitcoms, etc etc.

The book is also a great story of late-teen self-discovery where Parzival, our protagonist, must come to terms with who he is, his limitations and the differences between immersive simulated reality and the crude and mean 'real' world.

Finally, like all great books, there is a clear story arc, in this case, a Quest - almost a Grail Quest to solve a puzzle. Like all quests that matter, no one can get there alone.

This book easily moved into my top 5 of all time. Someone will probably make a movie and it will be horrible. Just read the book.

author: Ernest Cline
review_title: I thought the movie would outmatch the book, as usual. Man o man, was I wrong?
review_text:
I am not into SF/Fantasy novels, I have read "the Martian" by Andy Weir, but liked the movie better than the book, which is common for most people.
This is the first time it's the other way around. I missed the premier of the movie, so I bought the book until further notice.
I thought the movie would outmatch the book, as usual. But, man o man, was I wrong.
The book had me hooked from the start. The authors knowledge of the pop-culture of the 80's is both amazing and entertaining. There are things in here that I have never heard of or knew about, until I read this.

The story is about a dark future combined with existing technology and a passed decade's pop-culture, fancied by an eccentric genius, all woven together into a thrilling story about a young man who has a secret cyber-crush on a girl he has never meet before in real life, while competing against the entire world about the rights and ownership to what could be called, "the internet of the future".

It is also a story of fighting against an evil corporation who sees this competition as nothing more than another way to increase their power and to seize control over the internet. And their true goal is to limit the access of the internet to only those who have money, while leaving out everyone else.
This story has riddles, challenges, friendship, love, victories, defeats and setbacks. To win this competition you will need extensive knowledge of the 80's pop-culture and more. Buy it, you will not be disappointed.
If you haven't seen the movie, then dont worry, read this book first and you will get a story that is way more thrilling then the movie itself.

The idea behind the story was good- girl goes missing, family and friends in turmoil, everyone involved has a "what if" moment of guilt. But the writing was boring. There was no feeling or emotion to it, it was descriptive of a scene and nothing was ever really revealed within the writing, it was simply a boring way to lead you to believe a character was THE bad guy, but it would turn out that the character did something bad, but he wasn't the one responsible for taking the girl. review_text: I really wanted to like this book. I did. But I really had to force myself to finish and not just put it down. The characters were all highly unlike able and and made no sense! In the beginning I truly thought this book would be good, but this random stranger on the train was supposed to called around to track down the parents of teenagers on a train?? Really? I would’ve never even considered that a possibility in this day and age. Throughout the book you would think that one person is responsible and then out of nowhere a back story to a random person would come up to make you think it was them. This seemed to be a rambling novel with very little background information and not very well thought out. There was no- “oh, now I see....” moment. Then the ending! I can’t even believe that I read this whole book to find that the person responsible is so random and not connected to pretty much any of the book! A good thriller should’ve left me thinking ‘wow, we should’ve see that coming now that I know the ending”. But this is not one- the fact that it truest could’ve been a random person in the club that did this would probably be more believable.

title: I Am Watching You

author: Teresa Driscoll
review_title: boring and not clever at all
review_text:
Can not for the life of me understand how this got so many 5-star reviews!

First of all, the premise of the book is just ridiculous - that a woman on a train should have somehow prevented a girl she observed on the train from going missing. What could this woman have done. She kept saying she could have called the girl's parents. HOW? She doesn't know who the girl's parents are. And what if she did - how would that have changed anything at all. Or what - she could have told the girl (on the train going to London) to not go to London? Just preposterous.

Second, there were lots of hints about who might have been behind the disappearance of the girl. But then it turns out to be something completely different. A good mystery has one looking back at all the clues and then saying - oh I get it now. Not just some random other story that explains what happened.

Finally, it was just boring. I had to skip parts.

review_text:
I read Justice Redeemed and am half-way through the second book, Justice Burning. I will finish Justice Burning, but unless something changes, I won't be reading any more Darren Street books. Darren Street is not a likeable character. He creates much of the trouble he finds himself in. For a guy who is supposed to be a bright defense attorney, he does nothing to help his own case even though his Public Defender is an inexperienced young woman. His jail time in Justice Redeemend is brutal - I will accept at face value that it is reasonably accurate, but it is not something that I want to spend my free time reading about. A lot of violence in both books, and not a lot of legal intrigue.

Justice Burning finds Street taking vigilante justice against those who have wronged him in brutal, unforgiveable ways. Since there are more Darren Street books, I have to assume he lives through this - but I found I don't really care if he lives or not. Street is incredibly self-centered, does some really stupid things, and seems to be cheat on his girlfriend. What's to like about this guy?

Joe Dillard was a hot-head (like Street) and also caused a lot of his own problems - but he was more thrree-dimensional.

review_title: A Descent From the Dillard Books.
review_text:
First off, I enjoyed the Joe Dillard books (read all 8) so I was looking forward to this series. Not any more. I didn't care for the main character and for me that's a problem. He does stupid things (albeit for plot purposes). Example: "I want you to kill someone for me, here's the cash." Later: "I changed my mind but you can keep the money." Hmmm... I wonder how that's going to come back to bite him? The main villian is so over-the-top as to be almost cartoonish. Given what we learn about Clancey in the beginning of the book you have to wonder how he was able to continue his career. In the real world he would have been - at a minimum - fired and disbarred but, no, he ends up with a better job which he can conveniently use to repeat his underhanded methods to seek revenge on Street. Nearly every prosecutor, police officer, and prison guard apparently made their mission to make Street's life as miserable as possible. I skimmed through many parts of the prison chapters. The final chapters were a bit too implausible.
I have read many reviews of the second Street book and learned enough about the plot to conclude it's not for me. Too bad, Mr. Pratt. I think you went off the rails with this one. My humble recommendation: find a new main character and fewer implausible plot lines.

review_title: I devoured the whole series in about a month.  They're well written, a quick read and enjoyable through and through.
review_text:
A friend of mine "loaned" me all of Scott Pratt's Joe Dillard series books...1-8. I devoured the whole series in about a month. They're well written, a quick read and enjoyable through and through. My husband is a lawyer, and quite often I had some questions about the legality of some of the things that Joe was up against...each time, I was pleasantly surprised that the legal issues were well thought out and proved to be something that could actually happen. Now, all the situations that Joe is faced with throughout each book are very far fetched and quite extravagant...but that just kept me reading since it was so entertaining.

If you can get past the fact that it's a small town that is plagued with an abundance of drugs, murder, prostitutes, sex trafficking, millions upon millions worth of gold buried in a cave and a lawyer who is highly adept at blowing things up and chasing down criminals without regard to the law...then you'll love the series! I hope Mr. Pratt writes #9 soon...I'm going to have a Dillard-shaped hole in my life until he does.

title: Blood Defense (Samantha Brinkman Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Marcia Clark
review_title: Was Prepared To Hate It--But Got Converted
review_text:
This novel was a selection of First of the Month, and due to the timeliness given the end of the cable program about a particularly famous case of Ms Clark's, thought it poignant.

This is my first read of any of Ms.Clark's novels or other published books. I was expecting a somewhat recognised pattern of "famous person writes a book" quality. I can't speak to any other of the author's works, but I was unexpectedly reeled in immediately.The author has a commanding but not overweight use of the court system juxtaposed with an eminently agreeably disagreeable protagonist, a quasi-peer of the irascible Quincy, lawyer version. We get buy in rapidly with the main character, and the spiraling issues in which she is entangled, without becoming overly steeped in courtroom and legal micro-analyses. This is much more a character driven story, with process and procedure playing their parts, but not endless legal minutiae running as a surrogate for your post-JD law review.

If you're a semicolon hound, this is not the book for you; however, the dialogue and narrative are all appropriately written and roll effortlessly belying the effort to craft them. Many great one-liners, reminding/informing the reader at once that the author was not a trust fund grad or one who spoke only publicly consumable Latin or clench-jawed polysyllabic English. I've definitely thought of someone as 'an ass waffle' as a result.

Appreciated the twists and turns and their respective well written support. Don't want to give away anything as you should reserve those well-earned surprises from the text itself, but look forward to the second installment and where the characters go from there.

title: The Silent Patient

review_title: Reads like a Harlequin romance novel
review_text:
Honestly, if I could rate this a zero, I would. It reads like a cheesy Harlequin romance novel, with so much filler, it’s hard to remember what the actual storyline is. The dialogue with other therapists at the Grove is so childish, I almost could not read any further. Several times, Alicia is referred to as “a bitch” by doctors—I cannot imagine why the author chose to depict them as so blatantly unprofessional and adolescent. It’s quite disgraceful to the profession.
I stuck this book out, entirely because our book club chose it for the month. The more I read, the stupider I thought it was. I actually feel cheated for having spent full price on it. The conversations between people are poorly scripted, juvenile and unrelated to the storyline. The trite little sex scenes—-like a cheap trashy paperback. I’ve never rolled my eyes more than I did with this book. Every time the main character Theo says anything, he sounds like a teenager with a first crush. The famous plot twist at the end is deflating, at best. Predictable and ridiculous.
The whole diary thing reminds me of a high school essay, covered in red ink reprimands from the teacher, having been given a barely passable grade of D+. Unbearable.
I’ve always known that movies that get overhyped are usually way below par. This book is a perfect example of some great marketing through decent testimonials, but in the end, lacking any substance.
I would hesitate to recommend this book to anyone. I found it insulting, much like giving a 12 - year old a ‘See Spot Run’ book and telling them how wonderful it is, and how much they’ll get out of it.
Yes, you can make it through if you insist on reading it, but frankly I’d rather have my 20 hours and $25 bucks back. Let it go if you’re tempted to buy it. Invite a friend over for coffee and croissants, and enjoy some decent company. This book has no redeeming value whatsoever. I can’t imagine what possessed the publishers.

title: The Silent Patient
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Alex Michaelides
review_title: COULD HAVE BEEN SO MUCH BETTER!
review_text:
There was a recent article on the Washington Post about people no longer trusting journalists. Well, I no longer trust reviewers that climax on books ending up being disappointments. See, I have been burned and, frankly, I am tired of the hype circus. But I have been had again. Much hype has made about The Silent Patient, a ridiculous novel acclaimed by The New York Times, where it became an “instant number one bestseller.” Brad Pitt’s production company has optioned it. (Possibly, with a good scriptwriter given to rational thinking and serious editing, the picture could be an improvement from the novel.) I am relieved to find out that Kirkus Reviews was not part of the marketing propaganda, calling the mystery “amateurish, with a twist savvy readers will see coming from a mile away.” The Silent Patient has quite a few twists, in fact, starting from intriguing and developing into dumb and dumber.

The concept itself is seductive. I mean, speaking of dumb, I was caught. A psychotherapist wants to break the silence of a patient accused of murdering her husband, and through the exploring of her mind manage to solve the mystery. The minimalistic prose and short chapters with dramatic or cryptic endings are also appealing, both for readers who like a page-turner, and for the ones who hope that this will be intelligent, redolent, atmospheric, Hitchcockian.

Alas, alas!

What we have instead is a mystery with clues planted like artificial flowers, pretending to belong, but cheapening a tale that at first sounded promising. A seven-year-old could improvise a similar, disconnected tale.

While a lot of action happens in a mental institution and thus among experts of the human psyche, the story fills out with little character development. Superficial, it flows like a soap opera and ends with a grand guignol coup de theatre.

If I were asked, to the one who is just curious about Michaelides’s first novel, I’d say: No prob. It’s a fast read, you won’t waste too much of your time, and your grey cells will neither overwork nor will you catch a headache.

To the major critics who keep applauding rubbish, I may ask a couple of questions: Are you trying to kill literature? Who is going to give it a mouth-to-mouth resuscitation if you keep going?

To myself I’d mumble: Shut up and go back to your classics! Read once more The Murder of Roger Ackroyd, which has a similar approach to The Silent Patient’s. Agatha Christie, after all, knew what she was doing.

MJ Fortis – 7.24.2022

review_title: I didn't see the twists coming...
review_text:
This book was engrossing from start to finish. I listened to it on Scribd, and initially didn't think I would enjoy the male narrator's voice who appears most frequently in the audiobook, but it definitely grew on me. There are two narrators, one male, and one female.

A quick synopsis, Alicia and Gabriel live a seemingly happy life as husband and wife, until one day, Alicia shoots Gabriel in the face five times after he returns home and refuses to utter a word going forward. Alicia is sentenced to a mental hospital where Dr. Theo attempts to use psychotherapy to get Alicia to speak and reveal what happened that fateful night.

The story is told in both past and present tenses and we get excerpts from Alicia's diary both leading up to and following the killing of her husband.

What takes place in the unfolding of this story is one that I did not see coming up until it happened. I actually had to pause the audiobook to rethink what I had just heard in order to comprehend what had just happened. The mystery behind Alicia's silence and the disturbing events of that night totally took me by surprise and offered the rare treat of allowing the reader to enjoy the telling of the story coupled with the coupled shocking ending.
