title: The Butterfly Garden (The Collector Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Dot Hutchison
review_text:
The writing is fairly good, except for the language used by Maya (the first-person narrator). It seems too mature/self-possessed for a teenage girl. Maya had a strange emotional superiority as she worked to display no emotion or care. I have a hard time connecting with a character who may withhold from other characters but also the reader. The author may have had a conscious choice for this character, but given the intensity of the story the reader needs a reason to care about Maya beyond her horrific lifelong trauma.
As for content/story, anything involving sexual abuse of minors is tough to read (especially in fiction where it gets unnecessarily graphic or gratuitous). I understood the need to explain the backstory and why the reader would want to root for Maya, but there was too many visits to things already established. I had a hard time staying with this book and the resolution didn't seem worth the investment.
With this said, other readers may love this book for all the reasons I didn't. I like complex and imperfect female characters who get tested and prove their mettle and I didn't feel that way about Maya.

review_title: Incredibly dark, but the world building is intense and shudderingly thorough
review_text: This book is really good about getting the whole story to the reader, eventually. But there are two things that might be an issue. The story mainly comes as an interview of one of the victims, which isn't weird in itself. But you might have to use some suspension of disbelief on the have that she remembers literally everything. The tiny tiny details, from years ago. She's presented as someone who doesn't forget anything, but it's still somehow too much. The other thing, at one point in the story, she gets important news on someone and reacts against expectation, but there is never an explanation for this. More than anything else, this grated. But, the story did actually resolve itself, as much as it could I think. Details we might have wanted on what happens next aren't there, but I'm not sure they had to be either. If I didn't have these few issues, maybe I'd rather it higher. As is, 4 stars seems fair.

review_text:
Stupidest book I have ever seen. The pictures shows are certainly not going to be the first words of any child.
Firstly, there are 4 pictures per page. Toddlers cannot focus on multiple things at once, why not have a single picture per page?
Secondly, some of the pictures are just stupid. For example, there are pictures of a dog and a puppy on the same page. And the size of the puppy is the same as the size of dog. How is a toddler supposed to know or care about what differentiates a puppy from a dog when they are both depicted of being the exact same size?
This book is not written with a toddlers perspective in mind.

review_title: Bad layout of items. Geared for boy babies.
review_text: I was really looking forward to this board book, however I am disappointed. I don't like the layout of the items. I think -simple- words and "more meaningful to young kids" words should be listed in the beginning of the book, and more complex items/words towards the end. Like banana, orange, cat, dog should be before dump truck, train, and fire engine. Start off simple and then get more complex. The illustrations for some of these items in the beginning of the book are also more complex, while simpler illustrations/words are in the back. It makes no sense unless you are teaching these to a kid that already has a great understanding of all these things, though the age for the book is 0+. Lastly, there are way too many boy babies in this book! 17 boys (very obvious) and 2 girls. What about girl babies!?

review_title: Awesome, but get a 9v power adapter
review_text:
Love this thing, the 9v battery option isn't the greatest. I bought a few of these as gifts and one for me. Once I powered it up I immediately ordered a few 9v adapters to give along with the WWITG. It requires a 9v power supply with a 5.5mm x 2.1mm plug, center positive. They are common on here, I paid 8.99 for each one but what a difference it makes!!

Also, don't grab the cheapest one, look for one with a substantial cord on it so you have some leeway as to where you plug it in!! The $6-7 ones appear to have very short cords.

title: Say You're Sorry (Morgan Dane Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Melinda Leigh
review_title: Tone-deaf take on the criminal injustice system, written at a YA level
review_text: While there are some plot twists that could be perceived as interesting, they're barely believable, and the author of this book would really benefit from reading The New Jim Crow or watching 13th, or learning ANYTHING about how broken our criminal injustice system is. There are countless examples of hypocrisy in this sub-par novel—from being outraged at the way one poor, innocent white kid is treated while simultaneously calling everyone in pre-trial detention "hardened criminals," to the myriad jabs taken at Public Defenders, because "how could anyone help a 'criminal' get away with a crime?" (Hint: constitutional rights.) This is a completely tone-deaf portrayal of a really truly, very broken criminal "justice" system that prioritizes white people over people of color and rich over the poor. The author borders on Hero Worship when writing about police officers, talks often about the importance of carrying guns, and ascribes throughout the book to the general narrative that prosecutors are heroes, and most people in jail are guilty, worthless, and deserve to rot there. There is no critical thought whatsoever - though I kept reading hoping that through Morgan's journey from Prosecutor to PD she would understand how often the system drags someone (mostly people of color) through it and destroys their life (see: Kalief Browder), but there was no such revelation. The book itself is written at the level of Young Adult fiction, and at times borders on softcore porn. I would never read anything this woman writes again unless she gets some education on the widespread, life-destroying injustices inflicted onto kids and people of color by our prejudiced system, and stops trashing the people who work to defend those who stand accused.

review_title: Woke? Check, Politically Correct?  Check  Good Story?  NOPE  Interesting lead character?  NOPE
review_text:
I guess it's pretty difficult to get any manuscript past the "woke" police now a days, but you would think that a writer as prolific as Michael Connelly would not have to check the boxes. The main character, Renee Ballard, is a wanna be detective with a chip on her shoulder that Robert Conrad would have trouble lifting. She is rude, overbearing, ego centric, and wears her tragedy like a thorny crown. In everyone's face, works behind everyone's back, hides evidence to be able to release it to her own advantage, makes tactical mistakes and rationalizes them, she is a one woman wrecking crew determined to destroy her and her partners careers as long as she gets her man.
The reader is constantly reminded that trans are people too, women on the job are persecuted, being homeless is wonderful, well organized and the actual homeless are reasonable, rational people who really want to do better. Renee is the only angel in a city of evil and she has to constantly remind other officers, even nurses and doctors that being woke is the only religion worth practicing.
I'm calling bull puckey. I only made it about 25% into this before I had to stop, that or die aspirating my own vomit.
I really enjoyed the Harry Bosch series and I believe that I have read every one of that series. Harry had years to build up his rep, and was a mature hard working dedicated detective that butted heads with the brass and won. Renee Ballard is none of these. Frankly, with her attitude, she would not make it on any police force in a city larger than Po-duck. I am sure that in the end, she will get her criminal, be the heroine and ride off in the sunset. Good for her.

review_text: I usually find Connelly's novels a fun read.  They draw me in, keep me engaged.  Not so with this one.  I found it hard to care about any of the characters in The Late Show and impossible to become involved in the story.  What's more, the book is consistently burdened with painful detail. There are endless descriptions of characters' every movement step by step, of all the details in detectives' written reports and with what fingers they type them, about where they choose to sit in the station house and where they place things in their cars, and much more.  Sadly, few if any of this deepens our understanding of characters or adds anything to the plot.  I almost always complete books I've begun, even when they're less than compelling. title: The Late Show (Renee Ballard Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Michael Connelly
review_title: Fast fiction with a lot of filler and a weak heroine.
review_text:
The plot in and of itself is basically LAPD Det. Renee Ballard who's transferred to the night shift, referred to as the 'late show', after filing harassment charges against her superior and her previous partner chose his career over backing her. All she does is start investigations by collecting evidence and statements then gives them to various departments the next day. But one shift changes her attitude and compels her onto two seemingly unrelated cases that she can't help but finish to its conclusion.

I have never read anything by this author but the concept of the blurb intrigued me. However, I found Renee to be a male's idea of a 'strong female lead' that really has no clue how to write an actual, strong, interesting female lead. Renee was just odd and it's no wonder she's a loner. She has weird, random habits, a strange lifestyle that really makes no sense other than that the author wanted to make her 'unique'. She has this 'I'm a tough guy' mentality but backs down at the slightest hint of a fight. I really disliked her and never warmed up to her but she was not developed at all. The secondary character were pathetically rendered, nothing but cliches.

I like details in a police procedural and I actually found how the LAPD works far more interesting than the main character but that--and the mystery plot itself--both dragged on and was mostly filler. It just...meandered...and sort of didn't do anything for the story or help any aspect of this book at all. The writing style was not at all what I'd expected or had heard about from this author--in that he's a good writer. Really? This is clearly not a great example...maybe? The author didn't tell a story, he just stated a bunch of stuff that happened in a list-kind-of-way and checked off certain boxes that he thought would get the reader's attention and that was all that mattered to him (or his publisher, ghost writer, or both). That's not a writer/author, but someone who thinks they can write and hopes an editor can polish it. Well, the editor also sucks.

This is my first and quite frankly, I don't even want to bother with attempting to read anything else by this author.

title: The Late Show (Renee Ballard Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Michael Connelly
review_title: Not the suspenseful thriller it's made out to be
review_text:
I was really interested in The Late Show because I've heard good things about Michael Connelly as an author, and about his Bosch series. This is the first book of his I've read, and I chose this book to start instead of one of the Bosch novels because it marks the introduction of a new character/series by a well-established writer in the crime genre, so I thought it would be really good. Unfortunately, it did not live up to my expectations.

The story is mostly a dry police procedural story, with some small bits of excitement and edge-of-your-seat thrill mixed in, but not enough for my liking. The characters aren't that well-developed, which tends to be startling or confusing when they do or say something that seems to come out of nowhere. For example, the main character, Renée Ballard, is introduced as a loose-cannon detective working the night shift (the "late show") for the LAPD, but that is nearly the only thing about her personality that I was able to pick up on. I felt like her character was described to me, but not in a way that I could emotionally connect to her in any way. So when she decides partway in to use her womanly wiles to get assistance from a coworker, it came as a complete shock because nothing in the book leading up to that point even mentioned her sexuality, much less indicated that she would use those tactics. The other characters in the book are less like people and more like devices to move the plot along.

I also found that in some areas there was not enough information, and some places there is too much. The first time Ballard leaves work, she goes to the beach with her dog and rides on her paddle board for a while before pitching a tent on the beach and going to sleep. Why? Is she homeless? Does she always sleep on the beach? Or does she go somewhere else? It's never fully explained, and she doesn't do it again, finding all sorts of other places to sleep after her shift. There is also a LOT of police jargon throughout the novel, especially at the beginning, that I actually had to look up online because I had no idea what it meant. I started wondering if I missed out on some explanations of these things by not starting off by reading some of Connelly's older novels, like the beginning of the Bosch series. This is something I wondered numerous times throughout the book. However, as this is the start of a new series, a reader shouldn't have to have read other novels by the same author just to have a basis of knowledge to understand this one. (By the way, for anyone who is familiar with Connelly, The Late Show is in the same universe as the Bosch series, but is the introduction of a new character and the start of a new series.)

Later on in the book, it goes in the opposite direction with too much needless detail at times, and with some explanations spoon-fed to the reader. It's helpful to know what the things were, but there were a lot of instances like this one: "Ballard knew that bullet casings collected at the crime scenes and the slugs from the bodies revealed markings identifiable to specific models of firearms." I mean it's definitely good information for anyone who is not familiar with police procedural books or TV shows, but after reading explanations given in that exact way several times through the book, it begins to stick out to me, and not necessarily in a good way.

At the beginning of the book, during the first shift we follow Ballard's story, she and her partner respond to 3 different calls, one seemingly minor, one more serious, and finally the "big one," the one that will obviously be the focal point of the book. However, through the first half of the book, she's working all 3 cases, which is what gave me the impression of a dry procedural novel. It just bounces between the three with Ballard doing normal investigative work, and it comes off as being quite disjointed with a very slow pace.

To sum it up, would I recommend this book? Only to someone who is mostly interested in procedure, and not as much action. I think the parts with a lot of action and intrigue were really well-written, but it wasn't enough to make up for the its shortcomings. Taking this book on its own merit, I would not be interested in seeking out more novels by Michael Connelly. However, I have read a lot of other reviewers that say this book is so unlike Connelly's other books, they question whether or not he actually wrote The Late Show. Based on that, I may decide to try another of his books in the future.

title: The Late Show (Renee Ballard Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Michael Connelly
review_title: Love this new Michael Connelly character
review_text: Renée Ballard is physically small(buck and a quarter pounds), a Polynesian beauty raised in the Pacific surf, grit tough as nails, smart as a whip, and possessing a 9-foot tall spirit. What's not to like? MC is a master story teller of multiple plots. He knows the LAPD system and uses characters that are willing to buck that system even at the risk of losing their lives much less their jobs. The Ballard character is no less a risk taker than Bosch. Her attractiveness caused a superior to make an unwanted pass at her a few years back. Though she is very definitely a fan of the opposite sex she is not at all attracted to this bully. She filed a complaint. Her then partner did not back her and this detective was banished to the night shift where miscreants are sent to punish their deeds. With a chip on her shoulder she turns her night shift into a producer of results even with a now partner who is counting the days to retirement and understandably distracted by a terminally I'll wife. The story fairly quickly becomes a page turner. Even in the beginning the characters are revealed in the action. It's a fun read. Hope you like it as much as I do.

subtitle: Paperback – May 5, 2015
author: Fredrik Backman
review_title: Trite, boring, predicatable, poorly written...like a children's book for old people.
review_text: Backman writes about things he knows little-to-nothing about, and it shows. The book was an exhausting, boring read that I struggled to force myself to finish.  The characters are more like caricatures, and the continuity errors abound, from the nonsensical placement of a hook for hanging oneself in the center of a ceiling (not in a rafter or joist), to an obsessively meticulous old man not noticing a severely frayed rope, to every automotive repair requiring only a screwdriver and a few minutes of time, to the anti-cat (should have just stuck a dog in the story), to the Persian woman exclaiming "Jesus!" to any of a thousand other issues. This book was unbearable. There are no lessons or insights for the reader to learn or appreciate. The plot is so predictable that at times I actually sighed aloud. I wish I could think of any redeeming qualities, but I can't. I guess the one star was earned by Backman using few compound prepositions and the book having no spelling errors that I noticed. This book would have made for a decent 25-page, fully illustrated children's book.

title: A Man Called Ove: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – May 5, 2015
author: Fredrik Backman
review_text:
Here is a man called Ove. Some of his actions show caring and compassion, yet he is regularly name-calling, judging others by their appearance, and verbally spouting (or thinking) hate without restraint. He is obsessed by his own narrow interests. The author has conjured up an unlikable cardboard character who lacks ability to step outside his own restrictive environment. This book is marketed as humor. There is great irony in that because repeatedly Ove is very cringe-worthy. I do not find it funny for someone to be spouting verbal and mental venom and disrespect as Ove does on almost every page.

OK, a book of 300 pages must have some take away-words showing at least a modicum of enlightenment. They are sparse but can be found towards the end in a couple of paragraphs in chapter 39 in reference to life, death and old age. Why couldn't the author be more reflective in other parts of the book? The narrative seems to take place in a vacuum lacking historical time and geographical place. I did complete reading this book but the Swede in me felt confronted with a puzzle which lacked most of the pieces to form a comprehensible picture.

title: A Man Called Ove: A Novel
subtitle: Paperback – May 5, 2015
author: Fredrik Backman
review_text:
I would give it 2 1/2 stars if I could. I know I am in the minority with my opinion on this book. It was very predictable--which in and of itself is not necessarily a bad thing--but I feel like I've read this particular story in the not too distant past in terms of grouchy 'old' man becomes (more) lovable and then dies. Which brings me to my second, and more major criticism, this man was NOT elderly!! He was 59 years old, not the 80 or 85 year old I would have imagined him to be if the author hadn't reminded us, more than once, that he was 59.
I also did not understand what his late wife found so loving and appealing about Ove--it just didn't add up for me.
I realize the light and fun aspects of the book were meant to be enjoyed for what they were, and I did, to a point. But it seemed as if the grumpy Ove was a caricature more than an actual person. Now that I know the style of this author I won't pursue reading any of his future books but he will always have a huge following for this type of story--which is just fine.

title: A Man Called Ove: A Novel

author: Fredrik Backman
review_text:
A stellar debut novel by Fredrik Bachman. A Man Called Ove is remarkable. Funny, clever, quirky and heartbreaking.

Ove is a grumpy old curmudgeon. He is difficult, mean and doesn't like anyone. He just wants to be left alone. The only thing left that he likes in the world are Saabs. Ever since his wife passed away, he keeps trying to figure out a way to be with her, but he constantly gets interrupted, by a myriad of people, he of course, doesn't like.

He conducts a neighborhood watch, reports what he deems to be suspicious behavior and argues with everyone. He is most bothered by his new neighbors, Parvaneh, her husband and children. Parvaneh will not leave him alone, perhaps because she is used to people like him and needs a father figure. She pesters and pesters him, begins to "understand" his behavior and he warms up to her and several others as the novel progresses.

Underneath his funny, gruff exterior, Ove is an old man who I fell in love with and I think you will too. Fredrik Bachman writing style is truly extraordinary. I wish I had the opportunity to meet A Man Called Ove.

review_title: "All people want to live dignified lives; dignity just means something different to different people."
review_text:
I picked up “A Man Called Ove” because someone I was with insisted I read it. This is not great literature, the story is too convenient, and it is not very realistic. But it is a wonderful story to read. If I ever get to the point in my life where I read a book like this and guff about literary conventions over the story then put me in the ground.
In short, the text follows a man named Ove, who like all people, is more than what he appears to be. The story is told in alternating chapters, flipping from the present to the past, and as you read each chapter you discover more and more about Ove, and the folks who inhabit his neighborhood, and thus how they all came to be the people they are today.
The text is funny, I chuckled frequently while reading it, and the author does a very nice job with his characterization of Ove, and of his wife Sonja. You might also find yourself grimacing from self-recognition from time to time while reading this novel.
The ending of “A Man Called Ove” is too tidy, and it is what the reader needs. I kept thinking of a line from one of Kurt Vonnegut’s books while I was reading this text, “All the decent sentiments in life are corny.” That is very true, and that does not mean they are not valuable. This book brings a little goodness into the world. It will make you feel some pleasant feelings, and it is decently written. I cannot quibble with a book like that.

title: What the Wind Knows
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Amy Harmon
review_title: Can't understand all the five star reviews...  :(
review_text:
I would most likely give this around 3 stars, because the author definitely has put in a lot of work, and clearly has some talent. It's only because of all those (for me) misleading 5 stars, that I felt like I'd be balancing things out. Unfortunately, I just don't enjoy the writing style. This plods along with a lot of 're-telling' of details, as though the author doesn't trust the readers to remember what's been shown a little while before... However, as a reader who takes in the details, and loves to immerse herself into a storyline, I find it even more annoying when the main character is written with contradictions.
SPOILERS FOLLOW:
The MC is a world famous author who is supposedly a brilliant researcher. In the beginning, "...Even as a child I found myself entranced by the past, wishing I knew the stories of the people who had come before me...."
Then later, when she's in the past, living it...
"With all the ... I hadn't thought to ask Eion (her beloved grandfather, and seemingly the only person in her life, who she spent all of her time with) about his early life.... I had never thought about the time before, when he had existed separate (sic) from me, without me. ..."
At one point, a child's book is finished. It's wrapped. Then a few pages later the MC is rushing to finish it...
There's an excruciatingly overly detailed account of shopping in The Past. Normally, I can vicariously enjoy these scenes, but a lot of the details of the clothes could have been later wound into the story, making scenes come more alive. When each and every item is then listed with their respective prices, I was feeling like one of those poor guys you see sitting in department stores' womens' departments, trying not to look at the time.
Unfortunately, I found the whole book boring. Well, not the whole book. I still haven't finished it, but don't think that I will.
And I also have to agree with a few other reviewers. This is a poor cousin to the Outlander Series. The first book in that took me a few chapters to warm to, but then it grabbed me by the throat and never let go until the end, (where I was crying because the whole beautiful ride had finished.)

review_text:
Did not work for me at all. In fact, it was painful to sort through the history that wasn’t fully explored and the relationships that were a mix of weirdness and confusion. The time travel thing is so far fetched that there were a couple of moments while reading that I felt a sense of embarrassment for even reading this kind of thing. Frankly, I am blown away by how many people give this book such good ratings. I guess folks are really into the unbelievable, especially when it involves a sappy, forlorn damsel in distress.

To call it a “page turner” like some people have is just not true. There were many sections that were total yawners like the shopping trip Anne makes when she needs new clothes for her old Ireland time period. There was near-zero relevance in all those boring details as it did nothing to develop characters or add meaningfully to the plot. Further, and this is what really irritates me, there isn’t any significant and deep philosophical pondering by this woman who suddenly finds herself a couple of generations back in time...just flutter-flutter heart palpitations over the doctor healing her gunshot wound (eye roll).

If you are looking for a historical novel that helps you learn about a time period—especially with a believable sense of reality—this isn’t it.

I loved the architecture of the novel that alternates between history as written by Thomas Smith and the transition to 1921-22 by Anne Gallagher as well as the very clever use of lines from one of my favorite poets, William Butler Yeats. But, in the end, it seems close to plagiarism of Outlander and I was unable to fully embrace it as original, creative writing.

review_text: I have read 4 or 5 Amy Harmon books and enjoyed them, so decided to give this a try.  I borrowed this through Kindle Unlimited and am glad I didn't actually spend money to purchase a copy.  I generally like historical fiction, and I like time travel/fantasy stories, but this was a poor blend of the two genres.  The overall tone of the story was gloomy and depressing throughout, full of actual grief and anticipatory grief.  By the last chapter I'd resigned myself to an ending in which the heroine moves on with her life without a happy-ever-after scenario, but with strength of character learns to live the life facing her.  Then, in the last few pages the author threw in a sudden happy ever after resolution to the plot that just felt abrupt, sloppy, and incomplete.  It was very dissatisfying.  I didn't wish for the protagonist to have a miserable existence, but the resolution was too abrupt and left me with major questions about practicalities that were not addressed.

What the Wind Knows is a historical novel with a romance that travels back in time. It is full of the history and culture of Ireland.

title: The Wonky Donkey
subtitle: Paperback – Picture Book, May 1, 2010
author: Craig Smith
review_text:
It's not a story per se. It's written as a song, by adding one line of the song to each page. In the song, a donkey with a missing leg and prosthesis, and an empty eye socket, is humiliated, berated and ostracized just for his physical condition. I presume the author opines handicap as "wonky". "Wonky" has nothing to do with the donkey's behavior nor personality. He is berated and cruely treated in lyrics, words and frightening illustrations. There's even a (taunting) song that can be downloaded. Theres no way i would want the music to these words touching my ears. i wish i could erase the words and pictures from my eyes. I cant phathom how this author got the book published ... I really question if the publishers actually read the book!

The message is that it's "okay" to humiliate and taunt the handicapped.

This book teaches children - people- that it's acceptable to hate, humiliate, taunt and bully.

This will be the first book i've ever destroyed. i wish i could return it but I don't want to pay return

author: Craig Smith
review_text: My husband and I initially thought this book was hilarious based on the popular video of a Scottish grandmother reading it to her grandson, but we realized the message the actual book sends is not one we want to share with our daughter. While it is harmless from an adult's perspective and "all in good fun," a child may not know any better and take the message at face value. We felt this book was teaching that someone with a different appearance warrants name-calling - wonky, lanky, stinky, etc. We, as adults who should know better, wouldn't say these things to someone, but small children have not learned this yet. It is up to us to teach compassion, kindness, grace, understanding, and that the idea of normal looks different on everyone - this book is not consistent with those teachings.

title: The Girl in the Ice: A gripping serial killer thriller (Detective Erika Foster Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Robert Bryndza
review_title: Promising Start That Devolves into Unoriginal Police Procedural 1.0
review_text: I haven't read the other works by this author, but this is apparently a genre switch, with opening of this thriller being quite good. That's the sequence where we meet the girl the title tells us is headed for an icy end, intoxicated and vulnerable as she stumbles through a sketchy neighborhood on a winter night where more than the weather is turning nasty. The descriptions are vivid enough to induce some shivers for readers following the young lady lurching toward death, and the daylight discovery of the body in eerie circumstances delivers more. Yet the promise of that introduction goes largely unfulfilled, as the book quickly devolves from a story well told to a generic conglomeration of characters and events printed up as if from a basic police procedural template 1.0. The leading detective arrives in a new position as a widow trying to recover from policeman hubby's on-duty death, practically with a sign blinking "Tragic Past" over her head, but her fellow detectives need the newspapers to give them the scoop. That occurs when her first-case-back, high-profile investigation quickly goes sour, thanks to her maverick, f-the-politics attitude that bucks against the lords and ladies in the peerage and the Met set of command officers, portrayed as sycophants all too eager to carry "establishment" water. Before long, we discover there hasn't just been a murder, but a whole string of them, committed by "the figure," a gender-free moniker used to preserve the not-so-surprise identity of the killer before the big reveal scene. Mind, choosing that term literally makes the murderer a shadowy figure, and that cardboard cutout of a character promptly latches on to the tragic detective as his next obsession/chess-match adversary, which we know because the author has "the figure" following her around London with running commentary in its head. That's at least a switch from Ms. Detective's own thoughts, including how she identifies with these murdered young girls because she was a Slovakian au pair lucky she only had to handle the vaguely "bad atmosphere" of domestic employment instead of being sex-trafficked. Now, the tale of how a teenage, immigrant au pair managed a climb up the Met  detective's ladder would have been an interesting story, but we don't get to hear that tale. Instead, we get the standard scenes of conflict with superiors, up to and including her suspension under official investigation when her heroic insistence that "we're here for the victims" leads to breaking the boss's rules. So, of course, he has to come grovel he needs her back when the case is fouled up, and she makes a triumphant return to a squad that is now happy to handle her CCTV requests and spend the rest of the book doing cheerleader routines and backup-dancer performances in her top-cop spotlight showcase. Meanwhile, the predictable case is plodding along to the obvious conclusion no misdirect could hide past about chapter 5, with the appearance of shocking porn photos, explanations of how consensual anal intercourse is distinguishable in corpses from the forced variety, and a bunch of caterwauling over dead cats (the furry animal kind, not just the cathouse ho's being knocked off) taking the place of actual plot twists. That doesn't make the overall book terribly bad, but it's not terribly good, either. Given the glut of works in thriller/mystery/police procedural genres, delivering something truly fresh is a holy grail kind of aim, but for this genre switch to work, the author needs to transfer the original voice that was on display in the first few chapters but collapsed into stereotypes and cliches after that.

review_text:
I love reading crime/mystery/thriller books and I love it even more when I find one that is so engrossing, thought provoking, violent (I do expect violence in books like this) and entriguing and compelling characters.

This is definitely one of them. Set in London, the discovery of a dead girl underneath a frozen lake sparks off a story fill of twists and turns, standoffish and belligerent 'v.i.p' parents, police unable to do their jobs properly because of said parents obstruction and the bodies of 5 more women.

The class system rearing its ugly head to show that, maybe we're not actually moving forward, just trying not to show it as much.

I thoroughly enjoyed this book and am very, very much looking forward to the second book in the series.

*Huge thanks to Robert Bryndza, Bookouture aand NetGalley for this copy in exchange for an honest review*

Ugh this book is a slog; I only finished it out of anger. I see all 5 star reviews and am really surprised—What the heck is wrong with me?

I suppose this is the book for you if you’re the kind of person that can find deep meaning in motivational posters. Hang in there, kitty.

How about this for a plot twist? Rich Milanese family bribes local politicians to secure a position for their oldest son to be a driver for the top local general in Organisation Todt. This guy does this and gets to bang the maid to boot. After the war, He hides his service because he was a friggin’ Nazi. 70 years after most of the verifiable sources are dead, he tells a whitewashed version of the story. Here are the believable bits: Watching his cousin assassinated while he stood there in fear—watching his girlfriend die in front of a firing squad while he watched like a coward. These two scenes are completely out of character from the rest of the superhero nonsense.

Sorry, I know it’s fiction but come on.

review_title: A mediocre book by a mediocre writer.
review_text:
In spite of its enormous popularity, this is a mediocre book by a mediocre writer. First, for a project that allegedly took ten years to research and write, there are too many errors. Let me give just two examples. Apparently unaware that Panzer means tank, Sullivan keeps writing about "Panzer tanks;" at one place he makes the Germans pay in Kronen instead of Reichsmarks.

Second, there are too many coincidences to be believable; as when the hero, Pino Lela, during his final drive from Italy to Austria meets the very four highwaymen who robbed him a over a year earlier, kills some of them, and recovers a wallet the man had taken from him. That, at a time when the total number of partisans fighting the Germans throughout northern Italy was said to be about a a quarter million!

Third, though Sullivan in an interview he gave claimed to have been looking for "a deeper emotional truth" than non-fiction can normally provide, in fact he is is not good at writing about emotions. Describing his own, at the very beginning, he does OK. However, his way of talking about those of other people, primarily Pino, can only be called jejune.

That is why it is as I said: a mediocre book by a mediocre writer.

title: Beneath a Scarlet Sky: A Novel

author: Mark Sullivan
review_text: I have read dozens of Holocaust and WWII memoirs with each tugging at my heart in different ways, each revealing a horror of WWII that I hadn’t known, and only a couple historical fictions of the same subject, and now I know why. Though the main character (and all the main characters) are real people, it’s impossible to know exactly how much of this really happened. If just half of it had happened, then why wasn’t an incredible memoir written? Instead we get an ala Forrest Gump account of a man that was inconceivably at all these major WWII events in Italy. But that wasn’t my biggest issue with the book, my biggest issue was the writing. Mr. Sullivan’s very wordy descriptions got very old and boring. I found myself skipping several paragraphs at a time just to get to the actual point. A good deal of editing could’ve made the book read much better. Though Mr. Lella did do at least something in this book, not knowing what’s true and what’s not really is a waste of time. I would recommend reading one of the many non-fictional memoirs of survivors of this dark time in history, where you know what you’re reading truly does show what hell people had to go through to survive while showing how good can live even amongst pure evil.

The protagonist of this tale sometimes acted heroically and somsetimes compromised himself in ways that were morally ambiguous at best.  That is the story that could have been told.  i do not judge the protagonist ; i judge the author who could have told  a human tale of struggle that would have better honored the character than this sanitized story of heroism.

review_text: I purchased this ebook awhile ago but hadn't read it until recently as I have been reading books about WWII. "Beneath a Scarlet Sky: A Novel" by Mark Sullivan tells the story of Pino Lella, an Italian teen whose life is overturned by the the atrocities of the Second World War. Sullivan states upfront that this book is based on the true story but because not all of the details can be verified, he created scenes and dramatized parts of the story. The book is a quick read although I found the action is stronger than the prose. Several reviewers compared this book to "Unbroken" by Laura Hillenbrand which I can see except for setting and quality of writing. This is a window into the lives of Italians during the war and the valiant efforts of the Resistance. Some might say that Pino couldn't have done all of the things he does but war makes men of boys overnight and the impossible possible whether horrors or heroism.

review_title: How well do you know your co worker ?
review_text:
5 stars ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
The One That Got Away
Simon Wood

Description:

Graduate students Zoë and Holli only mean to blow off some steam on their road trip to Las Vegas. But something goes terribly wrong on their way home, and the last time Zoë sees her, Holli is in the clutches of a sadistic killer. Zoë flees with her life, changed forever.

A year later and still tortured with guilt, Zoë latches on to a police investigation where the crime eerily resembles her abduction. Along with a zealous detective, she retraces the steps of that fateful night in the desert, hoping that her memory will return and help them find justice for Holli. Her abductor—labeled the “Tally Man” by a fascinated media—lies in wait for Zoë. For him, she is not a survivor but simply the one that got away.

With an unforgettable heroine, a chillingly disturbed psychopath, and a story that moves at breakneck speed, The One That Got Away is thriller writer Simon Wood at his finest

This book is riveting and not for the faint of heart. Yes, there is some extreme violence in this book, but what would you expect from a story involving a serial killer? The murderer tortures his victims before killing them. Some of the scenes are creepy , very vivid ,will make u flinch ,and very gut wrenching. But the story is so well written,full of excitement and pretty terrifying to be honest . The mystery of what really happened to Zoe and Holly that fateful night, is a compelling read that will keep you glued to the action. In The One that Got Away, we know who the killer is by chapter three, and the book alternates perspectives between Zoe and the killer, (the man who kidnapped her). To the killer, Zoe is only a girl who escaped, who still needs to be taught a lesson.He's not done with her.I thought killer was really a creepy dude. His thought process was so twisted and disturbed that he was definitely a scary character. Especially knowing he lived a relatively normal life outside of his nighttime life, and no one suspected a thing. He was just your typical co worker. Great, Great book !!!! I'm now a big Simon Wood fan and will be on the hunt for more of his books. This is a great thriller that will keep you on the edge of your seat and turning those pages so fast you won't even realize you stayed up all night reading it ! And Zoe is an awesome heroine! Simon Wood did an excellent job of developing each character and keeping your heart rate at full speed. I really enjoyed this tense, nerve-wracking story! I finished reading it in one day and highley recommend it .

I am knowledgable of the WW2 concentration camps and the Nazi atrocities but to read about them in such graphic detail in a novel was far toooooooooooo much for me to handle.  My father was a sharp shooter in the war, fought throughout Europe from 1943 to 1945 inc., the Battle of the Bulge.  He liberated a concentration camp in Germany in 1945 and then was sent to the Pacific theater.  I never knew my father in all of those years when he was away at war.  I am incredibly proud of my father and "the greatest generation" who fought against the horrible atrocities and won us our continued freedom  --  for which way to many of the current generation show no appreciation and even worse are not even educated about it.

title: Lilac Girls: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Martha Hall Kelly
review_text: At the heart of this story are the inconceivable and horrifying surgical experiments performed by Nazi doctors on female Polish political prisoners at Ravensbruck during WWII - a weighty subject worthy of far more than the three personalized stories of an American socialite, a Polish victim and a German doctor presented here.  The true-story postscript at the end of the novel is the only part of this overly frivolous if well meaning first novel worth reading. From the brief background facts presented at the end, it is apparent that the real women were far stronger characters, good and evil, than they appear in the novel.  How much more powerful the story would have been in non-fiction form, without the morass of "chick-lit" additives of syrupy love stories and inane dialogue which drown the historic facts of a true and very unsettling wartime experience?  The American and Polish female players deserve so much more as a memorial to their actions and their suffering respectively; it is encouraging to read in the postscript that they seem to have received timely and appropriate accolades and recognition in the post war period.  If their true story has indeed been lost to the general public, it is sad that it has been resurrected in the format of LILAC GIRLS.

title: Lilac Girls: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Martha Hall Kelly
review_text:
I enjoyed reading this book. I want to thank NetGalley and the publisher, Random House , for sending me this ebook in return for an honest review. This book follows three women at the start of WWII in 1939. The first is Caroline Ferriday, an American socialite working in the French consulate in New York city. The second is Kasia Kuzmerick, a Polish teenager who is arrested after caught working as a courier for the Polish underground. She is sent to Ravensbruck, a women's concentration camp. The third is a new doctor, Herta Oberhauser. She is unable to find work as a doctor in 1939 Germany, where women doctors are rare. She answers a newspaper ad for a position as a camp doctor at a "re-education" camp at Ravensbruck.
The book follows these 3 women until about 1960. Once I was halfway through the book, I found it hard to put down, reading 50 to 100 pages a day, because I wanted to see what happened in the lives of these 3 women.
The author has an explanatory note at the end of the book. Several of the characters, including Caroline and Herta, were actual people. Others were based on actual people, specifically, "the Rabbit women," a group of Polish women who underwent gruesome medical experiments at Ravensbruck.

Much of this story is very depressing. The horrors of medical experiments at Ravensbruck are graphically described. There is a humorous line when Caroline describes her father's color blindness: "One morning at breakfast, he appeared in a yellow jacket, burnt orange trousers, and red socks."
This book is a solid 4 out of 5 stars.

I hesitated to stir my brain and just add my concurrence to the very astute and intelligent observations made by the the bulk of the negative reviewers. I don't have anything original to say tonight and it looks like it's all been said already.

review_text:
I was so disappointed with this installment of the Prey series. I had read that many authors were using ghost writers and I have to wonder now.

It was as though he did not know his own characters. The characters were not well thought out and had no depth. Letty has never had dark hair, and the error is ridiculous. There were several situations in the book I was unable to believe, Letty was a street wise kid, and I do not believe she put herself in a position to be killed by Pilate. I found that very difficult to read. Her naivete with Skye and allowing her to sneak out of the hotel while she was out of the room. The absence of Rose Marie was noticeable. Lucas was driving all over several states as though he had no other duties, and that was shocking to me. The ending was predictable and after all the situations he would quit, he did with this book? While I expect a darkness to the Virgil Flowers series, as he is a rougher character but Lucas has always been smarter and less violent and this book is the complete opposite.

Typically after I read these books, I continue to think about them for several days, but not on this book. I won't be reading any more at this point.

title: Gathering Prey (The Prey Series Book 25)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: John Sandford
review_text:
John Sandford doesn't owe me anything: I own every single Prey book (except this one) in hard copy. I've read most of them several times, and enjoy them without reservation. However, Gathering Prey is an unmitigated disaster compared to his previous Prey novels. He has either lost his muse or handed this one off to someone else to write. I actually gave up reading this less than halfway through.

I've read that Sandford has enlisted new authors to write his Virgil Flowers books, and the result has been very similar. Zero depth to the story, banal dialog, flat descriptive language. I appreciate his supposed efforts to give a leg up to new authors, but from a reader's point of view this is sort of a violation of trust. Honestly, I hope the same thing happened here because at least there is some hope that Sandford will take back the franchise.

I'm glad I bought the Kindle version. No trees needed to die for my copy of this book. It's unlikely that I'll ever finish this one, much less read it again.

review_title: He shouldn't have written this book
review_text:
This is what happens when a superb author writes too much. It's Sandford's 25th Lucas Davenport [Prey series] book. This reminds me of Tom Clancy's demise. Gawd, next thing you know Sandford will have a "co-author". The book isn't that bad UNTIL you compare it to a couple of his best works [e.g. the two Clara Rinker mysteries]. Then - ugh.

I saw an interview of Sandford on You Tube conducted by his son. Worth watching.

I feel really sad about this. I really was looking forward to this latest Davenport mystery. Maybe he should make it Davenport's last. Sandford does Virgil Flowers stories [another cop] but they pale in significance when compared to one of Sandford's earlier Lucas Davenport books. I just write this off to a greedy publisher and an author that doesn't know when it's time to quit. How sad.

The violence in this latest book is large in numbers but somehow it just feels churned out and considering the acts comes across as pale. If you want graphic sex, Sandford doesn't do it. This is a mark in his favor. With some luck some unknown will pop up and start a brilliant career. Unless Sandford undergoes some literary nuclear fusion, it's over. Oh, if Sandford is reading this, dump Letty. She is not needed and in fact hurts his stories. Possibly she could be Davenport's replacement, but she needs a solo act.

title: Gathering Prey (The Prey Series Book 25)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: John Sandford
review_text: I have read every Sanford book  and watched his skill as a writer develop with each new entry.  I felt his most recent books (both Davenport and Flowers) were his very best and most enjoyable.  Although I was looking forward to his newest release,  I had heard rumors about the plot and that this character (and Sanford) might be winding down and possible handing over (some of) the writing to his wife.  Letty has been on a path to get more involved in detective work, so it's no surprise that she is the center of this story.  Having said that, I found this book to be a disappointment and the worst of any I have read.  The story was not well done and the quality of the writing was not anywhere the standard that Sanford has achieved previously.  The characters didn't seem to be real or themselves.  Letty in particular seemed to act contrary to her nature; she is very savvy and intelligent but not so in this story.  Her character seemed to do stupid things that her character's intellect and instincts would not normally do.  After enjoying all of his book series, I am let down and thinking I need to find another writer.

review_text:
I have read all of the Prey books and this is the first one that disappointed. The plot was predictable and repetitive. There was little character development of the villains, except to portray them as Manson cult re-treads. None of the characters from the earlier Prey books were involved besides Lucas and his daughter.

The plot seemed more violent and bloody than Sandford’s earlier work. In an apparent effort to lighten things up, he interjected cheap shots at all things Californian (where most of the cultists in the story originated) which were neither amusing nor accurate.

This may be Lucas Davenport’s last hurrah. I for one will be sorry to see him go, but it seems like the right time.

Uncharacteristically, a key figure in Gathering Prey dies midway through and I'm trying to figure out if that detracted from the story for me. There's a reason I rated this book four stars instead of five, but I'm not quite sure what it is.

What is next for Lucas? Can't wait to find out!

I have been reading the Prey series for many years now having been hooked after Rules of Prey. I've followed other series books and eventually they become less appealing with each new book, However, this has not happened with John Sandford and book 25 still has be interested and reading very quickly to the end! I look forward to his new releases in this series so much that it seems an eternity till I can purchase the next one!!

If you've never read any of the Lucas Davenport (main character in the Prey series), I highly encourage you to read the first in the series (Rules of Prey) and you will know from that one book if you're a fan or not. When I read the first few books of the series the one thing that struck me most was that it's written from the male perspective which was new to me at the time. Mr. Sandford does such a great job in making the characters so realistic, I found myself getting mad at Lucas Davenport for his womanizing ways and attitude about them. But, the storyline is excellent, and over time, the characters have stayed true to life in that they grow, mature, learn lessons, and age through the years. That is a very difficult thing for an author to do and not only do the characters grow, the storylines are just as interesting and new with each book he writes. I am never bored or disappointed and the writing style has stayed consistent leading me to believe that John Sandford is still actually writing the material versus 'ghost writers'. I love his books so much that I'm now just as hooked on the other series that have evolved from characters in the Prey series. This helps me get through the wait for the next Prey because these are released at different times of the year. It's also nice that the characters make their appearances in all of the books keeping in line with their relationships to make it believable to the reader.

I recommend these books and cannot express enough how excellent and entertaining the writing is as well as the storylines. If you are a fan of crime novels, then you will love them. I don't really consider them a mystery per say because usually the bad guy/gal is known to the reader as you follow an investigation from the detective point of view, but, you feel like you are part of the investigation.

review_text:
Mr. Grisham, where have you gone? I liked this book even less than Gray Mountain and that is saying something. At least Gray Mountain contained a plot of substance. It was going somewhere. It was building up. It had a climax. And then it...ended. Unresolved. With absolutely no indication that the protagonist was going to follow through with anything that the plot had been building up to. But I digress.
The Racketeer gives us Malcolm Bannister, who cons the Feds into letting him go based on knowing who killed a Federal judge, and then while evading the relatives of the man he accused of killing said judge even though he's had all kinds of expensive plastic surgery, he sets up a fake movie company with the help of a woman he's just been flirting with for the last several years during prison visits, and lures young Nathan Cooley into giving over who really "done it", and then strands him in Jamaica with a first aid kit full of cocaine, while he and his girlfriend find stolen gold, give the Feds the REAL name of the guy who killed the Federal judge, and frolic in the surf happily ever after. Or something.
Where's the man who wrote A Time to Kill? And The Firm?

review_text:
There is an author's note at the end of this book. It states: "This is indeed a work of fiction, and more so than usual. Almost nothing in the previous 380-odd pages is based on reality. Research, hardly a priority, was rarely called upon. Accuracy was not deemed crucial. Long paragraphs of fiction were used to avoid looking up facts. etc." That says it all.
I enjoyed the first half of this book and then the whole premise got so convoluted that it was difficult to even understand what was happening. For me, up until almost the ending, I wondered what was going on. I ended up wondering why I had even bothered to finish the book. I agree with the author's note and it should have been placed at the beginning of the book. Had I realized how off-the-wall this book was, I wouldn't have bothered with it.

title: The Racketeer: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: John Grisham
review_text:
How can you care about characters that bore their very author?

The story, as it goes, comes around enough to tie up the loose ends so that you don't feel that this was a poorly designed novel. But that is about the best thing I can say about John Grisham's new book, The Racketeer.

The book is not badly written, Grisham too good for that, but it is written without enthusiasm. Everything seems to be told on a sedated even keel without passion and without any excitement whatsoever. There are no highs and lows. The passion is totally passionless. The horror - after all, two people are murdered and a woman is tortured viciously (or so we hear)is sterile and evokes exactly zero emotion or outrage of any sort. There is no tension anywhere. And above all, there is no vivid sense of danger or that anything is truly at stake - and that condemns any art to mediocre, elevator-music level of entertainment.

Alas, I spent the full price for it. I'd say anything above $3.99 for the ebook version is too much.

Better yet, wait for the movie. It's bound to be better.

review_text:
The first critical thought hit around page 3, when it caught up to me that I was reading horrible crap. I figured (and still think) it might be an earlier failure dragged out and gussied up to pass for the real thing in the eBook stampede.
I also thought/think maybe Baldacci's got himself a protege and in a fit of laziness (or a dry spell) is passing off her/his crap as his own.
Or, it could be that he's just losing it.
The prose is awkward and overwritten; the dialogue varies between prosaic and ridiculous. There's the odor of Sophomore Summer Gifted Writers' Camp about it.
It says something very sad about our culture that drek like this can receive a 4.4 rating from its readers, with 845 5-stars out of around 1350 ratings.

At least I will question this perception we cannot say anything against the lie that women are like men, especially when it comes to how stories like this try to distort the facts.

review_text:
I enjoyed the novel. It is not great literature, but it is a good summer read. Two assassins employed by a secret US agency are intent on killing each other. Of course, it is a love story. Of course, it is pure fiction. There is no secret US agency empoying assassins. Or is there?
Think of the disclosures by Edward Snowden. Think of secret juries and secret decisions. Think of US drones taking out terrorists in a "neutral and friendly" Pakistan. Think of the special forces that took down Osama bin Laden. Are US assassins all that far fetched? The novel is fiction but it may mirror the truth more than anyone intended. Still, it is a good read.

I gave up when he took a DVD and "ran it through an algorithm program". As someone with a degree in computer science, I am qualified to say this is an utterly meaningless phrase. It sounds like something George W Bush would throw into a speech. In the author's universe, intelligence agencies openly recruit at universities. This is why he was chosen. I swear this is a direct quote: "I was smart, I had always been a loner and I was damaged deep in my soul." Yep, the government only wants mentally ill people with no personal skills to work as intelligence agents. Seriously, he couldn't find someone in IT or law enforcement to disabuse him of these silly ideas? There is just too much good writing out there to waste your time on the admittedly enjoyable exercise of "hate reading". This is aggressively, suffocatingly terrible writing. title: I Am Pilgrim: A Thriller
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Terry Hayes
review_title: Not as original as I'd hoped
review_text:
I picked this up in a book store and perused the dust jacket. I kind of got a vibe that this was a new type of thriller. It's not.

That's not to say it's a bad book. It's also not. It's just not that different from earlier generation of thrillers. I started with what I will call first-generation thriller writers: Robert Ludlum, Frederick Forsyth, Clive Cussler and Jack Higgins. I read most of their respective catalogs. I tried reading some of what I call second-gen thriller writers (Flynn, Baldacci, Metzler) but didn't find them to be qualitatively different. So for a while I just stopped reading thrillers.

It starts out promising enough with a gritty murder in New York that quickly has you wondering, what does this have to do with a terrorist plot? This is our introduction to the book's protagonist. (I'm not sure we ever learn his real name.)

The book is told in first-person and right off the bat the - I'm going to call him the 'hero' - hero starts making noise like he won't be your typical hero. However, Hayes quickly reverts him to type. Harvard-educated, recruited by a super-secret intelligence organization, meteoric rise. Yawn.

Even the organization the hero works for starts out promising but again reverts to type. The hero describes the organization as a sort of internal affairs for the intelligence world. Huh. Good idea. Then Hayes goes on to saddle the organization with the supremely unimaginative name of The Division. I get it. He's going for a banality of evil thing here. It's a choice but one I disagree with. It just seems like we've seen this before.

Cue meteoric rise followed by disillusionment and walking away from The Division only to be pulled back in. It all just feels like we've been here before.

The villain is mildly interesting because he's a cleanskin (i.e. someone with no criminal past and hence hard to trace) but his origin story isn't very interesting. Raised in Saudi, father beheaded, heads off to Afghanistan and becomes a muj. Honestly, his back story seems like it's lifted from Osama Bin Laden.

The plot feels borrowed from Tom Clancy. I won't rehash it here because I don't want to spoil.

One of my big problems with Hayes' writing is his world building. I've already mentioned The Division. In The Division, the hero (at the ripe old age of twentysomething) rises to head The Division desk in Europe where he's the youngest ever Rider of the Blue. I'm not making that up. Rider of the Blue. WTF kind of organization would call it's people that? According to Hayes, one of the occupants of that position used to be an admiral so they called him the Admiral of the Ocean Blue and from there it mutated to Rider of the Blue. Later on the ex-Rider of the Blue (now known as Pilgrim) works with legendary Director of National Intelligence, Whispering Death. I'm not making this up. For short Hayes refers to him as the Whisperer. How do you read that and take it seriously?

I will say that I did like the character of Ben Bradley, the NYPD detective. He felt orders of magnitude more original and believable than the Rider of the Blue and Whispering Death.

Another small issue is that Hayes is an Australian trying to write from the point of view of an American and he's not particularly successful. For example, the villain is known as the Saracen. Saracen is a just not a word that many Americans - not even the Rider of the Blue - would know or use. Most Americans probably wouldn't know what it means. There are other examples, for example, when he refers to tennis shoes/running shoes/athletic shoes as 'trainers'. An American just wouldn't use that word and probably wouldn't know what you meant if you used it.

I feel like I am being harsh with this book. I didn't hate it but it just felt like I'd been there/done that. Perhaps I've just read too many other thrillers.

What I hated most is that as a work of fiction, the author's plot was during real world events that would only add to more people thinking this was closer to a non-fiction work rather than fiction.

Things I hated most:
The usual commentary by the author from one chapter to another: "Thank you Saudi Arabia" for giving us terrorists, "we, like the Jews, believed in the goodness of mankind" implying that Americans and Jews believe the good in people unlike Muslims, "over 45% of Muslim women cannot read or write" ~ where the hell did he get these statistics from, and the overuse of the superior tone and implying Ara bs and Muslims in general are stupid and inferior, how Arabs are garbage... There is backtracking and repetition, often it seems word for word. There was much gratuitous violence and the Pilgrim endures excruciating pain at regular intervals, but miraculously recovers in a couple of pages in order to pursue the plot.
“The Pilgrim” needs a rigorous editor and could be reduced by half to make a fast-paced page turner. I finished it only because I wanted to see what happened to the virus. The Saracen was effectively written out of the script and disposed of.
I’m glad it was a kindle unlimited. You know what they say - you get what you pay for.

review_text: Very believable central plot, which propels the main interest.  Lot of seemingly plausible plot details and insider-ish looks behind the scenes at high level governmental secrecy settings.  But also lots of completely implausible, coincidental twists and other stuff that sometimes seemed almost cornball. You get the feeling the author is trying really really hard to make this work and is wracking his brains to keep things tense and surprising.  Graphic gore and more at times; not for the faint of heart.  After a while, some of the suspense is lost because you know that something unexpected will happen.  In the end, I decided it was at the level of an x-rated (more for the violence and gore than the sex) adult cartoon.  The author has a lot of experience with Hollywood movies etc and this seemed to be written with the inevitable film adaptation in mind.  It was a page turner, but I can't really say that I enjoyed it.

review_text:
I have always enjoyed spy thrillers. I had sort of given up on them after the Soviet Union gave out. I don't care for the economic books that took on the spy market. This book harks back to the days of the best of the spy adventures which feature the hero working alone, in the cold.
Mr. Hayes is a fine writer. He is able to hold many strands of story, weaving in each at the proper time. The story marches relentlessly forward, each strand adding its weight to the overall picture. Each exquisitely drawn character jumps in at the perfect time.
Many reviewers recap the story. I won't do that. I'll just tell you it may be the most thrilling, intense book you will ever read.

review_title: If you haven't got taste....this book is for you.
review_text: Let's see what's in my clutter:  a group of antique Limoges boxes, a display of old chocolate boxes from the 1920s..15 paper weights, a grouping of chinoiserie vases...and on the mantelpiece, lots of Staffordshire.  I've got traditional English taste in spades and for many of us, we wouldn't think of parting with our treasures.  In fact, most of the very best decorators, from Nancy Lancaster to John Fowler to Sister Parrish to Keith Irvine would sneer at Ms. Kondo's advice.  My daughter and I both agreed that the popularity of this book must be linked to an abundance of "no tasters."  They must have stuff that needs to be thrown out.  As for me, I like my home packed full of treasures and beautiful things--even beautiful useless things.  A certain confidence in decorating comes from those of us who've been raised with lovely things and curated collections of "clutter."

Half of the book is about how getting rid of clutter inhibited her life. So... wait... The clutter, itself, didn't inhibit her life- the thought of what to do with it inhibited her life. Meaning, her obsession with the problem far outweighed the actual problem. That's just not the type of person I want to be taking advice from. The part where she tried to sell me that "folding is fun" is where I pretty much fell off the boat. Consider me uninspired. I guess I will just have to suck it up and throw out my useless stuff on my own.

title: The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up: The Japanese Art of Decluttering and Organizing
subtitle: Hardcover – October 14, 2014
author: Marie Kondo
review_text: This book has some good qualities, but for the most part I feel like it is just another way to promote minimalism. You can find plenty of inspiration to become a minimalist for free on the Internet and FB. Specifically Joshua Becker has some great advice and a blog called becoming minimalist. I found him more relatable. Ms. Kondo recommends asking yourself if your items spark joy, if not they should be discarded. I agree. However she also says you should appreciate things and speak to them to show appreciation. Honestly it seems bizarre to me to talk to inanimate objects. I would skip this book and look online for the motivation you are seeking to get your house in order. Cutting back on your "stuff" will definitely bring your more joy and make it easier to keep things tidy. And if you still want this information I would get the audible, so you have one less book to store! :)

title: The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up: The Japanese Art of Decluttering and Organizing
subtitle: Hardcover – October 14, 2014
author: Marie Kondo
review_title: Main point of book has helped, details were useless
review_text:
A few years ago, I was given The Life Changing Magic of Tidying Up as a gift & had never heard of it prior. Once I googled it I realized there was tons of hooplah surrounding it & got excited to read the book & start decluttering.

This is an easy quick read & yes, there are some good points that I honestly had never thought about before. The main point Marie Kondo drives home, literally over & over & OVER, is only keep items that bring you joy (other than items you need & absolutely have to keep).

And I think that basically sums up the entire book right there. The book is rather redundant & she tells several personal stories where you start to think she has serious psychological issues. She comes across as completely obsessed with decluttering. She talks about taking everything in her shower & drying it off after she's done showering & then putting it away. She does this after each shower!?! What in the world. I don't know anyone who has time or if they did have time, would want to do this! That's what those amazing shower caddies & organizers are for. The point is, there's things like that in the book where she loses me.

I love having a clean clutter-free home & life but I also want to HAVE an actual life, not spend inordinate amounts of time decluttering.

I don't want to give any spoiler alerts in case you haven't read it & want to. But she talks to/communicates with her personal items & advises us to do the same. I get the idea behind it (to give respect for the items & enable yourself to more easily let go of it). But for me personally, it feels silly & takes so much time since she advises to do this for every single item you own. I already have respect for my home & belongings & don't want to or have the time to have a chat with each individual item before deciding to let go of it. The technique could totally work for some people, but I tried it & felt ridiculous & just got frustrated.

There were a few things that really frustrated me about this book. She never talked about recycling, just kept saying to get rid of it. Sure we all know we can recycle items, but I thought it irresponsible that she never mentioned recycling. The main thing that really bothered me is she discourages people to give their belongings to people they know, saying it puts undo pressure on them to feel that they have to take the items & therefore can cause them to now have access clutter. I absolutely understand this concept to a point & of course no one should put pressure on anyone to take their junk they don't want. However, I have a huge amount of family members & friends that are SO thankful for my hand me downs. I myself am very grateful for certain hand me downs, so I don't have to spend excess money.

There are a few practical tips like how to fold clothing. But I found it confusing trying to figure out her folding method just from reading in her book. So I googled it & there are lots of very simple tutorials now online that make it simple & easy to understand if you can't figure it out from reading or you just don't want to read the book.

In fact, since the book has been out a while now, once I finished it I googled & found all kinds of blogs, videos etc that made her techniques super easy to understand & apply in your own life. So if you want to read the book, she definitely goes into major detail all about her methods & techniques. If you don't want to read this or just don't have the time, you honestly can find out all about it online, get the main info & get on to decluttering.

I feel that it's great to strive for a healthy balance in relation to our belongings, but this book seems to perpetuate some unhealthy practices.

Overall, I absolutely did take away the main point which is to ask youself if each item brings you joy & if it doesn't, get rid of it. I've applied this concept to my life & it's definitely improved my ability to declutter. The majority of the rest of the book didn't personally change my life in any greater way.

title: The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up: The Japanese Art of Decluttering and Organizing
subtitle: Hardcover – October 14, 2014
author: Marie Kondo
review_text:
This book is filled with conflicting suggestions and disturbing stories about the author that make me think she has some sort of disorder. She talks about how she threw away her families belonging without asking them as a child/teen. She once cried at soap scum on her shampoo bottles and has since kept them out of the shower, so she has to bring them in each time and wipe them off after each use. Her entire life has been a frantic struggle to control her environment and every thing in it. She tells you to throw away things you might only use seasonally or occasionally and just buy it again later. In one section she talks about how she stored seasonal items in purses she wasn't using, but then she decided that was a horrible idea because it was too much work to switch out the items twice a year. However, literally 5 paragraphs later she tells you to empty your purse each day so it can "rest" like that's not way more effort than emptying a bag twice a year. But, while she was writing this book sometimes she would come home and fall asleep on the floor (whaaat???) without emptying her bag and that's ok!

There is some good advice, which she takes pride in boasting about while bashing other methods. In reality the whole concept of keeping only what you love has been around longer than this book, she didn't invent it or any of the tips in here besides the extreme ones that most people don't have the time or energy to do. She talks about all the many, many methods she's tried since childhood and become unsatisfied with, I think she'll eventually get tired of her own methods and move onto something else.

I think if the author was more humble, less preachy, less obsessive, and less extreme I would have enjoyed the book more. Obviously a lot of people love this book but I'm not drinking the crazy kool aid.

title: The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up: The Japanese Art of Decluttering and Organizing
subtitle: Hardcover – October 14, 2014
author: Marie Kondo
review_title: Is this a book or a cry for help?
review_text:
This may be the first Amazon book review I have written, but this book spoke to me in such a way that I wanted to offer a few comments. I have given the book 2 stars; this seems to be the best way to describe my response to a book that is at once rather insipid yet in an odd way entertaining, and really quite remarkable in one unique way.
It is unreasonable to assign a literary-based score to this book since its purpose or function is in no way literary; it is simply flat in its writing, but then the reading of this book is not much of a cerebral event.

The entertainment (and the really brilliant part of the entire tidying-up tour de force) is how someone with neuroses such as Ms. Kondo's can actually capitalize on them and ostensibly continue to live out their personal compulsions and obsessions via the untidiness of her (paying) clients. Ms. Kondo's self-described interaction with the items she discards, the items she relegates to the bin, and in general the relationship she entertains with inanimate objects is almost dramatic. The strict rules concerning "rebound" and the tragedy of reverting to "untidiness" could be quite humorous if it were not for a few incongruities: "The act of picking up and choosing objects is extremely personal. To avoid rebound [the dreaded relapse into a shameful and sloppy life], you need to create your own tidying method with your own standards. Only you can know what kind of environment makes you happy."

I thought I did have my own method. Oh well, after gently scolding the reader a few times for a few minor failures , she forgives you with the reminder: "The fact that you possess a surplus of things that you can't bring yourself to discard doesn't mean you aren't taking care of them. In fact, it is quite the opposite."

The part of the book that really spoke to me was Ms. Kondo's "confession" regarding discarding items that belonged to family members without their permission (pages 50 and 51). This was beyond tidying. This was (still is?) a cry for help. I thought that this woman really needs to talk to someone, yet she really has succeeded brilliantly in her work. After all, who doesn't think they could benefit from a few tips on keeping the place a little neater....? Buy the book, but my guess is that peering into this woman's mindset will be considerably more entertaining than the strategies she espouses. The best part of all? I'm not married to her.

One last gem; (Ms. Kondo speaking) "I never tidy my room. Why? Because it's already tidy."
