author: Marie Kondo
review_title: helpful for hoarders, otherwise a load of spiritual jumbo-jumbo.
review_text: 90% of the focus of this book is about throwing out household items that do not "spark joy". No problem there, I like the idea of pairing down even further, although I already have a pretty Spartan home to begin with. My problem with this book is that there are basically zero helpful tips to keep your house from reverting to its cluttered state. Kondo promises that none of her former clients have reverted to their former cluttered lifestyle. She keeps mentioning this clutter free state of mind that everyone will reach once they get rid of all of their unnecessary items, a mindset that even her "lazy" and slobby clients reach, from which they never backslide. Yet there are no practical tips on keeping your home clean other than getting rid of things. What about those of us that are lazy about laundry piling up around the house, dirty dishes and countertops, incoming mail, etc?  I'm not buying it. I am the opposite of a hoarder and I already do periodic deep cleans and tidying sessions and (being fairly OCD about cleanliness and organization when I decide to be)  I've even achieved this zenlike bliss of having ones home in perfect order.  But I always revert back into a cluttered state eventually.  Nothing in this book offered any enlightenment on how to stop that cycle. Plus, I found the anthropomorphizing of objects more than a little silly. Sorry, I'm not going to start talking to my belongings or imbue them with some spiritual nature.  I don't understand how this helps someone become less of a slob.

title: The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up: The Japanese Art of Decluttering and Organizing
subtitle: Hardcover – October 14, 2014
author: Marie Kondo
review_text:
"The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up" by Marie Kondo is a cute and cozy read. However I found myself disagreeing with about half of the advice. I like balling up my socks and keep them in little baskets. I also like organizing one room at a time. That I can handle. Thinking of organizing a whole disorderly house at once gives me a headache. What I did agree with was that "tidying must start with discarding." This is essential advice that really does help the process or organizing. If you have less to organize in the first place, that makes a lot of sense.

As to the question of "Does this bring me joy?" - I'd have difficulty keeping most of what I own. I'd keep my desk, kitchen items, a book of poetry and a few outfits. I'd have almost nothing left. lol I guess I'm more practical and believe that not everything you own has to fit certain criteria. I'd like to keep what is OK, I like and what I love. If something makes me feel bad, of course I'll get rid of it and have.

I did like reading that the author still has a copy of Alice in Wonderland from her childhood. I do too and will never get rid of it. I have mixed feelings however about getting rid of photographs. I have all mine sorted into the years of my life but haven't put them in albums. I could get around to it in the next decade.

I think the author could have emphasized a bit more that people need to buy less to begin with. Buying new things is fun but if you have nowhere to put the new things, what is the point? You are just then on an endless treadmill of buying and tossing. I would have also liked her to talk more about donating things to charity. I hated to think that all the people she helps are just throwing things in the trash. She talks a lot about trash bags.

I'd also advise people not to use sponges at all. I'd suggest they use cloths that can be washed in the washing machine with bleach. Sponges are just too dirty to keep even if you put them out in the sunlight.

And I'd have suggested that people just keep one file box or one file cabinet to keep their important papers in. It is not possible to throw out all papers even though they do tend to pile up.

What some Americans may find a bit odd is talking to inanimate objects. I think I would rather talk to my cats who can talk back. I don't think I'll be talking to my house or purse anytime soon. lol There is also information about the Shinto religion and worshiping deities and gaining good luck. I think it is better to just pray to God for health, etc.

I do hope the author never comes by to see that I still have two closets of clothes. I change out my clothes twice a year according to the cold or hot weather. So far I'm happy with this arrangement. Maybe American closets are sometimes smaller than Japanese closets. I don't know. I just don't have anyplace to put most folded clothes except on the shelf in my closet.

Now as far as hiding books away in a closet I have to ask why? Shouldn't books be on display and show your good taste in books? I think so. And tossing away a book I haven't read yet...that is never going to happen!
I just read a lot more than most people I guess.

So while I found this book highly entertaining I did have some issues that prompted me to write this long review. Half the advice I agreed with and the other half did not work for me personally. I still am glad however that I read it because it has given me more motivation to keep tidy.

So thank you to the friend who gave me this book.

~The Rebecca Review

title: The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up: The Japanese Art of Decluttering and Organizing
subtitle: Hardcover – October 14, 2014
author: Marie Kondo
review_title: A long title for a brilliant book!
review_text:
So: the super excellent life-changing magic of tidying up... Here's the gist, the writer, Marie Kondo, is a professional organizer, who goes around Japan to help people get rid of clutter and organize what's left of it. If you think all Japanese are all minimal and zen, think again! They are just as messy as the rest of us. And they have even less space. That is, until Marie has visited. She doesn't sell storage solutions, she wants you to have so little you don't need storage solutions.

Marie is Shinto and so thanks all her stuff when using it, after using it and when throwing it out. I thought it was brilliant. I am not a Shinto animist, but I am "barking mad", and one reason I cannot get rid of stuff is that I feel sorry for the stuff that gets discarded. Marie has a different take, on storing and keeping stuff.
Two examples:
Gifts: their purpose is to be gifted, to be received and to bring pleasure. Once that has been accomplished they are ready to move on. Which immediately negates the guilt you would otherwise feel in getting rid of a gift.
Clothes: their purpose is to make you comfortable and look good, if they get old you thank them and let them move on. If they were a mistake and did not make you look good you thank them for teaching you what doesn't suit you and you let them go

The key is: "Does this give you joy". And this works for all kinds of stuff, and papers, and books and mementos. You start from easy to difficult, I did do the easiest category: my clothes. I piled them in a large heap and looked aghast at the enormous amount I actually had, and then I took everything in my hand to see if it brought me "joy". If not you can let it move on.
Because; things, clothes, stuff which are stored in dark places are not happy.
They are not fulfilling their purpose. And the fact that they are there, slowly mouldering away in darkness will weigh on your mind. Out of sight is not out of mind.
For me this is perfect. This is exactly how I feel about stuff, about storing stuff, and now I can suddenly let them go and feel really good about it. So I did phase one, my clothes. I happily got rid of half of my clothes, shoes, etc.
Another excellent tool the book gave me is "how to fold clothes". Yes, the mind boggles but luckily there is You-tube where the writer actually demonstrates what she means.
And gosh! Does it work!!!! I now not only can fold beautifully, I actually enjoy folding my clothes! It used to be one of my biggest nightmares! But, within half an hour of watching the videos, I was brilliant at it! And it is a joy to open my drawers! All the clothes are there, clearly seen and easily chosen. You also stand all the folded clothes on one end, so you don't stack, so when you open a drawer you see the top of every shirt.
You see, clothes don't like to be crumpled, or squashed at the bottom of the pile. So the extra benefit is that all my clothes are now very happy too!
The next phase, the second easiest, should be books, but for me books are very emotional, and sort of holy, so they will have to be one of the last projects I tackle. There is no reason not to be flexible, easiest first, and ''Komono'' (read the book) are definitely easier for me than books. But the magic of tidying up is working already... I come across books which I didn't want to get rid off, which I have been lugging around for decades, and suddenly I realize, "This particular book brings me no joy.... It can go!"
I suppose it is clear that I really love this book and as long as it gives me joy it will remain on my bookshelves!

The book itself is very pretty and a pleasure to hold, it is well printed on decent paper with an easy to read typeface. It is quite small and well bound in a hard cover.

subtitle: Hardcover – October 14, 2014
author: Marie Kondo
review_title: This is a GREAT little book — not for just reading; but for changing your attitude and life
review_text:
Daughter read it and told me it was great. She said so enough times that I finally ordered and read every word.

It is a great book in several respects: [1] substantive content is very good; the methods and rationale for them are all well explained and backed up with authors experiences (personally and with clients who consulted with her on Getting Organized; [2] It's well written and a small book and a good, easy read; [3] it is very motivating; it tells you exactly how to go about "tidying up" your place and how to do it in steps and this and her enthusiasm and explained benefits to expect, will encourage anyone (even a hoarder) to make some effort to at least see how it works.

For me, and surely many others, the hardest part of getting organized or "tidying up" is the GETTING STARTED and having a METHODOLOGY/PLAN. I found this book easily cranked up my motivation, gave me some good, new ideas and, best of all, motivated me to get started. From that point, I had great results.

One thing that might seem simply logical but is far greater than it sounds is: Even for a guy like me, not ever into tidying up, cleaning up or straightening out a household (now a necessity for bachelor again) ... the feeling of SATISFACTION from doing it and seeing the results was really significant. And, further, it's hard to believe how greatly you feel (how much better) when you change your surrounds from disorder to tidied up and orderly. No doubt, it does affect your subconscious mind and senses of surrounds and increases a sense of well being, comfort and tends to even uncluttered your mind (thinking) as well ... she addresses that (so do some other researchers/writers) ... but with her book, you will not only hear her, and her examples of various clients, but you are sure to FEEL it, if you read the book, grab hold of the motivation offered and START to TIDY UP ASAP ... and then keep it going. I am reluctant to over-state and say it makes it "fun" ... but it almost does if you really get the motivation up and go at it (i.e. "get into it'). I read many books over many years; this is one of the best little, simple and most effective books I have read in a long time.

You will NOT regret reading this book, if you have any issue or concern over cleaning up, straightening up, keeping things orderly and having a neat and organized space to live in. Enjoy.

review_title: brilliant book! I read this in one go & ...

Fabulous, brilliant book!

I read this in one go & it's just brilliant. It really does clear the cobwebs from your mind in how your *think* about your possessions &
tidying was fun, really! It's incredibly uplifting w/a wonderful message that I consider it a *must read* & it is so much more
than tidying, but a wonderful way to view & live your life. Many thanks to Marie Kondo!

Also, too, I wanted to note, my home is already incredibly organized & in good working order, but something just felt off -- I had too many items (altho beautiful) that held bittersweet memories for me & after donating/selling them my home feels so much happier & vibrant. I had in the past tried to edit these items, but just felt *stuck* -- Marie walks you thru what can be holding you back & offers
a fresh perspective. It was a wonderful experience, fun & uplifting -- highly recommend this book!

review_title: Put this one down and read her book “Verity” instead!! You can thank me later! Ha Ha!!
review_text: The only reason I finished this book is my kids and I sort of do a book club type thing. It was horrible. to not only myself, but my daughters were annoyed with it too!! The whole “writing letters to Ellen”….I found that boring and wanted to just stop reading!! She’s a grown adult, why is she referencing her child hood journal…and who the heck writes to Ellen? I don’t know, that just annoyed the heck out of me. Also her relationship with Ryle was lacking substance. . It just didn’t make a lot of sense. Then she opens a business just with the poof of her fingers…again missing detail and oomph!! The whole book just wasn’t great. My daughters want to read the second one just for S&G AND because this is a series. Gotta finish what we start. Ugg!! My oldest daughter has finished it and said it was a little better but still not great so it looks like I’m gonna be reading letters to Ellen again. Ugg!! Good thing these books are quick reads. The things we do for our children. My opinion…put this book down and read her book “Verity”!!! That’s a great book!! It’s a much better book. Better story. The end leaves you thinking and questioning everything!!!  I hope that one turns into a series! Well if she can keep the momentum going, which I’m sure she can!! It’s still cheesy and a little unbelievable, but it’s a book and that’s why we read them. They don’t have to be believable but they do need to feel like they were written with feeling, as if the author didn’t have a deadline to meet! Maybe this wasn’t her story to begin with!! Someone else’s idea. Who knows. This book felt rushed and empty. More like an after school special rather than a series starter.  Hopefully the second one is better. Fingers crossed!!

review_text:
I cannot tell you how angry this book made me feel. I’m not sure if I’m the only one, but considering all the five star reviews it seems I’m one of a few that flat out didn’t care for this book. I gave it two starts because 1) I still love Colleen and will continue to read her work. 2) I do love the way she writes, her style is still one of my favorites.
Starting out this book moved way too fast for my liking. The middle got extremely slow. Then the end sped up again to the point where I almost stopped reading it. She stayed in the apartment her husband beat her up and tried to rape her in? And then you let him be a part of the child’s life!? I can’t even with this book. This guy never gets in trouble for his actions, and is free to do what he did to Lily to anyone else. Yes, they loved each other, and the result of that love was heartbreaking. However, I can’t say the end result didn’t make me anything but mad. I loved Atlas, and if the story had started with him, broken off with him leaving and her attending college, and then them accidentally meeting up again at his restaurant…THAT would have been a great storyline. I know this book was personal to Colleen and I give her mad props for sharing pieces of her and her moms life. Partner abuse needs to be talked about more.
As I said, I still love Colleen Hoover and the way she creates a story, I just can’t get on board with this one. *All personal opinion*

review_text:
>Book Review – It Ends with Us

>I am an independent reviewer. This book is the 1st in the It Ends with Us series and ends HEA-ish. This book is a love story gone bad and fate gone good. Lily is a survivor of an abusive father. Her thoughts are so black & white on her parents. She hates her father and can’t respect her mother for staying with him. When Lily meets the charming Ryle, she (and I) were charmed. He is rich, funny and thoughtful. Their relationship takes place over awhile as Lily and Ryle create lives for themselves. When Ryle’s sister starts to work for Lily, Ryle’s and Lily’s paths cross again. I get that Lily and Ryle needed to meet again, but the sister was an odd character. She is uber rich and just walks into a dirty store front to work for peanuts.

>A secondary story takes place as Lily is reading her diary from high school. She fell in love with a homeless boy, Atlas and the reader learns that whole story. When Atlas and Lily meet again, Lily is in love with Ryle. Ryle has issues with anger and jealousy, which turn into violence toward Lily. How eye opening to see how someone can rationalize away domestic abuse. The author really had me loving Ryle. My heart broke when his fatal flaw was revealed. Ryle mentioned he attended anger therapy, but after he hurts Lily in anger he doesn’t seem to go to any therapy. Couple's therapy could have been an option to show how committed Lily and Ryle are to each other.

>This book is appropriate for an adult audience. I am giving this book 4 stars. I hope the next book gives up more Atlas.

title: It Ends with Us: A Novel (1)
subtitle: Paperback – August 2, 2016
author: Colleen Hoover
review_title: Preventing your heart from forgiving someone you love is actually a hell of a lot harder than simply forgiving them.
review_text:
*Review originally posted on Goodreads*

'I wish cutting my feelings off for the person who hurt me was as easy as I used to think it would be. Preventing your heart from forgiving someone you love is actually a hell of a lot harder than simply forgiving them.'

It Ends With Us was beautifully complicated. It was hot and cold. Up and down. Good and bad. Beautiful and ugly... I'm still trying to figure out how I really feel about it all because I'm genuinely torn on how I want to perceive this storyline. I loved it but in all honesty, I really do think I hate it as well. Not the "I-hate-you-Colleen-Hoover-stop-writing-books-and-find-a-different-career" type of hate but rather "I-hate-you-Colleen-Hoover-for-making-me-hate-everything-that-I-came-to-love" kind of hate because it pretty much summarizes all my thoughts and feelings about It Ends With Us in one sentence.

My opinions were completely divided. One side of me, the hopeless romantic, was utterly unsatisfied and angry with the outcome of the story. The opposite side, the one that's all about women's empowerment, was cheering on #TeamLily like it was Independence Day.

Rather than trying to sugarcoat my thoughts, I'm just going to be completely honest. I was 100 percent team Ryle from the very first time we met him. Just like Lily, I fell in love with every word and every gesture that rolled off of his body. I. WAS. HOOKED. It also didn't help that I kept fantasizing Doctor Mike as Ryle Kincaid. *heart eyes emoji* I loved his ambition. His personality. His confidence. To be honest, I think I might've loved Ryle even more than Lily did but that's another story for another day. That more than likely explains why I took the second half of this book like a blow to the gut.

Once we got to the second half of the book, that's where it started going a bit downhill for me as a Ryle and Lily shipper. Every happy moment that ever happened between my ship came barreling down as it collided with pain and abuse. I was angry. I was thrashing. I was yelling at the pages in front of me, "Why are you doing this Colleen?!" But most importantly, I was just heartbroken to see such a beautiful couple become so toxic. Everything I loved about the first half of the book was slowly unraveling right before my very eyes as if it never really existed in the first place. I can't even remember how many times I wanted to put the book down because my hopeless romantic self just couldn't handle it anymore. But I just kept on reading because I was guiltily hoping that Ryle and Lily would still have their happy ending despite all that had happened. :/ Sadly, this was where I was torn the most.

I have the upmost respect for Lily. She is definitely one of my favorite female characters that Colleen has ever created because she did what a lot of us would've struggled to do in the end: walk away. Lily was such a strong character and I admire her so much for having the strength to stand up for herself. There were numerous times towards the end of the book where I knew I probably would've gave in and forgave Ryle for his actions but Lily was inflexible. She was in a tough position but she put her foot down and demanded better for herself. In the end, no matter if I ship Ryle/Lily or Atlas/Lily, I'm glad that Lily was able to find peace for her and Emmy.

As for Atlas, I liked him but I didn't love him. Definitely nowhere near my love for Ryle. I wasn't exactly rooting for Atlas but I wouldn't have minded if Lily chose him in the end. However, I still very much preferred Ryle regardless. I just felt that Atlas was the typical knight in shining armor. Typical good guy you run to. His background story was interesting but him as a character... not so much. He just felt so ordinary and predictable. I wanted to ship Atlas and Lily because let's face it, the signs were practically being shoved down our throats, and although the relationship between Ryle and Lily was developing, Atlas's presence was a like a thorn on your side you just couldn't shake off. But I just couldn't bring myself to ship them blindly like I did with Ryle and Lily.

Unfortunately, I was too far gone and too far in love with the idea of Ryle and Lily to make room for Atlas and because of that, I'm not sure if I'll ever be fully satisfied with that ending. I was happy that Lily was no longer a victim of domestic abuse. I'm glad that after all that happened between them, Lily and Ryle parted on good terms. I'll forever be heartbroken over the idea of what could've been. And I feel indifferent to Lily and Atlas. Sorry not sorry, Atlas. That basically sums up all my feelings in a nutshell.

To be honest, I was actually feeling a bit more bitter than I'm making it seem after that ending. But after reading the author's note, it really put things in perspective for me and made me look at the story with brand new eyes. I developed a new understanding and appreciation for the story behind the story.

I was dying for Ryle and Lily to have their happy ending. Until the very end, I was still rooting for them. It's such an ugly confession to make especially when the couple you're rooting for is toxic and abusive. And I think I feel this way because I never, and hopefully I never will, had to experience abuse. I don't know what it's like and what goes on in the minds of the abused. Colleen did such an excellent job at creating the perfectly imperfect man that was Ryle. Abuse in books has always been a trigger for me and if it were any other book I think I would've put this book down by the first incident of abuse. But Colleen just made you fall so deeply in love with a character that even you couldn't bring yourself to hate him even if you wanted to. YOU were the Lily of this story. But unfortunately, I don't think my Lily would've had the courage to leave. I really wish I could say that I would leave in an instant, but I think I would honestly be lying to myself. You can tell yourself that if you were in Lily's position you would leave in a blink of an eye, but things wouldn't be as easily said and done if you were the one who was actually experiencing it all. And in truth, I think this is exactly what Colleen wanted us to actually sit down and think about because victims who've experienced abuse wouldn't be rooting for Ryle and Lily. I wouldn't be rooting for Ryle and Lily. It just goes to show how much of a struggle it really is to walk away from someone you love and loves you back in all the wrong ways. I usually never read the author's notes after the book but I'm really glad I took the time to read Colleen's story. It really did make me see the situation from a different perspective.

I'd been having a bad CoHo streak for three books in a row (if you're curious, the books were — in order — Hopeless, November 9, and Too Late) and for a moment there I was beginning to think that I was doomed to never enjoy another book written by Colleen Hoover again. But PRAISE. It Ends With Us restored my faith completely in the CoHo hype. Not that I was ever planning NOT to read any more of Colleen's books! Colleen Hoover is 100 percent my favorite auto-buy author. I will always buy her books no matter if I end up loving them or not, and with good reason because Colleen is such an exceptional writer. It Ends With Us still wasn't able to top Ugly Love as my favorite CoHo book of all time but I really enjoyed this book more than I thought I would.

title: It Ends with Us: A Novel (1)
subtitle: Paperback – August 2, 2016
author: Colleen Hoover
review_text:
It has taken me a while to write a review for this book. In the simplest of terms, this book destroyed me. I went in knowing very little about the plot and theme. I think that was a good thing, but probably contributed to why I was so destroyed by it. I wasn’t expecting an emotionally heavy book, but that is what this is.

I’m not sure I’ve felt this much anxiety while reading a book before. I read it fast. When I’d force myself to take a break and put it down, my hands, arms, and shoulders were actually sore from me being so tense. That should indicate just how attached and emotionally invested I get to characters and their stories.

The description on Goodreads, as well as the one on the back on the book are quite deceiving. They make it out like it is a love triangle. I wouldn’t classify it as such. Lily’s relationships with Ryle and Atlas happen separately from each other. I’m not giving anything away here when I say that Atlas does come back into Lily’s life unexpectedly, but it doesn’t quite happen in the way one might think or expect. It certainly doesn’t progress the way I thought it might. So no, this isn’t a love triangle.

Like I said above, I didn’t know a lot about this book when I decided to read it. I knew there was a lot of hype surrounding it’s release, but that’s about it. I’m not going to say much more that is specific to the plot, except that it is not a “light read.” It deals with emotionally heavy topics. If you’re one to look for ‘trigger warnings’ you may want to look at other reviews for those warnings. I don’t want to say much for those who don’t want to know.

This book did have sweet moments, funny moments, lovely moments, but it was also heartbreaking, sad, and at times really tough to read. Thinking more on it, one reason why this book destroyed me so much is because I found myself thinking like Lily. Making excuses, saying ‘if only.’ If I reacted like this to characters in a book, what would I do if I was in Lily’s position in real life? That scared me.

Lastly, I’m not sure I’d personally categorize this as a romance. Yes, it is about love and relationships at the core. Yes there’s some sex, but it is definitely not your typical romance book. That said, I would say this definition I read about romance novels does apply to it:
“Two basic elements comprise every romance novel: a central love story and an emotionally-satisfying and optimistic ending.”
(It just might not end in the way you expect it to.)

Colleen Hoover wrote a novel that affected me in a way I didn’t expect. The message that you will find within these pages is deeply important. It had me evaluating myself, my thoughts, and what my “limit” would be. I think it’ll make you think about things in a different light as well.

It’s real, raw, emotional, powerful, happy, sad. There were so many things in this book that broke my heart, and by the end, it was only partially put back together. I don’t think I’ll ever fully recover from this book. I felt all the emotions deep down and still do when I think back to this book. There were definitely tears. I don’t know what else I can say except for:

READ. THIS. BOOK.

review_title: Wow! My heart is cheering and breaking all at the same time.
review_text: First off... WOW! I am part of a book club and we wanted to pick a love story to honor Valentine's Day, and boy did we ever! I'll admit, I have read a lot of romance novels, but this was the most realistic (in a sense) story I have ever read. This is the first book of Colleen Hoover's that I've read. The complexity of the two romances in one really kept me hanging on the edge of my seat. I really didn't know what to think. I didn't know who I wanted her to choose. I honestly felt as though I could feel how Lily was feeling through Colleen's writing. It was "magical" (cheesy I know). And Lily was such a dynamic character that I can truly say I never under appreciated. Most romantic novels lead to find things about the leading lady that are irritating, and at times ruin the rest of the book for me. Not the case here. I wanted to just keep reading the book when it was over. I needed more. So much so, that as soon I finished this book, I bought and stayed up reading until 4 a.m. one of  Colleen Hoover's other books "Maybe Someday". I read the entire thing in one sitting. I couldn't put it down either. However, that's a review for another day. Truly, do yourself a favor and read this book.

title: The Woman in the Window: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: A. J. Finn
review_title: Come on.....basic at best. Derivative tropes and truly lacks any punch. Characters 2D at best.
review_text:
I wanted to enjoy this book more. More than that, I wanted to be surprised and taken on a roller-coaster of a ride bearing in mind all of the hype surrounding this book. Well...I wasn't riding on a roller coaster. Not even the kiddie coaster. In fact, I wasn't even riding on my nephew's hand-me-down Gun-It-and-Go-Chopper.

The descriptive writing was basic (you can't have rattan carpet on stairs either....coir, sisal or seagrass yes....rattan? No. Nitpicky. Maybe but considering how much they referenced it. It bothered me).

The Protagonist...a literal wet bathrobe and dumb considering she is a shrink, regardless of her situation.

There was no anxious tension. No depth to characters and the pacing only served to give the plot away. I'll explain below (spoilers).
**SPOILERS**
.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.
.
I love a good mystery and thriller. I've seen a lot of movies and read my fair share of books, so for me, the pacing is the most important element in a book with an unreliable narrator. Particularly, at what point the author chooses to reveal this fact to their audience.

In this instance, Finn begins to overtly set up Anna as unreliable from the start. She’s an alcoholic, agoraphobic shrink also addicted to pills and B&W noir films. That plot device - overt from ”go”- made Finn’s reveal of this, anti-climactic.

However, when an author has an unreliable narrator, I’ve always felt there are only three options an author can truly go.

One:
The big reveal at the end that our MC is freaky, dead, psychotic or has skewed perceptions due to whatever reason and the unreliability factor is a shocker.

I’ve found this the most effective when the author has fine-tuned that plot so tightly, the pacing is so on point and the Easter-eggs are hidden better than the Elf on the Shelf, that the audience (myself included) doesn’t see it coming. Then when the MC is revealed to be as unreliable as the US’s voting system and the narrative goes back and reveals all the things that have happened that pull the plot together? Genius. This works in books and in movies to excellent effect! For example; Fight Club (book and movie), The Secret History, American Psycho, Atonement, The Sixth Sense, The Usual Suspects, Wild Things to name a few.

Two:
The big reveal that our MC is truly unreliable early on in the book – as early as 20% and before the halfway mark. Take for example Gone Girl. I wasn’t surprised by the reveal, but it was really well done. And once that was out of the way, as a reader you were able to go on the true journey of Amys whacked up mind and manipulations. Of course, all the while praying you never meet anyone like that or if you do (that thanks to Gone Girl), you are able to identify them as a sociopath PDQ and run away faster than an escaped fart during Downward Dog. Now that’s tense.

Three:
The least effective for any true effect IMO because of where this reveal is placed. As in the case with this book. Three is when it’s revealed that our MC may be lying to us about 75% the way through. Why is this so bloody lame? Because of pacing. The crucial element for a great suspense thriller. Think about it……
At the 70-75% mark, you know you have 25% of the book left so the true, big reveal is left to come. In fact, you only have 15% to the reveal because the last 10% will be spent tying up loose ends and watching our character receive apologies for everyone thinking they’re nuts and, a few pages spent on their recovery, so they can swan off into a less murky sunset.

Therefore, you can’t help but consider the cast of characters who are likely to havedunit and when you do that, as in the case with The Woman in the Window, logic dictates there are only two…TWO possible suspects.

The obvious Alistair and the more obvious psycho-next-door, 17-year-old Ethan.

1 - Because everyone else is on the periphery except her tenant Dan who went away right after they humped. Zero credibility as a suspect even though Finn gave him the boring red-herring of jail time for assault (and what’s with this freakin' lady?? No background checks when vetting tenants? I don’t care how stoned she is).

2 - Because Alistair is the only blatantly unlikeable and middlingly menacing wanna-be baddie with any sort of character development.

3 - Because Anna is as dense as a bag of bricks….and not to mention unreliable. Let us not forget that Ethan is the only one she’s ever let in her house, given keys to and really communicates with. So of course, it has to be him! It had to be him even before it was revealed she was talking to dead people!

And so why is that? Well, because she likes him, she initially describes him having a halo over his head, invites him into her ONLY safe space, worries about him plus she is deluded, an addict and comes across as red rag to your friendly neighbourhood psychopath that’s why!

As Ethan tells her; “I guess you’re not the world’s best shrink.” Finn, A. J.. The Woman in the Window (p. 398). William Morrow. Kindle Edition.

In fact, here’s some trite end game dialogue between Anna and Ethan and I gotta say…..he’s not wrong.

“How f-ing stupid are you?”
I say nothing. He glares.
“I asked you a question,” he says. “How f-ing stupid—”
“Very,” I say.
“Very what?”
“Very stupid.”
“Who was?”
“I was.”
“Very f-ing stupid.”
“Yes.”

Finn, A. J.. The Woman in the Window (p. 406). William Morrow. Kindle Edition.

So, there you have it. When the hero and villain of the book are agreeing that said hero has been very f-ing stupid….well then, I guess I didn’t have to spend too much time explaining why this book is about as suspenseful as watching our 95-year-old granny being escorted to the car after holiday dinner.

title: The Woman in the Window: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: A. J. Finn
review_text:
Oh my, another one of those Women-in-Jeopardy books. I promised myself that I would not read another of these, but the hype just kept on with this book and there was the promise of the Hitchcockian element. I regret that I did not follow my basic instincts and leave this one alone. Finn’s book, in my humble opinion, was written to be made into a movie—as are all the others of this genre. Chick lit on steroids.
I guess the thing that I dislike the most is that all the women in this type book are portrayed as alcoholic, damaged, unsalvageable souls. Its bad enough that Paula Hawkins and Ruth Ware are portraying women in this light, but for a male writer to do so is insult on top of injury. At least in this one she didn’t vomit.
There are just too many good books out there to spend time on a mediocre one.

title: The Woman in the Window: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: A. J. Finn
review_text:
Imagine a drunk, disoriented, and sad woman is telling you a story..and she’s pretty sure that it happened, but then also, maybe it didn’t? Also imagine that she loves Hitchcock movies and other movies in that vein. That pretty well sums it up.

I did like this book, even though one element of Anna’s life is truly heartbreaking. One thing I will note is that the writing has kind of a staccato feel, mainly because Anna is impaired for most of the book. The rhythm was hard for me to follow at points, so I’d have to reread a sentence every now and then to make sure I was picking up what the author was throwing down. All in all, it’s a good read. Plenty of content, and I was surprised by the killer.

title: The Woman in the Window: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: A. J. Finn
review_text: SO...unreliable female narrator? Check! Posh locale or extravagant homes? Check! Despair? Tragedy? Helplessness? Check, check, check! Like Gone Girl, The Girl On The Train, and The Couple Next Door, this book has a female protagonist with major issues, most of them brought upon by herself. The main difference is that the author this time is a male, who actually suffered from depression, so he knows how it feels to experience anxiety, loss, and helplessness. Good references to Hitchcock and other classic thrillers add depth to the read, though I figured out one of the three “big” reveals quite early on. I did expect a tad more action and suspense towards the resolution, which is why I’m giving it 4 out of 5 stars. For me, not quite as engaging as Gone Girl, but definitely more of a good read than The Death of Mrs. Westaway. Though the latter is itself a good imitation of Jane Eyre or A Murder is Announced by Agatha Christie.

review_text: I am done with Grisham.  I thought he had finally gotten back to his lawyer "genre" like his original books but this was his political diatribe.  He should be a writer in the Charlottesville paper for his little ultra liberal UVA students.  His numerous discourses about the police, lawyers and the courts are a pain in the neck to dig through.  His apparent dislike of lawyers is strange since that was what he was.  Perhaps he is now self-loathing now that he has made a bundle of money writing stories about them.  I will not be mislead by further reviews of saying back tot he old Grisham.  I will not buy another of his books.  Too many other good writers out there in this "who done it and lawyer" genres.  Live the rich man style of living in your mansion in Charlottesville John and don't bother writing more editorials as books.

author: John Grisham
review_title: Poorly written stories about a whiny lawyer
review_text:
This could be Grisham's worst book to date. It is poorly written, with plenty of repetition. It also feels more like a collection of short stories about the central character, rather than individual chapters in a complete, stand-alone novel. It reads like a serial in a monthly magazine. The book would seriously benefit from some additional editing.
Grisham has wriitten a book that panders to the anti-authority paranoics, cop-haters and all those that believe our legal system is completely corrupt. Rogue Lawyer is about an attorney that lives on the fringes of the legal profession, one who's not shy about breaking the law to win his cases because he believes the cops, the prosecutors and the judges are all corrupt or incompetent. He's just leveling the playing field, so his attempts at bribery and jury tampering are pardonable: an anti-hero run amok. The book would have been much more enjoyable if Grisham's title character had done a lot less whining.

title: Rogue Lawyer: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: John Grisham
review_text:
This is the book people obsessed over, saying John Grisham copied Michael
Connelly when he had his leading character, Sebastian Rudd, doing business
out of a van (like the "Lincoln Lawyer"). But, Grisham's van is not actually
an office because Rudd's legal work is outsourced to paralegal contractors.
He socializes in the van and he uses it for transportation to places where he
doesn't want to be seen. The book's structure is more confusing than the van.
This is not one long story but several seemingly unrelated stories that become
related in the end. Each has its plot, characters, irony and sense of humor that
has the evil works of bad guys offseting well-meaning adventures of good
guys (like a SWAT team that causes grief for Rudd's clients). This can be
interpreted as reflecting reality. There really are rogue lawyers and
a rogue in any field is required to deal with unique situations.

I am a reader, however, and I couldn’t stand reading any more of this book and gave up in chapter three. The descriptions given had me rolling my eyes. A fully clothed man lying in a pool of filthy sweat? “ His eyelids felt like they weighed a thousand tons.” Those are some seriously heavy eyelids! title: White Rose, Black Forest
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Eoin Dempsey
review_title: I don't understand the high ratings
review_text:
The story itself had a great premise and I was intrigued that it was based on a true story, but the execution fell very flat. The first chapter reeled me in and I was ready to overlook the simplicity in the writing, but the further I got, the worse it got. The dialogue was so contrived and forced it was almost unbearable to read, there was no flow or emotion to the conversations and it appeared that the characters were not even listening to each other, just waiting to deliver their next line. I felt nothing for the characters and even after getting 60% of the way it was only through reviews on Amazon that I learned this was supposed to be a love story.

Also, the dialogue is often used to advance the plot and state bits of information about the story that no normal person would actually put into a conversation. There are too many examples that I could include here, but I didn’t want to give anything away. It’s almost like, “I was so sad to hear what happened to you at that barn across the hill, next to the stables where the fire occurred six years ago.”

Had this been a YA novel, it would have been perfectly acceptable. As an adult novel, it became a chore to read. The sentence structures were short and read almost in staccato, for example, "They must have seen his parachute. The woman was a Gestapo agent. How could she have gotten him back here by herself? It didn’t seem possible. She must have had help. Her story didn’t check out. Her face appeared in his mind. She was pretty as a pearl-handled dagger. He checked his torso for wounds... She must have gone for help. They’d probably be here in minutes." or even, “Sleep had been a long time coming the previous night. Many questions were still left unanswered. No need to bombard [spoilers] now. They had other waters to navigate. They needed food first.”

Nope. Not worth the read and unfortunate that this wasn’t marketed to teenagers.

review_title: Fictional novel set in WWII not historical fiction
review_text: I listened to this book through Kindle Unlimited and Audible.  The narration was not that great, the female voice was really annoying. Why they chose a man to narrate a female point of view book is odd.  The book itself isn't a bad story, but I'm annoyed that this is the second book I have read recently that uses White Rose in the title to suck you in and has little to nothing to do with Sophie, Hans, and Christoph.  I want to hear their story, not some fictional hanger on to the White Rose movement.  In the case of this book, the story starts after Sophie, Hans and Christoph had been killed.  So the use of the White Rose was simply to suck you in.  Had this book had a different title, I would have enjoyed it more as my expectations would have been different, because the story itself wasn't bad.  However, this is a fictional novel set in WWII not a historical fiction book.

review_text: Of course with that plot, the story had to be somewhat formulaic -- with excellent writing, I might have gotten beyond that issue. I did not feel that I really knew the characters or why a romance developed between them,  despite their being thrown together under dire circumstances. The character of the gestapo ex-boyfriend was such a cliche that it almost wrote itself. I did appreciate the sentiments expressed by the protagonists,  especially in this era of increasing jingoism around the globe, I just felt that it could have been done better. The ending felt so dashed off it was almost pointless. On the plus side, I do appreciate how this novel illuminated the incredible bravery and humanism of Hans and Sophie Scholl and their compatriots,  who fought a losing but heroic battle of words against the Nazi propaganda machine. They are the true heroes of this story.

He jumped into the dark unknown of what laid below but he brought light and a sense of purpose to Franka-who felt guilty on her part for being alive while her comrades were dead. She aided him in being an integral part of the war- a calling that was momentarily snuffed out. Furthermore, John reintroduced love back into Franka's lonely life. The Ending-was a nail biter. It was action packed and my heart was racing. I was trying to skip pages just to see if I would be disappointed ahead. I would recommend this book and will most likely buy and reread this book -if and when I decide to cancel my kindle unlimited subscription.

title: Fall of Giants (The Century Trilogy, Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Ken Follett
review_title: Though Polar Opposites Politically, Follett's Political Bias is as Profound as Ayn Rand
review_text:
Having read some of Follett's other books (the Kingsbridge series, Eye of the Needle, etc.), I began The Century Trilogy series. What began as a fascinating read in books one and two, turned in to complete disappointment in book three. My mother's forefathers were coalminers in Wales, prior to immigrating to America, so I was captivated by characters who may have lived very similar lives to those who came before me. Given that I was not yet born during the early twentieth century, I took for granted the accuracy of quite a bit of Ken Follett's world view while I was reading his books. I knew there were atrocities committed against the working class in the UK and America during the early periods of the books, so I assumed much of his research to be correct. I have always been very open to the idea that different political parties owed their necessity to the time and place in which they were needed.

Unfortunately by the time I had read most of the third book, I realized Follett was an extremist in his socialist, political beliefs, especially with regard to American politics. I am an Independent, and I hate reading anything so far left and so far right, when it provides no basis for reality. I would rather see both the warts and the dimples, rather than be told a fairy tale of half-truths. His viewpoint is very singular in his condemnation for all things Republican, and nothing but praise for all Democrats; even to the extent that he gives Pope John Paul II's great success in Poland to President Carter...utterly ridiculous. Follett praises by intimating Carter's dealings with the communists was "cautious", yet Reagan was supposed to take on the Kremlin during the Solidarity movement perfectly exhibits the bias in his writing.

As I was reading the book, I reflected that all of the Follett books I had ever read, prior to the Century Trilogy were period pieces from a time I had not lived; however, "Edge of Eternity" covered a place in time I know very well. His revisionism of more modern times has left me bereft of any pleasure for reading the first two books. If I can't trust his completely biased viewpoint of modern history, than how can I trust any of his research. Unless you want to read a socialist manifesto, concealed in the vein of storytelling, I would strongly recommend you not purchase any of the books in this series. As for me, I will not be buying another Follett book. It really is sad, because I would have loved to find an author who would have me explore my Welsh heritage.

The book is certainly a page-turner, but it was not at all what I'd hoped it would be. It's really nothing more than a Downton Abbey-like soap opera (I like so many others, got pulled into Downton Abbey in the first two or three seasons, but then gave it up after Matthew's untimely death - at that point I knew my emotions were being toyed with). The sex and sexual tension seems to be a key theme with some of these characters, and reading those scenes made me feel as if I were reading a trashy romance novel.

I gave up reading the book about a third of the way through, so I apologize to anyone reading this review if it isn't at all helpful!

title: Fall of Giants (The Century Trilogy, Book 1)

author: Ken Follett
review_title: Trying To Figure Out What Went Wrong
review_text:
Ken Follett's not an elegant writer, but in "Pillars of the Earth" he told a fascinating, fast-paced if sometimes gruesomely tasteless story. "Fall of Giants" deals with another fascinating historical period, but in spite of a few moderately interesting characters, it never really manages to come to life.

Why not? I suspect when one is writing a "world turned upside down" historical novel, you need a central character and a central point of view to really engage the reader in the surrounding events. "Gone with the Wind," though seriously flawed by its endemic racism, works brilliantly as an historical novel because events are all seen through the prism of the author's brilliant creation, Scarlett O'Hara. Of course Scarlett has friends, relatives and servants that enable the author to broaden the perspective, but Margaret Mitchell does not try to give equal time to a northern abolitionist family and an English working class family struggling because the Union's blockade of Confederate cotton shipments has shut down English textile mills. Follett, in his attempt to dramatize the scope of World War I and the upending of ruling class entitlements and imperialist ambitions in several countries, sets up too many people doing too many things to deal with too many issues in too many places. The story moves among five intertwined families--Welsh miners, English aristocrats, German diplomats, Russian revolutionaries and American industrialists--shifting from domestic scenes to organizers' meetings to halls of power to battlefields--and in addition to everything else, throws the changing role of women into the mix. As a result, you never engage with any one character or set of circumstances long enough to care.

"Pillars of the Earth" works in spite of its wide scope and large cast of characters because it focuses on a single community and a power struggle between two central characters with whom the rest of the characters have logical links. While I give Follett credit for handling all the characters and plots in "Fall of Giants" without confusing the reader, it's like trying to stuff bites of five different foods in your mouth at once. You can hardly chew, and there's no distinctive flavor to savor or remember.

title: Fall of Giants (The Century Trilogy, Book 1)

review_title: and I enjoyed Pillars of the Earth aswell as it's sequel World ...
review_text:
Ken Follett is a skilled author, and I enjoyed Pillars of the Earth aswell as it's sequel World Without End tremendously. This book, was however a big disappointment.

I found that, whenever there would be some kind of suspense, some cliff-hanger to the next chapter, Follett would always switch to another character in a very dull situation. The amount of characters could be said to give depth to the storyline, but I felt it moreso hindered the story from being compelling in any kind of way. Some characters were interesting, but others were not, and this irritated me. Even if all characters would have been golden, I feel like the switches between them were far too many - in a single chapter Follett could literally go from Russia to the US to Germany, all in one chapter... It felt okay for the first part, where the chapters were long and characters were slowly introduced, but later or it just went downhill. Instead of seeing many characters storylines intervening as the story progressed, it felt like they all had very separate storylines, with very few contacts towards the end of the novel.

I sincerly liked a few parts of the book, and feel like it could have been a brilliant book if it was shorter. Or perhaps split into two books, separating the families storylines and not attempting to mash them together like this. Overall, it felt like a history book on the different countries points of view relating to the first world war, with some bland characters to represent each country.

review_text: This is not what I expected from Follett. He has written this first of a trilogy as if the reader is a moron who can't figure out the obvious.  I'm not talking here about our knowledge of history, I am simply saying that he adds too much where it is not needed. He has created characters that are watered down and just plain boring.  I'm finding myself rolling my eyes more than once at some of the scenarios. However, because I shelled out 18 bucks for this Kindle edition, I must see it through to the end.  To be continued...

title: Fall of Giants (The Century Trilogy, Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Ken Follett
review_text: As a historical fiction -- especially 20th century -- buff, it's hard not to be attracted at times enjoy this first book of the trilogy. Follet does put you in the middle of the events and social conditions of  Pre-WWI and the War itself. I was astonished, however, at how badly it is written, how unreal the characters are, and the incredibly and towards the end of the book laughable coincidences that would bring the characters together (two principal characters, one British, one German, literally bumping into each other at the famous Christmas truce soccer game in the middle of the trenches...with dialogue that doesn't suggest the slightest surprise).  The writing is often atrocious, such as when towards the end of the book one of the characters says that "it will probably get another World War to make them understand." How insightful of him!!! The reader, I gather, is supposed to empathize and feel "Oh how right he is."  Please.  Having said that, will I read the other two books?...Probably. In fact, I'm sure I will.  It is interesting history. I've enjoyed many of Follet's other works. Which makes me realize just how difficult historical fiction can be. I'd actually give it a 2.5 stars..

author: Rachel Hollis
review_text:
As a 52 year old woman, I was surprised to find myself looking forward to delving into this book. As the mother of a 22 year old woman, I was expecting, based on younger friends who had read this and the reviews, a great read to pass on to my daughter.

The author has certainly experienced devastating loss, parental issues, relationship failures (and triumphs!), pain of separation and business ups and downs. I did love Chapter 2, hence the Two Star rating.

Unfortunately, I will not hand this book to my daughter and encourage her to read it. I kept on waiting for Rachel to address the elephant in the room: when your partner, in Rachel’s case her husband, makes a significant amount of money. When I say significant, Dave Hollis left his position he held since 2011 as the chief of Disney’s movie distribution. I don’t know his salary, but I can’t help but feel it was enough to allow his partner certain freedoms that the average woman does not enjoy: babysitters/nannies, errand runners, convenient/high end grocery stores, an option other than 4 am to workout, sitters to allow for work travel, etc.

Having said all this, some would say I am not giving Rachel the grace she describes in the book, and I’m ok with that because what Rachel has accomplished is amazing and she is someone I would love to meet. (She may not want to meet me!) I can honestly say that my husband and I would have made many different decisions, large and small, if my income was not essential to putting food on the table, a roof over my families head, carrying insurance for a family of five, purchasing used cars, etc. Perhaps Rachel’s income is needed for the day to day essentials of running a family, since she never addresses how money plays a part in becoming who we were meant to be, we don’t know. With all of the other personal issues covered in Girl, Wash Your Face, a reader may wonder why their personal financial story wasn’t discussed.

review_text:
In Girl Wash Your Face, Rachel Hollis debunks lies we believe about ourselves by sharing her own fallible moments. Each essay — 20 in total — addresses one lie. Hollis discusses happiness, saying no, not being good enough, weight and diet, being bad at sex, among other topics. As the book goes on, the “lighter” lies from the early chapters give way to more serious issues. She is candid about her brother’s suicide, her trials through attempts at adoption, and drinking too much.

This book is just the confirmation we all need that all those Instagram and Facebook pictures that make other people’s lives look amazing are actually hiding the real, boring, normal, crazy, unbecoming stuff that happens behind the scenes. It is confirmation that no matter what we think everyone else is doing right, they are dealing with their own challenges or insecurities.

Hollis is able to tackle issues of all sizes in this book and she does so with honesty and humor, which makes her lessons that much easier for the reader to relate to.

I recommend this book to young adult and middle-age women who need to recognize that their own challenges are shared by others. Most people will be able to relate to at least a few of the lies and Hollis’s own stories.

author: Rachel Hollis
review_text:
I never write reviews, but I felt compelled to after reading some of the critical, mean, and down right savage remarks from other readers on Amazon. In Girl, Wash Your Face, Hollis gives solid advice, teaches tough lessons, and at the same time makes you feel like you are her best friend. Other reviewers seem to criticize her lack of formal training, acknowledgement of how far she has come, and verbiage. In my opinion, she's simply sharing her story, and there is plenty to be learned from it. Do you really need formal training to inspire and motivate others? Does recognizing your wins, and sharing them with the world make you a bad person? Does the use of casual vernacular hurt anyone?

Haters are going to hate when you succeed. But, if you are looking for an authentic voice, that shows you a realistic path towards self-improvement, do yourself a favor and pick up a copy.

author: B. J. Novak
review_text:
How does this book have over a thousand 5-star reviews??

Breaking the fourth wall is not new in children's literature, and it has been done better (and funnier). Mo Willems' [[ASIN:1423133080 We Are in a Book!]] is laugh out loud funny, and an excellent choice for emerging readers. Children can also still enjoy the Groverian classic, [[ASIN:037582913X The Monster at the End of this Book]]. Either way, kids will learn that reading can be fun and empowering but not hurtful.

The Book With No Pictures is, perhaps aptly given the lack of pictures, a naked emperor. The realistic usefulness would be as a read-aloud for book-phobic kids. Its anti-authority vibe would be an easy sell, though perhaps the benefit even there is short-lived. This will not provide a pervasive incentive to read, given its laugh-at-you nature. Why would a child want to read when they just laughed at the reader's expense? That sort of embarrassment is the opposite of the "warm and joyous" experience the publisher heralds. The BooBooButt doesn't bother me as much as the overall meh-ness of the book.

Conclusion: B.J. Novak may write for a living, but this is not good writing for children. Not funny, Not original, Not recommended.

review_title: kids love it, Mom just likes it.
review_text:
When my kids (5 and 3) first got this book they were pretty upset, "what?! no pictures?! I dont like this book!" they went on and on about how they didnt want me to read it because it wouldnt be a "fun" book. Well, I read it and....THEY LOVE IT! they laugh hysterically every time I read it. So for them its a definite 5 star review...

for me however, its 4 stars. I like the book, and I like that the kids love it, but there's something missing. The book seems rather short, and not filled with as many funny, random words I was hoping for. Unlike other interactive type books, this one has the reader (me) engaging in a weird, mostly, one-sided conversation. I know I would have been pretty mad had I spent the amount the book retails for. Also, and this is a bit nitpicky of me, I wasnt a fan of the 3 pages where the book mentions refers to "the kid Im reading this book to" It only mentions one kid and talks about how the kid is so smart for choosing this book. I have two kids so I have to change it to refer to two kids during those 3 pages and they dont always chose the book, so saying they did seems a bit weird to me.

Either way, if you can get this book cheap, get it. The kids will love it. Its fun to read and be goofy with it.

author: B. J. Novak
review_text:
This book is startlingly simple, yet amazingly creative. It is both a pleasure to read to a kid, and it's subtle message is a respect for what books can do -- i.e., the power of words and ideas -- that I really like. And all this is done while providing plenty of laughs.

We bought the book for my three- and five-year-old nephews. It was a bit over the head of the three-year-old, but the five-year-old found it very funny. He asked each family member to read it to him.

The only downsides of The Book With No Pictures are that it is short, and I have a nagging suspicion that it could grow old. But, for me, the laughs I heard were worth the probably too expensive price tag. I definitely recommend it as a gift for any child close to five-years-old.

review_text:

author: Lucinda Berry
review_title: I feel so many things yet they all lead to disappointment...
review_text:
Where to begin....?
Well.... When I first read the reviews, I kept reading how disturbing this book was and how horrible it played out, little girl killing cat, killed sister, she tortured her own self, blah blah blah. That didn't phase me, for i personally enjoyed disturbing psychological books. They always kept me at the edge of the seat, and I really like that. In the beginning of this book, it kept me hooked and at the edge. I was really into it.....

However.... Towards the middle, early in the middle of the book.... I kept getting more and more curious at the characters, and then I started hating the author. And then I went back and forth hating the characters more. The ignorance is so high on this book that as I finished it..... With no inexplicable ending or no ending at all.... The only thing I'm satisfied about is me not spending ANY of my money on this book. Let me repeat that....

I AM SATISFIED I DID NOT SPEND MY MONEY ON THIS BOOK. 100% COMPLETELY SATISFIED I GOT THIS HORRIBLE BOOK FOR FREE AND I PAID NOTHING.

Because now I can delete it and pretend it never existed. I'm very sorry Lucinda Berry.... But this piece of work was horrible. You got me hooked no doubt the first maybe 7-8 chapters, but after that, I was down right disappointed, I was hoping all through my experience through this book that I would change my mind, that I wouldn't agree with the reviewers.... Well, I agree with them. Now I don't agree with them that this is a very disturbing book, trust me, this is NOTHING compared to what I've read before. If I would say the least, this reminded me of the horror movie The Orphan, just more brutal, at least I can say The Orphan was a good solid movie and it had a great ending. This book was not disturbing, I'm eating it by how horrible it carries itself and how frustrating it makes the reader feel. And quite honestly, a book should not make you feel that way. If it would of had a good ending, I would of probably given a good 5 stars, but this book was just down right a bad read and a very huge waste of my time.

That's why I am saying I am so glad I didn't pay for it, I am 100% satisfied I did t pay for it, I would be very angry right now and would call Amazon's Customer Service to return my money back. That's how bad this book was.

I thought Becky's body wasn't found... so after we find out how she died (which, let's be real, we all figured out pretty quick), where did the body go? HOW did it go missing? review_text:
SPOILERS IN REVIEW.
At one point, I thought it may be 4 stars, because though dark, I found it interesting and did not want to stop listening. But then I immediately took 1 star off for a kitten getting tortured and killed. Then another star for that ridiculous cliff hanger of an ending. Too bad those things really spoiled an otherwise good book.
It was very sad, but also fascinating to read about Janie’s life and her subsequent behavior.
The husband was a jerk. Everything about his character was wrong. Beginning with first meeting Janie.... it was to be kept top secret, and he immediately told Hannah’s sister and husband all about her. And his behavior toward her in the hospital would never happen. Then he never ever took Hannah’s side. He was blind to Janie’s behavior.
I’d really have liked the ending to be more firmed up. What did they do when they heard Janie killed her mom? Who was the guy in the trailer they heard on the video? What happened to Janie? Did Hannah ever return to normal again?

review_title: So much more than I was expecting!  Give this one a chance...you won't regret it.
review_text:
I'm not sure I've ever read such a crazy, intense, non-stop, haunting, anxiety producing novel...but only in the best and most desirable way. I didn't want it to end.

Once this book has you in it's grips, it won't let go. I started it this morning and literally could not put it down. My poor husband probably feels deprived.

Having received The Perfect Child free as a Kindle First February option, I honestly didn't have high expectations. These freebie books are hit or miss for me. Sometimes they're decent, sometimes they absolutely stink, and sometimes, they slowly mesmerize you with their intensity and unparalleled chaos.

The Perfect Child was like that...it gripped me from the start and didn't let me go. The characters, particularly Hannah, were so beautifully tragic...she felt very real to me. I could relate so very much to her feelings, her anxieties...virtually everything. Having said that, at times I also felt frustrated, primarily with Christopher. His choices and actions were questionable, even during the best of times. But the character who had my jaw-dropping at virtually every turn of the page was Janie. HOLY COW! I don't want to say much for fear of giving anything away, but Janie may be the best "villain" I've read in years. Little girl was beyond vile!

Is the story a bit predictable? I'd say yes, which is why I didn't give it a full 5 stars. One of the main threads was incredibly obvious to me, but that took nothing away from the story-line. And there were a couple twists which shocked me...not necessarily because they were unexpected, but because of how they actually occurred. There is also some animal torture/death, which is another deduction for me. I HATE animal torture in any book. Fair warning.

I can't end this review without making the obvious comparisons to Baby Teeth. Clearly, Lucinda Berry was somewhat inspired by the Zoje Stage novel. There are many similar threads throughout...but the stories diverge enough to make them each incredibly readable in their own ways.

I'm a fan, fellow readers. I haven't checked to see if this is Ms. Berry's first novel or not, but she has definitely become a must read author in my eyes. I'll be thinking about this novel for a long, long time.

Sure, he was stupid sometimes, as was his wife, but not unreasonably so, and they mostly snapped out of it when things got serious. Mostly. They still did things that annoyed me (irresponsibily adopting a pet and keeping it when things were so bad... Acting like Greg was in the wrong when he very much was not), but again: it didn't feel unrealistic. Nor did Janie, unlike some evil fictional children who seem to be masterminds with superpowers. Nah; she was just an effed up kid. The only thing that really rubbed me the wrong way was Piper's obsessive involvement... I kept thinking she'd end up boning Chris, for all obsessed with his GOODNESS and risking her job to help him that she was. what seasoned professional acts that way???

review_text:
I think that the misleading raving reviews that took me to buy this book are a sign of how poor are some readers standards for literature. I have even read one review comparing this decidedly poor book to those of Stephen King.
The characters are incredibly dull, almost unidimensional. The won't stop taking really bad decisions even in the worst of cases. The author has clearly written himself as the main character, and it comes out as a rather obvious effort. The writing is like a 14 year old attempt at writing fanfiction. Your suspension of disbelief goes out the window when he decides to tell a nurse, for example, that he is a police detective and she must let him see the patient, describing that if he does it with enough authority she should buy it. It looks as a bad tv show, and I was like, "really?"
The secret (I am so totally gonna spoil it: its a cabin in the woods where two sereotypical bad guys keep women they have kidnapped, rape them, impregnate them and then sell the babies, and kill their mothers) is so far away from being the dark, traumatic, soul shattering horror the author tries to make it be. I don't say that is not something awful; it is, but I think the horror reading audience is quite desensitized to such things already. The entire story is based on this secret, that takes forever to be told, and it's not even good.
I hated it. I'm never reading this guy again.

review_text: This was my first time reading anything by Mark Edwards, and I was pleasantly surprised. For a Kindle Unlimited offer, it was really pretty good. This story of a couple who's trip to Europe goes terrifyingly awry, and continues to haunt them even back home, is a real page turner. Edwards's dialogue is sometimes a bit clunky and cliche; and there is a time or two then the plot veers into far-fetched territory, but overall it is a riveting story and Edwards does a great job of setting a very creepy mood. I got a bit of an Eli Roth vibe throughout the book. He is also very good at structure and pacing, always giving you just enough to keep you wanting more, but never in an annoying or obvious way. This is a very intense, very quick read. I have 3 small kids, and was able to read this book in just a matter of days. I couldn't put it down!

review_text: I listen to many audio books and have learned that not all books are well suited to this format ~ often because when reading the printed page, it is easy to skip over the filler and nonsense that is becoming all to common place.  Possibly "The Stranger" would be more interesting to read but not likely.  The initial problem was introduced in the first few minutes but after 5 chapters, nothing had transpired beyond a detailed discussion of an internet search and a description of a body building MILF.  An occasional product placement is fine but when there are so many as to be jarring, something is amiss.  The plot moved sluggishly and was bogged down by threads that did nothing to enhance the suspense or the credibility of the story.  Coben has turned out some decent novels in the past but maybe it is time for him to hang up his pen.

review_title: An entire chapter (or more) are wasted on our hero
review_text: (Preface: As a newbie to Coben, I rented this book from the library and thus it will not appear as a Verified Purchase, but rest assured I read it. Also, review may contain ****SPOILERS****). The book starts out strong and immediately hooked me. A tight, solid thriller: I couldn't turn the pages fast enough. And then came the final quarter of the book, which devolved into the predictable hero-gets-blindsided-but-still-wins-the-day along with oh-look-the-cops-show-up-just-in-time. The main cop doesn't show up until the second half of the book. An entire chapter (or more) are wasted on our hero, who is also a respected attorney, assisting an old man who is about to lose his home to eminent domain laws. These passages serve no other purpose than to show how adept at lawyering our protag is. The titular villain--The Stranger--is a flimsy caricature and in no way threatening outside of his ability to destroy fragile lives by exposing "family secrets." If you're a reader who prefers the journey to the destination, this may be the thriller for you. I will be giving Coben another chance, but he's already skating on thin ice after this one.

review_text:
We were given this book when one of my older kids was a toddler. It had been on the shelf for years because we didn’t like it. The person who gave it to us said that it would have me in tears. It didn’t....it had me questioning their sanity.

Today my 4 year old asked me to read it. I did. I had blocked out how creepy it was. The mom creeps into her sleeping son’s room, rocks him and sings to him. This goes on even into his adulthood (when he lives in his own house across town) and then she gets old and sick and can’t stalk him anymore, so he rocks her in his lap and sings the same song.

My child said “This book is weird and I hate it.” It is boring, predictable and makes me cringe.

Plain weird and should be read as a joke, or as a cautionary tale of when to cut the apron strings. If I could give it 0 stars, I would.

title: Love You Forever
subtitle: Paperback – Picture Book, September 1, 1995
author: Robert Munsch
review_title: Creepy - make sure to read the 1-star reviews - don't go by the high rating!!!
review_text:
I regret no reading the reviews with one star. In fact, I think I simply saw that 1,159 people had given this 5 stars and figured this book must be perfect for my kid. It's probably the first time that I was misguided by reviews, which I truly rely on!

I don't know who could like this book or even consider it appropriate for a child, or an adult for that matter. My husband and I read this together and kept laughing in that disturbed kind of way we all do when we come across something that's just creepy but not supposed to be. I don't know how else to describe it.

Brief summary:
About a mother and son (there's no father). First page has mother holding baby, rocking him, and singing a little song. After that page, the pages are devoted to the boy is growing up, at various very random ages. At each age mentioned, the boy does something naughty or misbehaves and the mother yells at the son. Then at night, AFTER he's asleep, she crawls into his room, holds him, rocks him, and sings him a little song. This happens at EVERY age. Read below for more details of the creepiness.

There is no doubt value in books for mothers and sons, especially single mothers with absentee fathers, but this really can't be it. Seriously? I haven't looked for such books, but please tell me that children in this family situation have healthier stories and children books, where the mother isn't creepy, infantilizing her son throughout his life.

Who this book may be for (to give a benefit of doubt)
--I really tried to think of something, but I can't think of a single scenario, except that it ends with the son singing for a frail old mother in the way she sang to him growing up.

Here's what you need to know why my husband and I feel this book is inappropriate and creepy for child and adult:
1) mother crawls into his room on all fours after boy is asleep. Why does she need to crawl? Fine, you want to reassure your child that no matter what he does, you still love him. But wouldn't it have been more comforting if he's awake and the mother goes in with confidence

2) when the child is an adult and living in his own home, she drives at night, and CRAWLS THROUGH HIS WINDOW. And there is an illustration of an older woman holding a fully-grown man

3) the son holds, rocks, and sings to his mother when she's frail and old, but how does he know what to reciprocate when his mother always waited for him to be asleep to do the same! I'm being sarcastic... before someone thinks of the subconscious awareness this child developed, etc.

4) why is there no mention of father or a presence even in the illustrations? Perhaps it's for single mothers? As I mention above, even for sons with single mom's and absentee fathers, it's hardly a positive story

5) the verses are odd

"I'll love you forever, I'll like you for always, As long as I'm living, my baby you'll be"

--Not soothing or comforting in the sound, nor appropriate at all ages
--Not sure if the if the mention of "as long as I'm living" is this supposed to inspire a discussion between parent and child about death, to help the child know that mother's eventually die
--Are we no longer our mother's child after she dies?
--And why "baby"? The mother infantilizes her son long after he's a baby, even as a grown man

The author has a right to write whatever story he envisions, but at least the mother could have portrayed as a confident woman, a mother who can walk into her son's room on two feet (rather than crawl on the floor) to reassure her child that no matter his mistakes in life, she'll always be there for him.

She would worry and have nightmares about Mommy or Grandma getting old and sick.  Why go down that road?  I suppose if you're buying this for yourself or an adult child, it might be ok.
