review_title: Good intentions but did not work for me
review_text: I think that everything probably has been said in previous reviews- and there are so many of them! I was gifted this as a baby shower gift. My concerns with this book are several- 1) the illustrations are not very appealing, 2) the story although probably written with good intentions does not work out so well. I also agree with many other comments that the mom crawling into her child's room is creepy. I actually felt it was very demeaning to a mother to have this type of relationship wherein she has to creep and crawl to share her love and convey her attention to her son. And yes, it is very awkward to look at a picture of an elderly lady holding her significantly taller son in the baby position. The symbolism of love is conveyed too literally for me. Also the book is bound to leave you feeling kind of lonely/empty because there is no character development- we only observe the son going through tough stages, and the mom crawling on the floor. Last but not least, the lullaby song that they were singing was not rhyming well and did not seem very memorable except for may be the first line. Surprisingly- my son actually kind of liked- I guess he looked at it in a very innocent and non-judgmental way. I am not planning on reading it to him anymore though.

review_text: I am clearly in the minority here, but I found this book to be weird and disturbing. The beginning starts off well but the progression to breaking into a grown man's home to rock him to sleep is just ridiculous. It portrays a very unhealthy, codependent relationship between this mom and son. Even my 4 year old, when I first read this book to him, started laughing about her rocking a grown man to sleep. And though I love my mother dearly, she would never allow herself to be rocked in a chair by her own child; maybe a nice song, foot or back rub would be acceptable! Far from bringing tears to my eyes, I thought this book was bizarre and doubt we will ever choose it for story time again. Reminds me of Elf on the Shelf; so many devotees but I find the whole concept creepy and "big brother"-ish.

review_text: My husband and I received this book as a gift for us and our daughter (we have a 7 month old girl)...initially, we both cried when we read it together (I had heard about the book from friends but never actually took the time to check it out). Our mothers are older and the story really touched us. However, in looking at the book again, I can see why some might be creeped out by certain things, like the mother crawling into her son's room and rocking him back and forth after she's sure that he's sound asleep, especially when he's older (and I'm talking about a grown man here). I kind of wondered if my own Mother-In-Law did the same thing, would I EVER be freaked out...I'd be like, "OK, nice knowin' ya...enjoy each other...bye-bye now" LOL I kind of even put a black humor into reading it, like the son is Norman Bates (the mother in the book has that "granny" hairdo and old-fashioned dress) and it made me laugh, although I'm weird that way anyhow. In any case, don't speculate too much (I'm one to talk) over the book...it's not meant for it -I personally won't be reading it to my daughter until she's older and fully understands the concept of aging and death or using it as a teaching tool when I think that she's ready to learn about it.

review_title: Good up until the end, then it sucked.
review_text:
I don't read novels much but my wife and I got this on Audible and listened to it while driving to visit our daughter. It's 10 hours, and hooked us right away, especially with the special effects, it was like a dramatic reading.

I couldn't wait to get back to listening each time, and it kept us in suspense right up until the end. However, the resolution was laughable and now I know why I don't read novels much. Although the dramatic reading was lively and enticing, and the plot did keep us on edge, the way it played out was like a first-time novelist who had no idea what he was doing, and just explained everything in the last chapter, with some of the previous scenes being completely inconsistent with the resolution.

If this was an entry into a "first-time" novel contest, I think it would have taken last place. Or, if it had been written by an experienced novelist, it would also have taken last place. LAME !

review_title: Guilty --- of a shaky plot and a preposterous ending.
review_text:
I've read most of Baldacci's books and have found them to be uneven. Some are great and some take work to finish. But I though the first three Will Robie books were very good. The fourth installment not so much. So many of the plot elements made no sense. And while I like a book that give you a chance to figure out whodunit, this one was so obvious that it was unbelievable that the major characters didn't figure it out. Worst of all, though, was the ridiculous ending. You'll have to read it to believe it. But after you do, you'll just just shake you head.

The next point might be a petty criticism, but if you're going to write dialogue in dialect, at least take the time to get it right. Mr. Baldacci obviously hasn't spent much time in the rural South and probably got his ideas about the dialect from watching bad actors on television. I grew up not far from the setting of the novel, and he missed the mark. The one that's most maddening to me are the words "anythin'" and "everythin'". Nobody in the South pronounces those words that way. They may say "anythang" and "everythang" but they don't drop the "g" on those words. And it is confusing, because those of us from that area do drop the "g" on nothing (nothin') and something (somethin'). I can now add Mr. Baldacci to the list that gets this wrong along with every British actor trying to do a southern American accent.

review_title: An Assassin Returns To His Childhood Home. All Is Not Well
review_text:
Will Robie's career as a hitman for the government falters. Once by accident; once by delusion. Removed from field duty he needs to go back and clear up unfinished business from his past personal life before he can again move forward in his professional career.
The step back finds him back where he grew up; a small town in Mississippi. He finds his father is accused and is awaiting trial for murder.
As the story unravels, Mr. Baldacci does very well with introducing twists and curve throughout. His characters become nicely developed; and the reader turns pages waiting to see what little surprise awaits around the next corner.

The large twist comes at the end. All the twists in the novel are nicely brought together and tied up. It's a very good Robie novel which I recommend.
Incidentally, if you've ever spent time in a small, sleepy town In the deep South, Mr. Baldacci is pretty much on target with his descriptions; not good or bad, just descriptive.

title: The Boy, the Mole, the Fox and the Horse
subtitle: Hardcover – October 22, 2019
author: Charlie Mackesy
review_text:
It's cute, simplistic, and therapeutic. The characters carry on a directionless conversation filled with lines that range from petty (Is the glass half full or empty? I'm just glad to have a glass), to the borderline-but-never-quite-thoughtful (What's the bravest thing you've ever said? Help.), to the mostly saccharine (No matter how it appears, everyone has their struggles*). These are wanna-be inspirational quotes that never rise to the pithiness of aphorisms or poignancy of poetry. The artwork is cute, but not astounding, better than novice, but not prize-winning. Overall, the book is an overrated testimony to the American reader's need sentimental platitudes. It's just a shadow of Winnie the Pooh.

*I should note, my quotes are not exact, because I wasn't paying $23 for a 128 page comic book with a sentence on every page, so I read the whole thing while walking around the bookstore, and don't now have a copy.

title: The Boy, the Mole, the Fox and the Horse
subtitle: Hardcover – October 22, 2019
author: Charlie Mackesy
review_title: An empty selection of aphorisms. Our culture is doomed.
review_text:
The popularity of this book is disturbing. The various characters speak various dreamy aphorisms that are supposed to be inspiring and fill you with courage. You've seen some on buttons and bumper stickers. There's no narrative, and no reason for the animals to be the ones they are and not others. The author just needed various talking heads to speak witless sayings at one another, and he chose ones that looked nice when drawn.

The illustrations are fair, but there is no story, no change, no movement. It's just a kid and some talking animals all saying bumper stickers to one another. It's witless and forgettable. 10 years from now you'll wonder what came over you that you thought it was worth 12 bucks and 12 minutes of your time to read this worthless drivel.

Paper was not as substantial, the book was taller, but not as thick.  It also came with a silk ribbon bookmark which was affixed to the book. review_text: Do yourself a favor and borrow this book from someone before purchasing or get it at the library.  This is not a book for a child to read.  I'm so glad I read it first because I had to stop so many times to figure out the word that was written.  This is horrible cursive.  Some "n"s look like cursive "r"s which is confusing.  Some words are in print and some are in cursive.  I've never seen a book written in this fashion.  I love cursive.  It was my favorite subject when I was a kid but to read in horrible cursive is just confusing and frustrating.  It makes you lose sight of the story because you are frustrated on how horrible the writing is.  It has an "okay" story (the reason for 2 stars instead of one) but it's nothing different than what I've always told my children and grandson.  I'm really confused on what the hype is about this book.  I hope the picture helps.

title: The Boy, the Mole, the Fox and the Horse
subtitle: Hardcover – October 22, 2019
author: Charlie Mackesy
review_title: A five minute read if you can read cursive
review_text: I love the message....especially in today's world when most everyone wants to pick people apart for no better reason than group think tells them to.  For that reason alone....this book is a pleasure....if only a five minute distraction.  I was going to buy the hard cover as a gift for a couple of young readers (10 and 13).  I read on Kindle first to make sure it was  a good choice.  I won't buy the hard cover as a gift because the artsy cursive font is very difficult to read.  Cursive writing is no longer taught in U.S. schools.  Maybe the author and publisher are unaware of that. These kids are good readers and they are being taught at home to read cursive so they probably could read it, but why struggle to make out the words?  It sort of takes the pleasure out of soaking up the meaning.  This book is about 125 pages.  70 pages have words, some with just one word and most with one or two sentences, the other 55 pages have simple illustrations.  The illustrations are cute and the message is wholesome and uplifting...if you can read the words.

review_text: I was given this book to read by a Friend and within 2 pages, I knew I had to have my own copy.  Since then, (like a month?) I've given copies as graduation and birthday presents.  This is an amazingly touching book.  It's like walking into Narnia's wardrobe and being handed a book - it would be the Boy, the Mole, the Fox and the Horse.  It is one of those timeless treasures that you find so rarely - one that can be shared with young children, adolescents, teens, young adults - you get the picture, EVERYONE.  It is a story of Friendship and love.  One of my favorite quotes, "What is the bravest thing you ever said," asked the boy..."Help," said the horse.  It is lovely without being syrupy, profound without being preachy, and simply delightful.  The Author is also the illustrator and this is just another incredible bonus - gorgeous line drawings.  You NEED this book.  I am an avid reader, and rarely gush about about a book.  But I wish I had had this book a long time ago.  You will too.

title: A Criminal Defense (Philadelphia Legal)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: William L. Myers, Jr.
review_title: Attention Amazon - please fire whoever is selecting these Kindle First books!
review_text:
Attention Amazon – fire whoever is selecting Kindle First books please!

This book had two strikes against it out of the box:
It’s an Amazon Kindle First selection
It’s about lawyers.

And strike three: It’s bad. (And only secondarily actually about lawyers). Worse, the description kind of promises an evil legal mastermind at work, but that never really materializes.
McFarland has personal problems with his wife Piper and he has personal problems with his brother Tommy. But we’re not allowed to know why until the author doles out little tidbits over the course of a hundred pages. This makes for very frustrating reading.

And every time McFarland has the opportunity to do something about them he runs away. At one point he finally confronts his wife about why she is growing distant and when she accuses him of never being around, what does he do? He leaves!

The story is told in the first person POV – one of my favorites. But the reason for writing in first person narrative is so the readers will know what the main character / narrator knows. Unfortunately that is not true here. McFarland has no problem telling us when he goes to the bathroom, but when he views a critical video recording he doesn’t tell us who is on the video! IF THE AUTHOR DOESN’T WANT THE READER TO KNOW THINGS DON’T WRITE IN THE FIRST PERSON!

The author goes out of his way to be obtuse about everything. Every character has unknown secrets and we’re expected to hang on to the bitter end to find out all the loose ends dangling everywhere. The whole story makes no sense.

review_title: THE GIFT THAT KEEPS ON APPEARING
review_text:
A confession up front. I had to consult with my psychic adviser in order to decide whether this book was REAL or not. She looked into her whatever-she-looks-into (could’ve been a dirty bowl) and said: YES…NO…MAYBE.

But what did I think and feel? That’s what you want to know, right? Well, this book is really a worthwhile read. I checked into it while wearing a white sheet. First chapter shows you how this writer can grab you early—I was going WHOOO--WHOOO-WHOO. I was shivering so much I had to add a wool blanket to the sheet.

Our hero, Aubrey -- I love that name because that’s a good name for people who have ghosts in their life. You see how I talk around the specifics in this book? That’s what “reviewers” do when they haven’t read the book, perhaps just the synopsis or other reviews. But that’s not me! Remember, I worked through my psychic adviser!

So if you like to chill-out, have a strong constitution, and can control your heart rate well through meditation – this book could be for you. It took three days for my psychic friend to recover. And she was already into departed spirits

author: Sejal Badani
review_text:
We call these Saas-Bahu soap operas in India - sappy, full of tropes - the distant husband, peckish MIL, gossip mongering SIL, a handsome "Pardesi" with a sad heart, woman looking for trouble. None of them are sketched in any detail except for superficial conversations- the story - the secret - long drawn and winded - am going back to finish this book about the 3 rd time just to see how it ends when I already know what is going to happen. What a facile description of India, pandering to the popular taste, riddled with inaccuracies and made up words - Shrimati ??? Really ???? How hollow does it ring if sag is sakh? - It sounds as if the words are made up from reading picked up in the library than from a life lived and reflected upon. And how low does one have to go, to describe a girl in braces that extends all the way up to her neck? In the old days ( or even today ) a girl who had Polio may have been abandoned rather than fitted with braces that would have cost a fortune. And which child with polio has braces upto the neck, I wonder if this author set foot out of an air conditioned ride ever. Polio has been eradicated in India but why bother putting a good picture of the third-world into our head...just cater to whatever sells. I am just amazed there was no mention of a snake charmer, or maybe I missed it
Edit: I just finished the book and am going to give it a 1 - The condescension of it! Take way the man's great grand kids because she has money and a spacious apartment in New York. Wow! This is the true Brown Colonialism if any! Shame.

subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Sejal Badani
review_title: Has this book been written by two authors?
review_text: Like the story, this book seems to have two personalities. The life of Jaya and her husband in New York is painful and pregnant with grief at the loss of three unborn kids. It's painful because it's real. We get a far clearer idea of who Jaya and her parents are from these few pages in America than the rest of the book. Patrick, who has only a few scenes at the beginning, comes across as more 'real' than Stephen or Deepak - who have larger roles within the story. That's because the moment the book leaves the US and enters India, Jaya transforms into a dumb American tourist as the rest of the story morphs into a Bollywood soap Opera. Seriously, has the author lived in India for any period of time? A Dalit who cooks for an upper caste family in secret for twenty plus years? A little girl who has polio at the same time as laptop wielding Jaya? A school in rural colonial India where an Indian lady and a white man are able to carry on an affair in a garden for months? This story has more tropes than many Indian soap operas: Distant husband, Colorful Holi celebration, a ruined Hindu temple, Gujarati dances, evil stepmother and mother in law, Poverty, Orphanage, and sex scandals. I kept waiting for the characters to break into a song and dance sequence whenever I turned the page. None of this comes across as real. India seen through Jaya's eyes is a cartoon, drawn with stingy brushstrokes by a writer who really has no interest in the story other than as a conveniently exotic setting for her American audience. None of these characters are written with any depth or flourish. All the men that show up in the second half seem identical, made from the same clay. I wish the author had invested more in the Jaya's and Amisha's life. It is a good story that is totally ruined by a lazy author.

author: Sejal Badani
review_text:
I don't understand the gushing, over-the-top reviews for this book. For one thing, there is no extraordinary secret! I am irritated that there is such a long, drawn out build-up for a fairly common dilemma in fiction, especially romantic fiction. Based on the description of the work, I expected more than a romantic soap opera, as in suspense and a far richer depiction of India, especially during the colonial period. Relations between the British and Indians are barely mentioned while Amisha's and Jaya's thoughts and feelings are poked and prodded and repeated over and over again. Then the reader is subjected to several lengthy blogs from Jaya that hash over the same feelings yet again!
The plot is incredibly uneven, with the cardboard, rigid husband giving into most of Amisha's wishes. This is not at all plausible in such a culture. The inclusion of EVERY detail of lovemaking was a poor decision, as was throwing in the disgustingly callous and horrific treatment of Amisha near the end for some shock value. I am annoyed with myself for wasting time reading such a mediocre work and aghast that many people consider this to be fine reading!

review_title: Promising at first and disappointing later
review_text: This novel promised it all: an grieving infertile woman on a journey of self-discovery returning to the home of her ancestors and learning a family secret seemed like something I would love. The opening chapters detail the narrator's grief, as well as her joy in experiencing her mother's childhood home and meeting her grandmother's confidant, an "untouchable" servant she had rescued from a life of despair. As the servant relates the grandmother's story, however, the novel dissolves into just another predictable story of forbidden love. The narrator's role as a blogger became a thinly-disguised excuse for the author to lapse into essay mode, explaining to the reader what we were supposed to get from the story instead of letting us form our own conclusions. I loved the beginning, but found the final chapters tedious.

The book has a cast of strong characters that could have made for a fascinating story had it not been for the typical western construct of India and its culture - the 'smell of sweat at the airport', peeling paints, garbage strewn streets, hovels, beggars, loveless marriages replete with indifference and lack of respect for women, until of course,  she is shown true love and respect by the quintessential knight in shining armor, who had to be a white man!! And how can you forget the whole social construct defined by the vilified and favorite flogging horse "caste" with the centerpiece of an 'untouchable' - you name it and its strewn liberally all across the book, striking a very jarring tone. It is rather evident that the author has either never traveled to India or is seeking a western audience for the book.  Very disappointing and not likely to pick another book by this author.

title: The Storyteller's Secret: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Sejal Badani
review_text:
This novel is aptly titled: it stars several storytellers and unlocks many secrets. The story begins with Jaya,young, married Indian-American reporter who has suffered three miscarriages and in the process has lost her way. She leaves her husband Patrick who she believes doesn't understand her pain and takes off for India to visit her dying grandfather Deepak.

On arriving in India she finds her grandfather has died. At that point her story becomes entwined with that of Ravi, an untouchable whom her grandmother Amisha long ago brought into the house as a servant, saving him and his family from the miserable fate of his class. Ravi is devoted to the grandmother, and it is he who tells the tangled stories that reveal long buried family secrets.

His story of the grandmother reveals the reason her daughter, Jayas mother Lena has always been so emotionally distant with her daughter. As the story of her grandmother's struggle for personal freedom in pre-independence India slowly unfolds, Jayar begins to draw strength from the tragically deceased Amisha to begin putting her own life back together.

This is a complicated, bittersweet , perhaps overly long tale that presents human lives being shaped by the prejudices and traditions of Indian culture. The wide range of characters are realistic, drawing the reader into a memorable story.

review_title: Publishing for the sake of money
review_text:
Sometimes one of our favorite authors produces a work that we feel just isn't up to the pedestal we have put them on. It is a major disappointment when that emotional high of purchasing a highly anticipated new work is crushed down by the weight of an effort we feel just wasn't up to our standards.
This is one of those works for me.
All that anticipation and expectation aside, I still objectively feel that this is just not a good book.
Some elements always put me off, kind of like gratuitous language or violence when they don't contribute to the overall objective of the book. Racism is another topic that I just don't see a place for in most works. Unless you are talking Roots or 7 Years a Slave, then it is expected.
Excessive use of racial slurs just to further disenchant a reader with a character just doesn't work for me. Incest, nope, not on board with that one either.
Again putting that aside and trying to look deeper into this book, you can't. There is no deeper. It is a shallow, poorly structured race to capture a killer. Rampant law breaking, placing kids purposefully in harms way and even arming an under age child in hopes he will shoot and kill the antagonist.
So many things are broken with this book.
Let us hope that the next Stephen King offering in November eclipses this misstep.

review_title: A lackluster offering from Stephen King
review_text: Some professional critics regard King as a "hack."  Perhaps, but I am not a professional critic of popular fiction.  Leisure reading either engages me or it does not.  I have found some of King's horror novels to be quite interesting.  Such is not the case with Mr. Mercedes, a crime tale.  The novel offers little suspense and very few surprises.  The characters' behaviors are easily predictable, and although King struggles mightily to build toward a suspenseful climax, the outcome is foreshadowed throughout the narrative and in the telling seems contrived and flat.  It is not clear to me why King is venturing so far afield in more recent writings from the genre upon which he built his career and amassed a considerable fortune.  Perhaps he is just written out in the horror/fantasy realm.  If, however, he continues to turn out novels as pedestrian as Mr. Mercedes, he may well deserve the designation "hack."

title: Mr. Mercedes: A Novel (The Bill Hodges Trilogy Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Stephen King
review_text:
Stephen King's latest book is a pathological thriller. It's good, of course.

There's this guy they call Mr. Mercedes because nobody knows his name. A few years ago he stole an old woman's car and drove it into the crowd outside of a city job fair. He killed eight--he calls it his "score"--maimed dozens, and walked away into the crowd. He went back to his day-to-day life where nobody much noticed him. Except, perhaps, his mother. Lately he's been getting restless.

There's this other guy that recently retired from the cops. He sits on his easy chair all afternoon and watches daytime TV. While he watches he plays with the gun his father carried while he was on the job. Sometimes he puts it into his mouth, just to see what it feels like. Sometimes he thinks about the cases he and his partner couldn't solve. Mostly he doesn't think at all.

One day the first guy mails the second guy a letter. So it begins.

It's good, like I said. One of King's gifts is to faithfully capture pieces of ordinary life and show them to us, temporarily convincing us we are reading an ordinary story. Then he surprises us. It's usually not a pleasant surprise. We wonder why we were surprised. And so it goes.

There something new for me in each Stephen King book. In this one he finds a new thing to make us uncomfortable about. It doesn't seem directly related to the plot. It festers there below the surface. He explores it for us, finding new depths and reaching new levels of understanding. The understanding, stopping just short of sympathy, is the most uncomfortable of all.

Nicely done, Mr. King.

review_text:
I enjoyed Mr. Mercedes. I wasn't sure I would. I really didn't care much for Dr. Sleep, but on the other hand, I liked Joyland. I debated waiting to buy it until there were some more reviews, but I decided against that and just purchased the audio version the second day it was out. For the most part, I'm glad I did.

As other reviewers have said, I also felt that there was a difference of style with this book. Some reviewers questioned whether King wrote this book at all, and I can't say for sure, but there were definate King moments. Missing, though, was King's usual long introduction of in depth character descriptions was missing. I, for one, missed it. I really like King's extensive, detailed character histories. Characterization, I think, is one of his strengths, and, perhaps just because I was expecting the usual style, it left me feeling like the characters were lacking.

I particularly liked the bad guy. I usually like King's bad guys just as much as his good guys, and Mr. Mercedes was no exception. I did think he was a little predictable, but maybe sometimes crazy often follows the same lines. As other reviewers mention, I felt like the end dragged on and on a little. I'm not sure why. It was exciting, I listened hours in a row, and them about 2/3 of the way through, I found myself only listening to an hour or so at a time, and when I did, I was easily distracted. Part of me thought what the good guys did at this point didn't really ring true. And, small things began to irritate me, such as a computer genious that attaches herself to our hero out of the blue halfway through the book and becomes a major part of the good guy posse when she wasn't even there in the begining, or the worn out trope of the woman 20 years yonger, but who of course looks 35 or so, about half the age of our retired, overweight, apparently unattractive hero, a stranger who suddenly jumps our hero.

So, though the last 1/3 was kind of slow and a little irritating for me, the first 2/3rds held my interest much better than Dr. Sleep, and the ending was satisfying enough to rate this book 4 our of 5 for me.

The only negative I experienced was a spoiler posted on King's Twitter/Facebook account...it revealed the names of some of the characters who survived. I was at a point in the novel where I felt the fates of these characters were genuinely in question--while King is no George R.R. Martin, it's still never a good idea to expect favorite characters to ride off into the sunset--and knowing that they lived did have an impact on how I read the rest of the story. I was tempted to lower my rating due to this but that had nothing to do with the actual quality of the writing.

author: Anthony Doerr
review_text:
Don’t like being a naysayer, but this book seems overly wordy and pretentious. It also jumps around time-wise, with very short chapters and very long sentences, for no apparent purpose.
Let’s face it. This is not “The Grapes of Wrath”, “A Bell for Adano”, “The Old Man and the Sea”, or other very well-written novels that won the Pulitzer Prize.
But there have been, especially recently, works of fiction that were questionable, or political, winners. There are far better novels about war, especially WW2. Personally, I’ve read and reviewed several of them, and appreciate those that are well-researched and engaged me.

title: All the Light We Cannot See
subtitle: Hardcover – January 1, 2014
author: Anthony Doerr
review_title: 50 Page Novel inflated to 500 pages with postmodern gimmickry,
review_text:
Post modern literature style means -- non sequential, verbose and unfulfilling. The jumping around from character to character, back and forth in time is a gimmick. It makes the story "seem" more meaty. But there is not much here. The book is quasi lyrical but the chip-chop of the narrative detracts from whatever is there. Extraneous characters, scenes, and thematic initiatives just cloud the book and I guess to some, make them feel intellectual.

This book took 500 pages to say what could be said in 150 pages with the same amount of lyricism. The book was recoommended to me, that's why I read it, but I felt cheated. So take my recommend, and try to read a few chapters before committing the effort required to wade through a 150 page novel spread out over 500 pages.

My instinct is that the people who read this book want to flatter themselves with thir sophistication, and tell others about how great this book is, hence the 5 stars some give..

title: All the Light We Cannot See
subtitle: Hardcover – January 1, 2014
author: Anthony Doerr
review_title: All the Light We Cannot See is weakened by flaws of structure, content, and style.
review_text:
I bought this book with high hopes but wound up very disappointed. Although Doerr is trying to create a sweet and poignant narrative about survival during WWII, All the Light We Cannot See ultimately fails due to serious flaws in both content and style.

I am a lifelong reader with a PhD in literature and 40 years experience teaching college writing and literature. The more I study fiction, the more I admire a writer who can use structure (the arrangement of the chronological elements of plot) strategically to develop the novel's themes. Some of the best examples of this technique are Chronicle of a Death Foretold by Gabriel Garcia Marquez, Ceremony by Leslie Marmon Silko, and The Death of Ivan Ilyich by Leo Tolstoy. Anthony Doerr, on the other hand, fragments his plot for no apparent purpose. It is disjointed and difficult to follow, with no payoff for the effort. He not only switches back and forth between the two narratives but also along the timeline. Switching back and forth between the two narratives--the one about Marie Laure and the one about Werner--would have been plenty; also switching back and forth along the timeline before, during, and after WWII creates too much discontinuity and makes the narrative hard to follow, particularly the story of Marie Laure. The narrative of Werner, Frederick, and Volkheimer is easier to follow.

Both plots also depend on too many farfetched coincidences, so much so that it strains credulity. In addition, the idea that Uncle Etienne would extend the length of his broadcasts to play music is totally unbelievable. There's no way he would have risked not only his own life and the lives of everyone in his household but also the lives of all the soldiers who depended on the information he was sending. The music makes for a nice story and helps connect the two plots, but it's basically nonsense. I made a timeline in an effort to follow the plots and connect them to the events of WWII, but couldn't make sense of them, so I really appreciate the review by Alexandra Grabbe on 12/18/14, which makes clear that his historical details are as inaccurate as his descriptive details.

People have praised this book for its lush descriptions and evocative language, and those are things that I usually admire, too. Occasionally, the language and descriptions are beautiful and work well, but far too many of the descriptive passages use words as words--a piling on of sounds--rather than to convey actual meaning. For example, Doerr uses some truly absurd or exaggerated metaphors:

Describing Marie Laure's eyes: ". . . those two eyes hang unmoving like the egg cases of spiders" (332)
"A peaceful place, insulated by fields, enwombed by hedges" (356)
"spiderwebs . . . crackle like burning paper when he moves" (428)
the tongue of a boot "lolls cannibalistically" (317)--no logical connection to the rest of the situation or to the boot, which has lost its lace
"six trillion cells get crushed in the vise of our mother's birth canal and we howl" (468)--I've given birth, and that's not what happens under normal circumstances.
"In a delicatessen, black flies swim over a half dozen tables" (317)--There's no apparent reason to describe them as swimming rather than swarming.
"His face gaunt and his teeth maniacal" (464)
"Metallic, tattered moonlight shatters across the road . . ." (356)
"The moonlight shines and billows" (482)

Notice that some of these are just hard to picture (how does moonlight "shatter" or "billow"?) while others are just plain nonsense, as when the "spiderwebs [...] crackle like burning paper when he moves." Not even frozen spiderwebs "crackle." Speaking of spiders, there are more spiders in this book than I've encountered anywhere except that old horror movie, Arachnophobia. What little girl has eyes "like the egg cases of spiders"? And "enwombed by hedges"? Seriously?

Doerr's style has other tics or mannerisms of style that are ineffective and distracting. For example, Doerr repeatedly uses sentences that follow this structure: The blanks blank and blank. Here are a few of the innumerable examples:
"The branches seethe and clatter" (195)
"things scuttle and slide" (458)
"Her fingers dig and reach . . ." (232)
"The dogs caper and sneeze . . ." (245)
"the dogs freeze and twitch their noses . . . (246)
"The dogs circle and duck and romp" (246)
"mussels click and sigh" (260)
"The wind gusts. In Marie-Laure's mind, it shifts and gleams . . ." (269)
"The grasses toss and shimmy" (293)
"The moonlight shines and billows" (482)
"Silver tongs and spoons hanging from the cart chime and clank, and the wheels clatter and wallow" (108).
"Hours wear out and fall away" (320)
"a place where surface planes disintegrate and sounds ribbon in shoals through the air" (390)

Some of his other mannerisms of style include using alliteration and other repetitions of sounds for the cumulative effect of the sounds themselves even though the meanings of the words sometimes don't actually make sense in the context; using a lot of fragments, usually participial modifiers with no conjugated verb, to add details; and using inverted word order way too frequently. Here are some examples:
"swifts swoop out over the sunflowers" (337)
"swifts swoop for insects, and the filaments of a spiderweb catch the light and shine for an
instant and are gone" (436)
"Sleet still falling outside" (219) [not a sentence]
"A peaceful place, insulated by fields, enwombed by hedges" (357) [not a sentence]
"Long fingers, a thatch of thinning hair beneath his cap" (317) [not a sentence]
"streets narrow and sloping" (510) instead of "narrow, sloping streets," which would
be more natural

Finally, I don't know if I believe the claim that a person who went blind as a young child would see things in vivid color in her mind or have such concrete images of things she would not have seen or noticed prior to going blind. Doerr writes as though the descriptions are Marie Laure's mental images, but I don't find that realistic or convincing. He uses countless visual details that Marie Laure cannot see. He's apparently talking about what she imagines, I assume. He exaggerates Marie Laure's abilities to see and hear things in her mind (390-391).

I'm still trying to figure out what the Pulitzer Prize committee saw in this book. Perhaps the best thing about it is that it portrays acts of courage and decency by people on both sides of the war.

title: All the Light We Cannot See

author: Anthony Doerr
review_text:
This book is a total travesty. Granted, Mr. Doerr writes beautifully. However, as a retired history teacher of 30 years, I was shocked to see him carelessly use August of 1944 as the date of Germany's invasion of France. I think even most high school students are aware that the Allied invasion of Normandy, France took place in June of 1944. Why did Mr. Doerr arbitrarily choose to use August 1944 and the beginning of the German invasion of France???? It would have taken him all of five minutes to pull up a timeline of WWII on Google or "Infoplease". Therefore, I am quite puzzled as WHY this book is categorized as historical fiction. AND, unfortunately it is rated as #7 on Amazon as historical fiction!!!!

I cannot recommend this book to anyone, due to the incorrect dates that Mr. Doerr chose to use.

This book could have been a wonderful teaching tool for young adults as to the history of World War II and/or those who slept through their history classes.

Likewise with Mr. Doerr's extremely well-written novel. Around 1974  "Something drops into" Marie-Laure's "palm. An iron key." Forty year later, "She lives still."  I want to know what Marie-Laure did with that "little iron key." As for the dustcover blurb about Werner's story converging with that of Marie-Laure's in Saint-Malo. Don't hold your breath. review_text: As an Aussie friend put it so succinctly yesterday upon giving her my verbal review:"It sounds like it just was not 'life affirming'."  Couldn't have expressed it better.  Initally, the author's writing flows easily, and draws one into thinking "what a story teller the author is" - keeping the reader turning pages through all hours of the day and night, but in the end the story falls flat and just fails - including the mystery of the stone whose value could have provided so much good in the end. Each of the main characters had all evolved and were each in a postion to really add value to life and to each other, yet they were either killed off or perhaps worse, end up in a grey zone - just "going through life" not happy or sad, but rather just "existing". Perhaps for Mr. Doerr life is simply a journey to "get through"....hope, happiness are momentary at best.  I believe life holds so much more.  I prefer the hope and promise of life to come opposed to a life whose light will be forever diminished by one's past.

title: All the Light We Cannot See

author: Anthony Doerr
review_text:
This book began with such promise—such luminous writing—that I was enchanted. As another reviewer said, "It has been a while since I have found a book that I wanted to read slowly so that I could soak in every detail in hopes that the last page seems to never come." As I began reading, I could absolutely identify with that reviewer.

You know the feeling you get when you've "discovered" a new author, and the thought that you'll have endless hours of reading enjoyment ahead of you? That's how All the Light began for me. The richness of the story, the beauty of the loving relationship between a father and his blind daughter, the mystery as to how they would travel the darkness of the encroaching Nazi threat ... all were beautifully done. What lessened my reading pleasure was the switch from luminous to frankly boring. The author seemed to get ahead of himself. The switchbacks in time were confusing, annoying.

But my greatest beefs with this book are threefold: his lack of clarity in what happened to a gem (although I'm pretty sure I know what was done), the lack of resolution about my favorite character, and the dismissal of another character we've been involved with since the first. It was done so abruptly, with so little fanfare, in the matter of a single sentence, as to seem a betrayal.

I don't know how many people will even read this review, as the number of reviews is still growing by leaps and bounds. But I wanted to suggest to readers that they obtain a library copy rather than plunk down their dollars (or pounds or euros).

review_text:
I was so looking forward to reading this book based on the summary and the outstanding five star reviews it got, but I just could not see how so many readers felt this was a great novel! Although parts of the story are beautifully written, it just drags, and confusingly moves so slowly with its short chapters that keep jumping back and forth between characters and moments in time. Every time I started a new chapter I had hopes that I would get a chance to absorb more about each character, but then it would abruptly be cut short and I would have to readjust my thinking for another character or situation. After a while it became so irritating and exhausting having to read this novel in this fashion. I even had to look back several chapters a few times just to understand where I was in the story. The main characters of Werner and Marie-Laure never have their worlds come together until the very end of the book which was a such big disappointment. It was like reading two separate stories that dragged along with so much unnecessary clutter. I really wanted to just stop reading, but I had hopes it would all come together in the final short, choppy chapters. Unfortunately, everything just falls so flat and the emotional moments I had my heart set on just left me thinking...that's it???!! This is what I plowed
through over 500 pages for was THIS??!!!

review_text: After reading, over and over again, that this was the best book of 2014, I couldn't wait to start this book. But as I continued to read, I couldn't wait to finish. The premise of the book is intriguing, but the the stories of the two characters take much to long to converge (page 410 out of 511). I grew bored waiting or this to happen and when it does, the characters spend a few pages together and then the author fast forwards 30 years to neatly wrap everything up in less than 100 pages. Way too long of a build up for an anti climatic, rushed ending. The story would've benefited from more balance in the before (the characters met) and after. Sometimes I wonder if reviewers simply lack the courage to go against the "popular opinion" because this book was definitely not the best book that I read, published in 2014, or any other year for that matter.

title: All the Light We Cannot See

author: Anthony Doerr
review_text:
I started this book at the recommendation of a friend and got about 25% through it and couldn't stand it. It kept popping up in my recommended reading guide and I saw that over 15,000 people gave it favorable reviews so I figured I would give it another chance. This time I finished it, hoping it would get better as it went, but it never did. This book was moderately entertaining at best.
The characters are wonderful and well developed. I really liked the characters. The story line was interesting. The issue I had with this book was the way it was written. There was far too much description. There is a point where you are creating an experience for your readers and a point when you are droning on, adding filer words and distracting from the story line. I found myself skimming over the over descriptions only to miss something valuable to the story. I had to go back and read parts over and over again because my mind stated to wander when the book went into descriptive mode (which was the majority). There are few books that I have read which I really dislike but this makes the list. I especially hate when so many other people loved it and I feel like I am an outlier. Ironically I have talked to a few other people who have read this book who had the same experience as me so perhaps those who disliked it are not reviewing the book.
Although I wouldn't recommend this book to anyone, I would suggest that people read the other more positive reviews for an alternate perspective.

title: All the Light We Cannot See
subtitle: Hardcover – January 1, 2014
author: Anthony Doerr
review_text:
All the praise this novel and its author have received are well merited. Doerr is a masterful writer. The flaws in this otherwise jewel-like novel are, to this reader, these: that its conclusion seems a bit rushed and a bit too pat; and that its characters, though well-developed in many respects, don't feel quite fully developed. Perhaps that's a consequence of the book being constructed of brief chapters that alternate almost entirely between the stories of its two principal protagonists. A novel of a related sort that came to mind as I read this one was Anthony Marra's A Constellation of Vital Phenomena. Both books are novels of war. Both are brilliant acts of imagination and superbly crafted. But Marra's digs deeper into the pain and pathos of its subject matter and lays its characters bare in ways this one did not quite manage to.

I don't hesitate to give the novel in review my strongest recommendation (I could just as well have awarded it 5 stars). But writing this review, as I am, with a strong comparison in mind, I feel compelled to award a weighted measure. All the Light We Cannot See is a very fine novel. A Constellation of Vital Phenomena is a work of art. I strongly recommend you read them both.

title: All the Light We Cannot See
subtitle: Hardcover – January 1, 2014
author: Anthony Doerr
review_title: “a rich tapestry...a stunning and unforgettable masterpiece”
review_text:
Confession:

In matters of music and literature, I am terribly guilty of reverse chronological snobbery, too often believing that if a work is contemporary, it runs the risk of being shallow and poorly constructed; however, based on a friend’s recommendation, I began listening to “All the Light We Cannot See” via the Kentucky Libraries Unbound free lending library, and Mr. Doerr’s lyrical writing and keen insight captivated me to the point that I immediately ordered my own copy to have in my hands as I listened. The book, which is set in World War 2 France and Germany, is a rich tapestry woven from seemingly disparate threads of plot and setting into a stunning and unforgettable masterpiece, worthy of the Pulitzer it won. I am so very glad a friend recommended it—and that Anthony Doerr spent ten years of his life creating such a poignantly beautiful work for the world. I hope you read it.

subtitle: Hardcover – January 1, 2014
author: Anthony Doerr
review_title: Provocative - Themes of Love, Courage and Sacrifice - 4-1/2 Stars
review_text:
Beautifully written and powerful, with well-defined characters and a huge canvas on which to paint them. We mourn the casualties and there are many -- in particular, the boys, Werner and Frederick, whose lives are ended by the war machine, in spite of their extraordinary brilliance and sensitivity. And Daniel LeBlanc who disappears early in the novel. A waste that is not lost on the reader.

Marie Laure, is an elegant rendering of the Hemingway exemplar -- filled with “grace under pressure.” She moves through the story touching all who know her, even Werner, whose most idyllic day is spent alone with her, and who saves her by insisting on the white pillow case. Later, she recalls, "The boy saved her three times over. Once by not exposing Etienne when he should have. Twice by taking that sergeant major out of the way. Three times by helping her out of the city" (p515).

We witness the horror of the Nazi Youth Camps juxtaposed with the sacrifice and courage of the French Resistance, of which Marie-Laure is an active part. It is all very moving and sad but I felt a little let down at the end. I wanted more resolution, even though happy endings shouldn’t be a prerequisite in story-telling. I felt Werner’s sister, Jutta and Marie-Laure might have had a bit more time together to re-create their memories of Werner. It was of course real – their moving on, as incomplete as they were, filled with memories of those lost and grief becoming a permanent part of their personalities. How rare, “living happily ever after” is in real life.

Volkheimer is another casualty, moving on with his mundane life until we revisit him at the age of 51. His redemption comes, after years of merciless and (apparently) emotionless killing in his youth, in not preventing Werner from rescuing the French girl who is broadcasting for the Resistance.. Later in the novel, he teaches Jutta's son to sail paper planes – again, I think, a tribute to his friendship with Werner.

And the Sea of Flames is left in the grotto, “Mantled with algae, bedecked with barnacles. Crawled over by snails. It stirs among the pebbles” (p520). Never again to tempt the avaricious Von Rumpel, whose dying putrefaction the reader can detect in the last pages of the book.

I loved the novel. After over 22,000 reviews on these pages, there's not much more to say.

It is set in WW2 mainly in Germany & Occupied France. The author’s gift for bringing these two young characters to life, as they try to maintain some semblance of integrity and individuality, while growing up in an age when choices where limited, is absolutely brilliant. I practically liked the way the author manages to draw the reader in, with regard to the chapters concerning Marie-Laure, by using all the senses except sight. review_title: I will read this book times over before I die
review_text: I love reading & have been reading books for over 60 years.  I have also read numerous fiction & non fiction books on WWII. In many ways this is & is not a book about the war.  So many themes, under currents of meaning, human choices & limits & consequences to these choices, the sucking of whole societies & continents into vortexes of political & economic  oceanic currents are just a few of the encompassing human experiences that weave through out this book.  Do we always have a choice?  Viktor Frankl thinks that we do & I am not so sure.  I do not know much about the author at this point & I am amazed of the unable to express spiritual vastness like pulsating northern lights that was experienced ( & no, I am not on drugs or liquor)  On another level, I have come to appreciate the other dimensions of the peoples of Germany whom with few exceptions suffered greatly as for example "the harvested" youth of Germany.  For myself, the connections seen & not seen between peoples, the connections that I felt to the characters, to the times & vast processes & to the ocean of life itself left me feeling mournful  when I finished the book.  This is a great book whose stories are the stories of these present global times.

title: Sycamore Row: A Novel (Jake Brigance Book 2)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: John Grisham
review_text:
I have a really hard time believing that Sycamore Row was actually authored by John Grisham. I have to wonder whether it was largely penned by someone else and Grisham's name was slapped on it. The book does not read like Grisham *at all* and I cannot be the only one who found this to be the case. I have read every single Grisham novel to date. While some are clearly better than others, this one is just way out there in left field.

Where to start. The pacing is off from normal Grisham. Perhaps one of Grisham's greatest talents is the pacing of his novels. This one was up and down, and the down parts were downright boring. I had to force myself to keep going at times and that is something I never experience with Grisham.

The characters are two dimensional and uninteresting. In prior Grisham novels, his characters range from very real to so-so, but these characters have nothing to them, and they are not believable.

The entire plot of the story becomes clear about half way through, and the remainder of the book is just a rote exercise in flipping the pages to get there. Again, not like Grisham at all.

There are flaws in the plot and characters which do not reconcile.

I could go on, but that's enough. Anyone who has read a lot of Grisham must be able to see that this is not him.

subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: John Grisham
review_text:
First off, PLOT SPOILER ALERT!

Observation #1: I found it completely unbelievable that witnessing the lynching of a man in his childhood preyed on Seth Hubbard's mind his entire life to the point that he needed to "get right" by leaving his estate to the surviving grandchild of that man. It's just incomprehensible to me. This book is set in 1988 when I am certain few white southerners would have batted an eye at the lynching, burning or beating of a black person. Sure, a child witnessing an event like this would have been traumatized momentarily but it would have passed as the child absorbed and eventually reflected the culture in which he was raised. Please note I am not saying this is acceptable, but I traveled extensively in the deep south in my teens and early 20s during the Civil Rights era and the ugliness and hatred I saw will stay with me until my dying day. In most parts of the south the Civil War has never ended and I doubt it ever will.

Observation #2: This entire book could have been a short story if only Seth Hubbard had explained in his Will why he was making the bequest to Lettie Lang. Again, I guess we are to believe that 60 years after the fact he was still so overcome with shame over what his forebears had done that he simply couldn't bring himself to put it down in writing. Ain't buying it.

I have read all of Grisham's books and will continue to do so, but this one just didn't ring true for me and I felt kind of skunked by the ending.

title: Gone Girl: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Gillian Flynn
review_text:
This book is "unforgettable" but in a bad way. I will always remember struggling to get through this book because 1. It's the most I've paid for a Kindle book and 2. From all the positive reviews it should have been a book I loved.

I've tried to think of at least one positive thing I can say and believe about this book. I thought of one...only one positive remark and that is this Author can write. The story, as it slowly evolved, was convoluted and complicated and would take a talented writer to do what she did. What I disliked the most was there are very few likable characters within this story and the characters I could have liked were not fully developed.

I agree with the reviewers who basically think the ending was a mess. It was! I too felt the Author ran out of speed and was unsure of how to end the mess she created. I read 2-3 books a week. This book took me almost two weeks to finish. I hate that I wasted 2 weeks of my life in the belief that it had to get better and realizing after reading the final page that it didn't get better...it only got worse. It makes me sad that I have to write a bad review. I wish I could come up with one redeeming reason to read this book...I can't.

title: Gone Girl: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Gillian Flynn
review_title: Tied with Bridges of Madison County for the worst book I've ever read
review_text: If people had told me that this was a "guitly pleasure" book or "trashy" or something, maybe I'd understand its appeal. However, everyone said "good". Everyone told me it was a "good" book. To me, that means it has quality and value. This book was so bad and so trashy and so stupid, its popularity is making me question humanity's capacity to distinguish between good and bad. I hated myself for finishing. Yes, as many reviewers said, the ending sucked. But, really, the whole thing was sucky. The first half was less sucky than the second. But the extreme suckiness of the second half tainted the first, making its overall suckiness considerable.

title: Gone Girl: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Gillian Flynn
review_text: The presentation was good. The idea behind the flow of the chapters solid. But the result? I had to force myself to read it all. It plods along, carefully setting the stage for each piece of the puzzle to follow and fall neatly into place. It was drudgery to read.  But if so many people thought it was great then at some point it would redeem itself. Right? Wrong. It was boring, depressing, unrealistic. Drawing the length out doesn't change the story from a dime store whodunnit. Every book needs a character that you root for. Even if the story is thin you can cheer for your person. There aren't any in this book that I cared anything about. They all deserve each other. So you are left with characters who are unlikeable, a situation that is never resolved, a plodding, predictable story line that is flat. The author's writing technique and use of language are good. But, the story itself is weak. It reads like a tawdry, daytime talk show where you think go ahead, lock them all in a room and let them finish each other off. Who cares. And you change the channel. Click.

The reader develops the characters throughout the entire story, and you really feel as if you are being spoken to, mentally, by the character. The imagery is precise, the story DOES have a nice flow to it, even switching back from character to character. All of my praise goes out the window within the last 10 pages. The end of the story ruins the whole gosh darned thing. As a "tunnel vision" reader I was thinking about basically nothing about this book until I finished it. The ending is so dissatisfying, I was actually really angry. If the nice customer service agent hadn't accidentally refunded my purchase, I would've been mad that I paid money to read this with such a craptastic ending. I'm weary to buy another book from this author because of that slap-in-the-face ending.

review_text: In hindsight, I'm not sure what I expected when I ordered this book.  I had just read a review in the magazine the author had been a critic for.  Great review for a thriller with twists and turns.  Well, that much is true and the book is well written.  In fact, it's very wordy.  However, I'm one of those people who likes to care for at least one of the characters.  The more I read, the more I hated both the husband and the wife.  Each chapter was written from either the point of view of the husband or the wife and the chapters would jump from present to the past and back. review_text:
I am still having goosebumps after reading Gone Girl by Gillian Flynn. From the moment I finished it, it got me reeling all over again, making me want to read the book once more. The story has a lot of harrowing twists and turns and completely astounding shockers that I didn't know which to believe anymore.

I liked that this novel not only involved murder investigations, but it also featured a story about marriage - the troubles that couples usually encounter in their everyday lives, the secrets that separate them and the unspoken agreements that bring them together.

Told in alternating chapters, Flynn effectively demonstrated a haunting mystery that makes readers think “who has really done it?” and “what happens next?” A highly recommended read!

review_text: I read this recently, like most, because I wanted to read it before I saw the movie.  It was a great book.  The story is basically about a man who returns home one day to find his house trashed, and his wife missing.  The book takes you through the events of the following weeks.  There are also flashbacks that give you some back story, which adds clues for you to try and figure out, whodunnit?  The reason for the 4 instead of 5 stars is that , ugh, i just didn't like the ending!  I hate to say it, but it was just anticlimactic.  At the end, I literally said, really????? So it's kind of annoying to really like a book and get to the end feeling unfulfilled.  For that reason, I almost lean towards 3.5 more-so than 4.5 stars.  I am still going to see the movie, but I'm not as excited about it.  A friend of mine went to the movie.  She said those that have read the book, found the movie pretty good, and those that never read it, LOVED the movie.  So it's your choice, which to do first.  Maybe if you saw the movie, this will fill in some pieces.  Anyway, good book. just not great.

title: From Sand and Ash
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Amy Harmon
review_title: Why....why did she go there. Truly upsetting!
review_text:
Most of you will not care what I have to say. And even more will hate me for it. But it's been bugging me for days now so I'll say it. I know it wasn't Ms Harmon's intention (it was out of ignorance) but this is horribly disrespectful to the Priesthood and the faith. I get that is not at all what she intended but the fact she didn't realize it and most of you won't, speaks volumes.
SPOILER ALERT...don't read further if you don't want to have the book spoiled.

The fact that Angelo is portrayed as being faithful is a joke. He's married folks. You might not understand or care (or believed it) but it's a fact. "For he testifieth: Thou art a priest for ever, according to the order of Melchisedech." Hebrews 7:17 Even if YOU don't believe, a PRIEST should! And a faithful man does the right thing regardless of his earthly desires. And to make him out to be a hero and faithful man yet an adulterer is very disrespectful and dishonest. BTW, in biblical times both the Jews and Christians didn't see the word adultery like most today. I didn't mean cheating on your spouse. It meant having any sort of sexual relations (not just intercourse) with someone who is NOT your spouse.
Saying he was 'a good man' is like those that say 'Jesus isn't God, he was just a very good man" well duh.....He said He was God....so he either is or he's a liar therefore not a good man. Because you can't be both.
I get that I'm one of those weirdos that believes faith means being faithful. And as the rare (actually educated in the faith) Catholic I know that God forgives. But this guy didn't want forgiveness. He gave up his soul for earthly lust. Why are we so ignorant that we think that love and sex go hand in hand. So sad. So petty. To push that notion cheapens love to so little. And a priest, a good priest, a faithful priest would worry more about her soul than his desires. He has a much higher responsibility than everyone else simply because he's a priest. So to pretend he's faithful is a lie. He married the church. In a vow to God. And vows are unbreakable. Its not just a job. He can't 'quit' like you and I can at a job. It's a sacrament that leaves a mark on the soul forever! Not just lin this life but in the next.
Had she chosen him to be ANYTHING but a priest I'd have truly LOVED the book. Truly! It's very well written. I love her books. But she did choose him. And she chose to make him an apostate. And it bothers me greatly that he's made out to be such a great guy. We so badly need good influences in this world. And books and movies do influence. But this one celebrated and romanticized opposition to Christ and his Church. Even if YOU don't believe it, Catholics should, and I certainly do. Yes I know most don't care, but a faithful person should. Too many already think priests are terrible men (yet they abuse less than their Protestant brothers and far less than men in general) and this had the chance to put them in a good light. And oddly she likely thought she was. You likely thinks it did. I read the author's notes. She meant no disrespect. But in her ignorance that's exactly what she did. I am very impressed with her historical research otherwise. As for the war, most don't even know how the Church in Italy saved so many. It was probably one of the largest secrets of the entire war. Note: watch My Italian Secret....excellent documentary. Yet we have most people believing the lie that the Pope was a Nazi sympathizer or at best didn't care. He led a church that saved thousands in one of the worst times in human history. And he certainly knew. He had a game to play to save as many as he could. If he got the Vatican taken he'd have lost them all.
She told that part of the story very well. Excellent history. But why didn't she make him someone who could fall in love and not lose his soul doing it! It broke my heart and made me not like him at all. He can't even make it right without destroying a family. Super sad. Not a happy ending to me at all. He excommunicated himself. And to a Catholic...that means hell without confession and true repentance.

I would give this novel a 4.5! Eva is a Jewish youngster in Italy who befriends Angelo, a Catholic seminarian. They develop a very strong relationship and are possibly in love, but WWII intervenes as well as Angelo's beliefs that he should be a priest. They both decide to help out the persecuted Jews and both suffer the consequences of their actions.

I really enjoyed this novel. The author portrayed the horrific events of this era accurately and many parts of the story are true. The storyline of the main characters is fictional, but it is a compelling story and I loved the development of the characters. I highly recommend this book, and I will read more of this author's work.

In From Sand and Ash author Amy Harmon explores the strength of love and faith as Europe is torn apart by war and strife. Angelo and Ava are childhood friends whose losses create a bond and kinship that others will never understand. Under the watchful eye of Ava's father and Angelo's grandparents the two are pointed toward different destinies while trying to understand the opposition to anything other than a familial bond.

When Ava's father takes it upon himself to set aside his ideals to free as many Jews as possible he places himself on a dangerous path. That only leaves Angelo to protect Ava and ensure she fly's under the radar of the German army until the war is over.

review_title: Meh.  Not sure what the point of this series is (spoilers)
review_text:
Not sure why these exist. I gave two stars because Koontz writes interesting prose. But there is absolutely no suspense. Each book follows the exact same format: Nameless arrives in town possessing almost supernatural knowledge of his super evil target, Nameless visits a victim of the evil target, there's some internal revelation by the evil target, and then Nameless executes a perfectly plotted plan of "truthfulness" (not justice, there is no such thing in Koontz's world) and kills the super evil target in some appropriate way. Nameless faces neither obstacles nor any real danger (this is after four of these things, there are two more I guess).

At least I didn't pay anything for them.

And in reading these, I remember why I gave up Dean Koontz long ago: the very black and white characterizations. Good people in his stories are REALLY, REALLY good, bad people are REALLY, REALLY bad. And the world is a dark place full of an unrealistic number of super evil people, and there's always a preternatural dog. "Phantoms" is still my favorite Koontz book. I suspect if I re-read it today (it scared the crap out of me all those years ago when I first read it) I would still find it an effective horror story.

review_text:
This review and rating encompasses all six of the Nameless series. I thoroughly enjoyed each of Nameless's missions. The first story introduces Nameless - an amnesiac, truth-seeker, and orchestrator of consequences. Each mission further develops the character, Nameless. The sixth story of Nameless brings the reader to a climax of full disclosure and closure.

Dean Koontz is a prolific writer, a creative genius and an artist with words. I slow down whenever I read a Dean Koontz book, to better appreciate the flow of his words and his talent for description. He never, ever disappoints.

He has been a favorite author of mine for decades.

Thank you Dean Koontz - for the entertainment that you've provided to the reading public for all these years. And thank you for your charitable work with animals and shelters. 🐕 🐈

Happy reading, ya'll! 📚

review_title: To compare this author to Gillian Flynn is an insult to Gillian Flynn!
review_text:
To say this book represents a Gillian Flynn novel is an INSULT to Gillian Flynn! Whoever is the publist for this author decserves a big fat promotion....if any new authors are out there, find this publists because he/she is a genius! FIRST, I AM NOT RELATED TO GILLIAN FLYNN, despite my name, it's my maiden name. Although, I did graduate from Kansas University, ROCK CHALK!
I bought the audio version since I do a lot of driving for work. This book is painful to listen to. The ladies that narrate are good, the story is just aweful. The other reviews that you see with low stars are honest. There are no characters in the book that you like, can root for, or want to see suceed. I strongly disliked the main character, Rachel. A human being that gave up on life and blames everyone else and life for her current situation. All the main characters are miserable in their lives and take no responsibility for their actions. When the main characters find themselves in a bad situation nothing is done to strive forward or change the situation. Poor me, poor me, poor me. I was ready to smack my head up against the wall 90 minutes into the book. No matter how bad I think a book is, I can not stop, I have to finsh. I only have 3 hours to go and I can't wait to be finsished! I seriously considered going to the library to read the ending, but that would be cheating. I will be suffering through the last three hours to see the final outcome. Don't waist your credit or money. Ask your friend that read or listened to the book to give you the reader's digest version.

title: The Girl on the Train
subtitle: Hardcover – January 1, 2015
author: Paula Hawkins
review_title: A Repulsive Protagonist and a Lazy Plot Ploy
review_text: I needed a book to read on a 5 hour plane ride and a friend recommended this book. I knew nothing about it when I downloaded it other than it was a murder mystery concerning a girl who rides trains and sees something. Sorry to say after reading it, I was not impressed. First off, none of the characters are even likeable and are all a bunch of low-life's, especially the protagonist. Now I know, we're supposed to feel bad for Rachel because her husband dumped her and she's an alcoholic. But Rachel is so stupid, so totally void of any type of basic common sense, that I just couldn't stand her and I almost quit half-way through. But I pressed on. Then I get to the end and this lying, stalking, repulsive anti-hero who pees in her pants, pukes on her roommate's carpet and falls down in public all the sudden figures it all out and becomes the voice of reason?? Secondly, I hate the amnesia plot ploy. It's been done countless times and I think it's lazy. Yeah, I know, the alcoholic black out thing is supposed to be a new twist on it, but I'm not buying it. Hitchcockian?? Absolutely not. Next time I have a long plane ride I'll stick to the tried and true masters, Agatha Christie, PD James, etc.

title: The Girl on the Train

author: Paula Hawkins
review_text:
This is probably one of the more captivating thrillers I have read in recent memory. For a debut novelist (career as a journalist notwithstanding), Paula Hawkins has really produced quite an exceptional whodunnit, and with an ingenious structure and narrative style, that worked really well.

Three women, Rachel, Anna and Megan, share the narrative, and the chapters indicate the time and day of events, as each character sees and experiences them. Rachel travels daily to London on a train to her office and passes by a row of houses each day. She has become particularly enamoured with a couple in one of these houses, whom she names Jason and Jess. But there is more than just random voyeurism that draws her attention to that particular neighbourhood, and Hawkins takes her time revealing important details, as Rachel's story becomes intertwined with Anna's and Megan's, and how these women are connected becomes integral to the central plot, when a crime occurs.

Hawkins keeps the reader hooked to the many twists and turns in the story, and it is to her credit that she takes time to build up her characters, especially Rachel, the titular girl on the train, who is as pitiable as she is a deplorable parasitic mess. Despite these contrary feelings she incites in the reader, she endears as well and repels, and we are never quite sure if we can fully trust her. The sense of unease permeates the story and the reader cannot rest easy until he or she reaches the last page. A very intriguing read.

title: The Girl on the Train

review_text: I got this book based on hearing it was supposedly so good that they are making a movie of it, and I love mystery thrillers.  But I hesitated when I saw one review by a guy who described the characters in it as "vapid women with no life".  In hindsight, I'd have to agree.  The women characters in this book (as well as the lead male character) really do seem to me to be vapid individuals, whose lives revolve solely around "their man", and who I couldn't personally identify with in any way.  It was difficult for me to imagine the goings-on in their one-track brains, as each told their story in the first person.....INITIALLY.  As each individual's story unfolded, and more background to each was revealed, they seemed less vapid, or at least there was more of an explanation for their vapidness. The situation of seeing things going on in others' lives, via being on a train schedule every day made for an interesting premise.  I feel the same way sometimes just living in a neighborhood where I walk my dogs each night, and see and hear revalatory things about neighbors I perhaps would prefer not to know (?) Yet I'm sure plenty of thriller stories lie therein!  All in all, while it was a page-turner and I couldn't wait to get to what other reviews referred to as "an ending you don't expect"....I still came away from the story feeling like "Man, these people seriously need to think outside themselves and get a freakin' LIFE!"  And yea....it made me wonder how many people DO operate at this self-absorbed level and that accounts for much of society being like it is these days.....hmm.  Sad.
