title: The Girl on the Train
subtitle: Hardcover – January 1, 2015
author: Paula Hawkins
review_title: Great suspense story, marred only by poor finale
review_text:
This book is very well written. The story of the girl (woman) on the train, who passes her old neighborhood every day to and from London, and who imagines a fairy tale life for people who would have been her neighbors had her husband not left her for his pregnant mistress, is fascinating. Rachel, the woman on the train, is an alcoholic who has blackouts, which makes her a very unreliable narrator. The "fairy tale" neighbor, called Jess until Rachel learns her name is Megan, also tells her version of events beginning about a year previous to the story Rachel tells. Additionally, the mistress who took Rachel's place, Anna, sometimes gets to tell about events from her point of view. These three women share the story of events even if they do not get equal time as narrators.

Spoilers. Rachel is lonely after her divorce and she has lost her job. She still travels to work every day, if only to prevent her roommate from discovering that she is now unemployed. She drinks heavily, on the train, at the flat, in the park -- if she can drink, she does. This makes people doubt everything she tells them, especially when she tells them that she saw a woman who lives in her old neighborhood and who has gone missing with a man who was not her husband. Rachel has imagined perfect lives for "Jess" and her husband, only to see "Jess" betraying her husband with another man, just before Rachel sees her picture on the news as a missing person. Rachel inserts herself into the missing person investigation and also into the life of "Jess' husband", Scott, by telling everyone who'll listen that she thinks the "other man" may be responsible for her being missing. Though Rachel continually attempts to stop drinking, so that people will take her seriously, she keeps getting drunk, worsening her reliability and her own life.

"Jess" whose real name is Megan, may have a dream life in Rachel's head, but she has a "boring" life in her own opinion. She is, indeed, having an affair, but part of the clever setup of the novel is thinking she is having an affair with one man while she is actually involved with someone more surprising. Megan concentrates most of her story revealing how manipulative and promiscuous she is, showing her husband Scott is an unattractive light as someone who is "emotionally abusive" to Megan, in Megan's opinion. Despite that, her parts of the novel are compelling, if only because they are short and frequently interrupted by Rachel's story, where Megan is missing.

Anna, the woman who had an affair with Rachel's ex-husband Tom, and who is now living in Rachel's old house, near Megan and Scott, is trying to take care of her young child, protecting her from the "dangerous" Rachel, whom Anna believes is stalking her, and attempting to keep the romance alive in her marriage. Anna has the fewest sections of the novel.

The missing person/murder investigation and Rachel's involvement in it, including her "stalking" of her ex-husband Tom and his new wife Anna, is compelling. The fact that Rachel is an alcoholic with blackouts seems to make her the narrator you could trust least, but she does accurately recall some things in the story. Some readers found her extremely unlikable. I can't say that I liked her, but I didn't dislike her. The story was so interesting that I didn't mind one of the major characters being an alcoholic.

The only reason this book doesn't get 5 stars is because in real life criminals just don't fall apart and relate the entire crime, step by detailed step, to any interested persons, just before they attempt to kill the person to whom they are "confessing." So that was just an extremely long, unbelievable, weak ending to what was a very interesting suspense story. And the ending, involving Anna and Rachel, was also unrealistic. The two women do not like each other, and to present them as "fixing" things was just silly. I was not convinced.

The books deserves 4.5 stars for story, characters, and writing, but the ending, with its unrealistic confession, was such a letdown and so poorly presented (as an uninterrupted monologue from the killer) that is gets only 4.

The only flaw with this novel, in my opinion, is the 3 main characters' preoccupation with husbands, babies, and reproduction.  All of their lives, and personalities, revolve around men and babies, and they all seemed in competition with each other over who has the most idyllic family life.  It struck me as an archaic, artificial basis for their actions, which gave the whole novel an almost sexist feel to it.  Having said that, the novel is entertaining and seductive and I would definitely recommend it.

author: Paula Hawkins
review_title: Excellent novel and I definitely recommend the audio version
review_text:
The Girl on the Train sounds like it could be the long lost fourth Stieg Larson novel. Instead, it's a brilliant thriller by former financial writer and current New York Times bestselling author Paula Hawkins'. The novel was released earlier this year and hit the literary world like, if you'll pardon the pun, a runaway train.

Rachel rides the commuter train to and from work five days a week. Even when she gets fired from her job for being a drunk, she continues the daily commute just to keep appearances up. Her routine doesn't change. She stares out the window, gulps wine or gin and tonics, loathes herself, and tries not to look when, every morning and every night, she passes by her old house and her old life. Her husband has re-married, to a woman he started seeing when he and Rachel were still together. There's a baby now, and the beautiful little girl somehow puts an exclamation point on everything Rachel lost.

A few doors down, she notices a new couple. They're young, attractive and obviously very much in love. Rachel often sees them in their yard or on their small terrace. She fantasizes about them, creating names, occupations and all the different aspects of a storybook marriage. She's into the arts. He's a world traveler. Together, they've got the world on a string. Then, that woman disappears and is later found dead. Rachel believes she may have witnessed something that led to a brutal murder. She contacts police but her drinking issues, cloudy memory and history of harassing her former husband and his new bride make Rachel's claims less than credible. She's still convinced she can help but can't quite remember what she saw or what it might mean. Meanwhile, that old demon alcohol is never far away.

Because of poor eyesight, I've been an avid audio book listener for well over thirty-five years. I consider myself an expert on the subject. As a general rule, I don't care for books with more than one narrator. I find that style of production tends to be distracting and sometimes confusing. In the case of The Girl on the Train, however, that approach is perfect. There is a different narrator for each of the three primary female characters. The story is told from those three points of view and each has its own voice, literally. All three narrators are excellent, and their performance contributes to what's already a fantastic novel.

title: The Girl on the Train
subtitle: Hardcover – January 1, 2015
author: Paula Hawkins
review_text: I give this book all the stars in the sky! I absolutely loved it. For this to be Mrs. Hawkins debut novel, she has done a hell of a job weaving this story. review_text: The early reviews were right. Paula Hawkins' complex thriller is the book "Gone Girl" wanted to be but wasn't. (Sorry  "Gone Girl" fans.) Its heroine's alcohol addiction fuels her obsession with a house she passes daily on a train commute to London. Hawkins never quite lets us know if someone is heading for harm or salvation, and the imbalance is thrilling. Divided among three female characters, the chapters take the reader to the edge of one of two things - a purging reality or the embrace of unspeakable danger. Un-put-downable.

review_title: In the long run the only reason I finished it was because It actually became somewhat fun and humorous to pick out all the flaws
review_text:
I had higher hopes for this book based on all the postive reviews. In the long run the only reason I finished it was because It actually became somewhat fun and humorous to pick out all the flaws and anachronisms. My family lived in France during the war and several were resistance members, whose activities included hiding and transporting downed allied airman as well as jews, like the characters in the book.

I wondered as I read the book if the author had ever even been to France or talked with any survivors of the occupation or restance members?
Her characters were like displaced americans who just happened to be in France or at times cartoonish stereotypical figures complete with berets.They even sing Frere Jacque.

She seems to have no concept of how French people of the time dressed, spoke or acted or what they ate. She has no idea of what foods were available during severe rationing or how limited the quanties were. Some of her characters dressed ate more like they were from South Carolina; overalls, plaid shirt, gingham cloth... toast and eggs for breakfast in France? Making you own bread instead of going to the boulangerie? The restance members, we are told, wore brown pants and berets and just so we the (presumably stupid) reader understand that the hanged bodies, one of the protagonists sees in her village are village are restance members, the author describes the bodies as wearing berets. Really? Did someone put the berets back on their heads after they died, or were are berets such an integral part of a frenchman's head that they do not fall off even when the wearer goes through a viloent death by hanging?

Though some of the historical events and depictions from the war are factual, such as the massacre at Oradour, the author could use an extensive WWII history lesson, including life under German occupation. How does Isabel travels all over at will from Paris to the Pyrenees, when early in the book it is mentioned how hard it was to get travel permits during the occupation? Though parts of France were devastated by both German and allied bombing, the area where the fictional village of Carriveau is located did not undergo bombing. Does the author know that antibiotics other than some simple sulfa drugs were not available till 1945? She better check when freezers were available too. I could go on...

Did I mention that the stories romantic line and charater development are sophmoric and second rate?

review_title: the other younger and very beautiful, who joins the French resistance and
review_text:
This is basically a classic story of hope and faith eventually triumphing over unspeakable evil. The hellish Nazi occupation of France during the Second World War provides the ominously brutal background to this novel of two young French women who have to grapple with the basic struggle to stay alive amid daily Nazi humiliations, physical brutality and near-starvation.. They are sisters, one already a mother when war breaks out in 1939, the other younger and very beautiful, who joins the French resistance and, barely out of her teens, helps smuggle shot-down English airmen through the Pyrenees and into Spain.
It's a fetching story, but there are some caveats: Kristin Hannah is no Irene Nemirovsky, author of the acclaimed 'Suite Francaise' [2006], a novel about Nazi-occupied France and the ultimately futile struggle of a Jewish family to survive intact until the German defeat. Hannah sometimes gives the impression that she is writing from New England with the aid of Google research [and no doubt the odd World War history book]--in stark contrast to Nemirovsky's densely atmospheric, nostalgic masterpiece. Also, some of the love scenes between the younger sister and a young member of the Maquis [the French resistance] are redolent of the genre of the romance novel.
But these are only minor glitches in a steadily paced historic novel that is a timely reminder that some European nations have in the past exhibited the same sort of inhumanity towards their fellows as we witness almost every day from around the world.

review_text:
I absolutely loved this book. It brought so many different emotions as you follow the characters and their struggles and triumphs. This was not a typical, I know how it ends before I’ve read the first half book. There are so many truths, beautiful and ugly at the same time that, although a work of fiction, bring light to the real people who inspired this book.

People are often much stronger than they realize and I think this book gives a real sense of how courageous and selfless so many people were during this travesty of a war. So many stories are about the concentration camps that most people forget to think about the daily life of others who lived and fought secretly through the war. So many hid the truth of their former lives from the families because the pain was all too real and memorable.

This was such a good book. I highly recommend it. Not necessarily for means of entertainment but for a thought provoking, emotional roller coaster. You will finish this book changed. If we forget history, we are bound to repeat it. Let us never forget what these brave souls went through.

review_title: If you only read one book this year, make it this one!
review_text:
This book totally blew me away. I have never before had such an understanding of the hardships suffered by those in war in general or by the French during World War II in particular. This was a work of fiction, however, I'm sure the research Ms. Hannah did helped her get actions, occurrences and feelings as close to those of the French who suffered through that horrible time. This story of two French sisters was simply incredible. It made my heart ache, but left me in awe of what some people were capable of doing and the risks they were willing to take in order to help others. I loved that Ms. Hannah was also able to show that even though there were horribly cruel German soldiers, there were others who really were good men simply trapped in an awful situation that they couldn't remove themselves from.
The narration of this audio book by Polly Stone was incredible. There are reviewers who dinged her for her French accent, or her voices. I have no training in French, so I just sat back and listened to the story. Personally, I thought she did a fantastic job. Since the narration won Audible Best Narration one year, I don't think very many had a problem with it. I got this from my library, but I'm actually contemplating going back and using my Audible credit so that I can have it in my personal audio library. Great story, great narration!

title: The Invention of Wings: With Notes (Oprah's Book Club 2.0 3)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Sue Monk Kidd
review_text: This is a bittersweet tale of lives intertwined between slave owners and slaves before the civil war.  In spite of circumstances both good and bad, persons can be free in their hearts, souls and spirits.  Some slave owners knew slavery to be evil and worked to change the laws and to free the slaves while others remained prisoners of tradition and wealth yet in their hearts mourned their spiritual weakness.  The slaves yearning for freedom and respect form community and compassionately support each other in their physical captivity.  Yet they remain free in heart and spirit and strive to leave their story of survival behind for their children and grandchildren.  Do their captors ever realize they are unable to enslave these hearts and spirits?  Sadly no.  So in the end who is slave and who is free?  One must now ponder what if anything we have learned about slavery in any and all situations past and present. We may close the book after the last chapter but it will be difficult to forget that slavery still exists.

subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Sue Monk Kidd
review_text:
The story of Handful Grimké and her mom, Charlotte (two slaves in South Carolina) strive to find freedom where they can. In parallel, the Grimké's daughter, Sarah, yearns to break through the limits imposed on the women of her time. As Sarah and her younger sister, Angelina, find the courage to take up the fight for abolition, they also spark the beginning of the women's movement.

Most of us know that at some point in history, slavery ended, but few know of the important role women played in making this a reality. This book corrects that. I was pleasantly surprised that the book was based on two characters in American history seldom spoken about, the Grimké sisters. The book is beautifully written and you really engage with the characters in the book.

review_text: I really wanted to like this book more than I did. It felt too juvenile to me. I liked the story and am grateful to people like the Grimkes. We will always need more people like them. However. I didn’t enjoy reading this book. My friends loved and raved about it, and I’ve liked some of her other books, so I stuck with it, but I would’ve preferred reading an historical account rather than as an historical fiction. What bothered me the most about this book is that it can inadvertently cause people to keep persistently asking, "What about the nice slave owners? We had nice ones!" While the horrible treatment of slaves is highlighted in this book, I'm afraid people will overlook those and focus on the "nice slave owners," and totally miss the mark because they are so afraid to face the past of their ancestors.

review_text:
This double story of Sarah Grimké and Handful is oddly boring and predictable. There is almost nothing but misery for both girls throughout most of their young lives. When anything good happens, it is ALWAYS followed by some kind of disaster. Beyond Handful and her mother, and Sarah, everyone in the book is written as a stereotype--there's nobody you can get the slightest bit interested in.
Contrast this with Lily and her four mentors in the same author's The Secret Life of Bees. There, things don't just happen to people, they develop naturally from who they are.
P.S. I found the title, The Invention of Wings, and the legend of Handful's forebears as being able to fly, annoying, and at worst, a steal from Toni Morrison's Song Of Solomon. Kidd seems to use it as a formula for endorsement by the Oprah Book Club.
We KNOW this author can do better, and I look forward to much better future books.

author: Sue Monk Kidd
review_text:
The setting for this historical fiction is Charleston, S. Carolina in the years prior to the Civil War.  The story is told in  alternating chapters by Sarah, the daughter of a wealthy plantation owner, and “Handful”, a slave girl. 

Sarah’s earliest memory was witnessing a slave being whipped. She grew up with an intense hatred for the institution of slavery.  And although her childhood was  one of privilege, Sarah deeply resented the constraints put on her because of her gender.  She wanted to become a lawyer like her father and brothers, but the only “ acceptable” role for her was to find and marry someone of equal social standing.  Eventually Sarah and her younger sister Nina walked away from the privileged life they knew and became  ardent abolitionists and women’s rights advocates. The character of Sarah is loosely based on the life of Sarah Grimke who, along with her sister Angelina, became pioneers in both the anti-slavery and the women’s rights movements.

The second narrator of this book is Handful, a slave girl  owned by Sarah’s father. From her voice we get an inside look at the insidious institution of slavery.  The capricious and harsh punishments and daily humiliations meted out by the slave-owners is difficult to read at times, but can only touch the surface of this terrible chapter in our country’s history.  But, as historical fiction goes, this story is well researched and well written.  The book definitely deserves at least  four stars.

The intertwined lives of two women each seeking different kinds of freedom makes a wonderful story. Hetty (a.k.a. Handful) was given to Sarah on her 11th birthday. Sarah was appalled at owning another person. Handful was literally that, strong-willed, smart, and a bit sly. As Sarah grows into adulthood in the plantation class of 1820's Charleston, she grows more distressed by slavery and becomes involved in abolition. Handful learns to read and seeks a way to freedom as well. In her quest to free the slaves, Sarah realizes that she herself is a slave to the male dominated culture of the Deep South. These two characters become friends to the reader by the end of the novel. We are sympathetic to their journey and wish them well.
I had never thought about the fact that slaves were freed in America 50+ years before women were allowed to vote.

author: Sue Monk Kidd
review_title: Best Book I've Read in Quite a While
review_text:
This story of two girls -- a privileged white girl, Sarah Grimke, and a slave in attendance on her family, Hetty Handful Grimke -- drew me in almost immediately, and by the time I finished it, the characters had become part of my waking consciousness. As with any good book, I found myself musing, "I wonder what Hetty is doing now," or, "Where is Sarah?" Sue Monk Kidd, author of The Secret Life of Bees, does a wonderful job of weaving their lives together by means of alternate chapters, letting us move through childhood, adolescence, and adulthood with these two sensitive and impassioned women who are troubled in vastly different ways and who are bound to each other for life.

I see that many reviewers were distressed by Oprah Winfrey's notes. They appeared on my Kindle as frequent small "O" superscript notations (I assume these were click-able) which were initially annoying, but I became inured to them and was soon able to ignore them entirely. I appreciate many of Ms. Winfrey's gifts to our culture but I do agree that she often goes about sowing her opinions in fields that would be better left unplowed.

Back to the book: The veil was ripped from my eyes in terms of many exceptionally grueling hardships of slavery I'd never heard of and the inhumane punishments levied against slaves for even the silliest infractions. I didn't realize that Charleston, SC, was the gestational epicenter of slavery in the US. I admire an author who truly does her historical homework and Kidd exceeded all expectations. Toward the end of the book I learned that the Grimke family was real, and this made The Invention of Wings experience even more powerful. Highly recommended.

title: All the Light We Cannot See: A Novel
author: Anthony Doerr
review_text: There are so many things wrong with this book.  I mean I will start that it is wonderfully written and captures the intensity of an incredible time.  But it is also one of those books that when you put it down, you are disquieted.  First, it is a book that features leading female characters, written by a man..... yeah men just cannot write for women.  Second, when you finish the book and reflect..... you will be struck by the amount of hate in this book.  Think about (and I wont spoil) but think about who gets killed and raped.... and who does not.  Who is presented as heros.... and who is presented as scum.  Its amazing that the book seems to capture the violence and oppression that led up to WWII, and that so many were just pawns caught up in a hideous evil.... and then the book almost obsessively goes and kills off everyone the narrator hates.  Compare this to Vonnegut or Heller or even Hemmingway (or even Walker Percy's reflection on war).  We are 60+ years past the end of WWII and the author seems not to have resolution.  Finally.... the light.... the radio... is a theme that runs through the book and it is a bit like "gee whiz a radio is this invisible light that runs through all of us."  Really???  Radio is over 100 years old.  Yes, in the time of WWII there was a gee whiz factor to the technological advances that could be done with radio (consider radar)..... but at this point its not mystery or metaphysics.... its spectrum and science.  Post modern world view has moved past mysticism of radio waves to scientific advances of smart phones.

One minute a character is buried in a cellar and the next he's out three years earlier finding radios lying in the street. I never felt like I knew what was going on at any given time. Then the book is written  in present tense which in my mind makes it harder to follow. I guess authors see this technique as being creative. I see it as a gimmick. Anyway the book has obviously had  more positive effect for many  other readers and God bless them. For my part I was just happy when it was finally over.

review_title: All the Light We Cannot See
review_text:
Wow! Reading this book took much longer than most books I have read in the past year.
I had to take a break occasionally to visualize the characters, the scenes, the deprivation and devastation, the violence and the sometimes simple kindnesses.
This was a very different perspective on war, alternately told by a young blind girl who had to leave her home to escape the war with her father and by a young German soldier.
Though the story was somewhat tedious and too wordy, I enjoyed the "growing up" of the characters from naive and sheltered to aware and resilient, Mari-Laure, and Werner, optimistic and excited to jaded and resigned.
It will take a long time to forget the horrifying images of war as seen through the eyes of a young soldier.
It will be more pleasant to remember the life that Mari -Laure lead.

title: All the Light We Cannot See: A Novel
author: Anthony Doerr
review_title: "Open your eyes and see what you can with them before they close forever"
review_text:
This was an amazing journey through the eyes and hearts of children of World War II as I could have never imagined. I was introduced to Anthony Doerr and his novel All the Light We Cannot See through the Dallas Museum of Art's Literature and Letters series (next up on my list is The Book of Aron by Jim Shepard). The lecture was an absolute delight, and Doerr outlined his inspiration for the novel and within a mere 30 minutes remind me of all the wonders this world contains.

All the Light We Cannot See follows the stories of Werner and Marie-Laure, children on opposite sides of WWII, and how their lives eventually intersect in the occupied city of St. Malo off the coast of France. "Like a ping pong match," each chapter (often no longer than 3-8 paragraphs) flips back and forth to each child's story: Werner, a bright, curious, young German boy growing up in an orphanage with his little sister Jutta, and Marie-Laure, a blind, young French girl, living in the heart of Paris as her father's shadow, who happens to be the head key master of the Museum of Natural History. With the occupation of France, Marie and her father flee Paris with a museum treasure that creates a third story for the reader to devour (those familiar with the tales of The Monuments Men: Allied Heroes, Nazi Thieves, and the Greatest Treasure Hunt in History and The Lady in Gold: The Extraordinary Tale of Gustav Klimt's Masterpiece, Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer will feel similar heart strings ache). Reader be forewarned: time is fluid and like a picture book. You will traverse the four years of WWII, linger in hours and seconds of bombardment of St. Malo, and to my personal delight, you will also dwell in the "simultaneity of moments" in which you realize not everything is about you, and not every story has a happy ending, all the while knowing there is so much in this world we cannot see.

Doerr's novel is not any sort of "typical" WWII novel I have ever read because it makes so few omniscient references to the war as a whole; the kind a younger generation may easily label the events of the 1940's. The characters can only live each breath as it comes, and hope each imagined danger is just that - imagined. The Nazi machine and the Third Reich were not created overnight, and the "beginning" of the war did not occur as a singular event for many German youth, and neither did its end (for either France or Germany). I don't like to give away spoilers in my reviews, and although we already know how WWII ends, the stories of Werner and Marie-Laure, and the others around them (Etienne, Jutta, Madame Manec, Volkheimer, and sweet Frederick, von Rumpel, and even Jules Verne feels like a close friend through Marie-Laure's finger tips) are for future Doerr readers to discover.

While the most poignant lines to my soul were: "Your problem, Werner, is that you still believe you own your life." I will never read the phrase "listen, children" in earnest again, without feeling a certain ache in my heart.

Happy Reading!

title: All the Light We Cannot See: A Novel
author: Anthony Doerr
review_text: This is an exquisitely written historical novel  by Pulitzer prize-winner author, Anthony Doerr.  Doerr is a master wordsmith, and creates such vivid word pictures that the reader not only is privy to the innermost thoughts of the main characters, but  also can clearly visualize the details of what is happening and where.  This book is also a "thriller." The setting is Germany and France during World War II.  The story (stories) captures the lives of five principal characters, interlacing them, during this horrific time in history, in unexpected and extraordinary ways - a young German orphan, and his sister; a young blind French girl, her father, and her uncle.  The over-riding theme of this amazing book is one of self- discovery: the depths of bravery and strength of the human spirit in the face of desperate circumstances; and the struggle to come to terms with what is morally right and morally wrong.  This is a read that is hard to put down!

I have never come across so many totally unique, beautiful, accurate metaphors in my life...I highlight and read them over and over sometimes, wallowing and relishing in them.
This will be one I'll read many times...and definitely want the paper copy.

title: The Silkworm (Cormoran Strike Book 2)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Robert Galbraith
review_text: Following the world-wide delight with the Harry Potter series, it seemed reasonable to expect something equally remarkable from Rowling's mysteries, particularly one set in the publishing industry. Unfortunately, the murdered author and the troop of industry executives seem more like Murder Inc. than any legitimate group. Though there's only one victim in the book, that single murder provides enough gore to distract the reader from what should be the fascinating process of detection. With the exception of  the detective Cormoran and his winsome assistant, all the characters seem equally capable of capital crime. Less described than merely alluded to, the victim's book serving as plot sounds not only unpublishable but virtually unreadable. Horror fans may accept this venture into another genre, but those who enjoyed Rowling's wit and imagination and who read mysteries for diversion are bound be bewildered and disappointed by The Silkworm.

review_text:
The Silkworm by Robert Galbraith.

Cormoran Strike is called in on a case of a missing husband. Robin remains his gal Friday and then some.
There were a few spots in this story that brought out the best in story telling but...This story I found inappropriately much too long. This story could have been condensed into half the time/length and held my interest throughout. Unfortunately, the author decided to ramble on and on for no other reason than to fill up another page and lose my focus in the process.

The characters were repulsive to say the least. If this was intended from the start to try to emulate Philip Marlowe this book has failed miserably.
I will not continue reading this series(?).

title: The Silkworm (Cormoran Strike Book 2)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Robert Galbraith
review_text:
'The Silkworm' is a fantastic read! The few hours I spent every weekend morning reading this book was a great way to begin a sunny summer day energized! I don't usually read in the morning because it tends to put me back to sleep. Not a chance of such a thing happening with this novel!

As was true of the first in the Cormoran Strike series, 'The Cuckoo's Calling', the main characters are the best thing about 'The Silkworm' - fascinating and cute. The continuing drama surrounding Strike's and Robin Ellacott's personal lives mix seamlessly into the body of the mystery; the book is stronger for it. Robin's fiancé, Matthew Cunliffe, has a problem accepting Robin's job as secretary and Strike's quasi-partner in investigations; and Cormoran's disability issues from his missing leg alongside his annoyance at his connection with the aristocrat family of Rokeby he so doggedly ignores even as he uses the social power they give him are the spices which make this tale extra tasty.

Uh, perhaps I'm thinking of food metaphors because a disembowelment 'opens' the Pandora's box of deadly threats facing our brave duo. I guess it's how I roll.....but, perhaps I should mention this is an adult mystery, but not with unnecessary graphic violence.

Strike relies heavily on the skills he learned in the Special Investigation Branch of the Army while in Afghanistan to run his detective agency. Losing his leg has slowed him down tremendously, but he never gives in to the disability, though I found several tight spots because he cannot run or balance in the snowy weather of London that come up in the course of proving the innocence of Leonora Quine in the disappearance of her husband, Owen Quine, very intense and frustrating!

Owen Quine is disliked by most. He is a literary writer who became important when his first book proved a critical success. His personality and habits of betrayal did not win rave reviews with his publisher, editor, agent or friends, however. As a husband, he cheats on his wife. Only with his mentally disabled daughter, Orlando, does he remain a beloved man.

He produces a second book which viciously exposes the dirty secrets of all of his acquaintances. Somehow a draft version is delivered to most of the principals in the publishing house, as well as to his bitter ex-friends and now rivals. Whatever the devious reason behind this act, it succeeds in riling up everyone included in the vengeful author's book to such a heightened level, Quine apparently goes into hiding.

Leonora does not appear to love her husband, but she has bills to pay and a special needs daughter to raise. Not understanding that the police would consider her a good suspect for murder if Owen does not return, she simply wants him found to resume his financial support. Strike is aware of the bigger difficulty Leanora will face if he cannot trace Owen's movements. He is very concerned when he realizes that Mrs. Quine is one of the most honest, if idiosyncratic, people he has met lately. He can see how the more dull-witted police will not look for anyone else as a suspect because of her mannerisms.

He must find Owen Quine soon. Hopefully alive....

title: The Silkworm (Cormoran Strike Book 2)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Robert Galbraith
review_title: She could have been Agatha Christie (if that other thing hadn't happened)
review_text:
Plot-master JK Rowling returns for round 2 as the pseudonymous Robert Galbraith. And once again, she bubbles and seethes with plot twists, surprises, red herrings and good old-fashioned story telling.

We've returned to the world of private eye Cormoran Strike, illegitimate son of a world-famous rock star, maimed hero of Afghanistan. He's a sort of modern Miss Marple/Hercule Poirot with a dash of the giant Hagrid thrown in -- offering a difficult history, an uncanny intuition into human misbehavior, and a heart full of soul.

It's a classic detective tale, one that opens with a long-suffering wife who seeks Strike's services to find her husband, a once well-regarded, now fading author. And soon enough, Strike turns up a gaudy, horrific murder, a cast of colorful suspects, and a stew of painful histories/plausible motives that reach back 30 years. Does he solve the mystery? Does it satisfy? If you love JK Rowling, you know those answers already.

No spoilers here, but a couple of observations. Cormoran Strike (his first name referencing a Cornish giant, we come to learn) is the second male protagonist that Rowling has chosen to serve as the moral center of her stories. Through him, we once again feel her dripping contempt for snobbery, cruelty, lazy journalism and unearned privilege. These themes animate "Harry Potter" as well, of course; and it's been fascinating to watch Rowling bring her adult, non-magic universe into line with that world-famous creation.

I can't escape the feeling that all Rowling ever wanted was to live as a writer, telling clever stories and matching wits with her readers. World fame intervened with that modest wish, and introduced expectations and complications that no one could have expected. With these books, it seems that JK Rowling can return to her roots as an ace story teller, and she gets on with it splendidly. What a pleasure for all of us.

author: Janet Evanovich
review_text:
I love the Stephanie Plum novels for what they are - light but fun entertainment, with a bit of not-very-explicit Ranger and Morelli sex and a lot of snort-out-loud humor courtesy of Lula and Grandma Mazur. I don't expect a plot worthy of "War and Peace." But I do expect a plot.

If these are the reasons you read these books, I urge you not to waste your money on this one. I really wish I'd listened to the reviewers who said the same thing, but I thought, "I need something to read; how bad can it be?" The answer - really, really bad. It's not funny, there's no sex, and Lula and grandma seem like they are thrown in at the last minute because the editor said they had to be there. It's almost as if it was written by a different person. I read it about 2 weeks ago, and I honestly can't remember anything about the plot. That's how bad it is.

Please don't do what I did - you should listen to the legion of reviewers who say it is terrible. They are right.

Ms. Evanovich, this story line is done. Please do us all a favor and end it instead of churning out stale re-do's like the past four books. Please.

title: Notorious Nineteen: A Stephanie Plum Novel
author: Janet Evanovich
review_title: The Groundhog Day of Romance Novels
review_text:
There was a time when this series was fresh and ingenius. That ship has sailed.

These characters are stereotypical, two-dimensional people who do the same things in every single book. Lula eats, wears trashy clothes and shoots someone in the foot. Mooner smokes weed. Grandma Mazur goes to funerals and carries a gun in her purse. Somebody gets murdered and Stephanie finds the body. There is an explosion (shootout, robbery) on Stark Street. Ranger looks hot, tracks Stephanie and loans her cars while seeming to gain absolutely nothing from the relationship. Morelli and Stephanie have hot monkey sex. Stephanie's car explodes. Stephanie smells Ranger's soap. A skip talks to Lula and Stephanie at the front door, says they'll go inside and get ready to leave but runs out the back door while they're waiting.

Et cetera.

It seems that JE doesn't have a story arc for this series and keeps putting out new titles with the same plot in lieu of actually getting anywhere. It gives the impression that she doesn't know how to write anything else. The characters do not grow or develop. No one important gets sick, hurt or dies. Stephanie's hamster hasn't even died and those things are positively geriatric after three years! Stephanie stays in her one bedroom apartment and seems to have no aspirations to improve or change her life in any way. The Ranger/Morelli thing is ridiculous. I cannot imagine any two men would really stay in this stagnant situation ("Babe", "Cupcake") for YEARS with no resolution, no tension, no growth. Let alone the rest of the characters.

So the only possible explanation I could come up with is that this series is the book version of Groundhog Day. We wake up and read a Stephanie Plum book every day, thinking each time that the book will be new and different but realizing after a couple of paragraphs that we've done this before...

title: Notorious Nineteen: A Stephanie Plum Novel
author: Janet Evanovich
review_title: I'm done with these - boring boring boring.
review_text:
I was a fan of the Stephanie Plum books at first -- and kept up the enthusiasm for a long time. However, I'm finally done because apparently Evanovich is, too. Unlike other series with first rate continuing characters who grow, create interesting history, age, change, develop new relationships -- forget it with Stephanie Plum. Every book starts the same, has the exact same middle, and ends the same. Even for formula lit, this is a tremendous lack of imagination.

Grandma has become an annoying stereotype. Ranger? Morelli? Who cares anymore. If our protagonist had picked one a few books ago, that would have allowed her to move, allowed for creation of different plots and tensions, and some surprises left perhaps. Or bring on another man. Or woman. Anything really. Even Lula -- at first a great character -- has just become a bore.

My conclusion is that Evanovich is at heart a romance novelist (and this is everyone's choice but I don't read them) who got a huge hit on her hands going off the reservation with the clever One for the Money and has played it out beyond the end of the life of these characters. I read this one out of habit. But I won't make that mistake again. Evanovich just isn't able to delivery anything fresh.

review_text: I have been a Stephanie Plum fan forever but the last several books have been tired.  Notorious Nineteen is no exception.  I keep trying but Janet keeps putting out lackluster novels.  Perhaps it's time to retire Stephanie if she no longer cares enough to listen to her readers and put more effort into making Stephanie Plum novels what they once were.  Stephanie is whiny about her relationships with Ranger and Morelli.  Neither Ranger not Morelli have been fleshed out as characters.  In fact none of the characters have been fleshed out.  I hate to say it but if you're looking for a Stephanie Plum novel with some laughs this novel is not it.  I don't recommend purchasing it unless you are a die hard like me who refuses to give up on Stephanie or Janet.

author: Janet Evanovich
review_title: Better than the last couple of Plums
review_text: There are authors whose books I always buy, no matter what, Janet Evanovich's Stephanie Plum series is one of those. The last few in the series have been very disappointing, but Notorious Nineteen reminded me of the older Plum books. There was an actual storyline to it, an interesting mystery to be solved, and not as much silliness and improbable plots as in previous books (although it wouldn't be Stephanie without a bit of silliness). And there was a secondary storyline that was good as well. I get tired of the "is it Ranger or Morelli" decision to the point where I don't really care much about it. But I liked this one a lot.

review_text: Notorious Nineteen puts Stephanie Plum back into her thrilling role as a bumbling amateur detective who gets into dangerous situations that cause her to seriously question her lifestyle.  On the other hand, she enjoys the adrenaline rush provided by her "damsel-in-distress" escapades AND the two "knights-in-shiny-armor" who come to her rescue.  In this book, the focus is back on the realities of Stephanie's questionable job and her "loser" persona.  It's out of funeral parlors, onto the streets, and about the tough personal decisions she must make concerning her future.

review_text: This is a cringy read.Just because something is dark does not mean one must drag the reader through the muck. The first 100 pages is devoted to a young woman who remembers the murder of her family and yet tells us that she has lied about it, even though the flashbacks suggest otherwise; it makes no sense and the disconcerting portrayal of the MC just goes round and round without any clarity. And her brother Ben has some serious sexual issues that should not even be spoken of; unfortunately, Flynn insists on highlighting them. I didn't finish the story for these reasons and because the plot was so meaningless. Flashbacks included insignificant details, disturbing content, and repeated cycles of pointless dialogue.

title: Dark Places: A Novel
author: Gillian Flynn
review_text:
I was required to read this book as part of an assignment and can say honestly it was the most repulsive thing I've ever read, and I read Zombie by Joyce Carroll Oates. While Flynn is a skillful writer, the characters were utterly unsympathetic. There was not a single character to root for in this entire book. Was that by design? Also, there were a lot of plot twists which kept it interesting but they really added up to little more than a series of coincidences that strained suspension of disbelief. One or two, maybe...but there had to be at least ten coincidences that just happened to put all of the characters exactly where the author wanted them. That, to me, is lazy writing. And then, of course, there's the fact that this story's basis is a blatant rip off of the Robin Hills murders from West Memphis, Arkansas. (Misunderstood angry teen into devil worship and metal music regarded as the freak in town responsible for heinous murders...only this time there are no redeeming qualities to this teen unlike the real life teens in West Memphis.)

But the biggest beef (pun intended) I have with this book is the gratuitous violence and gore. It literally made me want to put the book down, but I couldn't because it was assigned reading. The book includes child abuse, spousal abuse, drug abuse, animal abuse and killing, sexual molestation, incest (yes, the teen even cops a feel of his MOM in bed), neglect, and let's not forget the actual axe murder, the shotgun murder, and the strangulation of a child. OH - and then there's the assassin/murder for hire plot thrown in for good measure. It was just too much, especially when you're not really rooting for any of the characters to begin with.

Flynn has the writing down pat. The structure was great, she kept the pages turning, and she writes really well. It's just a shame that she can't seem to create a decent character that a reader can root for to save her life. If I hadn't been forced to read this book, I never would have finished it.

title: Dark Places: A Novel
author: Gillian Flynn
review_text:
Like everyone else, I loved Gone Girl so much I thought I'd like this book. I read so many mixed reviews that I decided to just buy it. Right off the bat I was upset. Chapter one wasn't engaging because Libby comes on so strong and unlike any character I have ever encountered. I kept reading anyway and the book became so intriguing I couldn't put it down.

Libby isn't your average character, she's weird and matter-of-fact. I read so much criticism of her that I went in assuming I wouldn't like her but I ended up fascinated by her. I think many reviews are unfair to her and I think it's because she doesn't fit how we want our fictional characters to be. We want them to conquer their demons and rise above it all and she doesn't. There's no problem with that, in fact most authors play it up, but not this one. Libby is so real that I think it makes some people uncomfortable. Libby isn't all butterflies and rainbows, she is very dark and wounded.

What I think is putting people off about this book is that we like our stories to either be realistic and relatable or complete fiction. There is no fine line between the two in this book. Psychologically speaking, Libby is exactly what a real victim would be like; Gillian Flynn definitely did her homework with her. Libby victimizes herself, she engages in risky behavior, she is bitter and doesn't trust anyone, she is paranoid and entitled. Once readers get used to how raw this character is, the author changes it up by adding so many unrealistic coincidences. It's confusing to the reader because one minute you feel like you're getting a real-life look into the life of a victim and the next you're saying "yeah right". I like what she did with Libby, but I don't like what she did with the story. I was so engaged in the book, read it in one day, then I got to the end and felt like I had been seriously ripped off. This isn't a book to expect a happy ending from and that's obvious, but when everything starts coming together at the end, rather than being a place where loose ends are tied up, it is a jumble of totally unbelievable circumstances.

I am so disappointed with this book because I feel like a sucker. I started to think other readers were being too harsh because they didn't like the character and I was able to look past her. Yes, the animal cruelty is a bit queasy, but the overall the story was so fascinating that I just couldn't turn my Kindle off (I sat next to an outlet charging it just to finish this book). It was so incredibly engaging then it just does a 180 and takes a nose dive into unrealistic. I don't recommend it because even if you can look beyond a character who is strange and look past the graphic scenes, by the time you finish the book you feel like you have been totally duped.

title: Dark Places: A Novel
author: Gillian Flynn
review_text: ****SPOILERS****  I have to say in my history of reading books, this is one of the few I couldn't bring myself to finish. I looked up the ending, just to see if I wanted to finish it, and nope - glad I didn't finish it. I understand the characters growing up in the circumstances they did, brought about a lot of their demeanor; but the repetitive exposure to their "issues" got old real quick. Not a lot of action or character development. I couldn't find myself liking the main character (I actually hated her). She was lazy, rude, ungrateful, and most of all LAZY. I understand your whole family is slaughtered, that would screw anyone up - but there were no salvageable qualities to her- none. The mystery being the MOM hired someone to kill her? Really? At the very least Ben's girlfriend should have been the designated murderer, that would have been more believable. Hiring a hit man is expensive, they are so poor they can't afford bologna - now she has thousands to hire a hit-man?  I loved Gone Girl - this was just bad. Glad I only paid $3.

title: Dark Places: A Novel
author: Gillian Flynn
review_title: A failed second novel. Happens even to good writers
review_text: Probably the weakest Gillian Flynn's novel, not on a par with the "Sharp Objects" and "Gone Girl". I saw some reviewers complain about characters being non sympathetic. This is true - but they do not have to be. In fact, Libby, if anything, is an interesting character and in spite of her flaws, kind of grows on you. Which goes to the writer's credit - to be able to evoke sympathy for someone who is not easy to like. I think the weakness lies more in the portrayal of her brother - you can feel what kind of person he is, but not his motivations. Basically, he is not a shallow person, but shallowly described person. The same goes for his girlfriend Diondra and pretty much everyone else except Libby. This where I think Flynn has failed as a writer - she did not go deep enough under the surface to make the characters speak for themselves (or did not speak for them), and since there are too many pages dedicated to characters other than Libby, the novel fails to move (swim, fly, or even steadily crawl).

author: Gillian Flynn
review_text: Having seen, but not read, Gone Girl, I downloaded this book as my written introduction to Gillian Flynn. She is a very visual writer, which, I suppose makes screenplays easier to write. I understand that a film of this book is being planned, with Charlize Theron as the protagonist. Absurd casting, but that's not what this review is about. The theme of a young survivor of a massacred family was filmed years ago with Meg Ryan and Dennis Quaid in Flesh and Bone, a most underrated movie. The protagonist of Dark Places is far more damaged, and because of the damage, self-destructive. But, midway, she becomes something of a Nancy Drew, as she's drawn into reliving the night of the massacre and the question of who-done-it. The book is absorbing, but the resolution was pretty contrived. I expected more.

title: Harry Potter Paperback Box Set (Books 1-7)
author: J.K. Rowling
review_title: If I Had A Chance To Publish This, I Wouldn't!
review_text:
As an adult author reading this book, I hereby declare it garbage! The story is slower than molasses and there is absolutely zero action. At no point in the first two and half of the third book, did I feel like the characters were in danger. Not once! Nor was there any point where I wanted to come back and read more. I forced myself to finish the second one and I'm not going to force myself to finish the third.

Kids are smart. Buy them a good story to read like: Fablehaven or The Ranger's Apprentice or Pendragon: Traveler's Through Time. Those are good books. Harry Potter? Piece of crap! I seriously don't get how people like the books. They have no action and are slow. The two things that kills a story.

The fact I don't want to keep reading should be enough of a review. Save your money and buy/read a book that is actually good.

Fine, the one good thing about the books is the world. She did a good job building the world but the story is terrible. Which seriously makes me question peoples judgments on what is a good book. Because these are not!

The Harry Potter books are just a really wordy Magic Tree House.

title: Harry Potter Paperback Box Set (Books 1-7)
author: J.K. Rowling
review_text:
I, like others before me, was critical and kept away from the Harry Potter series. Wizards, witches, and magic? Please.

I could not have been more wrong.

I was taught, growing up, how wicked the books were, and that I had no business reading them. So I went along, wondering how ink and paper could shake so many people. However, I was curious, and that curiosity became overpowering to the point that I acted rashly. A friend said she had five of the seven, and I could borrow them. Curiosity won, though I was slightly terrified of what I was about to do. I'm so glad I did!! I love these books, and can't wait to read the last two! The way she writes is captivating, and not over your head or down at you. She brings you as long, and you see and feel everything the characters do. I was shaking the last book as I read, audibly saying "someone do something to Umbridge, or I will!" completely clueless of how I was going to do that. That is what great writing does. I would recommend this series to anyone and everyone.

title: The Short Drop (Gibson Vaughn)
author: Matthew FitzSimmons
review_text: The first two thirds of the book were engaging and suspenseful despite treading familiar territory. Then the plot started to deteriorate into a series of increasingly far-fetched or downright absurd events and explanations. It looked like the author took the elements from other successful novels (The Girl with a Dragon Tattoo, Tell No One, Absolute Power) but failed to fuse them into a coherent whole. The good characters didn’t have enough depth (no matter how much backstory was created for them), and the villains were so omnipotent and larger-than-life but then were miraculously and conveniently defeated. Two characters (Tinsley and George Abe) disappeared by the end of the book without much explanation. The core mystery turned out to be one of the worst clichés in fiction and thus was easy to figure out. It’s too bad because the book had a potential.

title: The Short Drop (Gibson Vaughn)
author: Matthew FitzSimmons
review_text: So that’s something, I suppose. Rather mediocre, overall. Characters are one-dimensional and boring. The dialogue contains some of the cheesiest stuff I’ve ever read (particularly during the “tense” stand-offs); rolling my eyes every three seconds at the dramatic, asinine exchanges really takes me out of the moment. The general plot is acceptable, but the initial development is heavily centered on hacking (Gibson is basically Lisbeth with a penis and Gerber), and that entire aspect is utterly abandoned halfway through the novel and never resurfaces. If your protagonist is developed around a superior skill set, you kind of need to keep that going. I mean, you don’t see Katniss chucking her bow into a volcano halfway into the Hunger Games and spending the last half bludgeoning everyone to death with an entrenchment tool, do you? No. Just, eh. It’s a first novel, and it’s decent enough. Probably won’t read anything else in the series, as there’s no real emotion there, but I do think the author has potential.

title: The Short Drop (Gibson Vaughn)
author: Matthew FitzSimmons
review_text: I disagree with most of the other reviewers. I found this novel a rather unpleasant read. The author shows acceptable narrative skills, but the plot is flawed, put together in rough blocks joint by heavy seams. Some characters behave very strangely according to perfectly well known human behavior, as verified every day in our experience. Without giving away too much, I'd like to say how strange it seemed to me that after receiving a life-threatening gunshot wound, an intelligent man chooses to disappear in the woods instead of remaining in a vehicle driven by a friend who's taking him to the nearest hospital. I stopped reading a few pages after that. Obviously the author didn't need that character around in the final part of the novel, and quickly got rid of him. A few chapters before this weird twist in the tale, the talented and experienced boss of a private security firm is abducted by villains because he didn't bother to ask for IDs when his car was stopped, and also didn't have a gun within reach when he already knew that serious trouble was very possible. Also, all characters are rather generic and undeveloped: hard-working, smart, capable men and even stronger, ruthless or unselfish women. Really? What does it take to be a woman in a novel nowadays? I'll be happy to give a five-star review to the first writer willing to describe the emotions of a woman who's not a beauty queen, likes to eat chips with medium hot salsa, and visits her local Walmart at least once a week. I agree that as an author you can do whatever you want with your characters, but you should dig a little deeper, and make them three-dimensional just like real human beings, if you want to stir passion in your readers.

SPOILER ALERT:  The direction of the plot critical to the sequence of events leading to the end of the story depended on a highly intelligent, responsible, hyper-cautious character getting up from a table in a restaurant and LEAVING HER LAPTOP ON THE TABLE while she went to the bathroom enabling the hero to hack into it.  I was absolutely blown away.  Nobody would be stupid enough to do this....a 10 year old knows better.  And the plot went downhill from there, as if this was the first step in the writer's completely running out of steam.  The careless, ineffective wrap-up of the plot/subplots was just plain dreadful.

title: The Good Girl: A Thrilling Suspense Novel from the author of Local Woman Missing
author: Mary Kubica
review_text:
I struggled with this review. But I felt that I had to be honest about the way I was jarred out of this story several times. And really, the casual racist stereotypes were unnecessary for what would have been an interesting thriller.
I started this story and was pulled in. A mother learns that her daughter has not shown up for work and we are introduced to a wealthy family in Chicago. The author, through alternate voices, introduces us early to Mia's kidnapping and readers then follow the story from several different points of view. So where did the author first lose me? SPOILERS TO FOLLOW.....Early in the novel, we have met many characters, none of whom are given much in the way of physical descriptions- and quite frankly they don't need it. The reader is not helped to know the race of the doctor, or random police officer. But when the kidnapper refers to another criminal member as the "blackest man he ever saw," I pondered whether that was something useful I would need later. This was one of the few references so far to race or color and so I thought there must be a story related purpose to it. I continued reading, still intrigued by the glimpses I was getting of the "good" guys and "bad" guys.

Then came this paragraph on page 203 "In Chicago, Gary Indiana, isn't spoken of highly. It is a hell hole. Much of the population is poor. There is a large African-American population." Hmm. I wonder "Is this true?" And that is a problem, because it really had no bearing on the scene and what was upcoming. It mattered zero for any character or dialogue to follow. But it kept popping up in my mind. And now with the early reference to the color of that criminal, my mind was completely OUT OF THE STORY. So now I have to contemplate questions about the author and her personal history-none of which I would have done if not for these awful inserts. But I really wanted to see how the story would end. Because it was intriguing. And then comes this at the end. SPOILERS!!!
" I think back to that September day, as I walked into the gloomy bar. It was a beautiful Indian summer day but inside the bar it was dark, nearly vacant, as a bar should be at two in the afternoon, just a handful of patrons sitting at their own tables, drowning their sorrows in straight bourbon and whiskey shots. The place was a hole in the wall, the corner unit of a brick building with graffiti on their side. Music played in the background, Johnny Cash. I wasn't in my own neighborhood, but farther south and west, in Lawndale, and as I looked around the bar, I saw that I was the only one who was white."
The author then goes on to describe Dalmar as black as the blubbery skin of a whale. Sigh. Not only did this criminal have skin like a blubbery whale, but he frequents an all black bar where Johnny Cash is the music of choice. REALLY? And more importantly WHY?
I love reading. I love mysteries, science fiction, horror, really most genres. But I am really tired of authors describing black characters only when a criminal or servant is needed.
I lost sight of the world she was building, because her casually placed stereotypes made me start wondering if they were necessary or something else. And once you are out of the suspense of a thriller, it is hard to return or even really appreciate the suspense building an author was doing.
So for me, a one star.

title: The Good Girl: A Thrilling Suspense Novel from the author of Local Woman Missing
author: Mary Kubica
review_title: The best thing about this novel is the cool looking cover
review_text:
Generally, with a novel, I’m good for one, big suspension of disbelief.
Faerie-Folk live among us? I’m in. But if halfway through the story, the gentle faeries suddenly start feasting on human flesh, I’m putting the book down.
A novel is a self-contained world and it drives me crazy when writers create consistent, definable characters and then make them act in ways they never would in order to serve the plot.
And so it is with The Good Girl.
Mia Dennett, an artist and teacher, is kidnapped and held for months in a secluded cabin. Told in alternating viewpoints from her abductor, her mom, and the detective on the case, the book starts out with plenty of potential, but quickly devolves into a bunch of silly characters who do things so outside their natures, so outside anyone's nature, they aren’t even believable as human beings let alone the people we’ve been given until that point.
The plot is clichéd and sloppy and the writing itself is completely forgettable.

author: Mary Kubica
review_title: I wish this story had been told from a different point of view
review_text:
Picked this up at an airport because I forgot my beach book and was looking for something suspenseful. Boy, was this not it.

It never really felt like anyone was in danger. The characters (particularly the ones narrating) seemed a bit shallow, more like charicatures than real people. I know these people are supposed to be somewhat fake, but when you see the same typical behavior and the same reactions hashed out over and over with no additional depth or explanation you haven't heard before, it gets tiring. The plot felt slow, and that's fine if I'm reading a slow book where it's all about how the characters are developing and changing. But this wasn't it. There wasn't anything in the plot to grab me, and there was nothing in the characters to do it either. It was just... okay. If I wasn't at a beach with literally nothing better to do, I'm not sure I would have read the whole thing.

I cringed at the love interest, once I realized what was going on, because it felt so unnatural and weird - and I don't think it was deliberate. There is a bizarre and strong political undercurrent along a major plot point that really bothered me, oversimplifying the struggle and consequences of a major decision into a simple "good vs. evil" situation. The twist comes so late on and with so little foreshadowing that it feels like it was never truly meant to be there.

I wish this story had been told from Mia's point of view and hers only, because honestly, hers was the only perspective I wanted to hear in this book. Ironically, it's also the only perspective deliberately left out.

Giving this a star more than it probably deserves because I did finish the book and although it is very, very low on my list of books, it's not the worst thing I've read and it did pass the time. But I kind of wish I'd picked something else at that airport stand instead.

title: The Good Girl: A Thrilling Suspense Novel from the author of Local Woman Missing
author: Mary Kubica
review_text:
I'm going to start by saying I did not like this book. The Good Girl is about a girl named Mia who goes to a bar one night to meet her boyfriend for dinner. Her boyfriend never shows up, so she ends up leaving with another man named Colin. Little does she know, Colin is not the nice man she thought he was. He was paid to kidnap her, but instead of bringing her to his boss, he drives her to a remote cabin in the cold outskirts of Wisconsin.

The Good Girl was told in three points of view over two time periods. We hear from Mia in the past ("before") and present ("after"), her mother Eve before and after, and the deceptive Gabe before and after. I'm finding that I don't like books that do this as much as I do having one POV. I think it can be done right, but more often than not, when it's done in a thriller it takes away from the suspense and mystery, because you already know what each character is doing and thinking. If the story was told just from Eve or Gabe's point of view, there would have been a lot more opportunities for reveals and surprises.

Almost everything in this book fell flat for me. Everything was really predictable, I didn't connect to any of the characters, and I didn't care what happened to them. The blurb on the book led me to believe that there would be a lot of suspense in this book, and to me, there was none. I honestly was bored throughout most of it, and there were a number of times I almost walked away from it and marked it as DNF. Additionally, I've see other reviewers mentioning that they felt it was fast-paced, and I didn't feel the same way. It could be because I was so bored, but I felt like the story dragged on, and considering the book was only ~350 pages, that's not a great thing.

Another thing I did like (that had no impact on my review) was that a lot of the story was set in Chicago. I live in Chicago, so I loved being able to understand references and locations!

Anyway, I can't say I'd recommend this book, though the book has decent reviews, so I'm clearly in the minority here. I have a few other books by Mary Kubica on my list, and I'll have to do some more research to decide if I still want to read them. The one thing I will give her is that she's a fine writer. I had no issue with her writing, just issue with the way it was executed (POVs) and the storyline.

title: The Girl on the Train: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Paula Hawkins
review_text:
THE GIRL ON THE TRAIN by Paula Hawkins was a big disappointment for me. I finally got around to reading it - to see what all the hype was about and it left me a bit annoyed that I spent that much time with it.
It is often compared to GONE GIRL which I also found to be an annoying read.
The characters were boring, nasty, selfish, narcissistic, full of lies - stupid, really. Rachel was a bumbling alcoholic. Megan, Anna, Tom and Scott were unlikeable and had no real personalities.
Scott and Tom were closet abusers and always on the brink of violence. The scenes with Tom and daughter, Evie, were creepy and gross.
I didn’t even like Rachel’s roommate/landlady. She came across (to me) as more of an enabler than a kind friend.
There was tension, but it was lost with all the focus on the abhorrent characters.
I did like the ‘rhythm’ of the train.
*One star and I consider that generous.

review_text:
The book was my Kindle First selection, and I’m glad I picked it! It’s well-written and suspenseful. Both the heroine and hero are likable and their characters well-developed. The story is told from both POVs plus the POVs of some secondary characters. I’m impressed the author could pull this off without confusing me!

The description of Sara/Olivia’s trauma is well done. I ached for her. I rooted for her. I wanted her to be whole again. And the sex scene between her and Cole is so raw and intense, it blew me away. Really masterful!

The only flaw with the story is the cop’s involvement. He set everything in motion and yet never warned Olivia. I kept waiting for him to fess up, but he never did. Plus, he put his daughter in danger.

Nevertheless, I was lured in and enjoyed it.

title: Nora Roberts Land (Dare Valley Series, Book 1)

review_title: An ode to Nora Roberts and La Perla
review_text: So the heroine, her self esteem at an all-time low after a divorce from her cheating husband, moves back home from the big city in order to prove that "Nora Roberts Land" exists. That is, that she can find Mr. Perfect within three months, in order to write a story about it. (Not to mention that her editor at the newspaper/magazine/whatever she is working for is actually willing to pay her for this.) In order to achieve her goal, she wears a selection of La Perla bustiers and dates every single man within reach apart from the one she feels attracted to. Yes. Sigh. And it goes on and on and on, with various obstacles and a few bad guys thrown in, which keep the heroine and the hero from getting into each other's pants. Will they get over it all and FINALLY live happily ever after? If you have nothing at all to do and are very bored and have run out of other free Kindle books, go ahead and find out. Otherwise, just skip this one.

review_text:
I don't know what Nora was smoking to allow her name to be put onto this childish story. Ok, her name is in the title and on every second page, but that alone can't be worth endorsing an author who is mediocre at best. I had to force myself to finish the book, hoping I would find the reason for those stars that were given by other reviewers, but no luck. Need an example of the credible characters? The sister of the heroine, Jill, had a crush on a boy in high school. He however chose a different girl and she never got over the rejection. After his return into their hometown, she now rejects him. Their common best friend dies, likely murder. Jill has a very emotional fight with her sister and is upset. So what are her thoughts as she runs into her former high school crush? Here they are: "But even though she was pissed at him, she still wanted to lather herself like body butter against that long, hard frame."
I gave two stars since there were no typos and the book was free, but I'll gladly invest into the real NR again.

Oh, how I wanted to like this book. After finishing all the books in Ava Miles' "Dare River" series in about a week, I rushed to find anything else she'd written. Those books were great - charming characters, great suspense, lovely story telling. I can't wait to read the next one. "Nora Roberts Land, on the other hand, was disappointing. My main complaint is the characters. They are not likeable in the least and their connection just wasn't believable. Meredith seems to have the depth of a puddle and spends most of the time talking about her underwear. Tanner isn't at all believable as a war journalist and has the least attractive personality I've ever read.

I never give up on books, but just couldn't get myself to finish this one. I will be looking forward to the next installment in the Dare River series, but will give a pass on the rest of Dare Valley.

title: The Atlantis Gene: A Thriller (The Origin Mystery, Book 1)
author: A.G. Riddle
review_text:
So the idea for this book seemed interesting enough that I had to read it. I also figured that because it was self-published and a best-seller, there had to be something to it. I was wrong.

The worst thing about this book is the writing. It's boring, unimaginative, and lacks any style. None of the settings are well described. It's impossible to visualize either the characters, where they are, or what they are doing. Words are re-used constantly. For example, Riddle uses the phrase "brain wiring" to describe anything dealing with the mind -- not just a lot, but literally every single time he has to refer to the concept. That he puts this repetitive and cliche phrasing in the mouth of someone who is supposed to be a researcher makes it even worse. Words and phrases are recycled within sentences of each other. The book lacks basic editing. And there is simply no creativity in how he describes things in the book which should, in theory, be pretty interesting. Almost all the descriptions in the book relies on cliches. At one point he describes something as looking like it's from "Star Trek" -- nothing more. It's like, really? Why did you want to write science fiction if you didn't want to describe anything in a new and interesting way? The dialog is horrible. The characters, even after their plot-twists, are shallow and uninteresting. It's just bad writing. The action in the book, of which there is a lot, is written in such a way that it lacks suspense, believability, or even the ability to visualize what's going on.

And the plot? Well, all those interesting elements -- human evolution, autism, Atlantis, even 9/11 -- none of them are actually welded together in a compelling way. And that was the main selling point of the book, really, the promise of seeing these disparate elements united in a thriller. Well, it just doesn't happen. They're just jumbled together with only the flimsiest of plot elements holding them together. This actually would be totally fine if it were a well-written page-turner, where the ride is good enough that you don't mind if the plot is Swiss cheese, but the writing is the worst part about the book.

If you buy this book, you'll be lucky if you actually finish it, and if you do finish it, you'll regret you had.

review_text:

However, the execution leaves a lot to be desired - the premise makes no logical sense, pretty much all the action and Bad Guy Motivation in the movie makes no real sense, the characters are 2-dimensional cartoons and the writing is extremely disjointed. People just run around for no reason, people are working together and also trying to destroy each other for no reason, people are attacking other people for no logical reason. There is a whole lot happening, and most of it makes absolutely NO sense whatsoever. This is the book Dan Brown might have written when he was 14 years old.

Oh, and any book which uses the word "ex-Patriot" to refer to a someone working in a foreign country simply should NOT be published.

I have no idea how this book gets so many 5 stars. I can only imagine most of them are the author's friends or he has hired some PR firm to boost up his reviews - if anything, this demonstrates to me how badly broken the Amazon review system is.

review_title: A sci-f/adventure screenplay pretending to be a novel
review_text:
Even though Mr. Riddle is a best selling author, I could not finish this book: had already put it down multiple times due to its rich frosting of cliches, characters straight out of Roger Moore's over-the-top 007 movies and poorly executed plot devices, It reads like a novelized version of a screenplay for a B sci-fi movie blessed with the budget of an A. I'd rather spend 2 hours watching the movie which would be immeasurably preferable to a dozen more groaning through the prose and the frosting.

I give The Atlantis Gene 2 stars because the author certainly has an imagination, even if his writing and plotting skills are not its equal.

title: The Atlantis Gene: A Thriller (The Origin Mystery, Book 1)
author: A.G. Riddle
review_text: My overall judgement of this book is that it was poorly written.  It is evidently a first novel and it appears to be self published. Clearly, it did not benefit from a good editor.  The story jumps from place to place, and from time to time making it difficult to follow the storyline. The author throws in gratuitous statements evidently meant for dramatic impact, but with no antecedent justifying the comment. I forced myself to finish this book but not with any joy or anticipation of what the next page held.  I was so disappointed in The Atlantis Gene it is one of the few books I've ever thrown away.  In fact I also threw away the sequel novel. I will not recommend this book to anyone.

title: The Atlantis Gene: A Thriller (The Origin Mystery, Book 1)
author: A.G. Riddle
review_text: My tastes tend to be in line with those of other reviewers, but this is a major exception.  I will first admit to not being able to finish it; I ran out of patience about half way through.  A little voice in my head kept reminding me that I read for pleasure, and none was forthcoming in The Atlantis Gene.  Off my device, darn book!  The writing is fine, the characters are okay, but the plot is...  annoyingly convoluted.  It may be that readers with a dogged determination to finish it are eventually rewarded, but I simply didn't think it was worth the effort.  With all due respect to the author, this just wasn't my cup of tea.
