title: The Atlantis Gene: A Thriller (The Origin Mystery, Book 1)
author: A.G. Riddle
review_text:
Upfront: I did not read this book, I listened to it, which may have had an impact on my view.

The book was ok. The story is interesting enough, although there were a couple points where I got lost in the flashbacks and rants about 9/11 conspiracy theories. I wish the characters were better developed and diverse. The women are weak and fragile, there to be taken care of and fall in love. Kate is a scientist, but painted as little more than a mother figure to care for the young and sick, who needs the male characters to protect her. If she is separated from her protector, another promptly swoops in. Every once in a while she has a line where you are abruptly reminded that she has a mind and is smarter than all the male characters, leaving you feeling that her character is too unrealistic to plausibly exist (even in a fiction book).
It did not help that the narrator uses a weak almost flippant tone whenever a woman speaks.

subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Barbara Nickless
review_title: Give It a Chance, but Don't Expect a Barnburner
review_text:
"Blood on the Tracks" is an interesting view of the impact of active military service in an active war zone on the mental state of an individual Marine following active duty and a return to civilian life. Framing the story in this way is interesting, but it slows the plot quite a bit.

Although the plot is predictable in the sense that the good guys eventually will prevail, there are some interesting twists along the way. The mood of the book swings back and forth between "dark" due to the psychological aspects and "suspenseful" due to the "who done it" type of novel. Likewise, the pace of the book is slowed about by the psychological angle, but there is sufficient suspense along the way, particularly toward the end. Given the framework of the book, the characters tend to be one-dimensional, but not to the point of creating significant problems for the plot.

I enjoyed "Blood on the Tracks," and I likely will give Barbara Nickless another read, but this one did not knock my socks off.

review_text: Decent story. Well written but two major flaws. First these people did not live in a bubble. Despite Nazi's efforts people knew how  rapidly Germany was losing the war. That is never factored into the story.. Secondly spare me the head in the sand politics in the end notes. The Nazis suppressed the church, controlled the media, confiscated guns, set aside the constitution, attacked dissidents in public, stifled free speech and used violence to disrupt opponent's rallies. Clearly these are all actions advocated by the US Left today. Ignoring all that & implying a handful of bigots marching non violently makes the right modern Nazis is the height of naivete and intellectual dishonesty. Would have given this 3  stars without the author's notes.

review_text:
Shame on you for advertising this book as historical fiction when in reality you duped people into paying to read your political rant.
Everyone has been granted the freedom of speech and the freedom of press in the USA. What Hawker fails to understand is ,if she wrote her political comments in her book in Nazi Germany she would have been executed.
I am embarrassed to say I suggested this book for club. I truly hope nobody believes I share any of the author's political opinions.
The story itself was terrible. I don't see how anyone could possibly describe this book as a romance; an ex-friar answers an ad and agreed to a marriage of convenience. Sex is not part of the convenience. The ex-friar is expected to support the woman and her children. Through out the book the wife is cold and commanding. I just didn't see the love.
Hawker gives the true story behind the book in her comments at the end of the book. She should have cut the rhetoric and stuck with the short version of the story.

My thoughts are I'm reading your book to be entertained much as I go to a concert to hear an entertainer, I don't want to know what your political beliefs are in any of these situations. It's not the place for it. I'm paying to be entertained for the things you are good at and not anything else. If you feel so strongly about how poor this President is doing his job then I suggest you go and get involved in your local government where you might actually be able to get something done. review_text:
(SPOILER ALERT!)

It has been a very long time since I have detested a "heroine" as much as I did Hannah. (I started this review and frothed at the mouth over it until I couldn't stand it either, so I'm redoing it to be more temperate in my opinion of the book.)

I nearly deleted it from my Kindle rather early on, so annoyed was I at Hannah and her incessant whine, her anger at the whole world which wasn't concentrating on HER nearly enough to satisfy her, etc. But now, having slogged my way through it to the end, I'm actually glad I finished it if only because I felt the author may have finally become tired of Hannah, too.

This woman, interested only in her own feelings of dissatisfaction with the world which refuses to share her opinions on how she should be catered to and appreciated as she whines, snarls, complains, etc., suddenly within a few pages of the blessed end of the book, becomes a human being! She treats her sisters with respect, quits running away from any semblance of responsibility, and, after one more jab at her dying mother, settles down to being pleasant.

Bah.

title: The Ragged Edge of Night
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Libbie Hawker
review_text:
A sucker for WWII tales, I really wanted to like this book. But it strained credulity, for me at least. I understand that the main character Anton was a real person and did his bit against the Nazis. Bravo! But the degree to which the fictionalized Anton found support for his resistance activities just doesn't ring true. A once fluent German speaker and German studies wonk (without a drop of German blood myself), I was an exchange student in West Germany just 20 years after the war ended, long enough for Germans to learn everything about Hitler's crimes, long enough to realize that sincere atonement was required if their country was to become a respected player in the international community. Yet I regularly encountered Hitler worship, covering a wide socioeconomic and geographic range (I lived with two different families, one blue-collar, one professional, in two widely separated corners of the country). In one of those locations, a former SS officer lived across the street and was regarded with enormous respect. Yikes. Guy gave me the creeps. I find it hard to believe that Anton so openly shared with fellow villagers his revulsion for the Nazis without being promptly betrayed and landing in some SS torture chamber.

Second quibble: inconsistencies in voice. I prefer third person narration to the current fad of first-person storytelling. But this third-person narration often confused me. The storytelling would suddenly switch to the first person, without the usual italics indicating Anton's internal monologue. Occasionally, I would eventually realize that the "we" in the narrative was not Anton at all, but the otherwise invisible narrator. Except the storyteller seemed to be, not the author, but some undeclared German entity of WWII vintage. The occasional single sentence might begin with a third-person discussion of the characters' exploits, but conclude with some comment about the need to rectify the evils in "our country" or to take "our government" to task for its sins.

After reading the author's comments at the end of the book, I figured she was equating Nazi Germany with the current U.S. Really? I had already tired of the preachy tone of the book, especially since little effort was made to show us the face of Nazi evil. Don't preach about the bad guys; show us how awful the bad guys are by what they do. Goodness knows, there's no shortage of examples to resurrect. Yes, we heard about the earlier (off-screen) gassing of the mentally impaired children in Anton's care and there was one effective anecdote where Anton realized that this ghastly mission pained one of the German soldiers marching the children away. Anton deduced that the soldier was forced to choose between the safety of his own family and the lives of these doomed children. Nice touch. But the only Nazi we actually got to know, the village gauleiter, was lackluster. His worst apparent crime was using his office to extort sex from the village women (again, the reader is told about it, after the fact, never sees the creep grabbing ass). What's more, the gauleiter's powers of persuasion weren't sufficient to seduce Anton's wife. Yes, Anton feared dire consequences for her, but they never transpired.

Another quibble: by 1945, was there really any village in Germany that had not been bombed to smithereens? The remote, rural one I lived in still had plenty of shell holes 20 years later. Yet Anton's village remains amazingly unscarred. Somehow the villagers all seem to have enough to eat and barter with. Even Anton's sister in much-bombed Stuttgart appears to have no trouble sheltering and feeding Anton's wife and three stepchildren. Really? In the 1960s, a common joke among West Germans was to point to a fat person and giggle, "DWW," short for German Economic Miracle. This relates to the era, beginning in the late war years and stretching into the 1950s, when Germans were emaciated from never having enough to eat. Hard to grow food on bombed out soil. Hard to transport food on shell-blasted roads and rail lines. Hard to buy food when you have no job. By the 1960s, things were finally changing for the better and plumpness was a sign of success.

Oy. So much potential for this book. But I was so disappointed.

review_text:
Historical fiction about Germany in an intentionally allegorical style perhaps meant to reflect trending current American events. Fear of foreigners, racial integrity and purity at all costs, moral indifference to infirmity and hardship, making a country great and dominant without regard to good and evil. The means do not and never will justify such horrific goals. We owe it to ourselves and to the world to learn from this dark moment in history and not to repeat the sins of our fore-bearers.
The inhumanity of the nazis is beyond the scope of belief, but such is the hunger for power that leads to an evil beyond comprehension.
I found this to be a moving and well written story, well worth reading.

But I skimmed quite a bit of this just to be through with it.  It was so far fetched with him figuring out what had happened and why just sitting in a motel room.  And it was so ridiculous that while they were going to all these places where he could just look at something and see all these things that everyone else had missed, the person from their group who was kidnapped was only mentioned from time to time almost as an after thought.  David Baldacci is one of my favorite authors and I hope he will get back to the writing style I have enjoyed for so many years until this one.

title: The Last Mile (Amos Decker Book 2)
author: David Baldacci
review_text:
I really enjoyed the first Memory Man book - I thought it was well written with a unique plot and good characters. This book is basically the opposite.

I won't get into major spoilers, but a semi-major plot point revolves on someone being able to sabotage a car so that it breaks down in a very specific location. What? Some of the characters come and go, are mean or nice without explanation and generally are annoying. And the "main" piece of evidence that everyone is searching for is rather unbelievable. Oh, and it's hard to get a sense of the time frame the book takes place over, but the main character losses like 50 pounds...in two weeks? Or three?

Fiction often requires the suspension of disbelief, but that is usually in regards to things like superpowers, time travel, etc. I don't think it should apply to the basic way 99% of people act and behave.

title: The Last Mile (Amos Decker Book 2)
author: David Baldacci
review_text:
This is the second of the Amos Decker series. In order to read it clearly, it is helpful to read the first, Memory Man as it explains Amos' condition.
The characters are developed to a certain degree; Amos more complex as he is the lead character. The story centers around Melvin Mars, a convicted murderer who is set free at the last moment from death row because of a confession from someone else, another convicted murderer on another state's death row. Decker is part of a special FBI task force who is looking into the case. Decker and Mars have things in common and that develops their relationship. Decker's extraordinary memory and ability to put together things others cannot moves the book along well, but some of the turns are rather obvious and the "mole" is some what obvious when one has read and seen many mysteries. It is a good mystery read and I like the characters so will look forward to a next book in the series.

review_text:
Just listened to the audio version of this. May be the worst Grisham book I have read or listened to. Making an abridged version of this book would be a piece of cake because at least 25% of the book is apparently just filler to hit a page count. Very slow moving, especially the first 2/3's of the book. Kept waiting for it to get better; it never did. There was a lot of repetition; like the story of the two murders that set the whole thing off. I think that was told in detail at least twice. And things like were inserted that were never touched again later in the book like the mutual interest between Lacy and a physical therapist.

Just a very disappointing book. If you are looking for a Grisham work to read or listen to, I would pass on this one.

author: Jonathan Stone
review_text:
What seemed like an interesting idea ended up bogged down by the writing style. The author loves fractured sentences. Yes, three word sentences are great to break up a paragraph, but too many paragraphs of three word sentences is disconcerting.

Also, calling this a thriller is wrong. Too many chapters ramble on about intent. The author tries too hard to "enter" into various character's thoughts. In truth, with proper editing, this might have been a good novella.

I read this is optioned for a movie. Yep, strip out the nonsense and it will be a straight to streaming flick.

However...this author wrote like he loved the sight of his own words and couldn't quite get enough of them onto the page. Blah blah blah....lots of information that, in my opinion, lent nothing to the story. I seriously doubted that the main characters - in the situation they found themselves - would have spent so much time in deep thought about....stuff.

Maybe it's just me.

While the basic story was interesting, I kept thinking...Naw. This ain't happenin'! Just not terribly believable for ME, anyway.

I think I'll stick with my non-fiction books for the time being, anyway.

Who would I recommend this book to? No one I can think of.

It got to the point that I was speed reading through the book to avoid the superfluous prose. And yet, the story was interesting. title: Moving Day: A Thriller
author: Jonathan Stone
review_title: Should probably have been a Novella
review_text:
Jonathon Stone's "Moving Day" has some issues and most of them could have been solved by making it shorter. Initially, it started out intriguing seeing the premise of the primary antagonist, until it is revealed that the first character shown is actually the protagonist. Nick, the antagonist, was the most interesting character to me and could have had more time spent on him. |

The main problem with this novel is Stone and his parallel narratives into Peke, the protagonist's, past. Consecutive pages were spent on his childhood, and would have been more effective if they were condensed and succinct, instead of continuing to trail on. It seemed to me that around 1/3 of this book was talking about his past like this (the events occurring 60 years in the past so by no means recent) and could have easily been cut in half. Because of all of these, "Moving Day" didn't read like a thriller until the last 1/3 of the book or so when it started to pick up, but even some scenes there were needlessly dragged out.

Something probably more akin to personal tastes is Stone's use of fragment sentences. There are an abundance of these and I'm not sure when he decides to use them. Instead of lists being written with commas, each list is a two or three word fragment.

Finally, Stone could trust the intelligence of his readers a bit more. Some parts were written in parenthesis, almost like expository explanations to show the meaning of a previous sentence and most of them weren't necessary. Stone wanted to make sure he told us exactly why events transpired the way they did instead of ending much more quickly, which sometimes helped (After reading, you'll likely question how the plot is remotely possible), but more often than not were unnecessary and takes the reader out of the story.

Now there were a couple of good twists and the premise at the first was intriguing that warrants it more than one star, but I feel like as a longer short story or a novella, this could have been a fantastic book if it were trimmed down considerably.

title: Natchez Burning: A Novel (Penn Cage Book 4)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Greg Iles
review_text:
I've been a Greg Iles fan since I read his first book. As a fellow traveler of Highway 61, I eagerly awaited Iles' newest book, "Natchez Burning." What a huge disappointment: repetitious dialogue, shallow characters, a meandering plot, unnecessary and hideous violence. The book is just boring. The only good writing in "Natchez Burning" appears in the very first part that takes place in the early 60s. It almost feels as if two different authors wrote it.

It is very irritating that Iles mixes his leftist political views into this story, alienating the "corrupt conservatives" across (and down) the river from Natchez, along with the "country cooks" of salty and sugary mush (that's how Iles describes it), who I strongly suspect represent a big portion of his fan base. Wilma Deen. (snort)

Worst of all, Iles reveals a complete misunderstanding of laissez-faire economics, a description of which is contained in the dialogue of one of the book's worst villains, as he describes the reason Katrina wiped out the people of New Orleans. Absurd. Mr. Iles might want to study the Flood Insurance Act written by Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA), and the excessive flood insurance rate hikes resulting from this law, and the effect it is having on the property owners in St. Bernard and Jefferson Parishes.

Mr. Iles, you know nothing about economics. Absolutely nothing. And, you only imagine that you know what white racists were like back in the 60s. Although very young, I was there, and they were not all ignorant, uneducated sociopaths. Understanding and writing about the complexity of this concept alone may have redeemed the rest of the blather that is your novel, "Natchez Burning." I will not be waiting for the next two books in this trilogy. I will delete "Natchez Burning" from my Kindle device. I regret that I have no physical copy; it would be great fun to burn it.

After 15-20 minutes I was looking for a place to pull off the freeway so I could change to a different audiobook.  I had to drive 20 more minutes.  The first forty minutes of this book (and that's all I heard) were sad/pathetic soft-core porn.  Engorged body parts, best-sex-I-ever-had scenarios, silly to the point of boring.  I have no idea how long it went on because I had to stop it.  Greg!  What were you thinking???  Actually, complaints about the narrator may have been unfair if one were consider that he/she is listening to an amateur porn show.  I'm no proud...but I want my pornography to be professional.

subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Greg Iles
review_text:
I liked Natchez Burning. The main characters are people we know from Iles' Penn Cage novels. In terms of action,
the plot moves along at a nice clip. By the end, many aspects of the story are resolved; however, Iles leaves us
dangling about Dr. Tom Cage, Penn's father. We still don't know the answers to his deep dark secrets or his fate, all
of which is fine because this is a trilogy. Those answers will come.

If you are a conspiracy theorist when it comes to the JFK assassination, you won't have trouble suspending disbelief
about this plot element. In fact, it's somewhat plausible.

My complaints are these: Penn and his fiancee get themselves into more tight spots than I can accept as reality. No way
should they have escaped this time; thus, it seems that the resolution, as always with Isles, is drawn out a bit too long. I
also find Caitlin's character a little unbelievable. First, she's "lightening quick" with her mind jumping ahead of Penn's
to make connections that sometimes seem paranormal. Then, she's melted into a quivering mess of nerves and feminine
fear. Yes, that's all possible, I guess, but I've rarely met a female that brilliant who doesn't have solid control over her
fear (then again, I've never been held at gun or flame-thrower point!).

Overall, I'm glad to have Iles back and in great form after his long recovery from the accident that almost killed him. Good
summer/beach read!

review_text: I could hardly wait to continue reading each time that I put the book down.  Iles wove an intricate story of love, loyalty, fear, intrigue, mayhem, race issues, and national tragedies with many characters who at times were difficult to track. (The book is very long!)  However, because I read Natchez Burning in a short time, I did remember who each was and their connections to each other.  My problem with the book is the ending:  the reader is left hanging with too many ravelled ends left untied.  My understanding is those "loose ends" will be tied in Greg Iles's NEXT book!  That, in my opinion, is a disservice to Mr. Iles's faithful readers.

review_title: Probably more fiction than fact - save your time and money.
review_text: I believe Tara grew up with an abusive father and an enabling mother. Much of the rest of the story strains credulity. As other reviewers have said, a lot of it doesn't add up. The review written by Drew seems to support this. He says in effect that her family was abusive and he has no knowledge about the first two thirds of the book. An oft repeated theme is that the siblings all have different memories of the same incident. I'm not sure this belongs in non-fiction. One reviewer said she wanted to throw the book across the room when she finished it. That was exactly how I felt. I was angry that I had wasted my time and money on this book. I think she is trying to get revenge on her abusive parents and make lots of money to compete with them. Ugh.

title: Educated: A Memoir
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Tara Westover
review_text:
I was really torn in my opinion of this book as I read it. It’s really not like any memoir I’ve ever read, but I also don’t read many memoirs from present-day writers. I will say that from an entertainment standpoint that this book is really good, if you can allow yourself to believe the details. I had quite some difficulty believing many of the details after about the first quarter of the book. As an educator with experience in a traditionally formatted American high school and as a former tutor of rural home-schooled kids, Westover’s claims about a number of things in her story about her non-education struck me as doubtful or preposterous. One of the first items that brought me to a full stop was her story surrounding her ACT scores. Without any science training, including such things we sometimes take for granted as training in analyzing data tables and interpreting graphs, I’d imagine reaching the 25th percentile would be a miracle; and her abysmal algebra ability, which she describes prior to taking the ACT and in her struggles with the BYU gen-ed class, would also mean getting to the 25th percentile in the algebra-centric ACT math would be quite lucky. This left me pondering how a score above 25 would be possible, given how improbable a composite of 21 would be, and that’s assuming she got perfect score on the reading and writing components of the exam. Either education was taken much more seriously in the Westover household, or it was at least less prohibited and more available than Tara Westover makes it out to be. In any event, having seen libraries both the carelessly “home-schooled” kids in rural areas, as well as the truly home-schooled kids I tutored, and having years of teaching experience in high school and college, I am sure there are omissions, at the very least, and probably complete alterations of truth or flat-out lies. So I was suspicious from then onward.

Another oddity I found in the story was how she claimed to have so much trouble writing essays in college, yet by her third year she was heralded for her essay submitted for the study abroad at Cambridge. The irregularity of her narrative is just so bizarre. I’ve seen plenty of college level essays from students, both from the standpoint of helping students with their writing at a writing center and seeing what grades essays of various qualities earned, as well as grading them in my classes; and the improvement of one’s writing is most certainly a slowly changing phenomenon. It takes reading lots of good books and practicing one’s writing to improve at this skill. It’s a long process. At this point in the book, I didn’t know whether Tara was a wunderkind, after all, and maybe scored perfect on those ACT reading and writing sections to get that ACT score, then forgot how to write on her first-year essays, and then turned it back on for the essay she had to write for the study abroad program. Here, I began sensing that she was constructing a narrative for the purpose of subtly and gently convincing readers of something, but I didn’t know what it was at the time, except that she wanted the reader to buy into her intellectual bootstrapping.

One disturbing thing I found within the pages was Tara Westover’s grim storytelling: for someone with so much at stake in telling these stories, claiming deep emotional trauma, I couldn’t help but note that the detail with which she told these gory and macabre stories. For someone to spend a paragraphs at a time talking about the charred flesh of her father, as if this were a fictional work, is psychologically telling. There are at least four instances in the book where my wife, an HSP empath, had to stop listening to the audiobook because of its grim detail. I have read some psychologists’ takes on the book, and what shocked me is that nobody had anything to say about the fact that Tara’s ghastly accounts don’t point to some sort of psychosis or sociopathy. It’s not unreasonable to think a girl, who has lived through some amount of terror from a bipolar father and highly abusive brother, who now tells of calamities past with horrifically graphically detailed precision, is telling stories thusly due to a psychological ailment created by the former circumstances. If this isn’t so, then Tara Westover has no qualms about putting sensationalism out there for dollars.

On this same topic, I’m also concerned with the portrayal of her father’s accident, as it is clear to me that the injuries, as first reported, were exaggerated. The injuries sustained were supposedly such that her father could only be hydrated by an enema, as his jaw, inner mouth, etc., were so burned that he could not absorb ice cubes in his mouth; and the muscles in his jaw were so burned that he could not hold ice in his mouth. I couldn’t tell whether this was an attempt at homoerotic imagery to embarrass her father by way of his fundamentalist views or whether this really happened. I couldn’t find any images of her father that confirmed this level of damage, but he was apparently so capable that he visited her at Harvard during her fellowship year away from Cambridge.

A major rub in this memoir is that Tara Westover is creating a narrative that pits traditional schooling against home schooling, and I find this deeply problematic, because it becomes clearer and clearer, as one reads, that Tara’s home schooling had to be decent: three of seven(?) kids in the family hold PhDs! Having worked with troubled inner-city teens with massive deficiencies in their public education, aged 17-25, I must firmly remind everyone that getting these people through a two-year community college has a tremendously high failure rate. For a detailed account of the gap that Tara Westover claims to bound without much comparative difficulty, look at Lisa Fenn’s (author of “Carry On”) absolutely gargantuan efforts to get LeRoy and Dartanyan through a four-year college, and the gap year(s) required to bring them to a basic college level ability because of the disparity between not being able to do the basics versus being college-ready; then compare that level of education and the effort that this trio put in, and reflect on Tara Westover’s story.

Compounding this point further, her brother, called “Tyler” in the book, has publically responded to the book, and I think his comments undermine a central support structure within the book. (Tyler is the oldest of the three PhD students in the family.) Tyler’s statement explains that Tara’s account regarding him in the book is plainly wrong. Tara tells the story as thought Tyler struggled to get away, to go off to college, and this required that he hide and study. Tyler says that the father was the individual who wanted him to go to BYU to get an engineering degree, particularly for the purposes of being able to have Tyler approve structures for the father’s business and whatever he wanted for his own property. This is a big problem for the whole of Tara Westover’s book, because not only was it the case that this home-schooling prison-break a fabrication in narrative, but the education at home had to be relatively good. Whatever the Westover family’s fundamentalist idiocies, it is impossible to claim that their home-school education was much inferior to the average traditional public school; which is an issue because, as the title suggests, Tara Westover has something she wants to say about “uneducated,” as much as what constitutes “uneducated.” As Tara’s interviews illustrate after the publication of the book, she very clearly pits her family, “rural folk,” and people of a particular political persuasion –collectively, the home-schooled uneducated– against regular people, urbanites with access to “education,” and people of another political persuasion. The subtext for what she’s saying in the book is so strong that she doesn’t need to make explicit the political point she’s setting up. Between the book’s development of the groupings of people, and the contrast classes she establishes in the book and in post-publication interviews, the axe she grinds suddenly becomes visible. This is also the reason for the many inconsistencies in the book, e.g., her father’s ability to solve ACT algebra problems.

Between the lying and the horrific things that most assuredly happened, e.g., Sean’s abuse and her father’s harm from probable bipolar personality disorder, it is really hard to say what’s true in this book, aside from the obvious chunks of reality that the publishers fact checked. Ultimately, I would give the book a 1-star rating for this alone, but I think things are worse than merely the authorial coercion and misrepresentation. Individuals genuinely challenged by life learn something, and I get no sense that Tara learned anything in her struggle, except how to manipulate people with words –and the number of times that she did this in getting to Cambridge will remain a mystery. I will speak to this further.

As a philosopher, I have an earnest love for ideas, knowledge, and wisdom, so seeing a PhD in intellectual history publish a memoir filled me with the joy at the idea that someone so educated would have blended the words of excellent thinkers past with her own experiences, arriving at some interesting insight about the world. This was not a product of the memoir. On this score, the memoir is completely vapid. The hackneyed motto, “you can do anything you put your mind to,” was as bad as any inspirational writing, and the cliché-heavy allusion to Quixote’s windmills when expressing her own illusions and mental breakdown was an embarrassment. Aside from a few regurgitations of titles and names of thinkers, I could not tell that the author had studied intellectual history (anywhere). She undoubtedly would have studied Mortimer Adler, given his extensive thumbprint on the discipline; so I think it would have been better for her to pull away from the mendacious narrative she was constructing to arrive at any new understanding. Maybe she could have remarked at how a new practical layer had to be added to Adler’s notion of “dogma,” between the religious and philosophical notions, where dogmatism is good in the former but bad in the latter. This would have made more sense of her father (and family’s) wrongs, objectively identifiable as wrongs. Of course, a life time of these harrowing experiences and reflection upon them through the great lenses of history would have been less superficial than this proposal I make; then again, the story has only been mine to reflect upon for a few hours, not a lifetime. In the end, she learned nothing, and simply expected that the reader would (dogmatically) side with her, without having an objective ground from which to condemn her father, which is what all of this “education” should have culminated in. Instead, she’s an emotional wreck at the end of the memoir, trying merely to convince readers that she’s in a better emotional place and empowered. Even in this, she learned nothing.

review_title: So yeah, religious zealotry makes for a terrible childhood
review_text:
I wish someone had mentioned to me just how much of the book was based on cultish religion. From the jacket blurb I knew there was survivalist craziness going on (in reality, not really), but the religious basis for every single poor decision and every survival of near-death experience made me glaze over. "The angels were watching over me" stuff got old. I was not moved or touched, as the other reviews promised, and it's not because I'm not religious. It's because it was ridiculous. Honestly, I was over it almost as soon as it started.

If the book were written more from the "all this before was terrifyingly nuts and we sooo know it now" standpoint, I'd be more accepting. Instead, it presents the wacko behavior as understandable and almost forgivable. The hindsight isn't giving me a "we've completely stopped drinking the Kool-Aid" vibe.

I realize Tara's (obviously) mentally ill father was doing his best while presiding over the family utilizing insane religious extremist views, but I'm not seeing enough astonishment. I can't imagine being forced to live under that kind of tyrannical rule in dirt and poverty, where everything is done without question in a certain god's name. But I have to believe most of the oppressed people understand that things aren't right and feel like they must find their own way, which should be FAR FAR FAR away from the crazed fanaticism and irresponsible choices. This is why books like Troublemaker: Surviving Hollywood and Scientology and shows like "Escaping Polygamy" work. People woke the F up and fled. But Tara seems to be telling the story from a state of shock, distant and removed, like it just happened and that's it. Where's the engagement? Where's the outrage?

So my big question is this: Is Tara's story as horrifying as she relates, or are we experiencing another A Million Little Pieces total exaggeration here?

Who knows? All I do know is that great ratings for this book just didn't translate into a great experience for me. Amazon forced me rate this, but I wanted my review to speak for itself. *sigh* This reader was clearly not this book's target audience.

title: Educated: A Memoir
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Tara Westover
review_text:
The writing in this book is truly gifted and well-crafted. Ms. Westover has a haunting voice that stays with you long after you read her book. Her story is truly remarkable. I applaud all that she has been able to make of herself.

That said, I came away with many questions and a few red flags. I know that Ms. Westover was careful to state that she is not criticizing The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints or its members, but I'm afraid that casual readers will come away with a very distorted view of the Church and its followers. We're not all fundamentalist survivalists who condone child abuse and consider women to be second-class citizens. If this story is true, the Westover version of "Mormonism" is a crude caricature. But a casual reader who has never met a member may think this family represents the mainstream of the Church.

As a practicing member of The Church of Jesus Christ, I also found some strange omissions in her story. She seems to indicate that the family was very imbued with Latter-day Saint teachings, but some things were missing.

She never talks about going to church services on Sundays, where she would have attended a worship service and then classes for children (ages 3-11) and young women (ages 12-17). In those services and classes, she would have met with many other church members who might have provided a more balanced look at life than what she found in her own home. She would have been taught genuine Christian principles, not whacked-out survivalist propaganda. She would have been taught about Jesus Christ and following his teachings as found in the New Testament and other scriptures. Where were her teachers? Who were her Church friends? Did she attend the annual girls' camp the Church sponsors? Did she attend a seminary class, even if she didn't go to high school? Did she participate in the goal-setting activities that are part of the Church's program for children and youth?

Did she and her family watch General Conference on television or at her church building, which is broadcast twice a year from Salt Lake City? Faithful members usually do. If they had, her family would have heard Church leaders condemn abuse and misuse of the priesthood of God. Men holding the priesthood are counseled just about every Conference that "no power or influence can or ought to be maintained by virtue of the priesthood, only by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned." Women are encouraged to make all they can of themselves and to be full partners in their marriage and in family leadership.

Faithful Church members are encouraged to send their sons on proselyting missions. (Women may serve also, if they choose to.) (You've probably seen missionaries around your town.) But Tara doesn't mention any of her brothers serving missions for the Church.

In the Church we try to take care of one another. Part of that care-taking involves men and women being assigned to visit other members in their homes, sometimes to impart an uplifting message, and also to see if the family needs help in any way. During Tara's childhood, these would have been called home teachers and visiting teachers, and they would have visited about once a month. She never mentions these people coming to her house, nor does she talk about her parents being home or visiting teachers.

These omissions concern me. I can think of three reasons why she may have omitted them: First, perhaps her family considered themselves apart from the main body of the Church, with her father in essence as its leader, so they weren't active in the Church at all. Second, she may have participated in these things, but her family life was so very chaotic that they didn't have any effect on her. Or third, and most troubling, perhaps she omitted these things because they didn't fit her story arc and advance the narrative she was crafting. This leaves me to question much of her experience.

I know that her family's lawyer has said the family encourages readers to take Ms. Westover's story with a grain of salt. I understand they have been the recipients of much negative feedback over the claims in this book.

Bottom line: I'm not sure how to feel about Educated. It is a powerful book; I'm just not sure about the absolute truthfulness of the story.

review_text:
4.5 stars

Wow, what a story! This was one of the most fascinating memoirs I've ever read and one of the most well-written ones too! From the moment I started reading, I was so engaged and drawn into Tara Westover's story that I found it impossible to put this book down – a first for me with a nonfiction book! Actually, throughout the entire time I was reading, I had to remind myself constantly that this was not a novel, not some fictional coming-of-age tale about a girl who was able to rise above her circumstances and carve out an existence for herself despite everything that happened, because in all honesty, this absolutely read like a novel. Tara's story is truly amazing and I'm glad she got the chance to tell it-- the way she was able to get an education for the first time at the age of 17, even being able to study at Cambridge and Harvard and eventually earning her PhD, was absolutely inspiring! I appreciate the raw honesty with which she relayed her story and am impressed by the tremendous strength and courage that it undoubtedly took for her to lay bare her inner conflicts and struggles so vividly for us, also going to great lengths to clarify the details and events that were part of her own memory versus the ones that were not. As we were exposed to one harrowing incident after another and bore witness to the destructive behavior and actions of Tara's parents – her religious fanatic survivalist father and meek, subservient mother – there were moments where I wanted this story to be a work of fiction because it was so hard to come to terms with all the cruelty and abuse that went on. It felt surreal at times, witnessing this family's brutality – more specifically the father and one of the brothers -- spurred by an unwavering, cult-like adherence to an ideology that obviously defied logic as well as all common sense yet was embraced so wholeheartedly and unquestioningly. Tara never once used the word "cult" in her memoir and it is unclear whether she ever thought of her family as such, but the way she described her parents, especially later on with how powerful they became and all the "employees" who not only worked for them but also admired them and adapted their ideology, it is obvious to any outside observer that's what her family eventually became. In this regard, I can't help but worry for Tara, with the publication of this memoir, what her future will look like, especially knowing that her journey is far from over and she continues to struggle with reconciling the new life she built for herself against the love and loyalty she still has for her family.

And this is the one area – Tara's continued sense of loyalty to her family – that made me struggle with rating this book and, to a certain extent, writing this review. I absolutely felt for Tara and it was heartbreaking what she went through, but at the same time, it was very difficult for me to reconcile her constant need to still seek validation from her family even after everything that happened. She acknowledged herself that her parents were abusive, manipulative, maniacal to the point of delusional, and their lifestyle was one that she no longer wanted to be a part of -- her parents, for their part, also made it clear that her refusal to conform and submit to their ideology meant that she was "no longer welcome" in the family and they wanted nothing to do with her anymore either -- yet despite all this, somehow, Tara is still not able to let go. The part where she talked about writing to her mother every year and basically "begging for approval" to see her was tough to read and in all honesty, frustrated me to no end. Even though her family outright rejected her time and time again and she already knew it was "pointless" to continue reaching out to her family and making the trip back to her family's compound every year, she still continued to do it – almost as though, despite knowing the impossibility of it, she was hoping for some divine miracle that her family might one day "come around" and change their ways. While part of me definitely understands the difficulty of cutting ties with family and empathizes with the conflicting emotions that Tara continues to struggle with, another part of me can't help wondering whether someday, she might succumb and everything she worked so hard to achieve – the education and new life -- may be in vain. I'm pretty sure there will be more to this story in the future and I can only hope that whatever happens, Tara can continue to find her inner peace and happiness.

Overall, this was a tough read, but a powerful one and so very important! It opened my eyes to so many things and I know Tara's story will continue to stay with me for a long time to come. Highly recommended and necessary read!!

review_text:
I began reading
Educated
because it was our monthly book club pick. At chapter 12, I chose to put it down. I had no reason to feel such pain and frustration from the abuse I was reading. I had plenty of abuse in my own family I didn't care to read about it as well. At the end of the month after hearing the other members of the clubs review in response to the book, and as I read reviews of the book and how well-received it has been across the board I began reading again and finished. I was also quite impressed that she finished her PhD at Cambridge.
The book saddens me. Abuse should never be allowed to be brushed under the carpet. And the powers in a family to release the abused from their pain should be acknowledged and given. Otherwise they should always carry that they are part of the abuse and the ugliness. Whatever medical label correctly describes Tara's father, he most certainly was warped in his beliefs and behaviors. And the reading portion of his responses to things that happened to his children reminds me of the lost time , instability, lost ability of peaceful mindfulness for children and people because of this condition. This is a true tragedy of a life.

review_title: The level of stupidity is astounding
review_text:
Reading other reviews I hoped this was going to be a better book, with more emphasis on science and action. Instead I ran across such a level of stupidity that I wonder how the book ever got past the editors and was approved for publication. Throwing scientific terms and lab equipment description around doesn't make it a good book. Expecting people to believe that preternaturally fast or powerful creatures would conveniently stand there waiting for the main character to complete 10 spells is beyond idiotic. Are we really supposed to accept that her magic is faster than vampires when she supposedly can't even register when they'd moved until AFTER the whole thing is over? Seriously? Or that a powerful wizard would wait for her to do her knots when he's known for his spellcasting abilities and has never been defeated, and yet he stand and talks and does absolutely nothing?
And then there's the whole chasing of the Book of Life.. Constantly trying to make it sound important and then doing ABSOLLUTELY NOTHING with it? Talk about a waste of plot line!
Add multitudes of characters introduced with absolutely no reason for their existence, no development and no purpose other than to fill in the pages and make the book unnecessarily longer. There was a potential to make it great but Harkness completely wasted it. Instead we're subjected to yet another rendition of mixed literary style with complete incompetence at plot development or conclusion.
Explicitly graphic descriptions of torture, sex and childbirth should be flagged as a warning to buyers so they would be aware what it is that they're getting. The level of detail and amount of these scenes crosses deep into obsession with sadistic torture and abuse.
Seriously, this book is beyond idiotic. It's absolutely abhorrent.

author: Deborah Harkness
review_title: I hate to write a bad review as I had such ...
review_text: I hate to write a bad review as I had such high hopes for this book.  But, it was such a snoozefest that I feel I must.  I was really disappointed with this book.  Like supremely disappointed.  It has all the bad aspects of book 2 (way over written, too many frivolous and unnecessary details, too many characters coming and going) but then she adds an entire new set of issues that make it just excruciating to read.  I literally had to force myself to finish this book, hoping there would be some great finale..sadly there is not.  The entire plot line about Benjamin and the blood rage is just silly.  She spends way too much time with the obnoxious DNA coding stuff.  Snooze.  Is this really such a needed plot point??  Then there is the scion stuff, so much build up for what?  Nothing, Baldwin has a minor hissy but everyone else (the dreaded congregation who is not so dreaded after all as they do NOTHING) is totally fine with it.  Sort of like how the Knights of Lazarus are so desperately needed, but in the end they don't do anything much at all to drive the story forward.  Really the entire story is convoluted, drawn out, and most of it is completely ridiculous (and its not the great, imagination inspiring ridiculous that captured me in book 1 and drew me in....this book is full of boring, contrived, boastful ridiculous).  I may be picky, but little things like writing that both twins just woke from a nap and then explaining that one twin (being part vampire) can't sleep....writing something like this nearly sentences apart from each other really forces a reader away from a fantasy type story instead of bringing them in because it's SO inconsistent.  I really can't even say how bad this book is.  It is just bad.  Do yourself a favor, reader.  Read book 1 because it really is a great book.  Try out book 2, it's not terribly bad if you don't mind lots and lots of detail.  But skip this one, make up your own ending, it will be better than this silly, thrown together story plot.  It really seems like there was no plan for this book or perhaps making money was a bit more important than taking the time to publish quality work.

review_title: The trilogy continued to be a slog and I just finally gave up and DNF'd
review_text: Second DNF of 2021 after multiple attempts to restart this audiobook. I just... stopped caring honestly. The first book really was enjoyable, and while definitely dense, there was enough new worldbuilding and character development that it felt immersive instead of slogging. The second book and this one: they feel like I'm slogging through for sure. I was listening to this on audio which usually keeps me moving through books that I'm having a hard time focusing on, but legitimately it took a good two to three hours of listening before anything really happened. I'm now eleven hours in/half way through the book and I still am not sure how/why the plot is going to progress. I know it's the third book in the trilogy that I'm supposedly half way through but I swear it feels like we've introduced so many new issues that the pace of the latter half will have to rush to finally accomplish things before the book ends or else it will feel like most of the dangling plot holes just stay there. And I just don't know if I care enough to see which it will be. Honestly, I should have known I wasn't going to finish this series when I gave away the physical boxset to make room on my bookshelf. I guess I just hoped that I'd be able to push through and keep going on the audio. Oh well!

title: The Book of Life: A Novel (All Souls Trilogy, Book 3)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Deborah Harkness
review_title: Ripped from the pages of Twilight....or how I imagine Twilight books must be written.
review_text:
This is actually the first time in a long time I have written a book review on Amazon, but I felt so strongly about it that I felt compelled to do so. It was just that bad. I almost didn't finish this book it was so awful.
The first 3/4 of the book is uneventful and boring. The writing is overwrought and ridiculous. I had to force myself to get to the end of it to find out what the whole Ashmole book secret was. (No spoilers...but it's rather anticlimactic when you do find out.) It had been a long time since I read Shadow of Night, so when I started reading Book of Life I was scratching my head about why I had anticipated the release of the 3rd book in the first place. I even went back and read most of Shadow of Night to jog my memory regarding the past events in the series. So I can say with definity that the writing has gotten much worse. It's not my imagination. It all went downhill after the end of Discovery of Witches.
The constant switching between 1st and 3rd person narration is jarring and unnecessary. I hated it in her previous books, but it seemed even more disorienting in this one.
The characters are 2 dimensional, conversations feel forced, and don't get me started on the ghastly sex scenes. Everyone is overly emotional (I don't know how many times somebody "gasps" in reaction to something), and she often uses the exact same words to describe an action. (Matthew "rakes his fingers through his hair" to indicate he is frustrated and his patience is running out. I get it. You don't have to write that in every chapter.) I felt like I was reading fan-fiction for the Twilight series or Fifty Shades of Grey. (I confess that I haven't read either of these. Just a suspicion that this is the type of bodice ripping literature that bored housewives seem to enjoy.) Maybe her editor saw the success of these lesser works and instructed her to adjust her work to be more vacuous?
I am not sure what kind of relationships that Ms. Harkness has, but none of the conversations in the book flow like normal human interactions. They all seem stagey and affected, as if she intends the dialogue to be performed by amateur theater companies. Everybody is a caricature instead of believable person. There is no subtlety or nuance in this book. Everything is beat-you-over-the-head obvious. Even if you can suspend the disbelief that witches, vampires, and demons exist, the juvenile rendering of events makes it feel obviously artificial.
Given Harkness's background, I don't begrudge historical facts and references to antique artifacts being thrown in. I just wish it was done with more finesse. Instead it feels like name dropping, as if she threw it in there just to let you know that she is a historian.

Obviously the people who are reading this book enjoyed the first 2, or they wouldn't be finishing up the trilogy. So the audience pool is limited. Given that, I am certain that most people who read this will like it. I may be one of the few dissenting opinions. If you are looking for an absorbing, believable escape into a fantasy world...go elsewhere. But if you want to get to end of the trilogy and figure out what makes Diana so special, then it is worth brute-forcing your way through to get that sense of completion that happens at the end of a series. I was hoping for a redeeming conclusion to the series, but no such luck.

title: The Book of Life: A Novel (All Souls Trilogy, Book 3)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Deborah Harkness
review_text:
I really wanted to like this book. I loved the first two - in fact before reading this final instalment I re-read the first two just so i could refresh my memory on the plot and characters (as i had read them a while back), and i thoroughly enjoyed them both again a second time. So it was with great anticipation that I opened the first pages of the third book.

Halfway in, I was frustrated, bored, and disappointed. I only read through to the end partly because I hoped it would get better, and partly because I wanted some resolution. But I finished it feeling less than satisfied (and definitely unresolved) - there were so many questions left unanswered.

There are many things wrong with this book, in my humble opinion. Here are just a few:

- Most of the book had Diana and Matthew flying around from one spot to another, without actually doing anything except expressing their undying eternal love for each other. YAWN.

- She introduced many new characters (eg the witches in the Madison coven) that didn't do very much that you wonder why she bothered with them in the first place.

-Some minor characters from the last books were also re-introduced which i didn't think was necessary at all to the plot line.

- The birthing scene - i'm sorry, but has she actually researched child birth? It was such a stereotypical presentation of how women give birth (eg lots of swearing at the husband - so trite and cliched) - when the reality is nothing like that?? Not in my own experience anyway!

- Worst of all, i finished the book still wondering - what is the Book of Life??? Isn't this last instalment supposed to answer that one important question??

- And what about the tats on Diana? Is she going to live the rest of her life with a Tree tattooed down her back, and palimpsest words in her eyes???

- And who was the informant feeding information to Benjamin? I kept expecting there to be some clever twist like it was one of the trusted inner circle people who turns out to be a traitor. But no, that would have required too much thought...

- I also kept wondering whether the author actually wrote this book herself, or whether she had other people writing different chapters for her. It all seemed so disjointed and incoherent.

- Alternatively, I wondered whether she was trying to write it like a movie (as I heard that the first book is now part of a movie deal) - there were scenes that felt like they would fit a Hollywood movie (eg the birthing scene), but on paper were just banal.

When the first two books were so well written, researched and thought through, this last one was hugely disappointing!

author: Deborah Harkness
review_text:
Its taken me a bit after reading this to even sit down and write a review for this book. I understand when you have had 2 bestsellers in a row that the expectations are extremely high. I must totally agree with another reader who said to the people who thought this book was great.....'Did we even read the same book?'

Disappointed doesn't even begin to cover it. The characters whose lives I fell in love with lost their luster in this book. The passion of a forbidden love and the urgency in a quest for survival just wasn't there. All through the book, I felt like l was reading stuff that was just pieced together. A traitor that knew every move they were making was never clearly revealed. Gallowglass simply disappears after making an admission. Even Matthew's love for Diana was subdued in this book. I truly felt like this book lacked the emotions and intensity that made the other books so valuable as a reader.

After reading this, my first impression was that this 3rd book was an obligation fulfilled. It filled in some of the spots but not nearly all. While I have re-read the first 2 books many times just to visit my favorite characters, once was enough with this book.
Sadly I was hugely disappointed in this finale.

title: The Book of Life: A Novel (All Souls Trilogy, Book 3)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Deborah Harkness
review_title: A big let down for me- *Spoiler free review*
review_text:
What a huge let down this book was. I'm talking EPIC proportion let down.

First of all, I am shocked at all the positive reviews I'm seeing. I feel like we didn't read the same book.

A Discovery of Witches was one of my favorite reads of 2011. I wasn't as much into reading then, and I stumbled across this one while randomly perusing my library for books. I fell in love with the story, the characters, and the magic of it all. I felt like the story was building up for something important, something powerful.

The second book was also pretty successful for me. It was lovely in the way that historical fiction is pleasurable for me. I also have a deep love of time-travel books, so I was practically guaranteed to fall head over heels.

A lot of time has passed since the second, and my expectations were sky high for the third. Unfortunately, the careful world-building fell to crap in the final installment. I'll try to break down my main issues with the story without giving away any spoilers.

1) The POV switches: I have very specific opinions about lots of POVs in the a story: Namely, I hate them. This book had at least 5 different points of view, which irritated me to no end. Why not just two? Those extra points of view just seemed lazy to me, just a way for the author to do some "telling" and less "showing" about the characters. To make matters worse, the author switched from 1st to 3rd person throughout the book! Talk about a headache. It was a terrible choice, in my opinion.

2) The number of characters: This book was like a who's who from the previous two books. I swear, no one was left out. There were so many people re-introduced that I had a hard time keeping track of everyone. The story felt so... cluttered. All of these extra people and their minor storylines weighed the plot down so much. It became sort of jumbled and confusing. I'm not sure why the author didn't just keep her focus on the main characters.

3) The lack of secrecy: I'm so confused! In the previous books, Diana and Matthew guarded the secret of their relationship, the quest for the book, and the secrets of Matthew's family fiercely. In this book? They let it alllll hang out. They tell everyone EVERYTHING! Everyone seems to know what they are searching for, that Diana is pregnant, simply everything! I have no idea why this had them throwing caution to the wind. They freaking told an entire class of students what they were researching. It was madness. Then they are looking for the person "leaking their secrets"... it could be the pizza boy for all they know! It was truly bizarre.

4) Diana's familiar: I won't say too much about this topic so I don't give away any spoilers, but I was utterly confused about the change in the firedrake's personality throughout the story, especially towards the end.

5) The haphazard plot: It honestly felt like the author didn't think this trilogy through very well. It was like the author had a brilliant idea for the first book and then had no idea how to carry it through. The third book had to reveal some mind blowing things to fit with all the buildup, but instead it was a collection of jumbled tangents. The main characters jumped from location to location, doing a series of things that didn't really make sense. They seemed like chickens with their heads cut off. The book didn't seemed planned. It was almost as though the author was making it up on the fly.

6) The blood rage thing: I hated this plot point. Blood rage was supposed to be this crazy thing, but some deep breathing and zen meditation seemed to snap all the characters out of it?? I was so confused as to why it was this big issue to begin with if it was that easy to control. I would have preferred it be a mindless, insane thing instead of the nuisance it was made out to be. It was a poorly fleshed out concept that could have been more powerful.

7) The Book: Okay, what is the deal with that book? We never truly get answers. I still am left wondering who created it and why. If you are reading this story thinking that something wondrous will be revealed, don't hold your breath.

8) Plot inconsistencies: There are so many plot elements that make no sense or are left dangling. I don't want to go into them all because I want this review to be spoiler free, but there were many instances where the book contradicts itself.

All in all, this book was a huge bummer. I give it 2 stars, mainly for nostalgia because I was happy to visit with these characters again.

Oh, and can Gallowglass get his own book? Pretty please?

**Copy provided by the publisher in exchange for an honest review**

review_title: Loved the first two.  This one?  Not so much.
review_text:
2 1/2 stars, leaning closer to the 2. Caveat: I read the first two books a month a part, and then waited a year for this one. LOVED them. Maybe if I had reread them before picking TBoL things would be different. But I didn't, and so I was immediately confused. So many people, so little memory of any of them. Out of desperation I downloaded the other two books on my kindle so I could easily search for people in the other books. Perhaps that got me out of the reading rhythm, but it was a real chore for me to finish the book. I'd get excited every once in a while --- for example, when Diana would return to academia* -- but then things would veer into another direction.

All that said, I love Diana and Matthew. I think I love Gallowglass even more and would definitely buy a book about him. Heck, I will still buy the next book that Harkness writes. I love history, which may be why I enjoyed this one less than the other two as there was less of that. I prefer Diana the Historian who is also a witch more than Diana the Witch who is also a historian.

*My opinion only, of course, but I'm still cringing over the scene that took place in the research lab in Yale, where the hip Professor was too impatient to learn real names, and so gave everyone nicknames based on their primary characteristic. I can accept the fact that witches, daemons and vampires walk the earth more than I can believe that people sit around and talk like that.

title: The Book of Life: A Novel (All Souls Trilogy, Book 3)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Deborah Harkness
review_title: A worthy conclusion to the trilogy, if not my favorite of the books
review_text:
When the second volume of this trilogy ended with vampire Matthew de Clairmont and his wife, witch Diana Bishop, returning to Sept-Tours from their "honeymoon" in sixteenth century Europe, readers were well aware that a final confrontation was looming: both with Matthew's renegade vampire son, Benjamin, and with the Congregation, who have for centuries banned just the kind of "inter-species" relationship that Matthew and Diana have forged. Now that Diana is pregnant, there is even more at stake, and Sept-Tours, the de Clairmont ancestral home, seems like the logical place to regroup and figure out how to do more than simply respond to attacks. Above all, how can they complete their quest for the missing pages from the Ashmolean manuscript that started it all - a manuscript they now know to have been made up of the skins of daemons, vampires and witches - and restore them to the Book of Life? Perhaps, if that can be accomplished, the rest will fall into place...

I found the first 100 pages of this to be relatively slow going, and was slightly disappointed to be back in the 21st century after following Matthew and Diana on their travels through the 16th century and their encounters with everyone from Christopher Marlowe to Rudolf, the Habsburg ruler of Prague. But the pace picked up, and soon enough Deborah Harkness had enough plot elements bubbling away to keep me entertained, as well as introducing some new characters and themes into the mix.

What appealed to me most here is the way that Diana, who only learned how to master her powers in the final chapters of the second book in the trilogy, really emerges here both as a powerful force and a powerful character in her own right. Until now, she had struck me as somewhat of a quintessential romantic heroine, swept off her feet by the handsome and domineering vampire (albeit being feisty and intelligent enough to command his respect). Here Diana's independent actions - magical and otherwise - will prove crucial as the story unfolds, and that was an interesting and welcome addition to the mix. There are some unexpected additions to the ranks as Matthew and Diana prepare for the final confrontation, and while violent magical battles formed a part of it, I was glad to see that Harkness didn't shy away from adding additional levels of complexity to the mix.

Criticisms? Sometimes the nature of the magical spells that Diana is casting (if not the nature of her powers - which is actually a very intriguing concept indeed, for which Harkness deserves kudos) felt rushed through or glossed over, as if the author hadn't really thought them through herself and thus couldn't explain them thoroughly. So I found myself reading, re-reading and re-re-reading several passages to try to figure out exactly what had happened, only to shrug and simply move on. I also found myself a little surprised at the ease with which the non-magical folks to whom the existence of vampires, daemons and witches is revealed in this final book is accepted. It's all very matter of fact; oh yes, of course, I thought there was something unusual going on - as if you'd finally learned that the person with the slight accent had in fact been born in Denmark. But there's a big difference between being born in Denmark and being a witch or a vampire who is 1,500 years old...

And occasionally the injection of moments of wit and levity felt out of keeping with the overall tone, as when one member of the team quips about having to restrain a stressed out-Sarah (Diana's aunt) from disabling the smoke detector system on a long-haul flight, or when Sotheby's employee, Phoebe - now the girlfriend of one of the de Clairmont family - spots a Holbein masterpiece hanging in a bathroom. Ysabeau tries to reassure her that Margaret More (the painting's subject) wouldn't have been worried by "a bit of exposed flesh." Phoebe responds, spluttering, `It's not the decorum of the situation that troubles me, but the fact that Margaret More might tumble into the loo at any moment!' " Now, this is about the seventh time that Phoebe has been awestruck by de Clairmont family treasures; the characters are about to conduct some serious magic; and yet all of a sudden they're getting girly and giggly about a Holbein painting? Some of these moments were fine; others were misplaced and the humor felt off-kilter.

That said, the novel was tremendously entertaining, and served as an unusually satisfactory conclusion to the trilogy. Unusually, because it went beyond the traditional "let's make sure the bad guys get their just desserts" kind of thing, and was an altogether more interesting conclusion, with an interesting and subtle reference or reminder of parallels in our non-magical world.

I also think that Harkness has left herself with enough leeway to come back to her characters in the future. True, the conundrums that Diana and Matthew had to face at the beginning of this book have been resolved in one way or another, but I would imagine that life for any supernatural creature is never going to be easy or straightforward, and certainly the struggle to carve out an independent path for themselves doesn't necessarily mean it will be happily ever after, undisturbed? Regardless, I'll be curious to see what Harkness does next. 4.5 stars; the second volume remains my favorite of the series.

Full disclosure: I obtained an advance review copy of the book at BEA (BookExpo).

review_title: Human nature pretty much mandates that we root for the underdog
review_text: Just a sign of the times we live in.....authors seem to feel a sense of duty in lobbing f-bombs on as many pages as they can jam in them into.  I'll not ever understand that.  At least I hope I don't.  But the book.  Yes, the book.  I read about a book a week and have for a number of years.  I honestly cannot recall ever reading a book that was 'darker' than this one.  Human nature pretty much mandates that we root for the underdog.  The boy accused was certainly that.  I don't know about anyone else, but I couldn't root for the boy.  He was thoroughly unlikeable.  But he wasn't the only one.  Virtually everyone in the book was unlikeable, with the possible exception of the dad's former best friend.  The storyline was miserable.  The nearby child-molester was miserable.  Jacob's best friend, Derek was miserable.  The end of the book.  Off-the-charts miserable.  Just really an awful book. Sorry, Mr. Landay.  I'll not be back for more.

title: Defending Jacob: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: William Landay
review_title: I should have paid more attention
review_text:
I should have paid more attention to the negative reviews.

First, I will say that I do not require a "Hollywood ending," and I don't mind that the author didn't wrap everything neatly in the closing chapters and paragraphs of the story. My complaint is not that I didn't like the end. I have many complaints to voice, and they're not all necessarily with the story itself.

I am not sure a story of this nature is best told in first person, and it seems the author, himself, was uncertain of his POV. He switches points of view within the story, and sometimes the 'dialogue' is presented as if directly from courtroom transcripts. The language and conversation during those exchanges are not authentic (even if the author and the narrator are attorneys).

Further, I was not able to identify with any of the characters, no matter how I tried. That, too, is the fault of the author. His characters are not fleshed out, and are far from complex.

I did read negative reviews prior to purchasing the book, as I am not someone who jumps on bandwagons and I don't necessarily agree with the 'must read' recommendations of others. This includes the opinions of professional critics. I can't say I would add this title to my own must read recommendations to my friends - or to anyone reading this.

Thanks for asking. :)

author: William Landay
review_text: I suppose when you are an attorney, this book fails. There is no real story here. The horrible crime is preempted by the "Nature vs. Nurture" argument. Many people feel this way about young people accused of crimes. Having appreciated the benefits of a good education I know there is so much more to the tragedies caused by pathological conduct. The theme reminds me of the Jorn van der Sloot case. That simplicity is the sum total of the message. The writing itself may be spectacular and the Shiva portrayal in this book was a welcomed change. However, being a parent, an attorney who occasionally represents young people, and a former educator, I cannot recommend this book. It is much too cynical for my taste. Furthermore, the criminal justice system is poorly represented here and it is critical that Americans are provided accurate information.

title: Defending Jacob: A Novel
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: William Landay
review_text:
There's a wonderful, dreamy scene late in William Landay's courtroom thriller "Defending Jacob," in which Andy Barber, his wife Laurie and their accused son Jacob are all lolling in the 14-year-old's bedroom musing about decamping as a family and sneaking off to faraway, exotic Buenos Aires to start a new life out of the spotlight and free of suspicion.

Jacob asks, "Is that true, Dad? Lots of beautiful women in Buenos Aires?"

"That's what I hear."

Laurie describes the South American city as a place of possibility where her son "will have children, and his children will have children and he'll bring so much happiness to so many people that no one will ever believe that once upon a time in America people said horrible things about him."

At this point in Jacob's first-degree murder trial it's evident to all three and to us that none of that is likely to happen, but still they can imagine and try to cope with an increasingly dark reality filled with dread and edging toward despair.

Jacob has been charged with first-degree murder in the slaying of classmate Ben Rifkin, a bully. Jacob's father, an assistant DA until the indictment, is helping with his son's defense. He narrates the story, which is a suspenseful legal thriller that spirals into a harrowing story of family dissolution.

Carefully plotted as any whodunit you've ever read, the theme takes on the same nature-versus-nurture argument as William March's provocative potboiler "The Bad Seed." Unknown to Laurie, Andy is the son and grandson of violent murderers and the question becomes has Jacob too inherited a "Murder" gene, the "Barber Curse?" Suspicion becomes as corrosive as rust as family loyalty and love are tested beyond reasonable limits.

A great deal of the enjoyment that comes from reading "Defending Jacob" is the pitch-perfect dialogue. Kids talk to each other and to adults just like the kids do in your house. When Andy articulates his life-long, adoring attachment to Laurie, the language is almost elegiac and in painful contrast to the harsh reality of their current relationship.

Descriptions are vivid and memorable. Jacob, Landay says, has a way of keeping his answers short "as if every word was a stick of dynamite." One soft-bodied character appears as if "His sides, belly, and tits all sagged against his black polo shirt, as if he had been poured and bagged up inside this black sack cinched shut at the neck."

"Defending Jacob" is in rare company as a courtroom drama that comes along very infrequently. Its most recent predecessor, to my mind, is "Presumed Innocent." Both stories had a final twist that you think you're prepared for and still it comes out of nowhere. In a single short sentence and a few words everything changes. "Defending Jacob" is bold storytelling, compelling reading.
[4.5 stars]

review_text:
A story really needs to earn 5-stars and I typically reserve these for works of non-fiction that are in my list. Defending Jacob was simply a dynamite story. While set around the courtroom drama of a murder trial, Landay has built a fantastic story about life relationships. Father and son. Husband and wife. How interactions with co-workers and friends can be dramatically changed by events. Of course, this all plays out around the events of a murder in their small town.

Landay has developed characters that evoke the desire to love them or hate them. The ability to draw out such emotion towards the characters in his story defines a story teller in my opinion. Landay does not disappoint. I seldom find a book that creates that type page-turning energy around the main and supporting characters. Well done.

To top it off, the ending will knock your socks off. I never saw it coming. Highly enjoyable and recommended read.
