title: The Professor (McMurtrie and Drake Legal Thrillers Book 1)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Robert Bailey
review_text:
I admit. I have an inbred curiosity about books I get that are free to me. The curiosity is that unless the read turns into a hidden gem, it was worth what I “paid” for it.
My take off for a book like this is mainly due to my own legal background. That is, I’m always on the look out for a decent legal thriller with good Legal Procedure thrown in on top.
This book was no gem. In fact, it was a “Perils of Pauline” story disguised as a legal thriller. By that I mean that at about the 20 percent mark on my Kindle, I not only determined how the plot line was going to play out, I didn’t even care enough to get into the Legal Procedure of the case.
The Plaintiff counsel, the protagonist in this read, was beset upon in his investigation of his client’s claim with one road block after another ad nauseam by both the corporate Defendant and Defendant’s corporate counsel. The legal Procedure at this point became little more than a kangaroo court in the offing, in favor of the Defendant.
Once I got to this point, I decided to put the book down, but, since it is my philosophy to give a book three attempts, in the hope that the story line will recover, I read on to the 60 percent mark, whereupon, I sped read to the end. Even doing that, I have to honestly say the read never got any better.
I am not going to go into all the a fore mentioned stumbling blocks thrown up by the Defendant to Plaintiff’s counsel. But, the word “ludicrous” readily comes to mind.
This was not, in my view, a serious attempt at legal thriller writing. It was in stead, a high school level primer aimed at someone who is more a lawyer wanna’ be reader at best.
Two stars, under the circumstances, is exceedingly generous.

The author says he wanted the professor to be bigger than life, like a legal version of Bear Bryant, and he sort of pulls it off, but because he didn't create the characters from the perspective of a professional novelist, many of them, including the professor, turn into caricatures of what he is after. The emotional swings in other characters happen too suddenly, and the hired bad guy is so overdone I almost didn't finish the book.

I see some people love it, so that's nice for the author, but if you are looking for a well written, compelling legal thriller, I suggest to look elsewhere.

review_title: Alabama, trucking, greed, attorneys, victims, evil people, and an English Bulldog
review_text: I decided to read this because I have family who drive large truck rigs to deliver heavy materials. The risks and liabilities in this business lead to laws and regulations to protect the public and the businesses. When owners, supervisors, and drivers violate the laws and common sense, injury and death occur. Such lead to involvement of lawyers and the court...in this case, in Alabama. Come to find out, a well known Professor has trained most of the attorneys involved in this case. At the same time, academic politics go astray and the Professor gets dumped. Not to be a quitter, even with health problems looming, the Professor makes a huge comeback. The underlying dynamics run parallel to the Crimson Tide of the Alabama football team. While football interests me somewhat, the best parallel story line comes via Musso, the English Bulldog who lives with the Professor. I am still crying....  I had some trouble keeping straight the two widows, each with two children. The single, female law student also parents two children. The woman plaintiff comes forth on behalf of her deceased daughter, son-in-law, and grand daughter. All had names and histories.  I was surprised that this was Robert Bailey's first novel; it's quite interesting; reminds me of John Grisham.

I am a voracious reader, but it has been decades since the book has wowed me like this one has. I am a John Grisham fan, and I feel almost sacrilegious in saying this, but this book outshines Grisham's novels.

The intricate knowledge of the legal system, something only an insider would know, combined with perfect prose - neither too flowery or too sparse- makes the reader lose himself or herself in the book, to the point that the writing falls away and one feels a participant in this world.

Mad props to you, Wayne Bailey. I can't wait to read everything you have ever written and everything you will write. The last time a book drew me in this much, I was 12 years old and reading To Kill a Mockingbird.

review_title: It is worse than the first book in series
review_text: Since I purchased both Fall of Giants and Winter of the World (book two), I felt committed to read both novels.  The first book was a disappointment and Winter of the World was even more of a disappointment.  As I read it, I felt like I was reading something written by a high school student, not a world class novelist, and began to wonder if Follett actually wrote it himself.  It was certainly not of the quality of his previous books.  The characters in this book were even more stereotypical than the previous book.  The shallowness of the book was revealed through the writer’s addition of graphic sexual activity which was totally unnecessary and distracted from the story line.  Such a strategy to boost book sales cheapens a novel.  The writer continues his devotion to socialism as a cure for all evils, even Communism.  After plugging through Fall of the Giants and Winter of the World, I’m not going to purchase book #3 and if Follett writes another novel, I highly doubt I’ll read it.

title: Winter of the World (The Century Trilogy, Book 2)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Ken Follett
review_text:
Follett knows how to spin out a lengthy tale effortlessly. If he adds nothing new to the drama of the world's slide into a second world war (and if it has been done better), still, it should be hard to make the story boring. But this book is deadly dull to the point of being annoying. Why?
First,because its characters are uniformly one-dimensional, being hopelessly stereo-typed. Granted, character development is not Follett's forte, but couldn't the characters be something beyond straw-man (or straw-woman)vehicles for social commentary, or at least present some occasional, humanizing surprises?
So, the characters are simplistic --- at least the plot should be strong. After all, the times and materials could hardly be more extraordinary, and Follett is practiced at his craft. Sadly, the plotting is so predictable, and so weighted with social preaching, that even the natural drama is diminished. An historical novel almost inevitably will have a social viewpoint, and this is not necessarily a bad thing; however, a well-written story need not sink under pedestrian politics. Good historical fiction meets the challenge of connecting characters and personal sub-plots with the grander scheme of events, e.g. offering insightful analogies, credibly injecting your "witnesses to history" into the right places and moments. Here, by contrast, the characters conveniently trip across one another by lazy contrivance, and rarely seem to come together naturally. Far worse, the reader is smothered with over-wrought analogies to drive home political points. To use one early example: Are Berlin Nazis systematically brutalizing and murdering political and racial enemies really the political and moral equivalent of thugs in a Buffalo labor dispute? For that matter, must all union reps be burdened with uniform nobility and all business owners and operators analogized to Nazis, as the author not very subtly insists? To put it more generally: Aren't the readers of historical fiction entitled to a little more respect for their ability to discern good and evil, or perhaps even occasional shades of grey? Follett's messages would be more persuasive if not for the overloaded adjectives and adverbs evidently intended to help us get the point.
So, ultimately a very disappointing performance by Follett. He has demonstrated a good command over broad periods of history, a nice instinct for historical detail, and (elsewhere) the ability to spin a fine story. Not this time.

1) Overpriced for Kindle. I know the publisher sets the price, but still. Overpriced for print as well. But I would not care so much if it was a better book.
2) Poorly written. Follett leans on romance and sex scenes repeatedly in a far more prurient manner than in his previous books. His sexual descriptions are more detailed, almost to the point of vulgarity. THIS IS NOT WHAT HE IS CAPABLE OF. Character development pretty much always includes sexual descriptions.
3) History moves way, way, way to the background. There is so much rich material available to deal with in WWII, yet Follett manages, even in a long book, to skim over virtually every important event. This is drama, mostly romantic drama with rivalries. Stereotypes abound.
Summary: When I write reviews, which is rare, I do not summarize plot/characters/etc. I let others write those types of reviews and I appreciate them. I only try and advise other buyers as to if, based on typical reader expectations, they will be satisfied or delighted. In this case, I doubt many will be nearly as delighted with this as they were with Fall of the Giants.

Yes I am finishing it. It is not as bad as some have reviewed, it just does not come close to the last 3 works.

Oddly though, he fails to recognize that the Soviet sector of Berlin represents socialism that is acting just as intolerant and unhinged as the Nazi fascists but seems to think that all socialism wants is free health care and free money for the unemployed as if this was their only agenda.

What is even more alarming is the tactics the Soviet lackeys are using in Berlin are the same ones we are seeing today in Seattle, WA here in 2020 from the socialists....intimidation, violence and beating innocent people. title: Winter of the World (The Century Trilogy, Book 2)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Ken Follett
review_title: Huge dropoff.  I'm not convinced Follett wrote this book
review_text:
Follett likes to write big historical epics. He did it masterfully in Pillars of the Earth and World without End. He did it pretty well in Fall of Giants (the prequel to this book). He did not do it well here. This book is a big disappointment. There's enough story that I managed to finish, but there were times I was ready to pitch it.

The critical problems
1) The Forest Gump elements of the story got a bit too extreme in this book. With a fairly small cast of critical characters, he still managed to put them into almost every significant event of the 1930s and 40s. The coincidences just reach the point of the ridiculous. It's not the worst problem the book has, but it's pretty significant.

2) The juvenile take on sex. This is why I wonder if Follett really wrote the book. I've never read anything where he reached this level. Almost every character is obsessed with sex and it keeps returning to events, fantasies, etc. And they just don't play out as real. One simple example--a sixteen year old boy who is totally infatuated with an older girl (she's about 20). She kisses him at a party. In this first kiss, with no other encouragement from her, he immediately moves to grab her breasts. Are you kidding me? An inexperienced kid who's intimidated doesn't do that even today--much less in 1935. Just ridiculous over the top trivialization of sexuality. It gives the book a low soap opera feel.
I just wanted to say "grow up" to the author.

3) He plays simplistically with the history. Fall of Giants gave a good picture of the different perspectives and involvements of the many different people involved in WW1. This book makes almost every character in Germany or Russia into a comic book villain. There is no subtlety or nuance here. There are just good guys and bad guys. It makes too many of the events predictable. And it would have been more interesting to see characters wrestling with making choices to join what turned out to be an evil society--and how even good people might have slipped down that slope.

4) While I was not as annoyed with the politics of the book as some reviewers, there are times when it is heavy-handed (and somewhat anachronistic) in its attacks on conservatives. There's not much subtlety about the politics either.

Overall a very disappointing book. If someone were asking me about the series, I'd tell them that if they can't be happy with the story ending in 1920, they might should just skip it entirely. This book doesn't leave me good hope that the trilogy will end well.

review_text:
Not quite as well done as "Fall of Giants", but still a page turner.

As in "Fall of Giants", Follett tells the story of a world at war from the perspectives of the common people of the U.K., the U.S.A, Russia and Germany. Once again he seamlessly weaves a mesmerizing fictional story line into actual historic events.

This time the main characters are the children of the people we got to know in "Fall of Giants", but I don't feel that Follett fleshed these new characters out as well as he did their parents. Although his new characters are absolutely believable, they just don't have the complexity that he achieved with his characters in "Fall of Giants".

Still, Follett's story telling is excellent, and I look forward to Book 3.

title: Killing Jesus: A History (Bill O'Reilly's Killing Series)
subtitle: Kindle Edition
author: Bill O'Reilly
review_text:
This was a very disappointing book. 0'Reilly has made a big point to say that this is not a theological book; it is history. Yet there is a lot of theology in it. From the discussion of Jesus' siblings to the Roman Catholic view about the assumption of Mary, it's really filled with a lot of Roman Catholic doctrine. And the history really isn't that accurate. From the first page to nearly the last, the authors have made clear that Jesus was 36 when he died. Not true. He was 33. The Bible never says how old Jesus was when he died, but it's not hard to figure out. He was 30 when he began his ministry (Luke 3:23). When you look at all the events in the Gospels including all Jesus' visits to Jerusalem for Passover, it's clear that his ministry lasted about 3 years. Even the authors admit as much when then talk about the second Temple cleansing on p. 192. They say it was 3 years from the first time Jesus did that. True, so where do you get 36?

There are a lot of things I really wonder about. Why the big discussion in chapters 2 and 3 about Julius Caesar? What did he have to do with Jesus? This is supposed to be about Killing Jesus, not Killing Caesar.

I would also like to know why the cross on the cover is a nonstandard type of cross. That is never mentioned in the book. I've heard Bill say on his program that he and Dugard believe that's what it looked like. Okay, how about some evidence? And if that's true, why do crosses look the way they do now? They've looked like the typical cross for a long time too.

I cannot recommend this book. I would recommend that people read about Jesus in the Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. They deal in facts. Not speculation.

review_text: Good story but sloppy scholarship.  The story starts with the implied truth of the murder of the innocents. Most serious biblical scholars tend to place this in the "very questionable" category,  O'Reilly states he is attempting to write an open minded narrative, but doesn't find any reason to offer any competing opinions. He also states that the Jews of this time spoke Hebrew, which is simply not true.  The language of the day was Aramaic.  Neither O'Reilly nor his co-author are biblical scholars or historical scholars of first century Palestine, which makes it quite difficult to present an accurate account of the life and times and subsequent execution of Jesus.  So my issue with Mr O is his contention he is trying to offer an historically consistent narrative.  If you are interested in well researched scholarship and an interesting story there are a number of excellent authors, including Bart Erhman and Elaine Pagels.  In the spirit of full disclosure I did not finish the book after finding major scholarship errors.

review_text:
There are several historically inaccurate statements made by O'Reilly and Dugard including the blatant error stating that the Philistines took the northern tribes of Israel captive in 722 BC. They should have stated that it was the Assyrians.

Additionally, they state that Jesus was 36 years old at the time of His crucifixion which is opposed to the biblical fact that Jesus started His ministry at the age of 30 and ministered to the Jews for 3 1/2 years. O'Reilly and Dugard apparently believe that there are years 0 BC and 0 AD since they calculate 36 years between Jesus' birth in 5 BC and His death in 30 AD.

O'Reilly and Dugard are both Roman Catholics and, thus, avoid any discussion regarding propitiation. This precept appears in Romans 3:25, 1 John 2:2 and 1 John 4:10. The precept is rejected by the Roman Catholic Church.

O'Reilly and Dugard incorrectly believe that Jesus was crucified on Friday, April 7, 30 AD. Had they made an effort to reconcile the "spices" contradiction between Mark 16:1 and Luke 23:56, they would have concluded correctly that the crucifixion took place on Wednesday, April 25, 31 AD. There was an ANNUAL sabbath for Passover on Thursday and the normal WEEKLY sabbath on Saturday. The women bought and prepared the spices on FRIDAY after the annual sabbath and before the weekly sabbath, then brought them to the tomb on Sunday morning. Jesus was resurrected just before 6:00 PM on Saturday and was long gone from the tomb by the following morning. The Wednesday scenario is the ONLY scenario that completely and unequivocally fulfills the "Jonah" prophecy of three nights and three days in the tomb.

Note: Tables generated by the Naval Observatory Astronomical Applications Department (NOAAD) prove that Wednesday, April 25, 31 AD was the only date between 26 and 34 AD when the new moon sighting would allow the Passover to fall on Wednesday.

There are a couple of unnecessary digressions into Roman Empire history which smacks of filler.

review_title: O'Reilly Stared Down A Deep Well And Saw Himself
review_text:
Two stories emerge when discussing Bill O’Reilly and Martin Dugard’s Killing Jesus: A History (O'Reilly, 2013): one is narrative, the other is scriptural.

From a scriptural perspective, Killing Jesus is a retreat back to the so-called “second quest” studies of the historical Jesus. First quest studies were fantastic narratives, loosely based on fact. In second quest studies like Killing Jesus, the author defers to the canonical gospels. In third quest studies such as Reza Aslan’s Zealot: The Life and Times of Jesus of Nazareth (Aslan, 2013), the author may defer to non-canonical works, both contemporary and modern. The result is that the Jesus of Nazareth depicted in Killing Jesus differs little from the Jesus depicted in the bible, which is likely how O’Reilly’s readers would prefer to know Jesus. As a result, Killing Jesus is a successful exercise in worldview maintenance.

From a narrative perspective, Killing Jesus is a testosterone-fueled romp through first century Judea, complete with whips, prostitutes, pederasts, STDs, belly dancers, corrupt officials and tragic endings. Children are hacked to death, slaves are cast off cliffs for fun, brothers steal from brothers. This is not the reverential stuff one typically sees in a story about the historical Jesus, but this is Bill O’Reilly, who is to Fox News what Hunter Thompson was to Rolling Stone magazine.

I have written A Reader's Guide to Bill O'Reilly's Killing Jesus, an in-depth analysis of the more controversial parts of the book, a survey of the initial criticism of the book, and an independent criticism of the book. It is available for purchase here on Amazon, I invite you to read it. The guide is useful for individual understanding Killing Jesus' context, and also for book clubs and discussion groups.

Search for: "A Reader's Guide to Bill O'Reilly's Killing Jesus"

title: D&D Player’s Handbook (Dungeons & Dragons Core Rulebook)
author: Visit the Dungeons
review_title: This edition is a reaction to Pathfinder and Online gaming
review_text:
As soon as I seen the authors on the title page in 5th edition PHB, I know there was going to be problems. They are writers and not game players. The combat and saving throws are simplified and under-explained to the point of you question its usefulness while playing. Might as well use or develop your own system for this. The weapons and armor are simplified too, which is good for the most part, but the limits of what certain classes like rogues and clerics can use are dissatisfying, unless you don't care as a DM what weapons they can use. The races and classes give to much description and worthless nonsense that you have to ignore. Plus once again, for what reason would anyone want to be a thief if everyone else can do there job. The PHB needs a streamline of what each race, class, stat, ect. can do so it is better for during play use or for creating a character. All the description stuff should be left to the player and role playing. Descriptions should be brief, about a paragraph, and then list the abilities of a class or race in a logical order.

Each edition of DnD rule books are written as if we are all 10 years old, never played role playing before, and have absolutely no idea what an elf or a dwarf is. This edition is trying to real back in their competition that developed from mostly Castles and Crusades and Pathfinder. It failed. These other games were developed by players, so they evolved into better gaming systems.

I would like to see an edition of a fantasy gaming system that gets rid of spell levels, streamlines spell casting and combat, gets rid of a strong alignment system, and has no need for secondary skills or non-weapon proficiencies. In other words, give the players and DM's some credit for wanting to role play. I seen some home grown systems like this and they are better than DnD right now. And all the races and classes are balanced.

title: D&D Player’s Handbook (Dungeons & Dragons Core Rulebook)
author: Visit the Dungeons
review_title: Ran a few campaigns; gave it a fair shake
review_text:
While I am certainly glad that the 5th edition of the venerable Dungeons & Dragons role-playing game has brought in a lot of newcomers (and welcomed back old hands), that is unfortunately where my praise ends. This edition of the game represents, in my opinion, the weakest edition of the game released yet. Honestly, I would even prefer to play or run a game of 4th edition (which isn't actually too bad of a system) than to play 5th again. There are many, many problems with this edition, at least from the perspective of a role-player (vs. roll-player).

This edition has to represent the most complicated and unfortunately least-accessible version of the game yet. While it's still not rocket science, new players are inundated with unnecessary amounts of minutiae. There is a heavy focus on "min/maxing," the practice of fine-tuning during character creation to create as many mechanical and mathematical advantages as possible- not only does it allow this, but it encourages it through the offering-up of many feats and skills that apply all kinds of numerical bonuses. I understand some people like this, but I think the more that the game specifically says, "here is what you can do," there is an implied "and you cannot do anything else." To the point that any conflict, physical or otherwise, comes down to picking a skill/ability and rolling. That leaves little room for player-driven creativity and improvisational acts. 5th edition tries to address the "crunchiness" of 3.x editions by throwing more variety into a system that, in my experience, discourages creative role-play in favor of rote and paint-by-numbers ability/skill checks. There is no *dynamism* in the system...everything is just-so and expected - it got to a point where nothing was surprising me from session-to-session. Every single encounter came down to the players picking a skill or ability to use; diplomacy here, bluff there, hide here, intimidate them, etc., with little to no flavor or personality...try as I might as a DM, the world we were trying to portray and animate just felt lifeless and flat.

I also think that making it extremely difficult for player characters to die was a big mistake. Again, this is personal taste of course, but as someone that appreciates the sort of triumphant feeling that comes with surviving and thriving in a harsh and potentially lethal environment, this edition of D&D consistently, at every level tier, feels SAFE. Parties are given many options to circumvent the consequence of death, and they are given these at pretty early levels, too. This is probably my main issue with 5th edition...that encounters with monsters and enemies that should be extremely tense and carry the risk of death and ruin, are left just feeling bereft of actual lethality and threat. This is maybe a good thing for new players, but ultimately - after awhile - the players realize that they can be tactically sloppy and disorganized and still come through most encounters relatively unscathed. That is, to me, entirely antithetical to what the D&D experience is and should be about. I'm not some kind of DM that enjoys wiping a party, or tries to play the game as an adversarial one; I'm just a DM that uses all of the tools and resources available to try and animate these worlds and settings with some degree of realism, or verisimilitude. Having dangerous and potentially lethal encounters- in which the party might need to hide or even flee- was a way to bring the campaign to life and immerse us in it more fully. When you can have a party roam through your hexes, relatively confident in the fact that most, if not all, encounters will be tailor-made to suit their level and will not post any great threat to them...that does something to a campaign over time, and it really detracts from the idea of a living, breathing world that is being cooperatively explored and detailed as play progresses.

As I mentioned, I am certainly thrilled at the prospect of more players coming into the hobby and I give credit to Wizards for that bit. But if you're someone that is keen on trying D&D - or even if you're currently playing in and thoroughly enjoying a 5E campaign - I would highly recommend checking out some of the older editions of the game or their simulacrums in the Old School Renaissance category. Both Advanced Dungeons & Dragons 1st and 2nd editions have solid mechanical foundations that give the group many tools for creating a rich and immersive role-playing experience that relies more on player/DM collaboration and cooperation than min/maxing and "munchkin" approaches. 2nd edition, especially, is a comparatively simple and intuitive system that is by its very nature the most modular and house-rules friendly version of the game; in the core books alone, the DM and players are given dozens of optional rules that can be experimented with and dropped in or out of a campaign. Throw in the Player's Options series and you can customize your AD&D game to such an extent that I've yet to see equaled in any published tabletop role-playing game. Even the original D&D rules (BECMI and B/X) have enjoyed a resurgence in popularity. Thanks to the simulacrum games like For Gold & Glory, Legends & Labyrinths, Swords & Wizardry, etc., many sourcebooks and expansions for these older editions of D&D are being published and put out there into the community.

So whether you're brand new to the hobby or someone that has been playing since 3.x, I encourage you to at least give vintage editions of D&D a careful examination, as I suspect that for at least some of you, you'll find them to be mechanically accessible and rich with role-playing possibilities that enhance and encourage immersion. Many of these editions are available in print-on-demand from various online retailers, but you can also get the original books from here on Amazon for surprisingly cheap (at least for now). Approach it with an open mind and see what happens! Best of luck in your tabletop journeys!

That is nothing but a pandering nod to some of the most toxic, intolerant and hateful group of people around. Of course any one can be what ever they want, its a freakin fantasy game for crying out loud! So why the need to spell it out?! Lots of odd pronoun usage that makes one feel as if they don't get that 97% of their audience is male. As you make your way through the book its as if someone stuck there nose into it and demanded these changes or else they would have been "offended" and then slapped "ism" labels all over the writers if they didn't comply with this SJW nonsense. title: D&D Player’s Handbook (Dungeons & Dragons Core Rulebook)
author: Visit the Dungeons
review_text:
How D&D stays on the top of the RPG heap, I'll never understand, since there are so many other better game engines. D&D's 5th edition retains so many of the faults of earlier editions--all the way back to the original--that one wonders why they bothered. The cookie-cutter class system for characters insures that you are forced to play inside a box defined by someone else's imagination (why do wizards have such low hit points and are limited to specific weapons? And the Vancian magic system--Still? Really?).

The only reason I didn't give this book a single star is that the the flow of the chapters is helpful--at least for a while. But in-text directions to defined terms (like "see page x") are not provided, which is utterly annoying. Many of the illustrations are puerile, which encourages sophomoric behavior at the gaming table. The paper in the book feels cheap and readily distorts in humid conditions.

If you want more (and better) game for dungeon crawling, get GURPS Dungeon Fantasy RPG https://www.amazon.com/Steve-Jackson-Games-01-1005SJG-Roleplaying/dp/B0714KH516/ref=sr_1_1?ie=UTF8&qid=1535582104&sr=8-1&keywords=gurps+dungeon+fantasy+roleplaying+game or go for an even more genre-spanning game with the GURPS Basic Set https://www.amazon.com/GURPS-Basic-Set-Characters-Fourth/dp/1556347294/ref=sr_1_1?ie=UTF8&qid=1535582050&sr=8-1&keywords=gurps+basic+set+4th+edition.

title: D&D Player’s Handbook (Dungeons & Dragons Core Rulebook)
author: Visit the Dungeons
review_title: May enjoy if have never played any other gaming system
review_text:
I've been playing AD&D since 1st addition. A friend recently stated that they wanted to run a game for one of their kids and asked me to play. They said it was going to be 5e, so I was intrigued. I didn't even know they had gotten this high. The last system I had played was v3.5. Reading through the Players Handbook I was very unimpressed. Some items are improved (I like the way they do stat increases), a lot of it is very basic and uncreative. I wanted to reserve final judgement until I had play tested it. Well, combat was faster with this new system because everybody only gets one action until they get to 5th level. At which point most classes get a second attack, but that is it. Only strait Fighters get more than 2 attacks in a round, and that isn't until 11th and 20th level. Only Arcane spell casters don't get a second attack. Playing a Barbarian or Paladin, congrats, the Bard can now attack as often as you. Oh, and To Hit has been replaced by "Proficiency bonus", and everyone has the exact same proficiency bonus. So a fighter that concentrates on combat his whole life gets just as much of a bonus to hit as a wizard. They have dumbed down skills. All you get now is your stat bonus and if you are proficient in your skill then you get your Proficiency bonus as well. As for skills, that is determined by your class (you usually get to pick 2 skills) and your background (you are given 2 skills, again no choice). Very few classes get more than this. So out of 20 some odd skills, you get to be "Proficient" in 4 of them with absolutely no chance to improve any other skill unless you multiclass. Leveling is a joke. From 1st to 3rd level takes 900xp, but to get to 4th level takes 2700? Then to get to 5th is 6500, WTF? There is no rhyme or reason on how much it takes to get to the next level. It is overly simplistic in the beginning, but exorbitant later on.

Definitely geared towards people who have never played any type of RP system. There is absolutely no thought in character creation. Even making a character background is already done for you. For a game that was created to expand one's imagination, they have taken all thought out of character development. Overall, I'm disappointed in the system and wish I hadn't purchased the book.

title: D&D Player’s Handbook (Dungeons & Dragons Core Rulebook)
author: Visit the Dungeons
review_title: Passable book construction. Approachable & balanced game rules. 2020 errata corrections included.
review_text:
The Rules:

D&D 5e may feel a bit lackluster to fans of older edition combat, but they also make the game fun and approachable to newer players, and ease the DM's burden for parties of more than three or four. To me, this simplification is a great strength. I would much rather spend my time adventuring and story-building with friends than endlessly waiting for battle accountants to grind through their floating modifier calculations before I can take a turn. The new rules not only streamline things for existing players, but also make it much easier to get newcomers interested in the game we love, which means that actually getting to play is more likely.

I also very much appreciate the introduction of bounded accuracy in the new edition's mechanics, which keeps monsters and characters relevant at all levels. (See also: concepts underlying The Monsters Know What They're Doing and Tucker's Kobolds.)

The Book:

Pages feel a bit flimsy; I accidentally put a crease and a ripple in one of them just by flipping through the book when it arrived, and I wasn't being careless. The text is clear, though, and colors are pretty good. Almost none of the warping, and none of the spine separation or page cutting defects reported by other reviewers are present in my copy, so I suppose I got lucky. This book won't win any awards for sturdy construction, and is therefore overpriced at full retail, but it seems a decent value when on sale, and I'm glad to be supporting continued work on the game. I'll just have to be careful when handling it.

I received a 13th printing (indicated by the lowest of the two-digit numbers in the sequence near the bottom of the copyright page). It includes all the errata corrections published by Wizards of the Coast as of April 2020. Seller was Amazon.com Services LLC.

title: D&D Player’s Handbook (Dungeons & Dragons Core Rulebook)
author: Visit the Dungeons
review_text:
UPDATE 1-21-14: My 2nd replacement copy is now coming apart. This is still the best version of D&D ever, but possibly the worst printing/binding job ever as well. Luckily, Amazon is, well, amazing! They are sending me a third copy on the house. Note, that I am likely using this book a bit more than the average player, as I've been developing a complete character generator in excel (pretty much done now). So, I've been referencing it a lot, flipping pages back and forth, etc. No abuse, mind you, just a lot of usage. None of the other 6 players in my group have reported any problems. And now that I'm done with my spreadsheet, I'm hoping this will be my last copy!

UPDATE: Unfortunately, I have to lower my rating to 4 stars due to my book falling apart after 1 month of use. What a terrible binding job! I read other reviews with this same problem, so obviously this is widespread. The good news is that literally 12 hours (on the SAME day!) after I complained to Amazon, I received a replacement copy. I wonder if Amazon will replace it again if this one follows suit. This alone is reason enough to purchase through Amazon or else make sure the retailer you choose will replace it. Caveat: I am a prime subscriber and purchase items almost every week; I suspect less prolific buyers might not get the same-day treatment. On to my review...

THIS is the best version of D&D yet, hands down. I was a huge fan of both the 3.0 and then 3.5 editions, and I *tried* to play 4th edition. I skipped 2nd edition, so I cannot comment on that (and 1st/AD&D was too long ago to remember). 4th edition played like a Magic card game and my group hated it, moving to Pathfinder and other games (including this playtest) after a 1 year trial. Third edition (and 3.5) suffered mightily from simply having too many options that made your characters so powerful that the DM could never keep up (without having a TPK...total party kill). Although our group really loved the customization offered by 3rd edition as well as Pathfinder, all of these systems were utterly broken around 10th level. Fighters (that are built fairly intelligently) in these systems eventually become impossible for monsters to hit without rolling a natural 20, but yet can turn around and destroy just about any monster in a single round of attacks. Wizards and clerics are even more imbalanced. High level campaigns are just really difficult for DMs to challenge players without outright killing them. Another problem with these systems (except 4th edition) is that every party is pretty much forced to have a healer (cleric) and rogue if they want to survive (and find treasure and traps).

D&D Next (hate this name, by the way...what's the next version, D&D Last?) (EDIT: It's called Fifth Edition on the back cover...just noticed that) is by leaps and bounds the most playable, balanced system there is, that takes the best from each of the aforementioned systems. Taking the healing system from 4th edition (its single best feature) removes the necessity to have a "party healer". You can actually run a complete campaign without a paladin or cleric if you want. Heck, you don't even need a rogue anymore. This is HUGE imo...now there is no more arguing over who has to play the obligatory healer/cleric (yawn). Of course, you'll probably still want a decent smattering of coverage (wizard, tank, stealthy type, etc.), but even the clerics are decent fighters. During the playtest, I played a melee-based cleric and almost never used healing spells during combat. Our current campaign features NO healers at all...the jury's still out on whether that will work out or not.

We had several skeptics in our group that preferred Pathfinder, but they are "assimilating". Combat no longer takes an hour to complete (this was TERRIBLE in 3.5/4/Pathfinder). Have they really "dumbed down" the rules? I actually don't think so. If you'll notice, the player's handbooks are about the same size. What they have done, and incredibly well, is streamline the rules. Having said that, we all know that more books will be released, and we can only hope that game balance will remain as good as it is right now. I do look forward to seeing more options for customization in future books.

My 2 main issues with 5E are the Reward system and lack of a character generator; until the DMG comes out, the jury is still out on the former. During playtest, our group felt like we weren't getting enough treasure, specifically magic items. Since Ye Olde Magic Shoppe is no longer in business, there is only so many caltrops and merchant's scales to enjoy spending your hard-earned gold pieces on. Luckily, if it's still an issue, it can be fixed easily by your Dungeon Master. I hope to see rules for magic item creation (and/or the ability to purchase at least SOME magic items) at some point that does not imbalance the game. But, our DM will allow us to "request" certain items show up during the campaign, which is probably the best solution in the end. Regarding the lack of a character generator, there is a 3rd party application being developed. I will simply finish up my Excel generator and just use that (it's free and I can update it whenever I like). Still, this is not remotely enough to bring it down from 5 stars (but the binding issue certainly was). Get it!

review_text: I got into D&D about 6 years ago, at the time my party was playing the 3rd and 3.5 edition, being very well developed and well thought out with many stats that made sense in my own opinion. After being introduced to this new world I began my research into a handbook for myself and all the different things that was available for purchase. Learning of 4th edition left me baffled by the amount of change, it made me uneasy, so the transition never happened, 3.5 stayed our go to handbook. While attending a convention in Indianapolis, called Gencon, this product was in display as it's release had begun, after sifting through it I realized how similar to 3rd edition this was. Immediately I knew I had to buy it, a few days later I had one for myself, 5th edition returns to the roots of 3rd edition, droppinguch of what 4th edition brought with it. If you are looking at getting into D&D or a returning player from 3rd edition I highly suggest starting or upgrading to 5th edition.

review_text:
The D&D Player's Handbook is very VERY dense with information. It's a little intimidating, honestly, but it has everything you need to make your first character and start playing, which was why I bought it. The pages are appealing and there's very well done illustrations that make reading the book a joy instead of a chore.

I bought this book on sale for roughly $30 when the usual price is $50. You cannot find a better price for this book in any comic or hobby store. I looked, and locally it was $50 all around. Amazon is by far the best place to buy this book.

Book was shipped in a box, which was nice, because I've had many a book ruined in transit by being shipped in envelopes. As a book lover, having books in pristine condition is of paramount importance to me.

I firmly believe every new player who doesn't have friends to guide them needs this book to get started in D&D.

author: Visit the Dungeons
review_text: I'd been away from D&D for many years. I played a lot of both Basic and AD&D (both 1st and 2nd editions) but lost touch with the game for a long time. I heard 5e was open source, so I got the basic rules from the WotC website to read up on the game. I loved the changes so I picked up the core books (PH, DMG, and MM) and started playing again. I love the new books. They are well formatted, have beautiful artwork (full color was never a thing for AD&D) and many of the online tools make references back, so they're great cross references as well. I don't play with a computer or tablet in front of me. I prefer paper, pencil, books, and imagination. That's how we had to do it before, but the newer story-focused aspect of the game makes it even more enjoyable to play that way. Adding maps, miniatures, and software just enhance an already incredibly immersive experience. I highly recommend the new books for anyone into fantasy role playing and this book is the first to get. For a player, it's essential.

review_text: Another touching story from Rhys Bowen, again tying a modern time (70’s), to the tragedy of the war years. Her characters are developed in-depth, and her plots complex. Just when you’re trying to figure out where it’s going, she drops a hint or two to give that ah-ha moment. We meet young Englishwoman, JoAnna, just as her life and goal to take the bar exam has taken a turn with a personal tragedy and the death of her father. With a bit of time off, and some surprising mementoes her father saved, she goes to Italy to try to learn his story and how he survived the war. Complications abound as she meets and grows fond of the little village of San Salvatore and a few of it’s special people. A hidden plot, and a surprising painting tie her to the son of a woman her father loved. Great entertainment.

author: Kendra Elliot
review_text:
Kendra Elliot writes well in this series. I received this book as a Kindle First with my Prime membership and was not disappointed.
Mercy (FBI) and Truman (small town lawman) work together to solve the murders of elderly end of time preppers. In the course of investigation they discover deception linking cold cases of murder. Together they work to bring peace of mind to the town as well as themselves.

A good mystery to the end!
